My name is SynificHD and I am a YouTuber who uploads many gameplay content, such as this game.
This review will show my thoughts and opinions towards the game, also including a link to the game for you guys to check out and hopefully enjoy; and give you an insight of the game!
The game "The Park" is a first-person walking simulator that isnt much of a survival horror, but is a psychological horror, where you play as a mother who is named Lorraine, who must re-enter The Park to find her lost son; as she explores the horrifying amusement park, she suddenly reveals who she really is, leaving you on the edge of your seat; wondering what the HECK happened!
"The Park" has a very basic story line (You're trying to look for your lost son and go through some freaky flashbacks) but holds a very interesting concept being held in what would be known as a "happy place"; a theme park. The price is also debatable being a somewhat short story but then again the game has a lot of detail in certain parts, especially in sidequests that makes the game more interesting. Overall I could put this game inbetween recommended and not recommended as the game has a few cons but I enjoyed playing and it all depends on your interest.
I recommend this game to players who enjoy a mind boggeling game, that leaves you questioning its meaning, and for people who enjoy walking simulators that are narrator based, that involves sitting through a lot of dialogue.
At the time, recording was an issue but it would probably be a lot easier now but I would give this a 7/10 due to long dialogue and trying to cut most of it down into a suitable video.

I've played this game for 10 minutes, and I already feel like I've experienced all it has to offer. Let me start off with my list of positives:
-Uh... I guess my heart rate did raise a little. So that's something, I guess.
Alright, with that out of the way, the negatives. Keep in mind that I'm a bit of a tech snob.:
-Locked at 720p. WHYYYYYY?
-Upon trying to window the game, it crashed. Holy hell, this is a technically bad game.
-No video options whatsoever. Have an issue with screen tearing? Sorry! Have a 1080p screen? Outta luck!
-Most of the graphics are prerendered. You can tell when you turn in your office and the monitors on the desk warp. This would be acceptable in the N64 era, but not now. I mean, just look at Final Fantasy 7. That aged well graphically, right?
-Even with the prerendering, the game is uuuuuuugly. I mean, I know a single dude made this game, and I'm not expecting Crysis level graphics, but still, the asthetics are butt ugly as well. Super Mario 64 is a more visually pleasing game than this, and it came out in '96. As an aside here, have you seen the trailer for the newest FNAF? It still looks like it was put together by a middle schooler in a video editing class. You have all that money and you can't make a good looking trailer? Sheesh!
-Minimal gameplay. It doesn't really feel like I'm in control. I know that's kind of the point, but still, if I wanted not to be in control, I wouldn't be playing a video game. Night Trap, back on the Sega CD, had an almost identical gameplay gimmick, but was lambasted for it. Why does this game get a free pass?
-Little story. One thing I always hear when people sing this franchise's praises is that the story is fantastic... I'm not seeing it. It's not really touched upon in game, other than one of the robots bit a kid.
-JUMPSCARES. ARE. GARBAGE.
-The motivations for the game don't make any sense. Why does someone have to be there to watch the robots? Why is the power grid so crappy that you can't keep a door closed? Why don't they frigging replace the killer robots?
-The escape key instantly closes the game without warning. And that's when I stopped.
In conclusion, I don't think this is a very well put together game.

TechRaptor Review by Mark Richard
After a development cycle interrupted by looming threats of legal action due to copyright issues, Chroma Squad, a a Kickstarter turn-based isometric tactical strategy with Super Sentai spices, created by Behold Studios, has made it across the finish line after reaching an amicable agreement with Saban Entertainment. Thank goodness for that, because it’s every bit as charming as the developer’s previous game Knights of Pen & Paper, only without those pesky micro-transactions.
Despite a few questionable design choices and small bugs, Chroma Squad is an enjoyable experience. The customization makes all the difference in the world, and it has an infectious innocence that evokes fond childhood memories. The campaign goes on for a solid ten hours, plenty of time to use the framework’s potential to the fullest. If that doesn’t appeal there’s also a branching story, talk of adding multiplayer, and the end credits promise an upcoming New Game+ mode.

- A whimsical love letter to Super Sentai and a must have for a fan, though far from perfect in design.

TL; DR This game is very fun, very easy to pick up on, and incredibly witty.
I've played Knights of Pen & Paper (which I would highly recommend as well) so I knew this team from before.  They take old ideas, revamp them, and put fun twists on them.  And they come out great.  The 8-bit graphics are awesome, so if that's a concern for you, don't let it stop you with this game.
The game is basically about your team, who are stuntmen, making their own TV studio to make a Power Rangers-esque show.  You have the 5 roles, and you pick which "person" is in each role, all with their own bonuses, so there's a lot of customizability in that. You pick colors and names, too, but that's pretty simple stuff.
And then the fun starts.  The combat is turn based, grid strategy, and your characters get powers (more as they progress into each "season") so you start of with not a lot and end up with a plethora.  You can use teamwork to add to actions (like throwing a team member at the end of the movement range to get that guy who's JUST too far away or comboing for bonus damage on the same target).  It takes some time to fully understand, but it adds a level of depth that's VERY enjoyable.
There's a lot of customization, but I won't spoil that part, as it's hysterically funny once you find what you can actually change.  The gear is cool, too.  You have a shop, that you can spend money upgrading occassionaly, that sells gear.  It's pretty basic, but you know what you're getting.  You can also craft your own, but that leaves the effects randomly generated, so you could get something awesome (like a pair of boots that give you crazy high dodge and counter chance, ♥♥♥♥ yeah!) or something absolutely terrible (like a helmet that gives 2% dmg increase to pistols, which you stop using pretty early).  You don't sell gear, you break it down for crafting components, which I feel was on the devs part a way to motivate you to craft stuff.  It does actually change the characters looks, so fun lil bonus there.
The story is pretty awful, but in a fun way.  At first you're filming episodes just to get viewers and fans, and no, they're not the same in this game and they have very different effects on your studio.  It gets downright hilarious, and they make a TON of references to other "sentai' shows.
All in all it's a great game, and the guys at this studio really need to keep coming up with more games, because you're that breath of fresh air in this industry that they've desperately needed.  It's not going to leave with you a deep message, nor is it a game with a gripping storyline or gameplay that leaves you begging for more, but it's highly enjoyable, easily understandable, and wildly entertaining.

The first thing you should know is that The Beginner's Guide is not a "game", but an ineractive tour through a handful of games allegedly made by developer Davey Wreden's friend, Coda, and is narrated by Davey himself. It's difficult to talk about this "game" without completely ruining it for those who haven't played, but to put it short: First, The Beginners Guide is best if you come into it completely blind (but not literally blind, like one of the games asks you to play at one point. Spoiler alert: it's not possible). And second, don't expect as lighthearted a story as Davey;s other game,The Stanley Parable, had to offer. While Stanley (great game as well, by the way) is a mostly humerous tale with some psychological moments, Beginner's Guide is the opposite; a story that starts out with a few humerous comments by Davey here and there, but eventually dives into something deeper and far more emotional. It can be finished in about an hour, so I reccomend you check it out whenever you have the time.

If you come at this expecting a game, you will likely be rather disappointed as this is even less of a game than the "Stanley Parable" was. You will probably have to go through it at least twice to get a good grasp on the central point of the fable, which appears to be about the level of correlation between art and its creator. It is best to treat it like a movie and go through the whole 1.5 hours in a single sitting.

This game unfortunately simply does not live up to all the hype
This game does a few things right, the atmosphere is executed very well. But it gets old fairly quickly. Many horror games sacrifice gameplay in order to deliver a scarier experience and FNAF is no exception. Underneath the atmosphere and jumpscares is a game that doesn't play all that well. The easiest way of putting it is that this game is a rhythm game with no rhythm to follow. You take actions too often you run out of power. You go too slow you get killed. There seems to be a set pattern that must be followed precisely and you die unless you can find and execute this pattern. This makes the game scarier, but makes the game more frustrating as well.
While the main reason I picked up this game was because of the lore behind it and while the lore is interesting integrated throughout the series it ends up telling a straightforward story that becomes less and less interesting the more I think about it. The story may help tolerate the gameplay, it simply isn't enough.
FNAF is a horror game that isn't really bad, it's unique and presents interesting interesting ideas. However, it simply is not as good or scary as many people make it out to be. The game has a fair price that I'd say is worth it if you absolutely want to play it. However, just know that it is overhyped out of proportion
Pros:
- Has an effective Atmosphere
- Provides unique game mechanics
- Story is told subtly throughout the series
Cons:
- The game has a specific pace you need to follow with no indication of what that is
- Jumpscares get old fast and will infuriate you more than scare you
- Gameplay is sacrificed for a better horror aspect

It's pretty clear that The Park was inspired by P.T. in a lot of ways. It's basically an interactive teaser for The Secret World which is a fairly decent MMO from the limited time I've played it. The execution here is just far too sloppy and predictible to come close to what Kojima did with P.T.
Predictible being the key word here. This is a stratighforward, linear walk sim. This hurts for two reasons. One, it takes little to no logic to get you from start to finish. It's not a rails, but it might as well be as you let the game holds your hand until the credits roll.
The second reason the game suffers from it's format, is there is no sense of danger or urgency. Part of what makes the best horror games compelling is the survival aspect. With P.T. you had the ghost Lisa that was quite hostile towards you. In The Park you know that nothing will hurt you. Any of truly dangerously feeling elements are in-game cut scenes and the remaining horror elements are a series of jump scares that were all so predictable, I found myself bracing and calling out each. I won't rob you of any, but you're gonna know when they're coming.
When it comes to price, I try to avoid saying a game is too expensive. If I really love a film, I have no issues dropping $20 for the blu ray. Games are the same. Even if it's only an hour long, an absorbing and fanstatic journey can be worth the price in my opinion.
The Park, however, doesn't come close to meeting those kind of expectations.

I really wanted to like this game.  It came so close.  But at the end, it's tepid at best, and it definitely left me with a bad taste in my mouth.
I enjoy experience games and walking simulators, and I enjoy short games.  The play time felt just right to me, and there weren't any bugs or lag.  I liked the atmosphere, I liked the idea, I liked the environments.  There are some solid moments in here, including one of the best-executed scares I've seen in a while--the
moment is perfection in subtlety, unreality, and understated terror.
Unfortunately, that happens within the first twenty minutes of the game, and it's all downhill from there.
From the beginning of the game I was already going
.  Seriously, from the opening lines.  It's not at all subtle.  With obvious dark magic tomfoolery gadding about, I was hoping that one of the other plotlines alluded to would go somewhere, but they devolved into cliches.  Actually, the entire game devolved into cliches.  The first few scares are inexplicable and intriguing, but they have explanations slapped onto them fast and hard.  WHAT'S BEHIND THE MYSTERIOUS MASCOT?
WHAT WAS THAT THING GLIMPSED FROM THE OCTOTRON?
WHAT IS THE SECRET OF THE PARK?
By the end of the game, there are literally bleeding walls, "scary" children's drawings, "eerie" nursery songs, dismembered baby dolls, the "throw a dart at the Horror section of Netflix" works.  Nothing we haven't seen before a zillion times,
That is admittedly some new levels of ham-fisted.

A survival game that's actually about surviving in a harsh environment, rather then dealing with zombies or cannibals.
Allthough the game is still in development it runs really smooth and new content gets added quite frequently. The new content mainly consists of new areas to explore or items to find/craft. It's still sandbox only, however the development team is working on a story mode.
The game relies on a simple hunger/thirst/sleep/warmth system like many other survival games.
What makes this game unique however, is it's artwork. The atmosphere is simply put amazing. The unique graphics and environmental sounds/music got me hooked straight away and is very well executed.
The only con I've experienced was that it tends to get kinda boring. Since as with every sandbox game, once you got your equipment and have settled for a bit, the challenge to survive disappears. However, you can make this game as exciting as you want. You can try to survive by staying out in the middle of the nights, survive snowstorms, wolves, bears and live like a godlike hunter, or simply settle down in a house.
TLDR; This game is one of a kind, and if you're into survival games this is a must have.

I'm a long-time player of Dungeons and Dragons games (Baldur's Gate, Temple of Elemental Evil, Neverwinter Nights 1-2).  Seeing this for such a reasonable price and for a recently published title seemed like a great deal.
The game started out well enough.  Graphics were decent, music was good, mechanics were workable for a board game representation of D&D.  The fact that there are only 4 pregenerated characters (whom I referred to as the lizard, Chuck Norris, Harvey Birdman, and Morris the Cat)  with no way to create your own was a bit disappointing, but not a deal breaker in itself.
Journeying into the jungle seemed good as I moved to the edge of one tile to expose the next randomly generated tiles populated with traps and treasure or monsters.  But then I realized that as soon as you slow down either to fight monsters or pick up treasure or disarm traps (the things that SHOULD be the focus of an adventure), you are absolutely bombarded with lightning bolts, swarms of insects, magical curses, or sometimes just heavy stones that inexplicably fall from the sky onto your characters.  Many of these effects are AoE, so if you are using teamwork and you have your party close together (like.. uhh.. a party) they will all be decimated in short order.
If you enjoy board games that simulate running at full speed through a jungle under threat of being bombarded by off-board artillery, this might be your thing.  As for me, I'm going for a refund.

So here's my review, might contain spoilers so be warned if you want to go in blind.
Really fun game with interesting elements sums up this game in a nutshell but also doesn't do it much justice.
Story
The city of Rapture itself is told via in game audio logs and not directly to the player, so you have to make an effort searching high and low, every nook and cranny to tease out the history of the once great city and how it fell into such a state that it is in now. Making the player find these and connect the dots is an interesting way to encourage exploration however this makes the story part mostly optional which is a downer since it it interesting.
Gameplay
Fun but with a few problems.
So you get a variety of weapons, cool.
You get a variety of plasmids (powers), cool.
You cannot use both at once, you have to switch between them on the fly to use them to their best extent. mmmm.. not very user friendly.
Most of the time I find myself just falling back into just using one plasmid, winter blast, because of how most fights tend to be fast without much time to scurry and switch plasmids.
The game transitions slowly from a dark, heavy, somewhat horror in the early part of rapture to a more continually action paced game. About as soon as you get the machine gun you will start considering that you can take on anything.
One issue for me is that there is No" aim down sights". You relearn gradually learn to target with the reticles. Hitboxes can be odd at best but at worst the can be bizarre. Catching an enemy in the edge of a shotgun? Killed them. Crossbow shot? Whiff if you/they slightly move.
Graphics
Well it looks good, especally so when it came out.
One big irk is when some powers flash the whoe screen trying to blind both you and your enemy.
Take note, turn down the brightness a bit.
Audio
Well this is hard becasuse it sounds good enough but the best part is when you get to a jukebox and listen in to the tunes.
That said voice acting, ambient sound and even the lack of it does well in building the world of rapture.
8/10
Good game, be prepared for a few things to relearn especially if you have been playing newer games.

Great game.  Unfortunately, it might die because it has become fashionable/meme-like to diss this game's DLC practices, and trash it at ever turn, even though I personally don't see what the hullaballoo is about.  Future publishers may want to take note, however--not necessarily because the haters are right, but because they are, at the very least, vocal.  I'll admit my opinion about the DLC/pricing set-up was skewed a bit, mostly because of the vocal hate.  Thankfully, I did some research on my own.  Here's what I've come up with:
This game's DLC is similar model to games such as League of Legends--cosmetic skins and future playable characters will need to be bought.  They have stated that new maps/game-modes will always be free (which will be great as it won't split the playerbase), and you will be able to play against others who own monsters and hunters you don't own.  Pretty much like League and other MOBAs.  The big difference, of course, is that Evolve is 60 USD for the base game, while most games that generate revenue from micro-trasnactions are free-to-play.
That said, Evolve has the graphics, gameplay, sounds, maps of a AAA title.  League, perhaps, is a great game, but it is not sylistically what we've come to expect from a AAA title.
As far as the gameplay, I have no complaints.  Every game has been different, exciting, and I look forward to putting in more hours this week on my medic.  There is a nice sense of progression through the tiers to unlock each hunter/monster.  If you like arena type gameplay, asymetical fighting, and strong group tactics, then you will probably really like this game.
I want to reiterate that NO ONE who purchased DLC day 1 has any advantage of someone picking up the game right now.  All they are getting is skins/monsters/hunters which are to be released in the future.  This is pay2customize, pay2playstyle, not pay2win.  If, perhaps, there is an overtuned monster/hunter that is released in the future that is a "must" own because it is overpowered or whatever, then hopefully the dev's will act quickly to rebalance it, as they seem to have done quite well with the monsters/hunters on release.

It's probably the first new Tropico game since Tropico 3.  Tropico 3 and 4 were basically exactly the same (4 having different UI and more stuff, but basically the exact same game).
Blitzing through Tropico 3 and 4 the past week to re-acclamate myself with the Tropico experience is of no help in Tropico 5.  It's essentially a completely different city-builder game now.  It actually feels difficult to do certain things at the start of a map which I sped through in 3/4 as easily as dressing myself in the morning, like setting down roads, quickly scouring for what metal resources are available, and setting down a patchwork of farms and garages to be connected by roads at a later date.  It's an unknown world to enter now.
Combat is somewhat incomprehensible, as there seems to be a severe disconnect between army size and army health, which only makes sense if by "army health" they meant "army morale" except the army health doesn't recover after winning a battle
The very first mission of the first campaign starts out normal and casual enough, then becomes suddenly brutal as you're faced with a foreign invasion that will completely wipe you out unless you've prepared with more than one military fort.
This isn't a particularly bad thing, but just starting off the one major complaint I have is the music choices are a whole lot weaker.  They're all instrumental now, and they all seem to have been chosen to be less spirited and soulful and more as just background noise, and it's an immense disappointment.
Another major issue is something that really shouldn't be an issue but somehow the game makes it one: You're doing a map, and finish an objective, and suddenly you get ripped out of your game and dropped into a map select screen.  There is no Victory screen or anything resembling one to let you know you've won the mission and are moving on.  As well, there's no explanation as to why you play the first map, win your independence, then in the very next mission you're back to being a colonial governor on a different map, working your way to independence.
The third mission then immediately drops you into a HUGE enemy invasion of your island, necessitating at least 4 or 5 military forts, basically forcing you to have planned ahead from the very start of the game for something you had absolutely no way of knowing was coming.  So if you didn't prepare for a completely unexpected invasion of 4+ infantry units at the very start of the 3rd or 4th mission, then you have to go back and play the game over from the beginning.
Another weird issue to have is something about the intensely bold colors and overall dim lighting and color choice of the buildings makes it difficult to actually make out individual buildings on the screen.  They start to mesh together and merge with the trees to a certain degree so it's nearly impossible to tell them apart without zooming in.  Even now I can't tell the difference between Construction offices and three country houses
Further playing experience leaves me realizing this game feels a lot more hands-off than Tropico 4 was.  A lot of the same style still exists, such as being able to track down and interact with citizens, but the difference in UI and game mechanics causes something of a disconnect between you and them, exacerbated by the almost complete lack of any real information in the Almanac.  The Almanac is now almost completely useless.
During elections, there's no option to give a speech and make promises and praises, and for the first time in ANY tropico game, I lost the election even after using fraud.  Somehow, there was just no way to interact with anything to affect the election --- I just somehow lost the vote, as it was somehow tied to the arbitrary Happiness.  There was literally nothing I could do to affect the election.
Inexplicably, after my third time re-loading the save, by NOT holding elections I got a boost in happiness.  There are only 4 factions this early in the game and none of them are loyalist
As well, the game keeps asking me to re-make my dynasty at random moments between mission successes/failures, resulting in there being multiple duplicate copies of my dynasty in the game menu
On the positive side, some good changes made include the Construction office is actually efficient now, so you don't need to build 4 in a single mission just so you don't have a backlog of 30+ buildings at a time, and you can actually see what people are protesting about and do something about it instead of just the generic "raise happiness"
The game also seems to think certain things are funny, like having you balance relations between two opposing superpowers.  Just like in previous Tropico games.  But those were about diplomacy.
In Tropico 3/4, when you choose to ally with someone, they reward you with a free army base of theirs which they pay you to keep on your island, as well as protection against potential invasion from the other superpower.
In Tropico 5, when you choose to ally with someone, they reward you by having a random HUGE invasion of your island, obliterating much of your buildings when you inevitably lose, unless you run through every single mission as a paranoid militant with dozens of army bases and military forts and virtually no industry.
And then you end up losing the game yet again when an election comes up and you lose because all your industry buildings were destroyed in the "friendly" invasion and you have not enough money to bribe every faction into voting for you (pretty much the only thing you can do in a Tropico 5 election)
On top of that, every other mission seems to have a sudden HUGE invasion of your island with little to no warning.
And another thing: the continuous island you return to and build upon instead of starting over every mission idea is a good idea --- it worked great in games like Zeus Master of Olympus and Emperor Rise of the Middle Kingdom.  However, when it's always the same two islands for pretty much the entire campaign, it quickly becomes boring.
Adding to this is the "genius" idea that despite it being a persistent island, the game thinks it's somehow a great idea to reset all your edicts between missions without you noticing.
Another massive "genius" move which makes absolutely no sense: there is a complete and total disconnect between Happiness and Unrest and Rebels.  As such, you can have every faction Indifferent or Happy with you, and still have nonstop Coup attempts and/or Rebel attacks in a certain mission.  Sometimes it's intentionally scripted just to be aggravating.  Other times, there's just no reason for there to be so much rebel activity when your society is free, open, and happy.
By the time you're near the end of the game, whenever you hear the phrase "Great giant Tropican spiders" you will completely explode with murderous rage

From the off the easiest thing to praise in this game is the visual style. The game looks amazing as it nails the classic 1930s cartoon look and paired with catchy as hell jazz music from the same period it makes for one of the best visually and audibly designed games in a very long time.
Keep in mind there are some platforming style levels but these are very few and far between with the big emphasis being on the boss fights. Like I said this doesn't bother me but this might be a turn off for some platforming veterans. Also this is such an unforgiving game. It isn't the hardest game I've ever played but is easily one of the hardest modern 2D games I have played. World 1 was fairly comfortable with a few rough patches here and there but once I got to world 2 I wanted to snap my controller in half. Despite this, the little line you get when you die saying how close you were to beating whatever boss is a great way of maintaining that "just one more try" kind of gameplay that this game excells at.
My only two problems with the game is 1. the hub world and 2. the shop system. This hub world was so unneeded. Sure it works and you could do worse but it just serves to break the pace of the game. Sure having hidden paths to skip parts of the game is a cool idea but you would want to try to beat every level anyway. It just felt like a forced addition to keep up with the plethera of modern games that use hub worlds these days, and once I had defeated the final boss it was a pain to constantly be going back and forth through the map to get to specific bosses I felt like retrying. Also the shop system is awful. You pay for new upgrades with coins you get from some levels which is fine but the bad part is that there are only ever four items to buy at one time. When you buy something it is replaced with something else and what it is replaced by is fixed for that item. So let's say there is an upgrade you don't want, but there may be a really good upgrade following it if you buy it so you take the gamble and buy it. It's a complete guessing game whether it was worth your hard earned cash. I get that's kind of a stratergy in gambling but it really made me relucant to buy anything in the shop without a guide so that I didn't miss something that could really help me.
Those really are my only problems with the game. As far as gameplay goes this is one of the best indie games I have played in years. A lot of the time some indie devs will intice you over with the promise of a great product, and they will get you to spend £15 on something that isn't even finished (I'm looking at you Derelict!). This isn't the case with Cuphead. Here you have an indie game with more love and passion put into it than most AAA games these days. Remember though the game is VERY hard so if that isn't for you then think twice before you buy this. If however you love a challenge then the game is selling for such a steal of a price so I would recommend it hugley.

Instead of reviewing the game based on the hype/fanbase/Youtube fame, I suppose it's time to write and judge the product on its own merits. I'm not someone who can get scared easily and this game didn't scare me at all but the idea of being perfect in the execution is what makes this game good. In other words, I was definitely sweating despite the fact that I wanted to stay focus.
The game is definitely not a looker but it got some atmosphere which is not too bad. Like I said, I didn't find the game scary... stressful is the word. I played the remake of Resident Evil before it gets released on Steam and I watched some horror movies. The true scares come from the not-so-usual "It's me" with the Golden Freddy (and possibly Nightmare) appearing out of nowhere because of those hallucinations. It was not my first experience into the point-and-click genre (I played the second Broken Sword game a long time ago, The Smoking Mirror) but I really have noticed some moments where the controls didn't feel that precise, especially when you need to click that button and you get that button being locked on because an animatronic decided to get in before you can have the time to close that freaking door.
Sure I laughed when Foxy "Sprinty Jackass" knocks itself on the closed door. For a first game, Scott Cawthon didn't do a bad job. Sure a Youtuber or two influenced my purchase but sometimes, you want to know what the fuss is about. A survival game that's actually about surviving in a harsh environment, rather then dealing with zombies or cannibals.
Allthough the game is still in development it runs really smooth and new content gets added quite frequently. The new content mainly consists of new areas to explore or items to find/craft. It's still sandbox only, however the development team is working on a story mode.
The game relies on a simple hunger/thirst/sleep/warmth system like many other survival games.
What makes this game unique however, is it's artwork. The atmosphere is simply put amazing. The unique graphics and environmental sounds/music got me hooked straight away and is very well executed.
The only con I've experienced was that it tends to get kinda boring. Since as with every sandbox game, once you got your equipment and have settled for a bit, the challenge to survive disappears. However, you can make this game as exciting as you want. You can try to survive by staying out in the middle of the nights, survive snowstorms, wolves, bears and live like a godlike hunter, or simply settle down in a house.
TLDR; This game is one of a kind, and if you're into survival games this is a must have.

I know what you're thinking, most likely. I know this is one of, if not, the most successful indie franchise of all time, and you're probably saying
. But I got solid reasons to hate it.
First of all, I want to clear up that FNAF 1 isn't a bad game.
I must recognice it was a pretty good game, and pretty original too. But, my reason to hate FNaF, doesn't come from the game. But rather the whole series.
Why?
Because in less than one year, Scott Cawthon released (at least)
, without actually improving the gameplay, and overexploiting it. What do I mean? That this is just a mold of every single FNaF game ever released. Yeah, FNaF 2 had no doors. FNaF 3 had traps for the only actual enemy, but, do you see a gameplay alteration? Do you see an actual improvement between FNaF 1 and 4? No, you don't. You see Scott basically altering the MECHANICS of the game, but NOT improving the game. He said FNaF 3 would be the last game of the
franchise. But, a month after that, we see FNaF 4 up on the steam store! Why? Because his fanbase is not only mostly consisted of kids that aren't used to the point 'n click genre, but because he knows that if he just adds the word "Freddy" on one of his games, the sales of it will rise up, mostly because people will think they're going to play something new. And it could easily be a simulator of Freddy taking a dump over a computer. But, where's the FNaF on it? On the Freddy sprite.
As nonsensical as it sounds, it's right. FNaF 3 is basically a game that could EASILY be deleted of the franchise, and yet NO timeline-related issues would occur! Because the lore itself isn't even present in the game. Whenever you're buying FNaF 2, 3 or 4, you're just buying this game I'm reviewing right now, only that it has altered game mechanics.
you may say. Yes. It does have minigames. But does it alter the story of 5 murderous robots that are trying to kill you? Nope. It's an add in. A filler. A way to fill the game, so it feels new.
Scott is just taking the same game over and over again, editing it a little bit, altering the way the characters look and behave, and replacing the game system over and over again. First it's a tablet and 2 doors. Then it's a light, a mask, and a tablet. Then a reset system button, with the ghosts of the past characters. And now? Yet another new concept. Don't get yourself fooled. If you're playing the game for the story, it would be better to watch a gameplay rather than spending your money on a carbon copy of a past game. Simple as that. Scott is taking your money, and he's releasing games faster and faster, because each time he says "Five nights at freddy's", lots of little kids that haven't ever played a point 'n click get their wallets ready to buy the exact same game again, only that with a different mechanic. Just like Toy Story 2 and 3.
Both blockbuster movies. Both go the same way. Both end the same way.
And it still made TONS of cash.
Same with FNaF.

I'm a long-time player of Dungeons and Dragons games (Baldur's Gate, Temple of Elemental Evil, Neverwinter Nights 1-2).  Seeing this for such a reasonable price and for a recently published title seemed like a great deal.
The game started out well enough.  Graphics were decent, music was good, mechanics were workable for a board game representation of D&D.  The fact that there are only 4 pregenerated characters (whom I referred to as the lizard, Chuck Norris, Harvey Birdman, and Morris the Cat)  with no way to create your own was a bit disappointing, but not a deal breaker in itself.
Journeying into the jungle seemed good as I moved to the edge of one tile to expose the next randomly generated tiles populated with traps and treasure or monsters.  But then I realized that as soon as you slow down either to fight monsters or pick up treasure or disarm traps (the things that SHOULD be the focus of an adventure), you are absolutely bombarded with lightning bolts, swarms of insects, magical curses, or sometimes just heavy stones that inexplicably fall from the sky onto your characters.  Many of these effects are AoE, so if you are using teamwork and you have your party close together (like.. uhh.. a party) they will all be decimated in short order.
If you enjoy board games that simulate running at full speed through a jungle under threat of being bombarded by off-board artillery, this might be your thing.  As for me, I'm going for a refund.

It is quite literally a parody of power rangers, because it was quite literally inspired by the same show.  The combat system revolves around the turn-based combat system, but with tactical movements and everything.  You have your basic healer, fast person, tech person, heavy hitter, and balanced fighter. I really wanted to like this game, but it's just not there. I can forgive the somewhat rough animations and moderately unlikeable main character, but this game just oozes other problems.
+Interesting art style
-Rather dull point and click puzzles
-Awkard writing and voice acting
-Clearly a prologue to a larger story, but does very little to entice you into that story
Some of the voice acting is ok, but a lot of it sounds like it was recorded using very low quality equipment or is very poorly mixed. Some of the characters are well-acted and memorable (the fisherman sticks out in my mind), but a few characters sound like they're trying to over enunciate or put emphasis on every line, which gets grating. Voice line clarity is all over the place and syncing is frequently off, with entire cutscenes being horrendously desynced. Even if you turn the sound off, the writing is nothing special.
This is very clearly a prologue to a larger story, but instead does little to actually draw you into that story. Most of the exposition is in a few large, obvious dumps. We aren't so much shown there's a large conspiracy as we are repeatedly told about it. Character relationships jump all over the place, making it hard to get invested in anyone, and it's very obvious from 15 minutes in that virtually all the characters are simply puzzles that could just as easily be replaced by a pile of items and a note. There are elements of a better story here, but for the most part it's just a game of busy work, which is a shame, since the world does seem interesting.
Speaking of puzzles, they're pretty bad, even for a point and click. Virtually all of them are use object on object inventory puzzles that may or may not carry a great deal of logic to them. There's a somewhat interesting if basic phone puzzle early on, but that puzzle style seems to be quietly dropped as soon as you leave the house. It's the "click around the map until you find an item then click that item on every other item in the world" school of puzzle design.
At exactly one hour in, the game crashed, and I just don't think I'll ever be going back to it. It just did nothing to pull me in.

So, I've been raving about this game on other platforms as I played it… I still need that one last achievement for bragging rights, but now that's I've basically finished the game I thought I should sum it up for all to see…
The ONE and only reservation I have isn't even a fault of the game: it's just that the creepy atmosphere, especially the gruesome (quite fequent…) death animations might not be to everyone's taste. If that's a major turn-off for you, this is probably not a game you should buy.
But.
Otherwise: run for it. No hesitation.
I love how the puzzles work: a few are timing-sensitive, but most allow you the space and time to think things through, without the usual stress I get from games where I'm going to lose everything if I don't get it right instantly;
I love how the game saves at each new puzzle, so you don't get annoyed with having to replay what you already solved over and over again, just to get back to the last point you failed. Again, it makes the game much less pointlessly stressful, and more engaging. If I had to rerun everything ten times when I come across a more difficult obstacle, I doubt I would have gone through the whole thing so avidly…
I also loved the ambiance, both the black & white theme that makes the gory deaths less in-your-face and distasteful, nd the sounds-but-no-music… which became so OBVIOUS a choice in the very last chapter. <3
And finally: I LOVED that last chapter. It really feels like a reward, an encore for players furstrated to have reached the end. You want more? Oh boy, here's more… and then some. It's like a hot cup of good coffee after a luxurious meal.
In conclusion: I absolutely, wholeheartedly recommend this game to all who like situational puzzles (kind of like in Zelda games, but more elaborate since it's the core of the game), as long as watching your cute little dude getting smashed, impaled & decapitated every two minutes or so doesn't bother you. (Or, you can try avoiding deaths… but good luck with that on a first playthrough!)

Simply put, Bioshock is a really good single player FPS. I will only go over a few things that I loved about this game.
Pros:
-Rapture has a really interesting and uneasy atmosphere to it, making exploration for supplies and recorders worth it.
- Using the environment around you, different ammo types, and a good variety of enemies makes combat fun and tactical.
- Plasmids are very fun to use in combination with your guns to spice up the combat.\
- Tenenbaum is one of my favorite characters, but I'm not sure why. I just love her character.
- Saving the little sisters instead of harvesting them is one of the best feelings in a video game I've ever had.
- The big reveal when you meet Andrew Ryan is very memorable in making you question your actions up to that point.
- All weapons can stay useful even to the very end of the game.
- It has a good game length  ( a good 15-18 hours to complete)
Cons:
- After Fontaine's betrayal, the game really slows down into a boring slog. I fell asleep at my desk twice trying to get myself to finish the big daddy suit.
- The final boss fight is incredibly easy. There is no challenge to it or mix-up of tactics. Just keep shooting until you drain his adam.
- Your reward at the end of the game is a pretty generic 30 second cutscene that depends on your choice to harvest of save the little sisters (hell, the neutral and the bad ending are just the same scene, just with different narrative tones), so I felt like my choices never had much weight or impact on the story.
TL, DR:   Bioshock is a good game that will give you a good amount of content and gameplay. Despite some flaws towards the end, it is still a good game.  Try getting it on sale (especially if you can get the Bioshock bundle.)

The gameplay is pretty good, mostly a normal fps with limited ammo type of thing but you also have RPG like upgrades called plasmids and tonics. Plasmids are like magic spells in other games, things like electrically shocking your enemies so that they take a little damage and are stunned for a while to freezing them to burning them to hypnotizing them in to helping you etc. etc. Tonics are like upgrdes in an rpg, they improve your attack defense allow you to move/swing faster etc. etc. There are 3 types of tonics, each with a maximum of 6 slots (I think) so you can have a maximum of 18 tonics.
The game is also very very lenient with respawning. You litterally just teleport to the nearest vita chamber, which means the map doesn't reset and you can whack a tough enemy 2 times with a wrench, die, then respawn, and whack him again. It still doesn't take away the challenge though.
This game has a mechanic called hacking. Basically, you hack stuff by redirecting the energy flow to a more desireable area. However, each puzzle is randomly generated and sometimes they come out to just being outright impossible. I put a picture in here showing an impossible puzzle. Also, when you fail a puzzle, even if its impossible, you are penalized with either loss of health, or with the alarm going off sending these flying robots with machine guns after you. The alarm things set off the alarms to get the robots to come after you, theres no way to cut corners to go diagonal, and you can't move them. Oh I'm sorry, did you want to live forever? Too bad, Zomboid cares little for your dreams! Prepare to spawn in a trailer park with a rolling pin as a weapon, whilst several zombies decide you look rather like a fine roast.
Zomboid is a sandbox, zombie survival game with a leveling and skill system which represents essential skills required to survival in a hostile world. It is by no means easy, unless you decide to go into sandbox mode with ridiculous amounts of loot turned on... but that's up to you and slightly unstatisfying.
If the thought of playing a game where you survive on crisps, orange soda and rain water whilst beating zombies to death with a frying pan  greatly amuses you, Zomboid is probably your type of game. The controls are not intuitive in my opinion, but they are relatively easy to memorise once you understand them.
It's a fairly realistic game and probably the closest you'll ever experience to a real zombie apocalypse. You can board up houses, rig up rope systems from windows for quick escapes, treat your wounds, combine food items and apply heat to them to create various things. At the more advanced levels, you can start building walls, doors and various other items such as rain collectors and your own house if you get enough wood and nails. You can also start your own farming efforts, taking advantage of seed packets and watering cans laying around to become self sufficent.
Really, how you want to try to not die as quickly as most is up to you.

Its like the Sim's in a Zombie apocalypse except it's just you, your the last person alive (that hasn't turned), no friends or family to be with (unless you play multiplayer). There will be NPC's added in future patches but the interactivity with these is still unknown, they will most likely be hostile.
In the early game your first challenge is finding a decent weapon, as a Spoon just doesn't cut it. However, breaking into peoples houses can set off security alarms, which attracts nearby Zombies that will chase you down unless your quiet and stay out of eyeline. During the first couple of weeks the Electricity is working so you can use household appliances like Ovens to cook food. It's not long before it turns off and you have to resort to eating canned food (if you have a can opener) or other dry products. Most food in the fridges will go off quickly as it is no longer chilled. You can cook your own meals by building a Campfire though I found this unnecessary as it's easy to stock pile large amounts of none perishables. Eventually the stored food will run out as well as the Water supply. You will have to come up with other ways of survival like Farming, Fishing and collecting Rainwater in Barrels. Learning Carpentry skills is essential as you can then use collected Wood to make all kinds of structures like Wall's, Box's, Furniture, even Barricades for your Doors and Windows to stop the Zombies getting in your safe House. BTW you can cut down Tree's with most weapons it just takes much longer than an Axe.
The game really is a survival sandbox with no real story except the one you make for yourself. Overall I enjoyed this game more so than games like DayZ. I like the isometric 3rd person viewpoint as opposed to 1st person as you can see if someone is sneaking up on you.
The developers have announced that future patches will contain NPC's and Vehicles which will add another dimension to the game.
I give this game a solid 8/10 and can recommend it to people who like sandbox style survival games.
TIPS: Always carry Beta Blockers with you as it reduces your panic level when around hordes of Zombies. Carry bandages & Painkillers as if you get bitten/scratched your less likely to turn if you attend to the wound immediately. Always carry a spare weapon as low durability can cause them to break. Take Drinks & none perishable Food with you as you may be away from your safe House for a long time. Find a "Large Hiking Bag" as it can carry the most items. When exploring buildings, whack Doors before you enter. This will let you know if there is a Zombie on the other side as they will start banging on the Door. Give yourself escape routes, when I enter a building I open all the Doors as you can quite easily get pinned down by charging Zombies. Take spare clothes with you (unless your already fully clothed) as you can die from Hyperthermia / Hypothermia if there is a sudden temperature change. Attack crawling Zombies from behind, they are slow to turn around and much less dangerous.

Every ship has limited ammo and you HAVE to posses ships very often. That's where the fun begin, as it brings a lot of strategy beyond the shooting.
If you possess another ship before you are out of ammo - the old "You" start shooting you from point blank.
If you jump from fast to slow ship in straight line - you'll get the collision damage with your old one and you'll be one hit from death.
If your old slow ship runs out after you cleaned all but the fastest ships - you'll gonna have bad time getting them.
It takes precision, calculation and holding fire to master it, as shooting all the time will render you naked to the incoming wave. So you kinda need to clear all but the ship you want, spending all the ammo you have and posses it without killing it first.

Been playing games on Steam for a while, but never took the time to write a review. I felt obligated to do this one because this game is a mixed bag for some, but I think it is an engaging interactive story, and that´s very much what this ¨game¨is. A spinoff from the MMO, The Secret World, you enter an amusement park, a setting from the original game to explore the sinister stories and tragedies that still haunt this decrepit theme park. You walk along and follow the rides and the narrative, and try to find and read the scattered letters and notices, and listen to Lorraine´s monologues about life. I call this an ïnteractive¨story because you can´t really lose, and even with my terrible sense of game direction, you can´t really get lost. While this game´s story was not a thriller, with some awesome twist at the end, I found it to be a tour de force that made me interested in finding where the story was going. The main character was enjoyable as a flawed and very human person, and I feel a lot of attention to detail was paid to making Lorraine seem like a real person with real problems, caught up in unreal circumstances. The ending of the game is a bit of a puzzler, but again, so interesting that I continued trying to research the game after it was finished, and even briefly piqued my interest in checking out The Secret World (but who has time for MMOs with almost 200 games in the library). While reading, I came across this quote from the creator that I wanted to share:
"Everybody's had that dream where they fall," Bylos says. "Most people have had that nightmare where they wake up because they fell from a height -- I want that feeling from people, especially as you go through the House of Horrors, the sense that the bottom is rushing up and you just can't stop it. It's inevitable."  --Joel Bylos
It was because of this quote that I came here to recommend this game, because it did exactly what the creator wanted to do, and I consider that to be a success. As the ending drew near, I couldn´t stop myself, and I did feel that rush of an impending end that made me both anxious and excited. While the game´s ending felt like a well-what-do-you-think-happened, I was glad for the experience. While some might want to wait for this to be on sale, as the game is maybe 1-2 hours at most, I encourage games to be the new medium for storytelling, and The Park is not to be missed for those who enjoy eerie atmospheres, realistic characters, and dark stories.

Fables from the Den is a digital children's book. Each story is a fable as the title suggests and so each short story teaches a moral lesson, using woodland creatures as characters. The dialogue is simple and effective. This would make a lovely print book, as the art work is superb. I read each of the stories out loud to my son (this should not take more than an hour even reading out loud slowly). He is too young to understand them yet but enjoys hearing my voice, and I liked reading them. We will be re-visiting this book later on when he can get the full meaning of the stories. They are definitely suitable from a young age, but I can't imagine they have much to offer people who don't have children in their lives unless you are a massive fan of the Shelter artwork and animals.
The downside is of course that these are on PC (or TV if you have yours set up that way), which is not an ideal way to read to children. I gave this a go, and enjoyed reading them out to my son - but quickly realized sitting with him in front of a PC for him to enjoy the pictures wasn't ideal. If this was a physical book, or even on tablet, it would make for a better bedtime story read. For this reason it gets a
recommendation for me.
If you are looking for a story book on the PC or have your TV set up in the bedroom where your kid is going to be able to see the words and pictures then I do recommend it - it is
. If this was on tablet, I could see myself reading these stories to my child every night and showing him the cute images - but for practical reasons, I don't think I will get much use out of it. I couldn't justify giving this a negative rating - it is perfectly executed, but for me, steam just doesn't work as a platform for reading.

5 reviews, game hasn't been out 24 hours yet, and already there's some pretty bad misinformation out there... I understand the game could describe what's going on a little better, but, no, you don't get an encounter on every hero turn. Just like all of D&D's adventure system board games, you only get an encounter when your hero doesn't explore a new tile or when the newly explored tile is of a special type that causes an encounter anyway. (Pretty sure the tutorial explains that.) Moreover, the game has several mechanics to cancel particularly nasty events as you progress.
Anyway, this is an excellent, digitized rendering of a D&D adventure system boardgame along the lines of Temple of Elemental Evil or Legend of Drizzt. It's not intended to compete with full-scale RPG's like Dragon Age or Neverwinter Nights and it's pretty clear about that from the very beginning. It's a board game.
I strongly disagree that the board game is poorly designed. The adventure system design is tried, true, and probably the best "RPG lite" board game design I've ever encountered - fast paced, builds and sustains exciting play. I've encountered a lot in the last 35 years of fantasy gaming.
Here's hoping they refine it a little further, smooth out some minor bugs, and continue support for games like this on the same level that Blizzard does for the Diablo series. More important, let's hope they add multiplayer. I think the game needs it.

Let's start by answering a common question.
Do you have to be a fan of the inspiration/shows to enjoy this game? No. However Chroma Squad does capture the magic and feeling of its inspiration. The jokes, winks, and nudges are all done hilariously and authentically. Poking fun and at the same time honoring the source material. Being a fan just maximizes your enjoyment and lets you in on some of the jokes.
That doesn't stop Chroma Squad from being a very deep, rich, RPG. From customization of your Cast(Party) to choosing what weapons(props) to craft. You will mold your team into what you see fit. Battling minions, bosses, kaiju, and a budget. No two save files will be alike unless you want them to be. Not only do you have that turned based tactical combat. You also must manage your own studio. Choose upgrades to boost ratings, and what ad agency will represent you. All these choices and options can deeply affect the flow of combat, crafting, and if you succeed or fail.
All of this seamlessly blends together in this over the top and humorous RPG. With wonderfully done pixel art, music, and steamy goodness. Chroma Squad is as wonderful of a homage, as it is a game.

Since you are probably skimming through the reviews to make up your mind on a purchase, I’ll save you some time and summarise this game with three words, they are cheap (price tag), stylish (graphics) and fun (game play). If that wasn’t enough to convince you, read on.
This title is essentially an arena game set upon a 2D platform with 3D graphics, the twist revolves around the clever implementation of gravity around structures and planets, with which the players will use to maneuver their mechs. The system can be confusing at first, but very rewarding once a player gets the hang of it, I was pulling gravitational slingshot and performing swing-by shooting within an hour.
The guns themselves are fairly mundane and standard among this type of game, but the twelve of them do vary a great deal in terms of play style and tactics. There are four utility tools available as well, but I rarely see people use them to much effect in game.
As for game modes, you have the basic Death Match which is self explanatory. Then you have Orbital Warfare, a territorial tug-of-war in which both teams race to charge up their main cannons for a devastating blast. Lastly you have Orbital Trials, a single player time attack mode that pits you up against patrolling machines on a map with limited weaponry; this was added by the developers after much request from the community.
The only problem I had with the game was the lack of bots, so if you just wanted a private match with a friend or two, the arena would feel very desolate. Other than that I felt the community could do better with a few thousand more players, so it would be easier to find games during different hours of the day.
The asking price of 10 USD is fine, but if you find this under 1 USD during a sale, it would be a practical steal.

VERY EARLY STREAM OF THOUGHTS:
first impressions are possitive.
The characters have a suite of abilties you can swap out before the map making it easy to change up tactics. Premade characters mean you can focus on the gameplay. the HP's and DMG numbers are all really small, which imo is refreshing. simple, easy to read. its great.
was and still am unsure about the way the maps unfold (created dynamically on exploration) but to my surprise its pretty fun. The system forces you to either uncover a new tile or take a dice roll which can result in damage to the party or status effects (possitive or negative), which creates an nice tension. So if you encounter a chest for example you have a risk/reward dilema, do you open the chest and risk taking damage from the penalty for not exploring? BUT, if the chest is adjacent to an exploration tile then you can open the chest AND explore bypassing the roll.
there appear to be many abilties that can manipulate the map, reducing or negating the penalties and creature spawns. there is also a meter that fills up that allows you to bypass the effects but it can also buff your party (more risk/reward - do you save your meter or spend it?)
the difficulty tuning seems pretty tight. with the constant pressure you really have to make use of all your abilties, and quite a few of them are one [per map] use. at the end of the maps my characters are totally drained.
you also find items which are basically just additional skills - their effects can be huge - allowing you to fine tune your character build even more. items are found on the maps, which can lead to exciting situations. example:  mage opened a chest whilst uncovering a new tile & enemy that charged me. the chest contained an item that allowed him to 100% dodge the next attack, which allowed him to survive just long enough for my paladin to run in and save him. the sigh of relief is shortlived tho - the paladin stepped on an explore tile to avoid the encounter roll continuing the momentum. the pacing is really great!
and there is a crafting system which is thankfully super streamlined - it clearly shows you what you can build for what characters with the items you have. I find crafting in games really tedious personally, but this system is so clearly presented with a quick glance and a couple button clicks you can further augment your build. nice.
technically, the product is very polished. clean readable ui, nice animations and effects. sound effects are crunchy, music is fine. its well produced.

Tales from Candlekeep: Tomb of Annihilation feels like a very good digital port of a very bad boardgame.
From a technical point of view it's top notch: pretty, with well-made user interface, nice animations, music, proper tutorial, no technical problems etc etc. But from a game mechanics point of view it has some serious issues.
My main beef is the encounter system. If you remember Warhammer Quest, event system there looked like this: After finishing player turn you rolled d6 and on 1 event happened. Here event happens every time after each character (character!) turn. Since you're controlling 4 characters you've got 4 events happening every turn. It's beyond ridiculous since they take like half of the play time, constantly stunning, poisoning, damaging, debuffing and annoying the hell out of you. It feels like being attacked by a horde of invisible enemies all the time. Normal enemies are easy to deal with, but the events are your main problem. Since you've got really small possibilty to influence them, every game feels like a race that you try to finish before all of you heroes die from random damage effects. I understand that it is anti-stalling mechanics but it is done terribly wrong.
My another beef is from game being really really slow. Considering I'm a guy with over 200 hours in Flashpoint: Campaigns I'm not exactly a fan of action games and my tolerance to slow is probably bigger than most of you. But this game takes slow one step too far. Why do I have to watch "Enemies turn" pop up and skip animation every time, even when there are no enemies on the table (80%of the time)? Why do I have to watch animations for the events bombarding me constantly for 1 damage, 1 damage, 2 damage and pressing space after each and every one of them? I know that this game is licensed and I even played this Ravenloft-boardgame old counterpart (wasn't stellar either) but this one is just plain bad. Wanna good D&D boardgame go and play Lords of the Waterdeep.
Another thing: balance. I realise that I can't judge that after 1-2 hours, and I need to make it to the endgame to see things from a proper perspective, but early game looks like this: You've got amazing paladin with best base stats, best passives and best abilities kicking butts left and right and 3 other sad excuses for adventurers just filling the spots and dying randomly from time to time.
Last thing, my personal beef. Names. Ranger Artur is ok, but others... Dragonbait? Who made this up? Birdsong? really? Why is my khajit-looking Bard named Birdsong? What do you have to do to come up with such a stupid name? I know it's D&D and I know it doesn't bother anyone else, but still. Dragonbait. Dragonbait. His parents must have really hated him to name him Dragonbait. Ok, nevermind, I digress...
Kudos for the developer - you made a very good port of a very bad game, now please make us very good port of a very good game.

About five minutes ago, I finished my first playthrough of "Chroma Squad". I could end this review here and now by saying/typing "Buy this game, NOW!", but I won't.
What kind of game is it? A Tactical RPG. Most of the time you have five characters to control in turn based battles, each characters may move once and then hit an enemy or use some ability, or it may move twice but not do anything else. The characters are like clones of the Power Rangers and you may name them and also choose their colors, but not how they look... per se. There's some identities with different stats and looks that can be chosen for each "Ranger", but that's it. But speaking of customization, you may name your studio and also different catchphrases that your team will use during battle - for when they're using their finishing move, when they transform into the alter egos etc.
The battles in itself are really good and gets progressively harder as the game goes on, the final battle was for me really challenging, mostly due to the fact that I tried to keep everyone on their feet and I tried to meet every goal. Oh, right, the goals. For each battle you get two "Director's Instructions" that could be "Defeat x enemies" or "Win in y turns" and other things. These goals keeps the game interesting and also, if met, generates more money and fans to the studio.
Graphics wise, it has a retro style, more 16 bit era than anything. Obviously it is modernized and polished to look a lot better. I liked it a lot, but then again I mostly like this graphical style. Sound though, the little I heard (mostly played it muted due to playing music meanwhile playing the game) sounded great but can't say much more than that.
In the end, if you're a fan of Power Rangers (which I'm not, so no requirement) and Mechas, you'll love this. Also, if you like Tactical RPGs you will probably like this, but the lack of depth in customization may put you off.
Like I said/wrote in the beginning of this review: Buy this game, NOW!

A beautifully done piece of art serves as the background for most of the space arenas and the sprites are very well drawn/animated with a good level of detail. The Beginners Guide:
I don’t know where to start with this game. It left me feeling something I haven’t felt before, and it was a strange feeling. It wasn’t a bad feeling, but it wasn’t a good feeling. It was something not happy but not sad. The closest thing I can liken it to is a sense of wonder and intrigue. The events in this game lead me in a very strange direction, a direction of knowing nothing while at the same time thinking I know everything that happened in the span of the hour and a half I played this game for. The events in this game lead you in a certain direction, as curated by Davey, but leave enough room for interpretation that they make each choice meaningful for each individual player. The Beginners Guide left a narrative with a linear story open to a wide variety of interpretation, which is something that Is hard to pull off. This game also has sparked a wide variety of discussion based on different aspects on the game, Coda specifically. This game has done something special for me, and many others, which is give an experience that lasts past when you close the game. It leaves a lasting effect on you, the characters are memorable and their actions are even more memorable. Each moment in the game is memorable, from the thought bubbles to the house cleaning this game made every chapter stick in my head. And that’s something I’d like to see more of.

It's a good game.

I have played through both the Alpha, Beta and now its live release and over the course of those couple months the game has been getting to an incredibly balanced state. There are somethings about the game that can be debated about whats underpowered or overpowered but for the most part its almost dead even due to the data Turtle Rock has provided (51% Monster and 49% Hunters during beta and internal tests). The Maps are just big enough to were it doesnt feel like an eternity walking across the Map without even seeing the monster although if the monster plays well by sneaking it should be a challenge and the hunters need to try and cut the monster off before staging up.
On the topic of DLC, the developers have stated that the game was built with DLC in mind. Meaning that throught the course of the games life span, content can be added at any point to allow players to try out new Monsters, Hunters or check out possible skins for them as well. THERE IS NO DAY 1 DLC. The pre-order bonus for just the base game was there for you to purchace if you wanted to get the monster for free down the line and you knew you wanted to buy it later anyways. With that being said, ALL MAPS AND GAME MODES WILL BE FREE. They do NOT want to divide the community by making map packs for purchace or possible game modes down the line and thus, everything is purely on the Hunters and Monsters, should you want to buy cosmetics for them or purchace new playable characters down the line.
Pros:
* The "Hunting" aspect is there as games can be tense due to not knowing were the monster is.
* Level Based Matchmaking. No getting paired up with low levels unless you queue up with one with you.
* Winning with teamwork is rewarded through good communication's either through pinging ingame or using in-game voice.
* High-Level play is definitely there in the higher level's. Multiple strategic choices for both Monster's and Hunters through perks, team compositions and map/game mode choices.
* Evacuation mode is anyones game, even if you're behind and you have balancing towards you, you can still win.
* Playing as the monster and you get to stage 3 quickly is satisfying as you outwited 4 people within a short amount of time in game.
Cons:
* There are a few bugs here and there but, for me personally it didn't bother me too much such as cursor showing while in game, matchmaking issue's with joining games somtimes booting you out.
* If the monster plays conservatively in a match and the Hunters cannot find him, it can seem to be drawn out/boring to some as most of the time you are running around/killing wildlife.
* Progression might seem very long for some later on in for character's as the requirements to rank your items up takes awhile but will come sooner rather than later just by leveling your account up while playing matches.
The game itself is a breath of fresh air from the normal FPS titles out there and even going off into a whole new genre as a 4v1 and more and more games are starting to arise with this model and even in Dying Light there is a 4v1 mode as well. The DLC is there if you want it. The DLC is not required nor is it impactful to your gameplay if you dont buy it as all it offers is cosmetics for Monsters and Hunters and more playable characters down the line like stated above. If you are looking for a game that offer's the thrill of hunting and being rewarded with teamwork that can have high level play then Evolve is a good place to start as it offer's all of that and interesting character design that gives each one a clear identity.

- In any case it is not mashed potatoes, rice or veggies to try out instead of pasta. When the menu is set, it doesn't get changed!
What Evolve's DLC offer:
-They're not mappacks as not to split community. That is commendable, but I wouldn't mind AT ALL paying for that kind of DLC, as it adds a new playground to a fixed gameplay.
-The DLC offer different monsters/hunters, i.e. it offers different gameplay mechanics. How come is this not chipping away at the core game?
Turtle Rock's answer:
The DLC content is going to be completely new and has not been thought of in the base game, we're not removing any content from the base game (or something in those lines).
Me:
So you're saying that, for an assymetrical multiplayer game, you're going to be releasing a stream of gameplay changing content that will inevitably mess the fragile equilibrium of the game and not even give access to that content to the entire comunity?
Also, as advantages are bound to happen, I'm sure you will not nerf down DLC characters too much, I mean: it's realistic for you to want DLC's to have a selling argument. Right? If so, isn't your game turning out to be a pay-2-win, although I have to pay for the base game?
TR:
But you get to play against and with the people who have that content, you're not going to be separated from the comunity, even if you don't purchase the DLCs.
Me:
So you're telling me that the code for all the DLC content is going to be downloaded to my PC as well, as I need to see it in action on other players, and that I will have to pay for it to unlock? Well thanks for adding every so months a few gigabites of DLC download that I won't be even able to use unless I give you some money...
In the end this is my point of view:
I would have gladly payed the pre purchasing price and even a season pass/game combo if the DLC's wouldn't have been gameplay related, but this setup is a recipe for disaster and I don't want to be caught up in the mess that is going to be balancing the game at each new character addition. Plus in a year or even less there is going to be a deluxe package for 30 euros where I can get all the content at once with most of the bugs fixed as well. (EDIT: I told it so, now it's becoming free to play! Best course of action was to wait and not buy...)
So in the end, don't buy this game as long as the gameplay balancing hasn't been achieved, and this will last as long as they're adding characters...

I'd first like to point out that this is recommended, but only on a sale. It's not worth it otherwise.
This game has a lot of potential. But it rarely does anything with it. The gameplay mechanics are great, online and local multiplayer is fun, the many different types of weapons provide many different ways to play, and once you get used to the unique movement mechanic, it's an amazing feeling to use gravity to zoom around different "planets". But the game just doesn't feel finished. It lacks things that I feel are basic to this type of game. It has no "normal" single player (which I'll expand on in a minute), no minimap of any kind, and really only 3 types of gamemodes.
So, there is a type of single player, and it's not that bad. You just have to kill a certain amount of enemies in a certain amount of time, and unlock weapons as you go. But the annoying part is, this is the only type of single player. There's not any mod where you just pick a world and dificulty, put in bots, and just have a deathmatch. Yeah, there's that in multiplayer, but multiplayer has it's own problems. First off, it's hard to be a "noob" in mutiplayer. A good amount of these people have gotten pretty good and using the weapons, utilities, and maps fully to their advantage. Not to mention, the community is tiny. For the whole US, there's usually only one game going on at once. Only one. With maybe 8 people. Not a huge community. Yeah, multiplayer is fun, but since it's so small, they should add more gamemodes for single player.
Gamemodes are another thing. There are only three. One for single player, and two for multiplayer. I personally would love seeing modes like survival, juggernaut, etc.
Now, as you can see, I am recommending this. That's because, with all this missing, it's still a good game. At least, it has it's moments. When you're playing locally with a friend, it's a great small game to have. And, like I said, the gameplay mechanics are pretty good. It just feels more like an early access game than a finished game.
So, overall, it's not a great game, but it's a good game. It can be fun to play sometimes, and it's a good game to mess around with friends. However, it feels like it's missing simple, easy-to-add things that would make it a far better game. So, feel free to get it, I'd just recommend getting it during a sale of some kind.

The Journey Down is a classic point and click adventure. The story (without spoilers) is quickly told: You are one of two friends who run a gas station at the habour. A woman comes over and asks for your help. You need to fix your water plane to accomplish that. There's a reckless bad dude in the background who apparently wants to stop you.
The majority of the game is you running around trying to get the missing pieces for the plane with no connection to the actual story.
You have a handful locations and in each location a handful of things to click on or one or two people to speak to. The first 40 minutes or so this keeps you interested enough until you've read/heard all discriptions and dialogue.
The game is extremely linear, you can't pick up stuff until you are told that you need it. This means that from a certain point on you have to revist known places again and again to find the one thing that has changed. Since there is no fast travel system and you can't even double click exits to skip through locations, you spend some time watching your character walk through the scenery. Thankfully, though, it is often pretty logical where you have to look so for the most part you at least have an idea where you should be going.
Puzzles are the heart of adventure games and here TJD actually does a fairly good job. There are only a few but they are logical and often slightly humourous, a definite plus. There are also a couple of minigames that everyone who has played adventure games before will know.
All in all, I expected more from the reviews that I've read. The first 45 minutes or so are nice, after that it becomes a bit of a chore since there is not much to explore after that.
I bought TJD for 0.89 € on sale and for that price I recommend it. The full price (8.99 €) is ridiculous. With 3 hours playtime if you explore all dialogue options and make yourself a sandwich inbetween, this is more of a demo than anything else.
Edit: After playing the second part I've changed my rating to recommended, since the second part is a lot better than the first part, definitely worth playing. To understand the second part you should have played the first one.
I still think you should wait until it is on sale, though.
