One of the best depictions of galactic war I've played. A fun, yet simple RTS.
PROS:
+Game uses primarily John Williams' score from the movies, which really helps with the atmosphere.
+Game is easy enough to pick-up and play for anyone with RTS experience.
+In-game battles promote the actual combat-side of the game instead of Starcraft/Age of Empires-style base-building.
+Galactic Conquest map allows for in-depth strategy between air/space armies and defences.
+Each faction has a unique playstyle, and their own strengths and weaknesses.
+Includes parts of the Star Wars EU, such as Grand Admiral Thrawn, Dark Troopers, Night Sisters, IG-88 and Mara Jade.
+Heroes are awesome, but not one-man armies (except for the really powerful ones)
+Graphics are good for its time.
+Base game covers A New Hope era, expansion covers Empire/Return of the Jedi era.
+Death Star is terrifying as hell, but not impossible to handle.
+Each faction plays as they should (Rebels are hit-and-run, Empire is a steady, unstoppable march, and Consortium uses black market tech to the extreme).
CONS
-Expansion doesn't have a story campaign for each faction, just for Consortium. Base game has story campaign for Empire/Rebellion, though.
-Multiplayer skirmishes can become drawn-out battles of "sending in the next wave."
-Only one resource (Credits).

Tropico 5 is NOT Tropico 4, that must be made clear. Tropico 4 was pretty much a beefed up Tropico 3 after all.
While I miss some aspects of Tropico 4 (apartment designs, some edicts, etc.), Tropico 5 is a truly great game in its own right.
I never did much of ANYTHING with the trading interface in T3 and T4, and while some lament the 'over simplified' and 'dumbed down' new trade interface, I love it. I am actually using it now and I know exactly what I'dm doing. What they made easy in trading, they made more complicated in everything else. Getting 100% happiness in a T4 sandbox was ridiculously easy. Even with $100k in a T5 sandbox, save games will be your friend. ESPECIALLY in the campaigns.
Factions are not the end all they used to be. While the people are easy to please, faction approval (and by extension the approval of their members) is not so easy. Happiness doesn't win elections. Approval does. Thus, you can be easily voted out if the largest faction doesn't like you for what ever reason. USE EVERY MINI-CHALLENGE YOU CAN TO PLEASE THE FACTIONS! Your life will be made significantly easier. Communists were easily appeased in T4 with food, housing and medical care. Now they don't give two hoots.
A huge amount of new features have been added, and I love them. From edicts to buildings to other mechanics. The added variety of army units is very welcome. Building managers make no sense to me though, since appointing them for each and every individual building is a micro-managing nightmare.
As a new edition of the Tropico series, I heartily approve. It is different, and a welcome challenge with many hours of gameplay fun (and frustration as you become accustomed to it). The game has that typical Tropico satire, parody and humour....and it is hilarious beyond what I thought T4 ever was.
Yes.

Alright, I don't want this entire thing to be a rant, so I want to give an example of my very first 4 player controlled hunter vs 1 player controlled monster experience.  In this example, I was the monster!
The game is divided into five matches, where the players vote on what each match type will be (except the final match, it's always the same).
The first match was a straight hunt, the hunters wanted to take me down! I was not prepared and did too much running amock, sadly I did not make it past stage one, they managed to take me out, but I did destroy the half of their forces in the attempt! Needless to say I realized I stopped breathing during a particularly long fight because I was panting by the end of it!
The second match: This one there were 6 eggs they had to destroy before they hatched, or they'd hatch into another monster and they had to take it out. I was ready this time, and took a bit more of a calculated risk as opposed to a blind one.  Instead of straight defending, I went out and immediately sought to evolve to stage 2 for more umph. The hunters were quick, having destroyed 3 of the eggs before I hit my goal, and as I went to hatch one of the eggs, they found me! It was a fierce battle, but I managed to escape, and while they took out 2 more eggs, I found the sixth one and hatched it! Now it was my turn, me and the second monster sought them out, and in a massive firefight, I devoured them all!
The third match: They went for another hunt. I tried to be a bit more stealthy this time, and though they caught up with me twice, I managed to evolve into stage 2. Riding the high of my previous win and feeling a bit invincible, I decided to take them on. This was a mistake sadly.  As I evolved too fast, and they found me while I was still trying to come out of my death shroud to take them on, so they had the advantage, and to my dismay they took me out, but again, I made them work for it!
The fourth match was a survivor rescue. This time they had to rescue 5 survivors or kill me before I killed the five survivors, or them. I got lucky on my hunting and found several big wildlife creatures that got me to stage two asap. They got to the first two survivors but I expected this, and as soon as the second two spawned I was already on top of them! I got one, but decided to make a retreat, and going off to feed more. Doing this allowed them to revive the survivor I incapacitated, meaning they needed only one more to win; however, I made it to stage three...and I was magnificent. I was no longer hiding, I was no longer peeking around corners and moving in stealth, I roared after them, destroying the five survivors as they spawned with no remorse! Destroying there very essence and claiming victory as my own!
The fifth match. This is a defense match, the hunters must defend 3 power structures and stop me, a fully formed Stage 3 Goliath from destroying their only escape! Unfortunately, as this was my first attempt, I was not ready for this challenge, and while I destroyed one generator, they took me down.
Despite the loss, this was an AWESOME experience. Even as a hunter vs the AI it was an epic game, and as a monster...from playing hide and seek in an attempt to get stronger to stomping around and laying waste to all that dare oppose me, it was extremely fun. And this is from a person who hates first person shooters as the hunter, I STILL enjoyed it!
Those of you with PCs that can run it, you are definitely in need of adding this to your collection! I'm still giggly from even just my first match, and I still have more monsters to unlock and many more hunters to try out!!

Unlike many of the reviews for this game, I actually own it.  Fancy that, eh?  Be warned that most of the negative reviews are from players who were in the Alpha, and don't seem to understand that the (admittedly BS agressive) marketing for DLC is not actually day-1 DLC, but rather stuff to be released in the future.
As it stands, the Evolve base game has a lot of content on offer for the dosh.  The twelve hunters all have their own nuances that can greatly affect how a match plays, just as the three monsters all have their own tactics in battle.  (Goliath is going to attack straight on, while it's in the best interest of Kraken to keep the hunters at a distance).  As such, I can't see myself getting bored of this any time soon, and with free maps on the horizon I do believe the game has longetivity.
The unlock system is also nicely done.  The character mastery gives a sense of progression and the unlocks it reveals keep me hungry for more, but at the same time it doesn't feel like a grind.  Part of that is from the fun "companion app" / bejeweled-inspired game they released for mobile, which has it's own twist on the classic match-3 gameplay that's pretty fun.  In any case, you can play the mobile game and earn mastery points, which you can then use to cut the already low grind in half for individual character abilities.
Really though, the game is a blast even when soloing as a hunter, and from what I've seen most of the players online do in fact use microphones so you won't die immediately.  But yea, make sure to have a mic if you're playing as hunter, and USE IT!
My only criticisms are the cosmetic skins in the store should be unlockable in-game without dosh, but meh, there's no gameplay impact there.  Also, no 3D Vision support.  Seriously, Nvidia actually went out of their way to disable it entirely rather than just calling it "not recommended"; the game renders completely flat.  Still, good performance on a GTX 680 on high quality.

Ah Outlast. This game is part Se7en, part One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest. I am going to be relatively brief about this game considering the length of time that has already passed since its release.
By default, the graphics and textures are not all that great- however this is easily fixable by a few quick INI edits as well as utilizing SGSSAA in something like NVidia Inspector; then the game looks great- other than some blurriness found in light blooms, etc.
The sound and music is very fitting for the setting, offering to the atmosphere versus taking away from it.
For a stealth game, it was well-done; offering enough tension to make the game enjoyable. I will note that the Insane Mode is not very friendly for most people and it took me several tries to complete the game. In fact, I really find it is not even worth doing ... they really should had Insane mode just offer saves at the end of every level instead of not at all.
The most intense moments I found were actually in the DLC involving the Groom ... who is one sick individual. In fact, it was the only scene in the entire game that actually made me whince. But, what man didn't.
I did find the rampant gore just a bit over the top, no scratch that- very over the top. It was used so much that by the end of the first level you really didn't care how many body parts and guts you stumbled across; as you've seen it all before.
By far the most disturbing imagery was that of the living inmates. From bashing their heads against the walls, or playing with themselves over a corpse or in the shadows was by far more visually distressing than the piles of mangled bits everywhere. Should had been more of this sort of thing instead of just the hackfest.
Overall, a good game ... one worth picking up for fans of the genre.

Wonderful presentation - lackluster game design.
That's how I would sum up Limbo in one sentence, and it is a shame. I love difficult games and I have a high tolerance for frustration, but this is the wrong kind of 'difficult'. Solving puzzles feels brainless and uninspiring in this title, especially towards the end. My main complatint is that you cannot use logic to do so, but rather have to apply trial and error in pretty much every situation. Usually, you will have a general idea of how to approach a puzzle, but in order to execute it correctly you have to repeat the same sequence over and over with just tiny variations.
.
In my opinion, a good puzzle game should give the player different elements to play around with and find out how they interact. Unfortunately, this is not Limbo's focus, as most puzzles feel very one-dimensional. Just compare that to Portal: In Portal, there is a general sense of achievement after solving a puzzle, even though the game is by no means hard. That's because the solutions are not apparent right away, and you have to mentally rearange the elements, thus making the player actively involved. In Limbo, on the other hand, you can see right away that you have to stop a cogwheel at the right moment in order to advance, but figuring out the right timing may take you about 20 attempts. What you feel after finally succeeding is not wonder at the imaginativeness of the devs, but disbelieve that you had to repeat the same boring task 20 times.
On the positive side of things, the atmosphere in this game is deep and brooding. If for nothing else, it might be worth checking it out just for the experience of the early game stages. If you enjoy it enough and do not mind the highly repetetive game play, this might just be the right title for you. Unfortunately, I just can't give it a thumbs up, as I felt more annoyed at the lacking puzzle design than enchanted by the artistic quality. This is one of those games that might really appeal to some people but not to others, so best try it out for yourself. The majority of folks here on Steam appear to have a different opinion from mine, which I am perfectly fine with. I am glad that others got more enjoyment out of this game than myself.
(BTW, the amount of hours played in my profile is misleading, as I played most of this game off-line)

Like the
, the game isn't perfect. It's interactive fiction, so there's little to be said about mechanics, and it's hard to write about the story without spoiling the message--but I'll try. The narrator (voiced by the game creator) guides you through incomplete games made by his friend Coda, who, from the outset, looms ominously over the narrative. Davey tells you Coda stopped making games but doesn't explain why, and he refers to Coda in the past tense, even when talking about the present. As you interact with the places Coda created, Davey shares his interpretations, which often involve over-the-top social and philosophical ideas. The game guides you through their relationship, and who they are (or who they might be, if you interpret it a certain way). Its conclusion asks you to look at your own relationships and what purpose they serve. I really enjoyed experiencing that in a game. It's rare, and it's different. That's the awesome part and why I recommend it.
I realized what was happening early on, but I didn't find that it negatively affected my experience. However, once the story turned, Davey (both the narrator version and the the creator) got a little too on the nose. His last few scenes basically tell you what to think and how to feel. That cheapened it for me. The kind of people that play interactive fiction games are smart enough to understand what's happening to a character without it explicitely being told to them. As a result, the ending didn't have the effect it should (or could) have had. He overplayed it, and the game suffers a bit as a result.

Alright, I don't want this entire thing to be a rant, so I want to give an example of my very first 4 player controlled hunter vs 1 player controlled monster experience.  In this example, I was the monster!
The game is divided into five matches, where the players vote on what each match type will be (except the final match, it's always the same).
The first match was a straight hunt, the hunters wanted to take me down! I was not prepared and did too much running amock, sadly I did not make it past stage one, they managed to take me out, but I did destroy the half of their forces in the attempt! Needless to say I realized I stopped breathing during a particularly long fight because I was panting by the end of it!
The second match: This one there were 6 eggs they had to destroy before they hatched, or they'd hatch into another monster and they had to take it out. I was ready this time, and took a bit more of a calculated risk as opposed to a blind one.  Instead of straight defending, I went out and immediately sought to evolve to stage 2 for more umph. The hunters were quick, having destroyed 3 of the eggs before I hit my goal, and as I went to hatch one of the eggs, they found me! It was a fierce battle, but I managed to escape, and while they took out 2 more eggs, I found the sixth one and hatched it! Now it was my turn, me and the second monster sought them out, and in a massive firefight, I devoured them all!
The third match: They went for another hunt. I tried to be a bit more stealthy this time, and though they caught up with me twice, I managed to evolve into stage 2. Riding the high of my previous win and feeling a bit invincible, I decided to take them on. This was a mistake sadly.  As I evolved too fast, and they found me while I was still trying to come out of my death shroud to take them on, so they had the advantage, and to my dismay they took me out, but again, I made them work for it!
The fourth match was a survivor rescue. This time they had to rescue 5 survivors or kill me before I killed the five survivors, or them. I got lucky on my hunting and found several big wildlife creatures that got me to stage two asap. They got to the first two survivors but I expected this, and as soon as the second two spawned I was already on top of them! I got one, but decided to make a retreat, and going off to feed more. Doing this allowed them to revive the survivor I incapacitated, meaning they needed only one more to win; however, I made it to stage three...and I was magnificent. I was no longer hiding, I was no longer peeking around corners and moving in stealth, I roared after them, destroying the five survivors as they spawned with no remorse! Destroying there very essence and claiming victory as my own!
The fifth match. This is a defense match, the hunters must defend 3 power structures and stop me, a fully formed Stage 3 Goliath from destroying their only escape! Unfortunately, as this was my first attempt, I was not ready for this challenge, and while I destroyed one generator, they took me down.
Despite the loss, this was an AWESOME experience. Even as a hunter vs the AI it was an epic game, and as a monster...from playing hide and seek in an attempt to get stronger to stomping around and laying waste to all that dare oppose me, it was extremely fun. And this is from a person who hates first person shooters as the hunter, I STILL enjoyed it!
Those of you with PCs that can run it, you are definitely in need of adding this to your collection! I'm still giggly from even just my first match, and I still have more monsters to unlock and many more hunters to try out!!

Chroma Squad is a Tactical RPG made by Behold Studios, the developers behind Knights of Pen & Paper. Chroma Squad is a love letter and a tribute to decades of Japanese superhero shows such as: Super Sentai, Kamen Rider and the Metal Hero series.
=STORY=
You start off as a five-people  team of stuntactors who decide to make their own Sentai-themed TV show in which they become a Sentai team themselves and fight against all sorts of monsters while managing their resources and fan-community behind the scenes. The first two seasons start very tame since you’re still an indie Sentai studio with a low budget, but from season 3 onwards the plot becomes more serious and fascinating.
Depending on your choice during the finale of season 4, you might either end up doing the Rider route, the Metal Hero route or the Sixth Ranger route. I won’t spoil much, but each route has their own scenarios going on with interesting mini stories that contribute to the game’s lore. The finale of the game itself is amazing, and is something to behold and be amazed at – I’ll try not to spoil it, but it’s definitely “empowering”.
Mind you, the game developers have suggested to implement more alternate endings or routes  within future DLC or updates, so this review might end up dated and not give a complete overview to what the story system of Chroma Squad offers.
= CUSTOMIZATION =
This is arguably my favourite part of the game, ‘cuz who doesn’t want to make their very own Sentai dream team? You can customize your team by choosing out of approx. 20 actors, each with their own appearances and bonuses. You can also name them and decide which suit colour they wear, i.e. if you always wanted to make an all-Red ranger team, well here’s your chance!
Throughout the seasons, the game offers various types of helmets and suits that not only give certain statboosts but also visually alter the appearance of your hero. Unfortunately, the amount of actors and visual-altering equipment you can choose from is quite limited, so you’ll have to either wait for future DLC or step up your modding skills.
You can also name your studio, your team, your giant robot, your transformation and lines of dialogue that call forth said mech, transformation and team attack. While it doesn’t give you the ultimate customization possibilities like customizing your own hero costume or actor from scratch, the game offers a decent amount of customization which will hopefully be expanded in the future.
= GAMEPLAY =
While the game is a turn-based tactical system, it’s not as complex or multi-faceted as Super Robot Wars, but neither is it overtly simplistic. You generally control five characters, each with their own stats depending on equipment, actor, role and bonuses you’ve activated through studio upgrades or siding with the more favourable marketing agencies. Each role offers a variety of skill, the Techie and Support role are for example more oriented on long-range and healing skills, respectively.
Your characters can generally do two actions per turn – in most cases you’ll (1) move to the enemy and (2) perform an attack or (1)(2) move to the other end of the screen. Your heroes can wield weapons which not only increase attack damage but also provide with an extra skill. Last but not least, there’s the Teamwork mechanic in which you can make two or more of your heroes pull off an combined attack at an enemy they’re both facing.
The giant robot vs giant monster battles have a more mini-game feel to it, but it can still be one heck of an intense battle. It’s a sideview turn-based battle in which you can hit the enemy multiple times until your turn is ended through missing the opponent, ending your combo with the defend options or ending the turn with a super attack. During the enemy’s turn you must step up your reaction game to minimize the amount of damage your mech will receive.
Outside of missions, there’s also a light Studio Simulation system going on – i.e. you’ll get to read and answer fan letters, upgrade your studio for additional bonuses, upgrade your giant robot, buy equipment, craft equipment or materials and side with the marketing agencies that give you the best bonuses or help you earn and gain more money and fans.
= OVERALL =
If you’ve longed for a game in which you can make your own Sentai team and fight against hordes of enemies with the help of unlikely allies and your trusty giant robot , then look no further because Chroma Squad is arguably the best Sentai game if not one of the best Henshin Hero games up to this point. The story, several dialogues and fan letters will make you laugh and smile – and perhaps, even give you the feeling that you’re being a true hero of justice. Gameplay-wise, Chroma Squad is a very accessible game but not without a challenge for those who want to step up their game. While the visuals and soundtrack aren’t AAA-tier, they’re still pleasing and amazing to see and listen to nonetheless. This game is definitely made with love, and it shows. I can’t wait for the future updates and potential-DLC this game has to offer. Behold Studios, you’re the best and thank you for this amazing loveletter to decades of tokusatsu heroism.

A great and at times, hilarious, retro tactical RPG. No level up system so the equipment system is the only way to change character stats. This causes a pretty simple tactical RPG system character-wise. Most of the strategy is in the battles themselves making sure you choose the right abilites to accomplish the objectives or "director's instructions". Marketing and upgrading your studio are the other two micro managing things you'll do between stages ("episodes"). Both pretty much letting you adjust rewards for completing episodes or helps you gain bonus stats during them.
The other major part of the game is the Mecha battle! Although they can get a tad bit tedious, it's Costume Quest-esque fun. You ugrade your machine parts, but in the end the pieces are all pretty similar. The mecha fights are all the same, your hits are die rolls, and missing a 95% hit is infuriating when they pummel you 3 times in a row after. The saving grace for Mecha battles is that you can hold Enter to fast forward them like cut scenes.
The dialouge is pretty funny and the story riddled with pop culture references, this makes for a special kind of humor. It has a pretty entertaining story and kept me hooked all the way through. When you do finish the game (I recommend it), keep clicking!

I don't want to do those all over again.  It serves best as a reminder of the caveat emptor nature of Kickstarter.

This game reminded me of a quote from Dr. Ben Sobel, in Analyze This: "I'm gonna go out on a limb here and say that this friend of yours, is you."
Except in this case, it is much less funny.
In fact, at a certain point, the game becomes quite unsettling and a little creepy.
I actually felt sorry for Davey Wreden in this “game”. But then I remembered that I actually paid money for this, and spent two hours of my time, just to listen to the developer ♥♥♥♥♥ about his schizophrenia, and about how his career sucks and how he wants to metaphorically kill himself.
Invariably, players will compare this to Davey's first game, The Stanley Parable, and invariably they will feel disappointed.
Overall, I can’t really recommend this game. If it were free, maybe. But as it is, it’s hard to justify paying anything for this.

The Journey Down is a very nice point & click style adventure game with humor that i would recommend to anybody who likes the genre. If you decide to buy, get the both chapters together. The game doesn't have tedious parts like some members of this genre does. You don't have to watch your character walk for ages, it skips to the place if you double click.
The story is not the most amazing one i've seen in a point & click style game but it's decent enough. It has some mystery elements and can make you curious at some points. In short, not amazing but good enough to keep you playing.
Most of the time the puzzles are pretty easy. You usually know what you need to do when you first see an item ,if not, you can figure out quickly. The game is rather relaxing than pushing you hard to solve a puzzle.
The characters are cool and their accents are really fun. Their heads are inspired by african tribal masks. You play as a young guy named Bwana. There are two other main characters named Kito and Lina. I liked all of the characters in the game especially our guy Bwana.
The art design is very charming. The game has a nice carribean and also noir atmosphere. The hand drawn places look wonderful.
One of the best things about the game ,besides its art design, is it's soundtracks. It includes some reggae and jazz tunes and the soundtracks become more jazzy in second chapter. The music fits well with the atmosphere of the game.

History lesson:
A long long time ago in this very galaxy LucasArts made a game called "Star Wars: Rebellion". It was a RTS game that was released under Windows 95. While this game was VERY fun, it did have a lot of flaws built into it. (one example would be an overuse of windows). The fans liked the game anyways, and demanded Rebellion 2. LucasArts developed Star Wars: Empire at War (originally called Rebellion 2)
Review:
This game is a must have for any Star Wars fan, but in reality, it is not the game that Petroglyph wanted to make. Unfortunately, LucasArts tended to be fairly impatient with the release of the games and would rush games to the stores before they were even really ready. While a lot of the errors can be seen if you know what to look for, and the AI will cheat (the higher the difficulty, the more the AI will cheat. The only real way it gets "more difficult" is by having things there is no way it should have. The tactics the computer uses aginst you is always the same), it is still a very fun game. I have spent many a hour playing this game. The graphics are good, the sound is what you would expect from a Star Wars game, and the voice acting is very good.

Full disclosure: I picked this game up from a giveaway on PC Gamer.
That said, I expect the vast majority of games I find in giveaways to be minor amusements at best, not even worth the time to download at worst.
This though? Definitely would have been worth paying 10$ for.
First couple of levels I was thinking "Oh, this is a fun little take on Gradius style space shooters, but not overly complex or challenging". Then I got to level 3 and suddenly the game made me take back that statement. The ship switching mechanic becomes very important for navigating each level, knowing when to switch and to which target is what keeps you alive. Each ship is easy to learn to control and vastly diffrent from the others in both how they move and fire, and I've yet to find one I didn't have a use for at one point. Though several I found myself jumping to briefly, taking out targets from their angle, then jumping again before I got stuck.
Graphics are sprite based and feel like something out of the SNES era, sound is on a simlar style and quality. Maybe not the best digital synthysizer music I've heard but very effective for the setting. The story I'm still getting into but it's revealed to you in short bits between waves and levels. Minor hints here in there as to why you're a conciousness jumping from ship to ship, and why there's a war between humans and an alien race going on around you. The pacing of the story is just enough to get you hooked and never slows down the action.
The game also has amusing extras that unlock at each level. The first one for example is "Flappity Mind" which allows you to play effectively a version of Flappy Bird. The others seem similarly ridiculous, but worth it for a few laughs.
So yes. Get this game, Even at full price. You'll have fun blowing stuff up and being the mysterious force making everyone afraid of who's going to turn on them next.
All I can say is: Choose wisely. This strategy game will make you work for those achievements!

I am a huge fan of the Tropico series but I unfortunatly cannot recommend this game. Also I should add I have logged about 70+ hours in this game at the time of writing this review even though my account says like 90 mins or something, I played most of it in offline mode.
Compared to Tropico 4 (which imo is the best Tropico in the series) this game just feels unfinished even with all the DLC. There was so much stripped from the game that I sometimes found myself spending time looking for something that was no longer present even though they were important features in previous games.
My main problem with 5 compared to 4 is that you have less control over your island and its inhabitants.
Here a few of my Likes and Dislikes
Likes
-Era and Research system was a good idea (poorly exectuted though)
-Dynasty members was a nice idea and looking forward to a return in futrue Tropicos hopefully
-Trade system was also a welcomed feature
-Online mode is a great feature but not enough people use it, (good for with friends though)
-New mining system
-New farm system
-Really liked the new combat system
-Manager system was a good idea
-Buildings look amazing (Best so far)
Dislikes
-New Almanac is just bad, lacks so much useful information (bring back the old one!!!)
-Lack of the Rise to Power, Background etc options when setting up a new sandbox game
-Where did all the trait options go?
-Labour camp removed (easily on of my favourite buildings, I would have bet money on it making a return in 5. Sadly not though)
-Lack of housing options
-Shockingly small amount of decorations compared to Tropico 4
-Grade school removed
-New budget system which replaces the ability to set the wages and upkeep of the building individually.
-Building options gone. (cants set schools to Military Education, newspapers to Word of God etc.) This was a huge disappointment for me.
-Not enough Tourism and Entertainment buildings
-Number of tourists allowed on the island capped
-Lack of variety in tasks, after a few playthroughs they become too familiar
-New Faction system is terribile (where did the loyalists go?)
-Advisors and Faction Reps Removed. Only Penultimo and Oaksworth advise and offer tasks now.
-Zoom levels reduced
-Criminals replaced with crime lords that justt appear on your island
-Election Speech removed (????)
-Rebel yell, Immigrants out etc starting options removed
I could list a few more but you get the idea. I will end this review saying that if you are thinking of buying this game. Don't do it and buy Tropico 4 instead.

Limbo is a puzzle platformer game where you play as a boy in a black and white environment. There is almost no story given in this game (although there are some clues for it) so you have to intepret it yourself. There are 39 set of puzzles which are separated into chapters.
Limbo is using black and white (and grey) graphics, with its eerie atmosphere in it. Despite of its black and white graphics, the graphic is very beautiful.
Limbo is using subtle and quiet bgm, which brought up the "Limbo" atmosphere. If you think that the bgm is very quiet, the sfxs are loud and clear enough to cover the bgm.
As i said before, there are 39 set of puzzles which are separated into chapters. Some puzzles are easy, and some are very hard. Whether it's easy or not, you'll need to do trial and error to get it right. You'll die if you fail though. Luckily, there are unlimited lives so you can try as many as you want.
Some puzzles, however, requires timing and doesn't allow any mistake. One wrong move and you're dead. The controls are also sticky and hard to control. You can't move your character when you are jumping, and your character will remember the key that you have inputted when you are trying to go down a rope (or should i said it a chain?). There is a chapter where you have to go down from a chain into a moving box which got me in a trouble because it still remembers the "down" key that i inputted when i was trying to get off of the chain although i have already moved to the box. You will also double jump when you are in the edge of a cliff and are trying to climb up if you still hold your "up" key after the character goes up. However, the control will be no problem once you get used to it.
Despite of the sticky controls, the puzzles are very interesting. However, you might get bored with it after several replays because you have remembered the mechanics. The game will also take a long time to finish, especially when you have no idea what to do and insist on not watching a guide.
Pros:
- 39 set of puzzles
Cons:
- Sticky controls

This game is part tactical RPG and part Business sim and the dynamics between the two is what makes the gameplay so interesting.
On a tactical level, you have a large variety of options to take in battle. Basic attacks, Team attacks (with 1-4 other team members) single or double moves, teamwork stances and acrobatic vaulting and 5 different classes each with their customizable special abilities. Multiply that 5 and you'll be doing a lot of strategic thinking each round of combat.
There is an actual strategically meaningful decision to be made between performing actions that are tactically sound and actions that make for good television. Because this game is not *actually* a set of heroes saving the world, but rather about a television show about heroes saving the world, your 'audiance meter' is of serious consideration. Often times the director's instructions (which, if completed, greatly helps your audiance meter) run counter to what one might do otherwise if thinking in a pure strategic manner. Striking a balance between the two is the key to maximizing ratings for an episode while still winning a fight.
The higher your ratings the more money you get. Money plus material drops allow you to upgrade your studio and further customize your 5 actors. Add to all of that a very awesome, and branching, story and you have a game that is WELL worth the cost of admission. The only thing that would make it 100% perfect would be to make an episode editor allowing players to easily create their own episodes and share them on the workshop. Regardless, this is an indie game that is worth your time and money.

Go-go SUPER LUCK SQUAD!
I'm reviewing this game purely on the gameplay aspect. There are plenty of positive reviews regarding story and sentai fanservice.
This is based on playing the highest difficulty:
This game is a decent turn-based game in it's own right. There isn't much strategy to it. A bit of planning is involved to complete the director's instructions, but in the end it all comes down to luck. The most important thing to making equipment, materials, all based on luck.
I have one save file where a certain material I obtain in abundance, and really dont need it as it's mostly for the starter equipment, and another save file where the only material I've been obtaining is the make the same pair of gloves. If you dont keep your equipment up to snuff, your rangers are as good as dead or too weak to complete director's instructions as the episodes difficulty increase.
_____
Now for the actual gameplay. Here is wear luck becomes absolutely infuriating. Let me give some examples:
Now, remember, you control a squad of 5 rangers.
The director wants you to kill all of a certain enemy within, say, 3 turns. There are about 10 enemies on the field, and you need to focus on 3 specific ones. Those specific ones need to all be dead in 3 turns. Sounds simple enough, plan out how you'll position your rangers to catch them and take them out.
Now, let's get to the problem:
- Most of the squishy enemies, unless you luckily score a critical, can't be killed by a single ranger. This means it will take two of your rangers attacking to guarantee that kill. After a ranger attacks, they're done for that turn. This means it should be no problem for you to kill 3 of the weak enemies within 3 turns. Let's not get into details about some rangers having to use up their turn just to move around and get close to these enemies. We'll just presume you'll probably be spread thin and only have a kill average of 1 enemy per turn.... wait, change that from 'kill' to 'chance to kill'. You have a 'chance' to kill 1 enemy per turn. So if you happen to miss this chance, you can kiss that director's instruction goodbye, and restart the episode. Let's type how this will play out if you're unlucky:
First turn: you manage to kill an enemy.
Second turn: you manage to kill another enemy.
Third turn, your last turn to complete the instructions, and you're only one kill away: you order your rangers to attack and... the enemy dodges. Well, you're screwed. Time to abort episode and try again.
This is how many of your games will play out. This may not be too bad when it's just the start of an episode. However, there are times when an episode has 3 parts and you can spend an hour of your time going through the episode, completing all director's instructions only to have some unlucky crap happen at the very end and have to restart from the very beginning.
That's a lot of time to be wasting over something that's completely out of your control, luck.
I'll give you one of my recent episodes as an example, there are three parts. The first two parts are simple enough, the third part involves a boss that can heal itself and many enemies around that heal. You have to kill the boss within 10 turns and finish it with a finishing move. A finishing move requires all your rangers to be next to the boss and attack together(use Teamwork).
Technically, you have to kill the boss within 9/10 turns, since he will stun your rangers(making you unable to use the finishing move on the 10th turn, as it requires all of your rangers) on specific turns... one of those specific turns being the 10th one. Now, that seems like a pretty decent time to take out the boss. That is, if you're lucky. Let's play this out:
(We'll skip the small details and say you manage to get rid of the healing minions within 3 turns. You now have 6 turns left to take out the boss, who will also heal himself for pretty hefty amount. If you're lucky, he wont heal too often. If you're unlucky, he might heal twice in a row, making all your damage done to him in a turn, null. You still should have no problems as long as you manage to keep hitting him every turn and wittle him down. Given you have proper planning, you'll be just fine!)
Turn 1/6: You manage to quadruple the boss, and dealing enough damage that will allow you to outdps his heal.
Turn 2/6: You deal enough to outdps his heal again.
Turn 3/6: He dodges, completely wasting a turn, and heals himself. That's okay, you see that you still have a chance to take him out in time.
Turn 4/6: He dodges again... okay, it might  be close, but just maybe you can make it.
Turn 5/6: He dodges again, and heals. He's now at full health again, it's game over. Time to abort and do the whole episode again, taking up another hour of your time.
_______
Let me give you one last situation. In this one, YOUR luck can be your downfall in completing instructions. Let's say you need to kill 4 enemies in a single turn. Well, remember how it can take two rangers just to kill one enemy? You have 5 rangers, it takes 2 to kill one. Simple math, you can't kill 4 in a single turn. Unless... you plan ahead and simply soften them up to kill at once later. You're so clever. A tactical genius in the making. This shouldn't be a problem, you've got the plan and the means to execute it! What could go wrong?
None of the enemies dodge, you manage to soften up 4 of them enough to where any single ranger can finish them off in your next turn. There's absolutely nothing that could go wrong. Unless... <.<
It's the enemy's turn: The weakened enemy attacks your ranger, it's super effective! At least super effective against the enemy, because your ranger decides that of all times he's going to choose this time to do a counter-attack. The softened up enemy dies. Now you only have three softened up enemies, maybe you still have a chance. You'll have 3 rangers kill the 3 softened ones, and your other 2 rangers can double attack some other enemy. Unless... <.<
It's still the enemy's turn: Another of the weakened enemies attacks another ranger. You couldn't possibly be so lucky you counter attack again, could you? I dont think I need to say where this is going. You know you're screwed, abort episode and try again.
The game could also stand to give some actual info on the stat points. There seems to be no info on the usefulness or effective amounts for Cooldown Cost and Skill Regen. There are other stats as well that have no explanation in the game, and you just have to guess and hope they're worth investing into.
If they cut out all of the luck crap, it would be an entertaining turn-based game that actually rewarded you for proper planning. Instead, it's always a roll of the dice.
I dont know how many hours Steam will say I've played this game, but my first save file is 11 hours. My second save file says 3 hours. So any beyond that was just wasted time from having to abort episodes.

I'll keep this short. First of all, if you're looking for gameplay, Chroma Squad has a semi-decent system going for it. In fact, it's quite fun. Not overtly complex, but it gets the game moving. Figths have some interesting mechanics to them, and you generally won't find yourself being bored. Gameplay wise, it's fine. A Seven out of ten, generally.
The reason I'm giving this game a negative review however, are these two.
First of all - and, I suppose, the less important one. The writing. It attempts to be this cheesy script played for laughs, but all it does is give you cringeworthy references that batffle you at just how badly they are handled. The kickstarter backer appearances are laughable and ham fisted. I'd actually feel embarassed for backing this and being put on it as it was.
It says it's an affectionate parody/homage to Sentai, but it instead feels like it's trying too hard.
Now, you might say that you don't give a crap about the writing and that's fine. It's a videogame. So what's my second complaint?
How awfully BUGGY the game is, and in the worst ways imaginable. It has a tendency to constantly shut down, crash ,or simply not do anything after a certain sequence of events happened. I've gritten my teeth and bore it for most of the game, but the last straw was, infact, at the very last mission of the game, composed of two long boss fights - the last one being especially long, lasting possibly hours. The game proceeded to crash on the first one, making me lose all progress. It then crashed again at the end of the second one, meaning it put three hours of gameplay to waste, as the game did not foresee it crashing, for whatever reason. That managed to make me give up on the game and not want to finish it. The fact that the bug report icon is ALWAYS there on the top right corner should actually tell you just how unstable this game is.
It's a fun game. It's an embarassing piece of writing, and an awfully coded mess that's unreliable at the worst moments.
UPDATE
After replaying the game post-patch, performance has indeed increased. I've encountered so far only minor visual bugs that did not break the game nor make it crash, so one can assume the stability of the game is indeed being improved. Previous complaints still apply, and the game still has a couple visual glitches, aswell as issues with the achievement unlock system, but right now, it's properly playable. With that done, I shift my opinion to a careful recommendation - if you're a fan of Sentai, you can probably buy it. If not, but you're really curious, wait for a sale.

Two brothers Bwana, and Kito are approached one day by a woman, Lina, from the University. the game itself is (as the title card says) a Shoot out to the classic Power Rangers series. You take over the role of 5 spandex wearing Super Sentai Actors who grew tired of their old director and start their own studio.
They use Blue Rangers Uncles warehouse to shoot their first episodes and find a prop from a huge Super Hero thing - which their old director finds out himself... From there on he starts plotting and you start raking in fans, money and cardboard to make awesome costumes.
First of all - the Episode stories are HILARIOUSLY terrible! But then, looking back to when Power Rangers was a thing in my life... WHo cared about story? I dont want to see those 5 people at school! I want to see them beat up those evil ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s! Come on, make an entrance and beat the crap out of those Baddies! And thats what those episodes are about
"F**k Story, lets kick some♥♥♥♥♥"
the fighting feels like its fitting into a SUper Sentai series, with acrobatic jumps, multi hit combos and dreadfully colorful Team Attacks, and at times, I feel less like a twenty-something years old dude playing a strategy game, and more like the 6 year old kid, watching those spandexed Actors beating the crap out of other spandexed actors, Striking poses myself and being the Blue Ranger in Kindergarten.
But I have to do some critic here as well. As first - the tutorial covers the basics. and only the basics. It covers moving, acrobatics, Team attacks with basic attacks. But thats it. Okay - other things can be found out within play, like that you can start a Team Attack with a Weapon Attack, instead of a basic attack and that the Weapon musnt be on Cooldown as well.
Secondly - Weapons. Your main weapons are your - gloves. You can buy and craft swords and Guns but they never seemed to use them in battle. just... punching the enemy. Until I found out that those weapons are Active Abilities, with Cooldowns and all.
The Amount of customisation is overwhelming in the beginning, and sometimes you may end up not knowing what to pick. But you'll come to understand.
However, overall the game is awesome, and if you are a fan of old Super Sentai Series and in need of a little nostalgia fix, get this game!
Random Fun Fact : When Haim Saban first bought the US rights for the Power Rangers Series, he only reshot the "Everyday Life" scenes with US actors and took the Fightng scenes from the japanese original series and re-dubbed them. A pretty intelligent move.

Do you enjoy a Jamaican accent (Cool Runnings Mon!)? Does a bluesy, rastafarian, carribean influenced world combined with Grim Fandango aesthetics sound entertaining? Then The Journey Down may just be for you!
The Journey Down is quite charming. The characters have silly, fun, eccentric personalities that makes them all feel unique.
This is in the style of a classic point and click and puzzles range from easy to medium - I wouldn't describe any of the puzzles in this game as difficult (of course this is all subjective).
The areas are quite small and there's only about 3-4 main screens you need to regularly travel between so the movement between areas is relatively quick. I only mention this because some point and clicks are plagued by slow pacing due to slow movement/large areas - but The Journey Down is not haunted by this. Very big plus here.
You can pick up this little gem for under 2 bucks - there's also a bundle where you can pick up chapters 1 + 2 for 5.99 on sale. That's more than a deal - that's a steal!
Overall, if you are looking for a charming point and click with some fairly casual puzzles (nothing too difficult) then I HIGHLY recommend The Journey Down!
The Journey Down takes about 2-3 hours to complete.

A cross between Super Mario 64 and Club Penguin (pre Disney), The Beginner's Guide first introduces us to the developer named only as 'Coda'. It shows his first piece of game development, a Counter Strike map with a
uniquely abstract view.
The game progresses with more examples of his work, only each game in turn shows a darker more troubling issue. I will attempt to give my analysis on the true message being conveyed:
---------------
The understanding of von Neumann machines is a theoretical obstacle. For example, many applications prevent embedded technology. Further, we emphasize that our algorithm is Turing complete, without visualizing information retrieval systems. Contrarily, write-ahead logging alone might fulfil the need for von Neumann machines.
In this work we examine how public-private key pairs can be applied to the construction of massive multiplayer online role-playing games. Our approach requests simulated annealing. Unfortunately, classical information might not be the panacea that end-users expected. Along these same lines, we emphasize that our algorithm creates the transistor. Though similar systems construct the simulation of information retrieval systems, we surmount this challenge without architecting courseware.
We question the need for compact symmetries. Although conventional wisdom states that this problem is often solved by the synthesis of virtual machines, we believe that a different solution is necessary. Though conventional wisdom states that this grand challenge is usually fixed by the improvement of the Ethernet, we believe that a different solution is necessary. The basic tenet of this method is the construction of systems. In addition, the basic tenet of this solution is the emulation of randomized algorithms. Therefore, our system can be improved to request Boolean logic.
The contributions of this work are as follows. Primarily, we consider how evolutionary programming can be applied to the deployment of object-oriented languages. Second, we use introspective configurations to disprove that reinforcement learning and the Internet can connect to accomplish this intent. We propose an analysis of semaphores (FumyPykar), which we use to verify that the much-touted omniscient algorithm for the investigation of rasterization by Miller and Thomas is Turing complete.
The rest of this paper is organized as follows. We motivate the need for gigabit switches. We prove the synthesis of robots. In the end, we conclude.
tl;dr - This analysis is as meaningless and pretentious as this game
---------------
All in all, this game is much like modern art, it's beautiful when you believe that you have taken something unique away from it, but really it is simply another piece of pretentious garbage that will be forgotten.

This game is absolutely amazing.
You've probably seen the trailer, so you know how the basic mechanics are. Taking over enemy ships and using them might  seem like a simple thing, but each one has a different amount of HP, ammo, speed, damage and bullet type, you can't keep a single ship for a long time because you'll eventually run out of ammo, and the constant bulletstorm will have you on your toes positioning your current ship on the field, thinking which will be your next move.
Your "switching beam" has a limited range and you can't spam it, some ships have limited mobility, some won't move at all, some can't turn left and some might even self-destruct, it's a unique and satisfying challenge, might be difficulty but it's not unfair at all.
On top of that the way it tells the story was very interesting, the game gives you only minimalistic details and provides glaces at the memories of the ships you've taken over, but different factions have different sights of what happened during the conflict and different ways of speaking (since they're different species).
In any case, I'd recommend this game for both it's gameplay and story. The price it's a little high for it's length, but I believe the quality greatily compensates for it.

The good!
- Solid atmosphere, good audio cues (if not a bit too good at telling you exactly what's coming), and generally good at being creepy.
- Nice variety of enemies and events, and seemingly pretty solid randomization and AI. Not perfect, especially with regard to item pickups, but we'll touch on that in a bit.
The bad.
- Items are totally randomized, but each item is necessary to counter a specific threat that can also appear randomly with little notice. It's near impossible to spot what an item is from a distance, so this means you'll spend a lot of time running between them and praying you maintain at least 1 of each lest you face certain death.
- "Running between them" is a bit of a lie, because your intrepid survalist is actually an 800 lbs man that hasn't left his power scooter in decades and has a bum leg. He's capable of sprinting for about 5 seconds. Total, in the game. It recharges so slowly as to be almost irrelevent, unless you like standing around in safe zones for several minutes doing nothing on a regular basis. This is also a problem because one enemy type can only be countered by kiting them with short sprints, meaning all of your precious stamina has to be saved in the event they spawn on you. So, mostly, think Dear Esther in the dark with spoopy noises. And bear traps, because bear traps.
- There's really no indicator of where to go initially. I get that it may be intentional, but you really have no indication that there's *anywhere* to go apart from an also-randomly-spawning npc that directs you. He seems to be pretty generous with his appearances, but I did have a couple attempts where I was already battered and bruised before he showed and gave me any indication of what to do.
THE VERDICT
I'm super on the fence about this one. There's great potential, but in it's current state it plays more like an RNG rage game in the guise of a horror game than an actual survival horror. Maybe I'm just missing something since I was playing pretty quickly on stream. My opinion would flip quickly with a bit of balancing work on the random elements.

Devil in the Pines is a great little survival horror game by the fledgling studio Rebelware Games. I was a bit apprehensive going into this thing, seeing how disappointing
was. How disappointing exactly? Several times I was seriously considering going back to that review and changing it to negative, something I've never done before IIRC. Not this time either but yeah, that's pretty bad. Thankfully, the last part of the Braveland trilogy offers a delightful, upward bounce in quality, matching the first
and probably exceeding it.
The grind was put in a "sweet spot" of sorts, where it still exists but isn't as excruciating as it was in Wizard. The English is vastly improved, at least in terms of grammar and spelling; the style is still awkward at times. Itemization and item stats are significantly more meaningful in this one, as items can now yield benefits of ex. 10-30% instead of 1-5%. The talent tree is also designed better than the previous one. The new units are interesting and come with well thought-out abilities. The story actually tries to have nice twists. I mean... it fails, but at least it tries. Perhaps most importantly, the world is far less linear now! There are whole islands that are optional. There are also random encounters (of sorts).
Improvements all-around. The pirate theme is charming but the music gets tiresome fast. The achievement design requires about... one and two thirds of a playthrough to get everything. Which is unfortunate, but acceptable. Definitely a thumbs up, no hesitation here.

Relaxing little puzzle game in which you deliver letters to various denizens of the dream-forest. I think...
PROS:
+ Interesting Visuals. I liked the landscapes I encountered, they were well done. The art is rather unique.
+ Calming Music. It's not upbeat, not catchy, not noisy or fast. It fits the game perfectly.
+ Simple Puzzles. I played this because I felt like some easy gaming. This fits the bill perfectly. The only puzzle I had trouble with was the one where you just have to keep moving, even if it seems like you can't. If you play the game, you'll find out what I mean.
CONS:
- Visuals made possible paths nigh invisible on several occasions. I would think I was stuck, then randomly zoom my mouse around the screen a couple of times and discover a new path to travel down.
- The premise and story are pretty weak. I'm not really sure who I am, except that I deliver mail. And I'm not sure where I am, except that I apparently deliver dream-mail?
- One puzzle had a poor solution, it could have been done better.
- Once you deliver the final piece of mail, the game is over. Unfortunately, since I missed an achievement on my first playthrough, that meant I had to start over from the beginning to get that one achievement. A bit annoying.
CONCLUSION:
Easy gaming. That's all this is. Nothing is difficult, just do everything you can. The puzzles are pretty simple. The music and visuals are relaxing. If you don't want anything demanding, go for it. Don't expect a particularly fulfilling experience, but I did enjoy what there was of it.
FINAL RATING: 5/7

I'm sorry to say that I wasn't a fan, and I wanted to post some of my issues to other prospective buyers. I'd like to clarify that I'm a big fan of both management/sim games, SRPGs and Sentai, so I fall right into the game's key demographic.
The game is spoiled by poor writing throughout the gameplay experience - I understand the developers are working against a language barrier, but this means that much of the dialogue has no flow or substance. Tonally, the dialogue never seems whether to indulge in the action fantasy of sentai, or provide a narrative about the stunt crew pursuing their own career. The result is that the characters are constantly breaking the fourth wall which is not only tiresome, but spoils the atmosphere the game's (very good) graphics are depicting.
The game has been designed without level ups: where this might seem beneficial to some, they've replaced this tried and tested mechanism with a bolted-on crafting system. You become dependent on crafting gear from items dropped by enemies - worse, you have to hope that the 'random bonus' is actually worth having. The removal of level ups takes away a sense of stable progression, and replaces it with gear-dependence, which, for me, sucks the fun out of the game.
The management aspect is not developed or interesting enough as a worthwhile distraction, and the two gameplay modes (simulation/SRPG) don't mesh with each other in a satisfactory way. The lack of depth in the simulation and the lack of levelling are disempowering - you're never sure where you sit on the game's difficulty curve, and ultimately your successes do not feel like they've originated from any choices you've made. This is poisonous for any game, but Chroma Squad simply fails to provide any grit, depth or detail beyond what is an impressive exterior.
TL;DR: It looks great on the surface, but goes to pieces once you get past the unique premises, references, and graphics.

Cuphead, I my opinion, is not really like that. Don’t get me wrong it is paced well and I felt that the game for the first two thirds was teaching me its core mechanics and making me understand them to use in each boss fight/level. Yet when coming to the end of the second area and beginning the third, I did not feel competent at all in the later levels and that rush you get from completing them didn’t come for me and fun was sapped away. Finishing levels felt more like a relief then a triumphant victory. It felt more like pattern memorisation then my actual skill with the game coming through when I beat the later bosses/levels.
The difficulty in this game is very different compared to other games and reminds me of games such as Battletoads. Is the game as hard as Battletoads? Definitely not and I do feel like I could complete the game with a matter of time. But I just found myself getting angrier every time a new challenge presented itself rather than getting excited about it.
In conclusion the game is great for those people who like this type of challenge but unfortunately it isn’t for me.

The Park is such an incredibly hard game to review. I really, really enjoyed many parts of it, but the price cannot be justified, and it's definitely weak in several areas.
What I didn't know going in, was that this game is made by the creators of The Secret World, an MMO I have heard about but never played, and ties into lore in that game. Knowledge of that game is not necessary for understanding the story of this game, and stands perfectly as a standalone title, but there is apparently extra story regarding the locations here found only in TSW.
Now, The Park nails atmosphere, it nails it hard. Small noises, flickering lights, all kinds of things make Atlantic Island Park feel incredibly haunting. The lighting and very nice graphics contribute greatly to the eeriness and mystery present here. It can be downright chilling at times.
What follows this unfortunately,
This game suffers from what I feel Among the Sleep is affected by as well. Atmosphere is built so well and so tensely, but then there are rarely moments when it pays off. One of the best and most well built up moments happens early on,
After that however, the game tries to use a few awkwardly placed jumpscares to scare you. Initially I thought each ride would have some spooky thing occuring, but in one of the most obvious places there was nothing, and it felt awkward after what had happened before.
In the final act of the game, however, it takes a really nice turn and paces itself well, becomes incredibly unnerving and very well done. The game then ends, however, with an interesting story conclusion, but all the buildup in the final section led to a section of suprising anticlimacticy, with the story then ending. The whole ending section feels like it takes great inspirations from another horror phenomenon,
, and it is honestly incredibly scary, but unrewarding in the end.
Speaking of which, the story is engaging and interesting, basically, the classic "Your son ran off into the Park and you need to find him", and while it starts seeming pretty predictable, it throws some twists in to allow it to break from the form generally taken by this style of storytelling, and it still leaves enough open to keep you questioning after the game ends. What's really odd though, is that your story has seemingly NOTHING to do with the story of Atlantic Island Park. There's interesting backstory to the park and some things you encounter, but the game could have been done in a completely different place, and the story would really have remained unchanged for the most part. There is lots more to be found about the Park itself in TSW I heard though, so really it only serves as a bridge to TSW.
There are definitely a few moments in this game where it tried to scare me but was hilariously poor, because the game thinks crazy, supernatural action can substitute actual fear, where there is danger to your character, and merely serves as objects coming at you fast. (Worth noting that the game is entirely an experience, and there is no fail state of any kind) Moments like these feel pointless and serve no greater purpose in the storytelling experience (save one).
But easily, the most unfortunate thing about The Park, is that it's unbelieveable short. My playtime is not trustworthy because I left it running through the night in order to get my card drops, because I didn't even hit two hours on it. I even had spent some time AFK and a bit of time alt-tabbing, so my real playtime drops to ~1.5 hours, probably a little less actually, considering I restarted a few times after beating to figure out how to get the final achievement. This runtime is appaling for a thirteen dollar game. You could buy a ticket to see a two and a half hour horror film at a cheaper price. I'm sure the price justifies the effort put in, but what is given is miniscule. There is almost no replay value (unlike a game like $10 Slender the Arrival, where if you really enjoy it tons of other difficulties, modes, secrets, and more extend the time beyond a single playthrough) I picked it up at a discounted price of $8.70, and I still feel ripped off despite my enjoyment.
Again, this is a good game, but $13 is no price to pay for this game. Look for a steep discount before buying this, but there is still enjoyment to be had in the short time you spend with it.
Definitely worth looking into if you're a big fan of psychological horror, and less interactive, more storytelling focused games, just watch the price, and know it's weaknesses.

I think the complexities of social living in the modern world lead me to find great peace in the simplicity of this game.  You are stranded in the wilderness and are only concerned with survival.  You must find shelter, keep warm, gather food, purify water, avoid hostile wildlife.  There are many ways to do these things, and many challenges that arise organically within the world.  A routine trip through familiar territory can turn deadly if a blizzard strikes, freezing you and closing in your visibility, testing how well you really know the landscape.  You can catch a disease that takes weeks to cure as you struggle to maintain your normal routines with a dramatically weakened body.  A surprise encounter with a bear can leave you critically wounded and desperate while damaging the warm clothing you've come to take for granted.  But all of these obstacles can be overcome, and if feels triumphant to do so.  So often the simple beauty of the game's environment makes you stop and just admire.
The upcoming story mode promises to add a whole new dimension to this game, but I can strongly recommend it even without that promise.

Evolve is a 4v1 competitive first-person cooperative shooter by Turtle Rock Studios (creators of Left 4 Dead).  The game offers challenging levels of competitive gameplay pitting 4 hunters against 1 monster in a hostile environment.  The hunters have four classes: trapper, support, medic, and assault.  There are currently 3 monsters in the game: goliath, kracken, and wraith with a forth monster (bohemoth) to be released soon. Monsters are designed similar to classes with melee, caster, and tank like abilities. Those that deal more damage have less health.  The classes of monsters and combination of hunter classes play out as being well balanced so long as groups work together.  But teamwork and communication become vital to continued success.
The game is built on the 4th generation of the CryEngine and looks great.  This is one of the best looking games this year.  The game plays very smooth but I have noticed some tearing in cut scenes and frame drops on some maps with max settings.
Games can end quickly or not depending on the skill level of the players.  Each class has a purpose and should be played to that purpose to win.  The environment alone can kill you if you venture off on your own.  This game stresses teamwork by design.  The community so far has been good although with a competitive game like this you can expect some less than mature behavior at times.
The game has received a lot of negative reviews concerning the DLC market.  The DLC in my honest opinion should have little to do with the rating of this game due to not only the design of the game but the DLC model.  The game has been designed to allow DLC content to not prohibit gamers from playing any game mode or maps.  The DLC offered will eventually add new personalities and monsters to the game but is not required to play with or against people with the DLC.  The majority of DLC consists of skins for monsters and hunters alike with a small amount being playable characters that will mix abilities of a class with a new look and personality.
Unlike many other AAA titles, Evolve does not restrict your ability to play the game with the exception of the characters not being playable without purchasing the DLC.  The alternative would be to add map packs and game modes that would cut the player base down to those that have the DLC and those that do not rather than the current DLC model that gives maps and modes to the community for free and charges for nonessential content.  It would have been nice to have had some skins rewarded for unlocks but that isn't the case, at least at this time.
The developers have put a lot of time balancing this game and it shows.  This game is a lot of fun and if you are a fan of cooperative games like Left 4 Dead, this may be right up your alley.  I have linked an older video from Alpha of my first impressions, not much has changed.  You can follow my link to my Steam page or my YouTube page for current gameplay if you like.

Once and for all: I know that many do not agree with the business practices of Turtle Rock and 2K. In particular, the preorder monster and the skins you can and will find in the ingame shop. I do also think it grossly exaggerated. A skin for € 2.99 ?? Never ever! This is almost a kebab (without health risks)!
For those who do not know, Evolve is "cops and robbers" with monster and space soldiers. You play a predefined group of mercenaries or the monster. You must complete various missions per round. That monster can, by feeding, "evolve" up to three evolutionary stages and acquire new skills. The mercenary can be revived up to two times. No, they do not evolve...but every faction gains new skills by completing skill challenges.
So is "Evolve" any fun? Yes! But the only question is, "How long?"
After a few rounds you have seen it all. But this is it for every multiplayer game out there. Which is not an apology. I think the variation lies within the players and the vast enviroment. For me thats enough...for €40 - 60€. Why?
There are groups that act tactically. They are using the enviroment, plan ahead and lure the Monster into a trap. Then there are groups which are rushing toward against. Some groups split up and others stubbornly pursue the mission objective, that is defined in each round, so they achieve a victory this way. You will forget that there are just a handful of maps to explore. You really do not notice.
And the environment is harmonious and just beautiful. Every detail has been placed with love. Kudos to the level designers! A moody and mostly believable game world. I guess thats the true content of Evolve. This is sometimes better than 30 sloppy maps.
In summary, I can only say that I previously had fun with Evolve. It plays well, offers interesting possibilities in terms of tactical diversity and movement. It's polished, despite a few bugs. The characters are not quite as loveable as the Left4Dead protagonists. I'm curious what Turtle Rock does next with Evolve. I hope the skins are getting cheaper...come on guys! You don't need that much money.
As for the REAL long-term motivation, I can't say anything yet. Maybe the few maps and missions ARE the problem? Or  it gets boring after you've unlocked every single♥♥♥♥♥♥ Perhaps it turns out that the the balancing is aweful after more and more players reach the higher levels? Nobody knows.
Buy it if you have friends to play with or if you are like that kid from the "ready or not trailer" who plays the monster.

NOTE: This is the same review for the other two games in the original Deponia trillogy aswell. I thought that as they are a continuation of the same story that they should stay together.
The
trillogy is a classic point and click game on a wold filled with garbage. In the trillogy, you assist the, at first forgettable/dislikeable, protagonist Rufus try to reach the floating paradise of Elysium. Over time, the originally forgettable Rufus uses his witty dialog to slowly get you on his side rooting for him on his quest.
+Amazing story
The story, although only really played out during cut scenes to new areas, is deep in detail. It pulls you in, really pulling you into the world.
+Funny
Not many games have blaitently funny dialog, but these games definatly do. Rufus has funny responses to other characters, his own acvtions, and stuff you try to have him do.
+Characters
All the characters seem fleshed out quite well. Each has a uniques personallity, displayes different emotions, and just act different. The variety is also pretty good.
+Enviroments
Most enviroments are well detailed with other people and objects to bring the scene alive. In some cases, youll get people who are from other games showing up in the envirments aswell.
+Music
The music worked well with each area you would be exploring. Although mostly being simmilar themed, it all was different and interesting.
-Animations/Movement
The walking animation on Rufus, for me was a bit weird. He didnt really face where he was going and took odd paths to where he needed to go.
-Duration
Some areas seemed too short, while others were too long. It was an odd thing and may have just been the way I solved the puzzles in each area, but it struck me as odd how I could clear one area in ~30 min and another in 2+ hours.
The
trillogy is an amazing set of games that brought back tthe nastolga of point and the point and click style. The quirky dialog was fun to hear and laugh at resonces. The story makes the narcissistic Rufus someone whos actions have you rooting
for the duration of his adventure. If you have some time free I can highly reccomend all the games in the
trillogy and
.
