The people at Red Barrels are pretty smart developers. Because if, to all apperances, Outlast takes most of its ideas from Amnesia: The Dark Descent (or the Penumbra trilogy) in terms of gameplay ideas, it puts it in a far less elegant environment and lets that dictates the flow of the game. Forget the gracious verbal jousting of Alexander and Daniel and the self-conversation, because your new nickname is now going to be "little pig" for almost eight hours - nickname given by a seven foot tall, disfigured killing machine, that rips people heads off with its bare (bear) hands. That is the ambiance here. Extremely stereotypical creepos in lieu and place of normal human beings with mental illness inhabit the biggest asylum you've ever seen, complete with a prison section, a church, sewers and all that with the flimsiest electrical instalation conceivable. The first steps in Outlast are made to freak you out with a pretty violent imagery, dismantled bodies, blood all over the place and all rendered in a surprisingly gorgeous engine for a team that small. You, a journalist that clearly as suicidal tendencies, simply follow the remarkably well paced and extremely linear story to uncover what went wrong.
So the gameplay is pretty much Amnesia. Except you are not finding tinderboxes to light up the place or oil to replenish your lantern; you are only searching for batteries to fill up your video-camera that happens to have a night-vision mode. Because the protagonist is filming all this. Despite the brutality of what he sees and suffers, he keeps on filming. You have the choice to play the game without looking in the camera, but the zoom-in and out and NV are your saving graces here to navigate the dark hallways. It also is your only advantage over the enemies in the game, that consists in the same kind of lethal stalkers that Amnesia had. You can't bit them, except for scripted events that the game will explicitely show you. So your only chance at surviving is finding the next door or crouching in the darkest place possible. Which is, again like Amnesia, a great way to create tension, forcing the player to either listen to the psychopathic a**hole in complete darkness, or looking where he is through the lens of the camera, wasting precious batery that could help finding the next place.
The story is delivered through environmental clues as much as the classic notes from RE. But contrary to Amnesia or RE, Outlast has some NPCs that can give short but efficient exposition.
And overall, I think that "efficient" is the best term to describe Outlast. It isn't a ground breaking game in terms of mechanics, that pretty much consists in light exploration, navigation, and light stealth. It isn't ground breaking in terms of art direction. It isn't amazing in terms of story either. But each elements is really well done, and well done enough that it creates tension from beginning to end. You are not going to be surprised by a second playthrough, since due to the linearity of the game you will see 95% of it in one run. But you will have some fun spooky moments. Not the lingering uneasiness of a Silent Hill, but a cathartic stream of build-up and pay-off, jumscares and stressful shunks of gameplay. It is pretty light in terms of mechanics but never to its disadvantage. Simply put, it is a fun horror game.
TR;DL
Proof that linearity and scripted gameplay aren't doomed to be associated with sh*tty triple A yearly releases, Outlast is the best example of a good (if not great with its excellent "Whistleblower" DLC) spook-house. The atmosphere is really neatly built thanks to an efficient art direction that aims somewhere between realism for the technical aspect and its decorum and over-the-top representation of insane people for the occupants. Enemy Mind is a nifty creative twist on the side-scrolling shooter genre. Instead of controlling your own ship, you play as a psychic entity that can commandeer an enemy ship at will. Just press the button and you can swap into a different ship. It's a simple enough premise, and the game executes on it pretty well--well enough that it feels like a key piece of the gameplay rather than a gimmick.
Each ship has limited ammo, see, so you're forced to jump from ship to ship in order to keep fighting. Levels are designed to nudge you toward playing a wide variety of ships--when you run out of ammo, you won't always be able to hop right into a new copy of the same ship. And the boss fights of each level are built around the mechanic--for example, you might have to jump around a circle of stationary turrets to reach the boss's rotating weak point.
The story is interesting. It's not you against Bad Guy Aliens. You're dropped into the middle of a war between aliens and humans. (You'll get a different ending depending on which side's ships you use more frequently.) The two factions are, visually, very distinct, and when they're onscreen together they'll actually fight each other. Furthermore, both sides quickly become aware of your presence, and you get to hear them reacting to how you're taking over their minds, which is pretty cool.
So I like what they did, generally. That being said, there are some flaws. For one, it would be nice to have more variety in the ships. There are a decent amount to choose from, but a lot of them are just variations on "shoot forward in a straight line." Oh, and another thing, it's always forward. You can't turn around. This is definitely problematic, because the enemies CAN turn around, and they WILL come at you from both sides, and you'll just be, like, well, I can't turn around and shoot the guys behind me, so...bleh. Also, you supposedly have a limited numer of extra lives, but in practice, you get unlimited continues, and continuing puts you at the exact same place as respawning, so...what's the point of having lives, exactly?
In any case, it's a short game--I'm not very good at shooters and I beat it in 3 hours--so it doesn't wear out its welcome. You don't need to invest much time to enjoy this game. I don't know if it's worth $10, but if you have it in your backlog from some bundle or other, I definitely recommend giving it a look, just because it's interesting and it does something new and unique. It's short, it's sweet, and while it's not the best shooter you've ever played, you've probably never played another shooter like it.
P.S. Make sure to check out the Rock Simulator in the Extras section. It is glorious.

It can be that challenging in spots, but unlike the classic shoot'em up arcade games, if you learn to master it, you can recover from near death over and over by jacking ships. Or, in some cases, asteroids. While my initial playthrough is short (4.1 hours), there's enough here to make me want to try it again, both mastering the stranger ships' playstyles as well as figuring out the story.
With all that available to keep the game interesting, it should be mentioned the art style, animations, and soundtrack are all wonderful in themselves. The alien ships tend to have animations that make them immediately recognizable (if the looks weren't enough, that is) from the human ships, making them even more of a joy to jack, but that doesn't mean the human ships don't also have some creative and fun designs and animations to go with them. They very much do, which makes it a tough choice at times to decide between which faction to try to carry through the game with.
This is only compounded by the differing story perspectives they also each offer, as you get to see each side's perspective in this game in more depth than you ever would in past arcadey games like this. It's a little disorienting at first, but starts to come together towards the end, however I suspect replaying it and trying harder to stick with one side's story might illuminate foggier areas of the story, which makes the length great where it's at. Any longer, and it might feel too tedious to explore the other perspectives in-depth, but as it is? It's great, and I'd definitely recommend it, it's far more than you might expect from a $10 game!

Published by: Funcom
Developed by: Funcom
Genre: Adventure/Psychological Horror/Walking Simulator
Release Date: October 27, 2015
Time to complete: 1.5 hours
Delve deep into the mind of a troubled woman searching for her son in this creepy yet enticing horror experience.
This game is heavily centered around the fragility of the main character’s disturbed mind. As such, this game tackles some pretty heavy/unpleasant themes, and may cause emotional distress for some.
After her son Callum runs into ‘Atlantic Island Park’ after hours, Lorraine must venture her way through the chilling macabre amusement park to find him.
The heavily narrated ‘game’ is more aptly considered a story or an experience; there is no combat or action involved, and very few interactions available.
The Park has mastered psychological horror perfectly, not relying on cheap jump scares or excessive gore, yet still managing to scare the player witless. The dark and disturbing scenery adds to the unnerving atmosphere of the game, and makes it easy to become fully engrossed in the story and the character you are following.
Lorraine first appears as the average mother, speaking of her worries and struggles as a parent. Venturing further into the park, and further into Lorraine’s thoughts, you realise that she is far from average. As you follow Lorraine’s journey, you begin to question the validity on what she is experiencing. Her paranoia and obvious mental instability are further emphasised as the game progresses, most evident towards the end of the game, with clues about her past shown in cutscenes throughout.
There is a clever parallel to a children’s fairy tale evident in the game. Similarities are shown through Lorraine’s stories (if you really pay attention), and hints are present throughout.
As this is more of a walking simulator, there really isn’t much to the game in terms of difficulty/challenge/gameplay. Essentially all you are able to do is walk/run, and interact with a few objects (usually notes or similar). You are also able to ride the few attractions in the game.
Because the game is more of a short narrative, there is no real replay value to it, and it takes roughly 1-2 hours to complete the entire game.
The Voice acting in this game is tremendous. The most chilling and unsettling part about this game isn’t the jump scares, the gruesome scenes you read about in the notes or the creepy park mascot, Chad, seemingly stalking you throughout the game. It’s the perfectly illustrated story, the emotion behind every word told by Lorraine, portrayed by Fryda Wolff. You can feel the struggles Lorraine is experiencing, the dread in her voice as she recalls past events. What makes this game go from good to great, is Fryda’s portrayal of Lorraine.
The graphics are fairly standard. There’s nothing over the top spectacular in this department, but it is still a pleasant viewing experience.
The Park is an immersive psychological horror experience, definitely worth getting if you like the genre. The storyline is compelling, and it’s definitely a game that will stick with you.

Like Star Wars? Like Command & Conquer? Remember Rise of Nations? This is a lot like that, but not turn-based. In the galaxy map strategy part of the game, you have to build all of the units you're going to use in the ground and space battle parts of the game. Aside from that, you have hero units that can be deployed in battle or sent on special missions. Smugglers, for example, can be deployed to enemy systems to steal credits, or deployed in ground battles.
There's a lot of strategy and tactics involved. Certain simple tactics (baiting/kiting) will sometimes work and sometimes not, depending on how the AI feels right then. Like any good Total War game, you have the option of just allowing the computer to calculate the results of a battle instead of playing it out yourself. And as with any good Star Wars game, the music reacts to the battle conditions.
I give it a B+. When it was first released, I would have given it a C, but patches have improved the mechanics a lot.

Ok so lets debunk some things.
first, the game is good.  its well polished, and at least for me i have experience little to no issues (other then a bug with my mouse cursor and steam overlay)

id even say the balance is good, each class has its own hook that nobody else can replicate, while sharing a main feature.
i dont even mind the searching for the monster parts as humans.
and being a monster is most fun ive had in a while.
if i was to rate the game based soley on the merits of its gameplay id give it a easy 10/10.  but its not that simple
first is its lack of real content, for a game in development for 5 years, it has very little going on.  there is a reason they compare it to titanfall.  thats not to say whats there isnt good, and a certain type of person will not ever get really bored of it but rather dig deeper and find the nuances and depth of gameplay to craft truly memorable experiences.
subtract 1 point for lack of real content, 9/10 is still stellar! at least for what it is.
now the nitty gritty.
this dreaded DLC stuff everyones been talking about.
This is the issue, not so much the characters that havent been developed yet (they are just planned to be made), thats not a huge issue.
no its two things
charging such high prices
and charging for things that should just be included in the game
skins, lets talk about skins, everyone loves looking unique right? thats probably what the publishers thought when they forced turtle rock to put up 6 dollars packs of 3 skins.
thats right
6 bucks
3 skins
these skins have been available from day 1, this is true day 1 dlc
some of you may go "but it has no effect on gameplay", that my friend is hardly the point.
Youve already paid 60 dollars (or more) on a game with very little overall content for the money (not that the content thats there isnt good), but apparently your 60 bucks isnt good enough for 2k, no, they look at that 60 bucks and go...its a start.  hence you see massively jacked recolorations of th same skins (they are in fact the same skins, just different colors).
they COULD have included them in the main game, 60 bucks is more then most mulitplayer only games cost.
they COULD have them put behind unlocks/achievements so people can use those skins and go, look, i achieved something, i did this, im good at the game.
but no, recolorations, thats it, the easiest of customization.
Then you have the price on the new hunters/monsters.
7.5 PER hunter, 15 PER monster.
youve got to be freaking kidding me.
this is not borderlands where you can level up and customize your character to absurd degree.  this is a multiplayer game.  its like charging 7.5 for a rifle in cod and 15 dollars for a bazooka.
7.5x6+15x3=90 bucks that you are gonna spend to get these guys.
on top of 2.99-6 bucks for up to 3 skins a piece
"oh but you get free maps and modes"
really? weve gotten to the point in time in a videogame where we are accepting of being charged for game modes now too?
Look, lets break it down, the games freaking tight, its awesome, if you love being the monster, you dont need friends, if you love being the hunter, its wise to have some.
but the game at release wasnt worth more then 40 bucks, regardless of time invested in the project.

As soon as I played it I IMMEDIATELY knew this had to be the same team behind Knights of pen and paper.
If you are buying this expecting it to have some simulation elements or have strong RPG elements then immediately stay away from this game. This development team has sucked me in many times with the premises of their games but they never follow through with this premise.
I certainly would have loved a game about making my own Sentai series where my decisions determine not only how popular the show is with the combat being real tactical battles with impressive "fakey" special effects with many of its comedic moments being just the sort of crud a studio would pull to save money. Yet that isn't how the game works.
Basically to understand the game you take the role of several stunt workers who have decided to make their own "power ranger" type show. You achieve this by having random fights at which you are given goals that you must succeed, there is a story but the characters involved mostly speak entirely out of character at all times.
In fact that is probably my biggest gripe about the game's comedy is that it has absolutely no grounding. The game makes no attempt to even pretend like there is a show actually being recorded because characters almost never say their proper lines and cannot shut up for a moment about their own special effects or plotting. So some jokes, such as the characters not being able to transform because their costumes are in the cleaners out of show, fall completely flat because it never feels like this is interfering with the show because it just feels like a Larp. Another joke that falls flat is their constant references to their cheap teleportation effects, which would certainly be funny if they didn't constantly refer to it. The comedy could have been this game's saving grace, the nectar that would sustain me through the simplistic combat.
Outside of this the vast majority of the game's comedy are references. The majority of them are "references for reference sake" rather then folding them seamlessly in the game's comedy.
What the game really boils down to is a tactical RPG nothing more and nothing less. The studio runs itself and your decisions are just buffs, you are not the one writing the plot, chosing the opponents, deciding on the scenes. Yet what is there is just the barest of a tactical RPG, in fact if they didn't give you the ludicrous goals at the start of every episode the entire game would be too easy.
Yet even in this there are some genuinely good ideas there. Viewership, which you will max a little too quickly, depends on how you fight. Boss monsters for example must be defeated by your finisher otherwise you get a stiff viewership penalty (for obvious reasons) and if you waste a finisher on a boss and don't defeat it? You also get a penalty. Yet even this can come off as forced when you cannot even transform until your viewership is high enough (what is this viewed live?) instead of just allowing the player to carefully contemplate whether taking a penelty is worth it.
These goals are usually things like "defeat all enemies before hurting the boss" which are decent ones. Yet as you go on they become quite complex requiring you to carefully map out the field. The issue with these isn't that they are difficult, and they are, but that they are the only source of difficulty in this game.
You then collect crafting items from ordinary enemies which you can craft into weapons that are usually "comedic" so expect a lot of "Bucket helmets" and "Tinfoil swords". They have their own stats as well as randomized bonus stats based on how good the item is. These are equipped like everything else and to the game's credit all the items show up on your characters.
You can get studio upgrades and even marketing using the money you earn on each episode. Marketing for the most part effects the money and viewership of episodes for a small fee. You can also use your viewers to activate additional powers unlocked by that marketing campaign which can easily turn the tide in a fight from easy to rediculously easy. Studio upgrades amount to buffs and bonuses to shooting or to crafting as well as unlocking more items.
To shoot you are given a selection of fights you must do, and you will do all of them so don't worry, and then you get into a fight. That is what it amounts to. All the shoots are usually fights with usually the characters chiming in, out of character, about what this episode might be about (as said earlier they barely keep up appearances that they are actually shooting this show).

I had played Bioshock about a year after it had released initially, but stopped about half-way through.  A few years ago I restarted the game with the intent of finishing it, but managed to get about 2/3rds in before dropping out again.  I finally replayed this game in the year of our lord 2015, and for once finished it.  Let me get this out of the way up top: The game is 100% worth playing (or even replaying).
-The setting is super original: an underwater laissez faire utopia filled with the best and brightest, ripped apart by civil war due in part to the discovery of a gene altering substance.
-Combat is pretty good.  Tons of guns (that you can carry all at once!) and a variety of magic powers called "Plasmids" that vary from shooting fireballs to hacking turrets.
-Passive buffs via tonics that you purchase/find and equip allow you to personalize your playstyle somewhat.
-Varried enemy design, with thoughts taken into enemy placement in the level itself to provide interesting fights.
-Great level design, from the layout to the art design.  Levels are open with multiple branches off the main 'hub' of each level that are typically explored throughout the level via progression towards your goal.  Although there is some backtracking, enemies are usually placed in a way that makes fights fun and interesting.
-Water and particle effects are still pretty good.
-Audio design is great, from the sounds of water puddling in hallways to the ambient effects your plasmids make when you equip them.  All the work goes into create a stellar atmosphere that lets you buy into the world.
-The first 2/3rds of the game are a bit predictable in terms of how the game delays your progress narratively.
-The last act of the game is a bit more linear than the first 2/3rds, and the final fight really stinks.
-Some people think the audio journals are an overused trope, but I personally liked them for how they build the backstory.
-Switching between your gun and plasmid is annoying at first, but you'll get used to it with practice.
-The hacking minigame got boring for me about 1/3rd through the game, but some people might like it.
-Most of the textures have this shiny look to them that makes them look like plastic.
-Be prepaired to work a bit to get this game running smoothly. I had a ton of crashes before turning off the steam-overlay and forcing the game to run in DX9 before it ran smoothly.  There are a ton of steam guides to help you fix that stuff up though.
-Audio can hitch and cut-out during combat when too many sounds are playing at once.  I couldn't figure out how to fix this one, but luckily no dialogue is cut out.
-Physics calculations in the game are played at 30 fps, making them stand out a bit on modern machines.
-Options menu is a bit dated and you'll have to do some INI editing to adjust things like FOV and proper sensitivity.
Bioshock is still worth revisiting, if just for the story and gameplay alone.  It's a decently sized game and took me around 12 hours to beat, with the only downsides being that the final act is a bit lackluster and that the game looks dated and might take some playing around to get it to run without crashing.  But you're rewarded with a good shooter with a fantastic story and world that makes you interested to find out more every step of the way.
Tip: You probably want to up the difficulty, the mid game and onwards is pretty trivial on medium difficulty.

Enemy Mind is an interesting take on the arcade style space shooter games like Galaga. In most arcade style space shoot-'em ups, you'll pilot your ship through a level, all the while collecting powerups or weapons that may make your craft stronger. In Enemy Mind, your ship has the ability to take over and "transfer consciousnesses" into any other enemy ship. Each craft also has a limited ammo supply, so you'll usually want to expend your entire ammo clip before transferring over to another ship. This creates a gameplay style where the optimal strategy is also the most fun one: blow all your ammo trying to kill everything on the screen, transfer to another ship, rinse and repeat
The playstyles and designs of the enemy ships are varied and interesting enough to make it exciting each time you encounter a new type of enemy craft. It makes the player want to take it over immediately and experiment around with how much armor the craft has and how its weapon systems work. Some craft are agile with fast firing, low damage weapons. Some craft are slower with huge area of effect damage style explosions. Some craft are themselves weapons and are designed to be torpedoed into other craft to drill through their hulls. There's also an accompanying story that is played after each stage in the single player campaign, but I almost entirely ignored it. It was doled out in little text lines one at a time and it seemed mostly forgettable and inconsequential.
Summary
Enemy Mind isn't a revolutionary arcade style shooter, but it's a lot of fun. If you like games like Galaga, you'll have a good time with Enemy Mind. Navigating the bullet hell that the enemies throw at you while throwing back a bullet storm of your own while simultaneously possessing and experimenting with new craft and different playstyles felt really good. The boss battles are challenging and unique. There's also a couch co-op multiplayer mode, but I unfortunately haven't gotten a chance to check it out yet. This seems like the kind of game that would be fun to screw around in for a little while with another friend. I wouldn't go out of your way to buy it immediately, but it's worth a look if you find it discounted on a Steam sale or something like that

Enemy Mind is a brilliant concept trapped in a game that's less interesting than it deserves.
The hook is simple, but oh so ingenious it begs the question why it hasn't been done before (the closest comparison that comes to mind is Driver: San Francisco): instead of playing as any specific ship, you have the ability to reach out and take control of any enemy ship you come in contact with, and it's just as cool as you'd imagine. Whizzing around as a tiny fighter and then jumping into a bombing tanker or alien starship creates a dynamic I haven't found in another game, one where enemies are less obstacles you need to remove but strategic pieces to manipulate the battlefield with. Prioritizing ships so as to save those with the most desirable features to take over later runs contrary to almost every traditional approach to shoot'em'up combat, and something that makes Enemy Mind feel so unusual to play beyond its novel mechanic.
It's rather a shame then that said mechanic is Enemy Mind's sole strength, and what it throws its entirety behind. Taking as just about every ship often feels weak, and unsatisfying, and though providing you with a finite amount of ammo keeps you from just sticking to a single ship for the entire game, it also becomes rather tiring having to constrain yourself so drastically in order to take enemies out as each shot needs to hit and that's not especially easy to do most of the time. As quickly and often as it comes, death is largely meaningless, with no penalty save the loss of your score and the requirement to replay a little before where you met your untimely doom. This caused the game to almost immediately lose all tension, and once the novelty of taking over enemies wore off I rather lost interest in what I was doing.
And I say this having completed Enemy Mind in a meager 2 hours, which is about twice as long as it has interesting things to show you. New enemy types are continually trickled in, but many of them were immediately written off as being rather a lot less functional than those I'd been using already. I wanted to become invested in the narrative, which pieces together the memories of the pilots you've taken over to try and give context to what exactly is happening, but it's so abstract and difficulty to piece together that I was all but entirely lost by the end and only had the haziest of ideas how I got there. I imagine there's a compelling story here, but it tries to tie itself into elements of gameplay that are more interesting in concept than ideal ways to tell a narrative.
Enemy Mind's genius mechanic is so strong that it's worth checking out for it alone, but it's telling that I'm more excited about its ideas being recreated and innovated on in other games than I am about the game itself. It's a solid curiosity and a great proof of concept, I just wish its broader foundation was as engaging.

This game is a quite excellent multiplayer first-person shooter, but it's demanding, requiring more time and skill than many people may be willing to give it. Although the game includes an "action" mode with the usual multiplayer shooter elements like crosshairs, kill cams, and other features, most people play the "realism" mode (or the even more realistic "classic" mode). The realism mode features no crosshair, no damage direction or grenade indicators, no reliable friend-or-foe indicator, bullet drop with no easy helpers to compensate, one-hit kills (except some limb shots), fear and morale effects, realistic reloading, etc. In short, it tries to be a realistic WW2 shooter. New players can expect to be repeatedly killed, to have no idea where the enemy who shot them was, to have a hard time hitting anything with the bolt-action rifles of the era, and to make more than a few teammates angry when they kill them by accident because everyone looks alike at first. But if they have the patience to stick with it and learn the game, they can also expect to have a lot of fun.
The graphics, sound, and music are all well-done. I have no complaints about any of them, and many aspects of them are praiseworthy. The sound effects are the most interesting of any shooter I've played, with each weapon having a distinctive sound which varies with distance and context (such as shooting inside vs. outside). With a full battlefield of 64 players, the sounds of combat are quite engaging. Some of the music is beautiful and stirring, and none of it is obnoxious. Each nation's troops speak their native language (or can be set to speak accented English).
The game has various classes: riflemen, assault, machine-gunner, sniper/marksman, anti-tank, engineer, light mortar, flamethrower, squad leader, team leader, tank crewman, and tank commander. There are some "elite" versions of the basic classes as well (e.g. elite assault) with slightly better weapons. All classes except riflemen have very limited numbers. (For instance, there are usually only two sniper slots.) Different nations have access to different classes. (For instance, only Americans have flamethrowers, only Japanese have light mortars, and only Germans and Russians have tanks.) New players are expected to start as riflemen and work their way up to the better and rarer classes, although if the server is not full you can often be whatever you want.
There are various game modes, but the most commonly played one is Territory / Campaign, where you have to conquer and hold territory on a (cartographic) map. Each battle is over control of a single region on the map, and multiple battles together make up the campaign. This adds a bit of higher-level strategy to the game, with considerations beyond winning individual battles. You can win most of the battles and still lose the war!
Within a game mode, there are different combat styles depending on the map design. On some maps, your goal is to capture certain objectives, and you have plenty of men and time. On other maps, men are the limiting factor and your goal is to basically kill all the opponents. On other maps, time is the limiting factor and your goal is essentially to take/hold objectives in/for a certain amount of time.
The game requires more teamwork and coordination than a typical multiplayer shooter, with squad leaders following the team leader and individual soldiers following their squad leaders, although some classes (such as the sniper) work on their own. Many players ignore the chain of command, but the best teams use it well.
The game features two campaigns that are quite different. The older campaign is the Red Orchestra 2 campaign, depicting the war between Germany and Russia on the eastern front in WW2. The two sides are well-balanced and their classes and weapons are largely symmetrical. Combat often takes place in industrial or urban areas with multi-story buildings, giving many opportunities for sniping and close-quarters combat. There are some open terrain battles as well, but built-up areas predominate. This campaign also features tanks, which can dominate the field of battle. Although the classes and weapons are symmetrical, many of the maps are not. In some maps, only one side gets a tank, or one side gets two tanks to the other's one. This is not a bad thing. It makes the combat style different on different maps, and keeps the game interesting.
The second campaign is the Rising Storm campaign, depicting the war between the USA and Japan in the area in and around Japan. The two sides are asymmetrically balanced, with the Americans having significantly better weapons and the Japanese having a stronger fighting spirit. (The Japanese are less vulnerable to fear, and can fight through pain while charging into melee combat, where they have an advantage. A fatal wound is still fatal and they may still bleed to death if shot during a charge, but they might take down an American or two before dying.) The sides are pretty well-balanced overall but the Japanese require better teamwork to win. Combat primarily takes place in the jungle or in small villages with primitive structures, giving a very different feel than the RO2 campaign. There are no tanks in this campaign, although a mod exists to add them.
The leveling and upgrade systems of the game are well-done in my opinion. You can level up your profile as a whole, each class, and each weapon. The upgrades provide small improvements that can be significant overall, but which don't unbalance the game.
The controls are good although the default key bindings aren't ideal. (You can rebind them, of course.)
On the downside, the community is relatively small. Typically there are between 600 and 2000 players online, usually about 1300. This translates into between one and three servers with a low ping and a full complement of 64 players. Usually there are two full servers and three or four half-full servers with low ping. (These numbers are for each campaign, so both campaigns have at least one low-ping full server at any time, in my experience.) This is good enough for now, but I worry about the future. (If you buy the game, you can help sustain the community.) It also means that there are few players playing any game mode besides Territory / Campaign. The community is also relatively demanding, and doesn't appreciate players who don't make an attempt to learn the game and learn how to work as a team. You can still be a lone wolf, but you're expected to ultimately support the team's goals while doing so, not just rack up kills for XP. (Kills alone don't win a battle, except on manpower-limited maps.)
The game also wants to install the annoying PunkBuster software, but you can say no to this and the game will still work. Some servers will not accept you, but the most popular servers have PunkBuster disabled. In 100 hours, I haven't noticed any cheating personally, and have only seen one person accused of cheating and kicked. So playing without PunkBuster hasn't been a problem. In that same amount of time, the game has crashed two or three times and the server has reset about three times, so it's quite stable but not perfectly stable.
Overall, if you're willing to commit some time to learn the ins and outs of a new shooter, Red Orchestra 2 and Rising Storm can provide long-lasting fun.

This is a work of beauty.
It's a Galaga-style shooter: two buttons, plus directional controls. The hitch is that one of those buttons allows you to hop your control to an enemy ship.
Gameplay hinges around the gimmick, and it's a good one, but what puts this title from pleasantly retro to a must-buy in my mind is its narrative.
Enemy Mind has absolutely no reason to have a story as good as it does.
The writing explores in full the wonder and horror of being a thing that slips from consciousness to consciousness, consuming and casting away bodies like shell casings out of nothing more than curiosity. Plot snippets are brief and frequent, and vary depending on which of the two factions' ships you end a sub-stage with. I found myself playing with as much as sense of horror as with retro glee, and out of everything else Enemy Mind gave me as an experience, that's what surprised me the most.
I'd impulse-buy this at 2.50 and regular-buy it at 5.00 or 6.00. It's fairly short--maybe a couple hours long, without major replayability--but just a single run-through leaves an impression strong enough to change your day.

This game is a sham, even more than traditional casinos. Avoid spending any real world money on it. It can be fun if you're just looking for a social experience and don't really care about going broke or achievement hunting. Read on if you're curious.
So before I go into the negative aspects of this game, I feel like I should talk about what makes Four Kings a positive, unique experience, and why I've spent over 100 hours on a game that I cannot recommend. The answer is that there is simply no other game like this out there. It's an MMO, but it's also a casino simulation, with a wide variety of games to choose from including blackjack, poker, slots, craps, bingo, and roulette among others. Seeing that this is an MMO, there is also a social aspect to this game, and most of the players are friendly, helpful people who like to see new faces.
Now, let's talk about the negative aspects.
The community that I mentioned? Yeah, that's also a
aspect of this game. At some point along the line, the game developers decided that it would be wise to advertise this game as a social/dating game. As a result, there are a lot of people who create accounts and just hang around the lobby and the bingo hall, hitting on anyone who happens to have a female avatar. The game gives you the option to block or report them, but it's impossible to keep up with the neverending deluge of new accounts that only exist to try to hook up with "hot chicks". It's very annoying, and I wish the game developers would integrate something like a "Do Not Disturb" tag that I can toggle to discourage these people from bothering me. This may seem like a minor gripe, given the existence of the report/block functions, but I would argue that it is negatively affecting the community overall. The casino is usually pretty empty, which I think has a lot to do with these folks who create accounts just to harrass people and generally be annoying towards others who just want to gamble away their earnings in peace.
SPEAKING OF WHICH...let's talk about the odds.
If you're just playing this game for fun, and honestly don't care about losing all of your chips to questionable RNG, then I encourage you to play this game. You'll probably enjoy it. For people like me, who are achievement-focused, it's a nightmare.
Poker is about the fairest game that you can play, as it is in a traditional casino. It's highly dependent on skill and game knowledge with only a bit of luck involved. However, finding a poker game can sometimes be a pain due to the small community, so the rest of us end up playing Blackjack.
Look...I'm aware that the house always has the advantage. But something is not right in this game.
At some point, I decided to memorize the optimal single-deck blackjack strategy that you can find on websites such as "The Wizard of Odds". In the beginning, the game seemed pretty fair. I won some, I lost some, and had no real complaints aside from some extremely questionable losing streaks. Lately, it's become even worse. Every time I sit down to play blackjack, I always see the same patterns repeat themselves over and over again, namely:
-I bust >90% of the time if I hit on 12-16. The dealer only busts around 25-30% of the time on these cards.
-The amount of times the dealer draws a 4 or 5 on a 16 is unbelievable, and, frankly, the reason I'm writing this review right now.
-The dealer draws to 21 far more often than I do on the same card combinations, *especially* if I have a 19 or 20.
-I never draw 10s/face cards on double downs. I just played blackjack for 2 hours prior to writing this review and drew a 10 only once on a double down that entire time. Most of the time, I'll end up drawing a 2 or a 3 and losing my bet.
-The amount of times that the dealer beats you by 1 is absurd.
Single-deck blackjack has some of the fairest odds in regular casinos. I lost 1.7 million chips in 2 hours using optimal strategy, as per the "Wizard of Odds" strategy chart. If you think I just got unlucky and that there's nothing fishy about this game's RNG, I challenge you to play blackjack for a month and tell me if you don't experience the ridiculous "bad luck" that I did.
I don't necessarily think this is deliberate on the part of the game designers. It could be a programming mishap - I have similar suspicions about the Treasure Trap bonus round, which I have not managed to win for 2 months as of the posting of this review.
Anyway, if you can enjoy this game as a fun little thing to do for free, I encourage you to do so. But I'd advise you against investing any real-world money in it. Going to have to concur with the other negative reviews that something is fishy here

I'm no statistician, but I'm sure there are some impressive odds associated a dealer pulling Blackjack four times in a row in a six deck shoe!  Fortunately for Digital Leisure, however, they don't have to worry about any  gaming comissions sticking it to em!  Having played a few thousand hands, however, I can tell you that such an occurance is NOT a rarity here.

This game will make you uneasy both during and after your first attempt. You might wish to return for the scares, or you might wish to never visit this "perfectly fine" pizzaria again. Some, however, are like me, creeped out by the atmosphere but always wanting a challenge. Regardless of which of these three descriptions fits you, continuing after your first try is the best step to take. You WILL fail. You WILL forget any advice which was given to you before playing. You WILL fail several times.
However, you will eventually begin to overcome the anamatronics, your finger poised over the left clicker on your mouse. Your reflexes will improve, allowing you to blast through the light-checking process and keep an eye on your two very special "friends." You will find yourself becoming less anxious as your power dwindles, and you might even gamble against the A.I. by blocking all entrances to the Office, risking an instant-kill from Freddy after the power goes out in exchange for keeping him and Foxy at bay. You will eventually notice that these attempts work in your favor.
The first gamble will most likely be an accident, but you learn. Most learning experiences in this game stem from near-death experiences. You continue to uncover how the animatronics act when unleashed, and eventually you learn so much that all fear will subside. At this point, it is only a matter of time until you complete the game.
As a player who has cleared the entire campaign, including the nightmarish night 6 (on my second try, no less) and has completed everything but the 20/20/20/20 mode (plus any other Custom Nights), I can tell you that this game is worth much more than the $5 price. The animatronics will try to deter you from their home, but staying opens the doors (pun intended) to an incredibly well-developed strategy game.
P.S. : I didn't call it a horror game for previously stated reasons. It is simply an amazing strategy game once you learn the ropes and tie up the A.I.'s plans with them.

Overall... I'll give it a YES, but be warned it is VERY short.   It may be the shortest game I personally have ever played.

It saddens me to see this game get so many terrible reviews solely for the fact that it has dlc on release and "Lacks content". May I remind you that 99% of the dlc is purely cosmetics. SKINS. You can buy these individually or in a bundle for the correlating pattern which is in fact cheaper than buying all of the skins on their own. The other 1% is the season pass; this offers you 4 upcoming hunters and 3 skins for the original launch monsters. Wonderful. So what am I getting at? I'm saying that everyone complaining about dlc is over exaggerating and jumping on the hate wagon of misconception. They say that this game does not nearly have enough content to be $60. Fine, I'll let anyone have their own opinion, but maybe they should look into the overlooked details and facts of the game before stating it so violently.
Let's talk about how much content this game really has. Evolve has a total of 4 classes, and for every class there are 3 characters, which puts us at 12 hunters total. Each character has their own story, personality, unique abilities and play-style (This also goes for the monsters). Every character has individual progression as well. Within this progression there are 3 tiers; each tier having different and more difficult challenges than the last. There are rewards for completing each tier as well. Most of the rewards are little icons you can use to individualize your profile badge. Although, when you complete the 3rd tier you unlock a special skin for that character as well. Not to mention there is an over all leveling system that all of your experience from every hunter/monster goes into. Also, by leveling up you unlock perks for both sides of the fight in which each side (hunter/monster) has 9 perks that have 3 tiers. The progression and rewards for monsters are in the same format as the hunters. So, if you do the math this gives us a total of 15 skins (1 for every playable entity), 45 icons, and 9 perks for each hunter and monster. Oh wait, and don't forget the game modes! There is Hunt, Rescue, Nest, Defend, and evacuate which is a 5 round game which includes all of these game types. I think that is a considerable and reasonable amount of content for launch, but that's just my opinion, remember these things folks! Everything else above that sentence in this paragraph is fact.
I see people commenting on how there are multiplayer bugs and un-stabilized play. I will have you know that I have not experienced any unstable gameplay while playing the game online or offline. I have experienced a few minor bugs, here's the list: un-wanted cursor appearances and disappearances, a small part in the wall on a certain map I cannot jet pack climb on as the hunter, and a small wall that can be jumped over, but cannot be climbed over on monster side. None of these were anything that shortened the length of my hair or had made me contemplate the quality of the end product of this game. I can think of plenty other games where glitches and bugs have been much much worse. I say that all of these things will be fix shortly, for they are certainly easy to spot and reproduce.
Conclusion? I say the amount content is sufficient for release. A big reason why I think people are complaining about content is because they were spoiled from the start. For those who played the game in the alpha and beta stages of the game (especially beta), they were nearly given the whole game on a silver platter! Every single character was available to anyone that pre-ordered the game through steam during the time of the beta. If you didn't preorder you were only missing out on the 3rd character of that particular class! From my knowledge there were not any restrictions on leveling up or character progression. The only thing missing from the game were the individual game modes! And skins.... don't forget the skins. Bottom line is I think everyone needs to see the game for what it is. That it's a really fun and exciting game to play. Whether it's just a game to run around large areas to shoot strange and interesting creatures or an in-depth strategic battle for monster and man alike. Look for yourself! Try to find comments saying that this game is just "straight 2k dumpster baby" or "10/10, uninstall simulator 2015" because I'm sure they aren't there. This game is good fun for everyone.
Danks for reading.

I like this game, I really do.
It has fun, silly weapons/support items that are situationally OP (depending on map) meaning you need to learn them all and understand when to switch to counter your opponents.
Movement is a blast, getting flung around planets at increasingly high speeds and then landing on top of someone with a pulse rocket explosion is great.
Visuals are simple but crisp, everything is low-poly but some excellent colour choice and parallax effects really sell it. Each stage is unique in both appearance and layout, every single one is worth experiencing. The mechs themselves look okay at best (very N64-steez), but that barely matters since you view them from such a zoomed out perspective.
The sound effects are stellar, and the music is a fun, pumping, Tron-style track that matches the on-screen action to a T.
It just has one huge problem: No one is playing it. The only time there is ever a server is when me and my friends go make one to play with 4 players.
So fair warning; bring friends who you can hit up to play with you. You will almost never find active servers with more than 1 or 2 people in them, and even then the lag can be just agony.

An amazing story based game, would highly recommend you play it without spoiling it for yourself by watching videos or summaries.
I won’t spoil the story here, but it’s really amazing. It’s a very different experience to most games released nowadays and left me thinking about it for days after finishing it. The story has a very interesting message behind it and encourages you to research the developers and their stories more after completing it. The pacing is solid and the maps are very well designed. Don’t feel the need to rush the story; it is much better enjoyed when you take it slow.
The game is made in the source engine, so the graphics aren’t quite Battlefield 1, but they use a large variety of ambient lighting and shading to make even the source engine look very pretty. The games appearance also works in favour of the story, which will become apparent as you play through the game.
The soundtrack is very atmospheric, and fits the game very well. A large variety of songs are used and they all fit their respective environments perfectly in my opinion. The voiceover work is also fantastic, very well written and acted.
To conclude, buy this game and don’t read any summaries. Going in dry will not only make the game more enjoyable, but also leave a much greater impact on you. This is all just my opinion, but I do believe this game is amazing and definitely worth the buy to complete.

I love this trilogy. This one was probably the best GAME for me - the puzzles were good, not too easy, but not so hard that the only way forward was to cheat (I only had to ask my friend Google for
, not just the answer like in some places in the other games where the puzzles were just too obscure) . The gameplay is also clever - minor spoiler here -
- and the humour is up to scratch (mostly).
But, alas, like seemingly all of my favourite games, this one has its flaws. For most of the game, it was bugs for me. From the start it was a bit buggy - quite unlike the other two games, which were fine - problems with the drop down menu, visual glitches, audio glitches when people were talking. All of these things were rare and minor - but occasionally it would completely screw up, and Rufus would start walking through things, and that meant I had to go back to my last save. That, on top of the minor bugs, was very annoying. Luckily, I save often enough that it wasn't a huge problem.
The other problem was - you guessed it - the end (no spoilers, I promise). Now, I don't have a problem with it
. On reflection, the actual way the
ended was fine, if not exactly happy. It was the execution that bothered me. It was over too quickly, I didn't expect it to be over and I was, at first, disappointed. The clips didn't seem dramatic or clear enough as to what was happening (It did NOT help that they were slightly buggy, and cut together awkwardly, in my case). When it was over, it took me a few minutes to work out what had actually just happened. It was a good ending - sort of - but it felt badly done, and rushed. I also wish that they'd tied up a few more loose ends, if only to give me a little more time in Deponia before it was over, to see where the characters ended up, after three whole games had made me care about them. As it was, I felt like I'd been kicked out prematurely.
As a trilogy, this wasn't always perfect - but I do love it. I like the world, the humour, the characters and the story. The puzzles throughout are mostly good - some a little obscure - but this game, the finale, was definitely the best, for the solidarity of the story (until the very end) and puzzles which actually left me with a sense of achievement rather than of frustration.
I'm very happy to have played them.

Red Orchestra 2: Heroes of Stalingrad
Multiplayer First-person Shooter
Tripwire Interactive
Tripwire Interactive
is a multiplayer first-person shooter set in World War II developed and published by Tripwire Interactive.
The main game is set during the invasion of Russia from the Nazis against the Soviets. There is also a standalone game called Rising Storm that features the American attacks against the Japanese after Pearl Harbor. The game doesn't have a real storyline, but the setting feels very grounded in history and there are plenty of real life locations, as well as actual guns and vehicles from the era.
The game uses Unreal Engine 3. There are your usual texture pop-ins and small performance hiccups, even though there aren't as many as usual. The game olds up fairly well and the decaying cities of Russia are well varied and full of little details that suck you into the experience.
The game features a variety of modes, including Territory (where you conquer different places on a map), Firefight (team deathmatch), and a Multiplayer Campaign (which is basically Territory played on multiple levels and stages). The levels are all very well balanced, and both sides feel equally as powerful. The game lacks a crosshair and an ammo count: while it is pretty weird at first, you slowly start seeing that it's the best way to get sucked into the game.
There are multiple classes to choose from, each one with its set of items and weapons to use on the battlefield, but in the end the game rewards the most skilled players, and there isn't a weapon more powerful than another: they are all balanced to suite each player to their favourite play style without making them too overpowered. The Squad Leaders work as spawn points, while the Commander has the ability to force respawn and to select sections of the territory to launch an artillery attack or bombardments.
I have never felt more paranoid in a game than when playing RO2: whenever you are getting shot at, you lose focus, your vision gets blurry, and you start losing the ability to hear. When crawling through the battlefield with a bunch of comrades, seeing one of the suddenly become a ragdoll fills you with fear of knowing that a sniper is probably loading the next bullet to send to your brain. This are just some of the amazing experiences I've had in this game that in my opinion shows how brutal and unheroic war is: people die, people scream, and in the end each side loses a ton of good soldiers.
The game features bullet drops and realistic damage: shooting at someone's leg will make him limp, shooting at his lungs will make him grasp for air for a couple of seconds without collapsing... When I started replaying the game for this review, I remembered how unforgiving it is for new players. But if you give it enough time, you will get better at handling weapons and calculating the difference bullet drops as well as the best tactics to win on both sides. It becomes a very rewarding game.
The sound is phenomenal, with realistic weapon effects, cheesy but fun voice acting and powerful explosions. The soundtrack is also very underrated, and it homages classic themes from movies like Saving Private Ryan.
The game is constantly being updated by the developers, and the community is pretty great too: many maps and modes can be downloaded from the Workshop to change the game's formula up. There are also over 140 Steam achievements that will keep you hooked for a long time.
Overall, Red Orchestra 2 is one of my favourite multiplayer games of all time, as well as a great war game that requires a bit of tactics and good skills. Everyone who enjoys online games and first person shooters as well as more skills than luck will have a blast playing this hard at first but hugely satisfying game.

Compared to the previous two titles, Goodbye Deponia pushes the limits of dark humor. You, the player, sell a black woman into sexual slavery. You lead children onto the doorstep of a pedophile and later into the  mouth of a child-eating swamp monster. You drive a man to suicide.  We were first introduced to Rufus as a well-meaning buffoon. But as we progress through the trilogy, he becomes increasingly despicable and unempathetic. It becomes difficult for the player to project themselves onto this character.
Rufus was given a redemption ending. I feel that this was too sudden a change of character. It makes the finale less tragic and memorable. Character development should not just happen and the end, but rather revealed as a continuous process resulting from an accumulation of experience.
Like the previous two titles, the production quality of Goodbye Deponia is very high. If you are a fan of the series, you should enjoy its finale.

The Journey Down is a point-and-click adventure game with very unique visual style, above-avarage music, fine voiceacting, and a silly storyline with dumbest puzzles ever imaginable. I usually don't look for difficulty in point-and-click adventure games, since I found story to be the most important thing to consider, but these puzzles are beyond any measurement of difficulty. I mean, Broken Age for example, also had pretty easy puzzles, but they made sense, progressed the story in one way or another, and they required some kind of thinking nonetheless. In The Journey Down, puzzles are like "There's a thirsty guy over here, there's a glass over there, and there's a water tap right there. Now you click them in order.", and they have no contribution to story whatsoever. By the way, you are a reggie guy who speaks five times slower than an avarage person, reviewing literally each and every action you do. Game consistently tries to be funny, especially with accents, but they are flat-out boring, with nothing happening outside. And that's about it.
Although it's not the worst point-and-click adventure game ever, there are so many amazing point-and-click games to be played like Monkey Island series, The Longest Journey series, Syberia series, Discworld, Full Thortle, Broken Sword series, and Broken Age, that The Journey Down is not even a competitor.
One last thing, if you can compare this game with Grim Fandango, you are clearly out of your mind.

"The Park" is a very short narrative horror game (approx 2 hours' gameplay) set in a spookily derelict theme park.  You are seeking your son who ran ahead of you and has vanished out of sight.  As you search for him, you'll start to unravel the history of the park as well as begin to experience more of the horrors within both the park and yourself.  It's a game that probably merits the unfortunate tag "walking simulator" but in a positive way.  It doesn't feel laboured.  It plays equally well with gamepad and keyboard/mouse.  The story is dark and mysterious as it unfolds.
It's VERY atmospheric.  If you like the idea of wandering around a small, desolate theme park in the dark, and to perhaps experience some of the rides as the story is narrated, this is a game you'll enjoy.  The horror elements are really well done, with a few small jump scares but no cheap tricks.  What was especially pleasant was to find my character had arms and legs, full reflection in mirrors and a shadow that occasionally made me jump when cast against a wall (bigger devs please take note - it was very nice not to be a disembodied head)!  The gamepad controls were very simple too.  A joy to play and, while sadly very short, a rich and dark experience as a psychological mystery unfolds, leaving you to ponder what on earth it all meant, and what your part in the story might have been.  The graphics, once inside the park, are tremendous, giving an EthanCarter-like vibe to the game.
I had a couple of glitches in trying to get it to run properly but a restart resolved it (my gamepad refused to be recognised at first).  The game is very short indeed, but I suspect it's meant merely to be a teaser game for Funcom's "The Secret World" (an MMORPG with free 7-day trial).  There isn't a concrete conclusion to the ending - which I imagine is deliberate, leading you to wonder who and what (can't say more because spoilers, but the story IS good).  There seemed to be a few loose ends where some things weren't explained, but again, that might have been artistic license rather than fault.
Personally, I think it's a wee bit short for the price, but the experience is worth it (if you played the equally excellent "Homesick" also on Steam, it's a similar sort of experience - different tale obviously).  On balance, I'm glad I bought it but the replay value (as with all games of this genre) is probably not that great.  I expect I will play it again at some point just like I'd watch a good movie again, but there won't be any variation in gameplay.

First of all, this game is a steal. I've seen it as low as sixty nine cents, sure, but even at twelve bucks for this and its sequel it's a heck of a value. Charming, pretty easy, and short.
But it does have a heavy dose of adventure game logic. The fact that the game goes to great lengths to poke fun at adventure game logic("I hate puzzles!" exclaims the main character) does nothing to ameliorate the fact that it relies on some goofy leaps of logic. That said, it's otherwise well written, well performed, and beautifully scored. The aesthetic is especially interesting, raster backgrounds digitally painted over free hand sketches with characters rendered in a heavily subdived prerendered 15FPS 3D meant to imply stop motion animation. However, it often falls short of this ambition and just looks like early CG. But when it works it's actually extremely lovely.
Obviously, if you really want stop motion animation in your point and click adventure game, go grab Dream Machine. The Journey Down is a unique voice in games. I found its characters goofily endearing, and enjoyed my time with them.

+ Does what it says on the tin, you get to piece together puzzles made of short videos of wild animals. The "image being video" often helps to complete the areas of the puzzle with the most movement first.
+ I love the grouping feature, where the game automatically separates edge pieces from inside pieces. Saves a lot of time!
+ Well-designed UI and very helpful feedback on matches / correct locations.
- The game doesn't actually offer all 3 difficulties for all puzzles to me. Eg. for the Koala one I can only see the 240 and 350 difficulty, not the 60. (Maybe they appear
I did all the puzzles, but it wouldn't make sense for the gradual difficulty curve.)
- It would be nice if the videos were seamlessly looped, that little jag every few seconds is mildly annoying
- All 3 of the background music options are annoying after a few minutes - I turned off the background music altogether after half hour of play
- Often the extruding part of a puzzle piece doesn't look the appropriate size or shape for a given hole, but it does end up being correct. This results in having to try to match the piece to many other pieces with broadly similarly shaped/sized holes. This is somewhat mitigated by the excellent "snapping" mechanic.
- It feels like the cursor is sometimes not that accurate. I only noticed this when trying to pick up a specific piece from the top bar.
- It would be nice if there was some way to discern which pieces are in the correct location. Currently the only way to tell is to try to move the piece, and if you can't, then it's correct. I have to remember not to leave pieces lying around on the board to avoid confusing myself.
If you like jigsaw puzzles and nature, give it a try, it has a mostly enjoyable gameplay. The negatives listed above are only minor annoyances to me.

, and no, I wouldn't recommend to buy it for £7. It's worth maybe £2-3 at most.

TLDR: This is an amazing game, but it hinges on one (or two) factors. This is an amazing game IF: You like Power Rangers or Super Sentai. This is the main reason I'm "Not Recommending".  I will still play for another 50 hours or so, but I'm a Rangers and Sentai fan.
9/10 - Power Rangers/Sentai fans
6/10 - Normal RPG, tactical fans
Chroma Squad has some mis-leading aspects, mainly that this is a simple tactical game, and not so much of a Manager/Studio Simulation, and it lacks any deep RPG elements.
PROS:
-Best Power Rangers game yet! No joke, easily the best. If you like Power Rangers at all- BUY THIS NOW! You will not be very disapointed.
-Blend of tactical, rpg, and simulation aspects
-Can customize team's colors, equipment, weapons
-Crafting is available
-Can upgrade the studio
-Great retro music and art (some people hate that, I like it)
-You do not gain levels. This is under pros and cons because to some this takes away from how much of an RPG it is. To others, this means no 'grinding'
-Great GUI/UI. It looks very nice, and it's easy to use.
-Contracts with different agencies. This is a really nice touch. I like this a lot.
CONS:
-The simulation/managing aspect is sort-of fake. You don't really become a fliming studio in the sense you get to create your own episodes. Nor does changing the 'actor' for your Rangers change their personality (a black guy with a mohawk has the same personality as an alien, who also has the same personality as a living beaver-man).  You DO get to choose the order of episodes, but this will only change the ending of the game (as of right now, when I write this).
-Virtually NOTHING you do has an effect on how the story/studio/managing/episodes etc. Some things effect how many fans you get, and it will change these end-of-episode fake tweets (Twitter) "Wow!  You ended with a finishing move! That was awesome" or "Lame, you need to change your gear! #OldGearIsLame". This is a nice touch at first, but it becomes annoying. Especially when 'fans' want you to change your gear every episode, when there isn't any new gear avaiable.
-Tactical elements are light: I did not feel I had to ever strategize to complete a level.
-RPG elements are light: Very few RPG-like choices. When you beat a season, you get new 'Season Abilities', ultimately only allowing for 5 different abilities/powers/moves per 'Hero'/Ranger
-Studio Management aspect is very light: Right now it only improves your heroes, and or Mecha. It can also give you more fans/money.
-Mecha Battle: This is nothing more than a simple time-reaction game. It does not feel engaging, and also Mecha battles do not happen after every fight. So when it /does/ happen, it feels anti-climatic because of how shallow the fights are.
-Crafting can be fun, but it also feels shallow. Instead of choosing the gear you like (like a damage suit vs a HP suit vs a magic suit etc) you just get scaling gear. So you end up re-crafting your old gear just so you can get the newest set.
-Due to crafting the items in the 'Shop' are either much worse or much better in comparison. (Level 3 shirt from shop: 120 HP, Level 3 shirt crafted: 87 HP and +1 random property (likely of equal strength)
-The story... If you buy this game for the story PREPARE to be disapointed. It's fully of tongue-in-cheek (aka humorous, funny, comical etc) elements. I am not a huge fan of this. The writing isn't very solid (Sorry Gui) and I never find myself wanting to know what happens next
-There isn't a lot of gear/items/equipment etc. Half way through the game: 14 'equipment' pieces to craft, 17 to buy. Weapons: 14 to buy, 12 to craft. Remember, these only affect some visual looks and your stats. Weapons give you a new attack (which is nifty) but ultimately it's going to be a variation on the same thing (axe doing more damage than sword)
-(Currently) no NewGame+
-There are even fewer studio improvements to buy, making the studio/managing aspect even weaker. (I'm half way through the game and I have 10 available to buy)
-Buying the "bigger studio' doesn't actually change anything for the episodes. Nothing at all. (It provides stats, but does not change the episodes themselves) At least in Game Dev Tycoon the visuals changed to a larger studio and gave more options to do things. That is not the case here.
-You do not gain levels. This is under pros and cons because to some this takes away from how much of an RPG it is. To others, this means no 'grinding'
Knowing all of this: I will still end up playing quite a bit. And I don't mind posting this, knowing a lot of fan-bois will dislike my review. I still find the game to be fun, but very misleading. You don't really manage very much. (Unless equiping & crafting gear in any other RPG counts as simulation/managing aspect :P ) The studio improvements don't change much. The gear changes your looks and stats (like most games) but there isn't much choice, so everyone at a certain point will be wearing either A) Gear that was Crafted or B) Gear that was bought. You aren't going to use an old gear-set that has worse stats, and there isn't a choice between visuals (you get what you get, right now)

I've been a fan of jigsaws for a long time, but never was happy playing a digital version of it. This title is no exception.
It's just so flawed. UI is poorly made, even if it's aiming for children - which it shouldn't, since jigsaw puzzles are a 3-∞ activity. BGM music is repetitive. The pieces lock in the right place (and you can't disable it). No need to turn pieces around to fit - they're always at the correct orientation.
Also, one important rule when designing anything is "You shouldn't do something just because you can". That means that while a digital puzzle allows you to do an animated jigsaw, doesn't mean its a good idea. The dev should've gone for some things that digital puzzles allows you and ARE important: hotkeys, keybidings and more auto-sorting options (the game allows you to auto-group pieces by edge and non-edge - it could also allow for colour group, for instance).
All in all, a weak title. I literally played some better jigsaw computer games in 1998.

First up: Please note, I do not recommend this game at full price. I got it at a discount, and that's probably the time you should get it.
As for the game itself: Do you remember that fun feeling of coming together with the whole family on christmas, and just grabbing a 1000 piece jigsaw? The feeling of the pieces as you rub your hands through them, looking for that distinct feeling of an edge piece? Well, this game has none of it, but I doubt any puzzle game can, but still.
The pieces are all already perfectly aligned, right side up, and picture side up as well, which means no hassle of pieces turning upside down when you go through them. But also, no fun of firguring out what goes on what side. But even more so, because alot of the pieces are moving, it's like a huge brain dump, where you can't distinguish from edge to normal piece as easily.
This also leads to an interesting mechanic. With the lack of space in the borders to have a lot of pieces separately, and the movement being different in different spots, soon you'll stop puzzling with the regular "edge first" mentality, and start with a new these pieces are very close together mentality, which can happen on any spot of the picture. Sometimes it's the sky, sometimes it's a single reed, and sometimes it's the one thing that doesn't move, like a tree.
In the end, it won't come close to a regular jigsaw on christmas for me, but the idea that the picture starts growing, and seeing the movement of an eye take shape, and become almost completely round does give a good feeling.
The downside is, that the first three puzzles start at 60 pieces, second 3 start at 240 pieces, and then 3, and 1 separately start at 350 pieces, without a way to play the easier ones first. This means you need to do the hard ones before the easy ones, and makes it a bad game to let your kid puzzle with.
It is a nice game, which does give a few different ways of puzzling, which in itself is nice, but eventually, you will still know you can't just use 9 square feet of your home just for a puzzle for the next two weeks, and thus your playing on a subpar computer screen to safe some room. Fun while it lasts, but not a whole lot longer.

It saddens me to see this game get so many terrible reviews solely for the fact that it has dlc on release and "Lacks content". May I remind you that 99% of the dlc is purely cosmetics. SKINS. You can buy these individually or in a bundle for the correlating pattern which is in fact cheaper than buying all of the skins on their own. The other 1% is the season pass; this offers you 4 upcoming hunters and 3 skins for the original launch monsters. Wonderful. So what am I getting at? I'm saying that everyone complaining about dlc is over exaggerating and jumping on the hate wagon of misconception. They say that this game does not nearly have enough content to be $60. Fine, I'll let anyone have their own opinion, but maybe they should look into the overlooked details and facts of the game before stating it so violently.
Let's talk about how much content this game really has. Evolve has a total of 4 classes, and for every class there are 3 characters, which puts us at 12 hunters total. Each character has their own story, personality, unique abilities and play-style (This also goes for the monsters). Every character has individual progression as well. Within this progression there are 3 tiers; each tier having different and more difficult challenges than the last. There are rewards for completing each tier as well. Most of the rewards are little icons you can use to individualize your profile badge. Although, when you complete the 3rd tier you unlock a special skin for that character as well. Not to mention there is an over all leveling system that all of your experience from every hunter/monster goes into. Also, by leveling up you unlock perks for both sides of the fight in which each side (hunter/monster) has 9 perks that have 3 tiers. The progression and rewards for monsters are in the same format as the hunters. So, if you do the math this gives us a total of 15 skins (1 for every playable entity), 45 icons, and 9 perks for each hunter and monster. Oh wait, and don't forget the game modes! There is Hunt, Rescue, Nest, Defend, and evacuate which is a 5 round game which includes all of these game types. I think that is a considerable and reasonable amount of content for launch, but that's just my opinion, remember these things folks! Everything else above that sentence in this paragraph is fact.
I see people commenting on how there are multiplayer bugs and un-stabilized play. I will have you know that I have not experienced any unstable gameplay while playing the game online or offline. I have experienced a few minor bugs, here's the list: un-wanted cursor appearances and disappearances, a small part in the wall on a certain map I cannot jet pack climb on as the hunter, and a small wall that can be jumped over, but cannot be climbed over on monster side. None of these were anything that shortened the length of my hair or had made me contemplate the quality of the end product of this game. I can think of plenty other games where glitches and bugs have been much much worse. I say that all of these things will be fix shortly, for they are certainly easy to spot and reproduce.
Conclusion? I say the amount content is sufficient for release. A big reason why I think people are complaining about content is because they were spoiled from the start. For those who played the game in the alpha and beta stages of the game (especially beta), they were nearly given the whole game on a silver platter! Every single character was available to anyone that pre-ordered the game through steam during the time of the beta. If you didn't preorder you were only missing out on the 3rd character of that particular class! From my knowledge there were not any restrictions on leveling up or character progression. The only thing missing from the game were the individual game modes! And skins.... don't forget the skins. Bottom line is I think everyone needs to see the game for what it is. That it's a really fun and exciting game to play. Whether it's just a game to run around large areas to shoot strange and interesting creatures or an in-depth strategic battle for monster and man alike. Look for yourself! Try to find comments saying that this game is just "straight 2k dumpster baby" or "10/10, uninstall simulator 2015" because I'm sure they aren't there. This game is good fun for everyone.
Danks for reading.

Pros:
+ Atmosphere is great: environmental sounds are immersive (from creaking trees, howling wind, opening up your pack, etc). The weather changes and effects you. You leave footprints in the snow. The colour and clearness of the sky changes, as well as visibility (eg, fog and blizzards). Sunrises are stunning!
+ Emotional music sometimes drifts in and out at certain points. Otherwise all you have is either silence or the sounds of the environment, which really presents a sense of realism.
+ Small details, like said footprints. My favourite is seeing the character's breath in front of her face in time with the sound of her breathing.
+ You have the option to write your own journal entries for each day, as well as to keep general notes.
+ The game automatically keeps detailed stats for you.
+ The ability to craft items. Some items require extra effort to obtain the materials and the use of time, again with the sense of realism.
+ Character vitals need to be seen to, which pushes you to concentrate on survival on top of the other things you're doing, such as exploration.
+ Use of a rifle if and when you find one to hunt animals.
+ Areas differ in terms of the terrain, buildings and the general atmosphere.
+ A sense of bliss is achievable when you've journeyed too far from shelter and you wind up at an unexpected new little area to find new supplies and shelter.
+ The game has a promising future (you can keep up to date with progress on their website at Hinterlandgames and see a video showing you exactly what they plan to do to bring the game to the next level in terms of, well, everything - environment, atmosphere, characters, story.
Overall I am very positive about this game and its future/upcoming changes. At the moment I enjoy roaming around the sandbox areas, exploring and pushing to survive, making lots of use of the journal. To think there is more to come, as well as a story mode, is really exciting and I look forward to it all. I highly recommend this game.
