I must say that when i saw the anoucement trailer a few years back, this game caught my attention immediatly. Not only because of the aestethic, but the frenetic pacing that the gameplay shown had. This was one of the games that i kept repeating in my head "please, don't be♥♥♥♥♥♥quot;. Now that it was released, i'm relived that my prayers were heard. I will refrain from talking about the art direction, because it has all the praise it really deserves. Just look at it. Even if you don't like this art style, you must admit the game looks INCREDIBLE.
So, about the gameplay? Really good, if you like a challenging platformer. You can shoot in most directions, but that doesn't mean you can just fire aimlessly. You still need to time and aim the shots well to kill the smaller minions or to chunk the bigger enemies or the bosses, even with close-range weapons.
The game is made mostly of boss stages, that you need to hit constantly to whittle them down slowly, and the only hint that they are taking damege is the feint glow after every sucessful shot, and the transition to a new stage of the fight. To make the boss hunting a little easier, you can get new weapons and upgrades from the shop, with the coins you collect in the few 'run n gun' stages, that have 5 coins each. Choose your power-us wisely, because you only have few coins to spend.
It is unfair to compare this game to Dark Souls
. I think it is better to call this a refined version of Contra, from the NES. In Contra you run, aim, and shoot, while dodging the enemy fire and getting new weapons. Cuphead has this exact formula, but adds in a Dash, so that you can dodge attacks faster
and a mid-air parry that grants you a power-shot every time you hit a bright-pink enemy projectile
. It becomes incredible the amount of stuff flying on the screen that you have to dodge, but, with enough trial and error, you get to do in a snap of the fingers.
Ok, i praised the game a lot, now lets get to the bad stuff. Not bad as in gamebreaking, but as in "It could have been better". Mind you that i criticise this game after beating it once, mostly single player, and loving every second of those 17 hours:
-Starting off, why in the name of guacamole you can
parry mid-air? I get that you are jumping most of the time, but having to use it as a double tap of the jump button is just odd. Even if the game has platforming challenges built around this particular aspect, i still can't think of a reason to not have a ground parry, even if a delayed one.
-I thought that the lack of a hard mode to challenge the most skilled or avid players being a negative, but the game already has a hard mode. Play it alone. The idea of having a game built for 2 players isn't new, but it feels somewhat incomplete not having a partner all the time, either to save your hide or to whittle the boss faster. It feels like you are trying to drive a car with a flat tire - Technically you can, but it is dangerous and you feel wierd all the time.
-I have a small gripe with the weapons and upgrades. It adapts to the players personal style of playing this type of game, selecting up to two weapons, a power up and one of three Supers. Sounds simple and awesome, but i cannot brush off the feeling that it is somewhat broken. Broken meaning that i used the exact same combo of weapons and powers in almost every non-aerieal boss, including the last one. Peashooter (the standard weapon, mind you), Seeker Shot and Invinsible Dash. Every time i tried a new combination (Spread shot, extra life with less damege, automatic parry), i just felt weaker, even after a lot of tries. I missed the safety of the Invisible Dash, or the practicity of not having to aim a lot using the Seeker Shot. I hope thats just me.
-This game has a lot of trial and error. The boss fights last only about 1~3 minutes, but you die A LOT, sobe prepared to spend some time on every boss, learning its patterns and planning a strategy. I dont think trial and error is a bad thing; it is just a tool of learning and incentiveses you to keep going, knowing that every time you get closer to the end, but don't think you'll just "kill this boss on the first try and move on".
-
One last thing that is not gamebreaking, but might be a bug: In the first stage of the last boss, The Devil, when he uses his head-snake attack, one of the ways to dodge the attack is to run to the opposite side of the room. When he retreats his head, the tongue animation is a little bit off of the hitbox, so when you leave your safety cover you end up getting hit when he  clearly has already retreated.
It may feel that i am criticizing the game a lot, but only because it is easier to list the few bad things i found out about the game than the mountain of praises i can give. Heck, i even sprinkled some fair points and praises in my criticism. Be the beautiful and talented art direction, that captures the magic of a long-gone era of animation, or the fantastic action-packed gameplay, this is the kind of game that just does not age. Simple, effective and just good.

I hate horror games.
Okay, okay, I'll admit it.  I don't hate them, I'm just too much of a ♥♥♥♥♥ to play them myself.  But for The Park, I grew some balls and sat down in the dark for a good scare.
I'm also going to admit that I'm cheap.  Normally, I regret pretty much anything I spend money on.  However, I definitely do not regret this game.
The atmosphere was the BEST part of this game.  I scare easily, and there were some jumpscares that got me of course, but it wasn't just that.  The game wasn't particularly scary; I've seen worse.  It was extremely unsettling.  It took the time to get under your skin and stick with you.  That, in my opinion, is MUCH more effective than any jumpscare.  I felt on edge even after the game ended for a while afterwards.
The voice acting was surprisingly great.  I didn't run into any glitches.  Like I said, I was completely immersed in the atmosphere of the park.  The story was surprisingly good; a lot of it left me thinking.  I ended up recommending the game to some friends just so I could have other people to discuss the story of the game with.  Overall, I find that The Park was worth my money.  It really packs a punch for the short game that it is.

I'm sure nobody wants to read another glowing review, but I'm just another voice singing with the choir. I hated it at first, until I found out I was able to use the joypad (push the "a" button to activate!) then I could learn the nuances of the game without inhibition. THE GAME IS a SURVIVAL SIM like nothing you have played before.
With the Dual-analogue concept, I was able to understand how the sight-lighting works, and how attacking works, and how to look around while walking. everything has an option (I accidently drank bleach because I didnt read, much like real life) food spoils if you remove it from the fridge, or the power shuts off, oh my gosh, this is the deepest game I have ever played.

Pros
-Gamepad control
-decent inventory management
-the BEST Isometric game since Diablo
-Real sense of Survival and despair
-Updates are frequent enough without breaking the game
-Detailed and deep gameplay: you WILL wonder where your time has gone
- Walking dead fans rejoice! you have something to do until the next episode and thereafter while waiting!
CONS
here we go
-Inventory management needs work. Solution: Think of Diablo/Arma how you could tell what Items you have and how much space without being over-encumbered. Maybe a grid system to allow for mixing and crafting outside of the inventory menu. for example, a Bat takes up 2-3 slots if I am correct, but its only referred to in numerical fashion.
-Inventory again: Icant at a glance see what I have, especially in a pinch, but then again, It could be deliberate.
-Stats! I like the stats, honestly, but I dont like that after killing 20 or more zombies, your guy is still scared. maybe anxious, but there so far is no levelling up like I would like, or maybe I didnt notice yet.
I LOVE THIS GAME. If you read the "zombie survival guide" from max brooks, you can apply many many of the philosophies here.
WISHES
-they already spoke of vehicles and Split-screen, so EVEN if its paid DLC I would get it.
-maybe an aiming system for the gun. or maybe its deliberately meant to make guns feel like you cant hit a damn thing unless its close. BUT OH MAN IS IT LOUD. I LOVE IT.

TL;DR Version:
It's lonely, harsh, and tense -- everything a zombie apocalypse should be -- but it needs the living to be really fun, either through NPCs or an easy-to-use LAN function.  When that comes out, it'll be hard to compete with this game.
Long Version:
It needs a streamlined (or STEAMlined) multiplayer set-up.  I can't deal with these IP's and ports just to open a LAN.  Without friends, "Project Zomboid" is just a well-designed but depressingly desolate zombie experience.  I don't just want to survive.  I want to LIVE.  That said, it really is supremely well-made as an open-world zombie-survival game, and it's getting better all the time.  Also, the choices given while customizing your sandbox difficulty really are fantastic and surprisingly diverse.  It's a game I already love, and I'll stick with it as long as it takes for it to get over the few problems that it has.  It's worth it.  Just be sure you don't play with weak stomachs, hearts, or bowels, because turning a corner only to come face-to-face with a zombie you didn't notice a moment ago, or having three corpses upon you while checking rooms in a supposedly-empty house can be the random-chance jump-scare that does you in.

Chroma Squad is a Tactical-RPG (i.e.: Final Fantasy Tactics, Fire Emblem), coated with some Management Sim mechanics.
In Chroma Squad you control an independent Super Sentai Studio trying to create its first series. As such, you'll have to manage your money, buy upgrades to the studio, new clothes for your actors and hire people to take care of your marketing strategy.
The meat of the game, however, lies between these management sessions. Whenever you record an episode, the game becomes a tactical RPG: you start giving orders to your actors on where to move, who to attack, stuff like that.
It's an amazingly stylish game. The pixel-art is awesome, the soundtrack is pure chiptune bliss (plus a main theme with japanese lyrics!) and the game is packed with references to pop culture and super sentais in general.
You don't really need to be a super sentai fan to enjoy the solid tactics mechanics in this game, but it surely adds to the overall experience. I recommend this game to anyone who ever enjoyed a Power Rangers episode or is just itching for a new TRPG game.
TL;DR: Awesome Tactical-RPG with stylish graphics, soundtrack and references. If you like Super Sentais you'll fall in love with it!

Definitely an interesting game. I've always been a fan of shmups and the unique mechanic of taking over enemy ships was what sold me on it initially.
The controls are a mixed bag. If you're more accustomed to 16-bit era shoot-'em-up games, you should be fairly comfortable with them. It's about on par with Super R-Type or Gradius III. If you're used to more modern shmups, however, it may be a problem.
The game itself is fairly short, which is to be expected in this genre. There are 8 levels in all, each with multiple waves of enemies. Each level ends with a boss fight. Some involve fighting a large formation of standard enemies, others involve fighting larger crafts which utilize the ship-swapping ability in different ways. The game can be difficult at times, but considering that you have infinite continues and you continue from the beginning of the last wave you've reached (which is also what happens when you lose a life, oddly enough), it's a little on the easy side. I managed to beat the game in about 3 hours. The replay value for the game stems from the storyline, which varies based on actions you take. So if you don't really care about that kind of thing, it's kind of a wash.
Fortunately, there are also some unlockable extras, like an arcade mode that does away with starting at the beginning of each wave (but eliminates contiunes), a boss rush mode, the original proof-of-concept game and two parodies of other games.
Gamepad support is great. I had absolutely no problems with my 360 pad. Best of all, there's even an option to switch between both analog sticks and the D-Pad to control both the ship in-game and the menu controls.
In summary, if you're looking for an old-school horizontal shooter with some unique mechanics, I'd definitely suggest picking this up. On the other hand, if you're looking for a bullet-hell shmup, this game probably won't offer much.

I played through and beat the main story of this game in about 2.5 hours. I don't really feel drawn to replay it or climb leaderboards.
Overall, it's kinda fun, but it's just not fun enough to recommend (compared to the plethora of other, more fun games you could be playing).
As a shooter/SHMUP, it just feels weak. This feeling of weakness comes from everything from the music and sound to the gameplay mechanics and art.
Your gun and the enemy guns shoot tiny bullets that just go "pew pew". You can't spam your shots either - you have limited ammo with each ship so you'll find the gameplay consisting of making tiny adjustments, trying to line up with an enemy ship, and tapping once only to hear a pathetic "pew" and weak "retro" explosion sound effect. The hitboxes don't match up with the enemy sprites at all - the actual hitbox for an enemy is usually smaller than the actual sprite, which makes it even more frustrating to try to line up shots.
The music is just as tinny and weak sounding as the sound effects. It's actually fine that it blends in with the whole soundscape of the game, but overall I just found it to be entirely forgettable and not add to the game at all.
Furthermore, and this is probably the most detrimental to the core gameplay: the art lacks hard edges/contrast and makes it difficult to tell what is going on. When there's a lot of stuff on the screen, it becomes a huge cluster of nonsense and makes it very difficult to parse the game state and keep track of yourself. A simple addition of a few visual cues, some nice hard outlines for the enemies or something like that would've done loads to enable more satisfying, skillful play. They did a great job of making the enemy types easy to distinguish so I'm surprised that the devs didn't consider this sort of issue.
There's also several other frustrating bits. Things like the enemies being able to turn around when they get behind you and shoot you. It's just not very fun to deal with.
At times, however, this game does manage to be quite fun when you're successfully stringing together several jumps and taking out lots of enemies as you go. These moments are few and far between, but I imagine if you played it more and got more skillful you would experience this more often. Also, the challenging parts of this game are quite rewarding when you finally beat them. They also avoided making it too frustrating by letting you continue from the wave you were on even when you lose all of your lives (though your score is reset).
The story is quite cryptic and so sparsely told throughout the game that I had a hard time following it.
In conclusion, just contrast this with the feel of playing something like Raiden where you're making tiny corrections to dodge through swarms of bullets, all the while firing away with an upgradeable massive weapon, wreaking havoc on the enemy and causing explosions everywhere while a rad soundtrack plays. That's partially one of the things that makes those games fun to play - the amount of polish that went into evoking a feeling of power and intensity. This game just doesn't evoke that feeling, and maybe it didn't intend to, but it just doesn't FEEL fun.
If you're just looking for something new and like climbing leaderboards and raising your high score, you might enjoy this, but why not play a more thrilling game?

The worst part about Tropico 5 is the extent to which I don't care about playing the campaign missions. The campaign leaves you with two basic islands to build off of, and your progress carries over mission-mission. This means that the actual act of 'city-building' gets extremely limited - because missions are now about tacking on some arbitrary requirement rather than striving for the most efficient/aesthetically pleasing system. Furthermore, as there are limitations on the number of consecutive times you can re-use an island, both islands have to be able to accommodate any industry (as missions can often boil down to 'make x, y, and then z industry'). Accommodating every industry makes the islands generic - taking away the adaptation game of Tropicos past of dealing with soil/resource/beauty variances. The overarching plot is dumb, and political tweaks (especially over-militarization as detailed in other reviews) just makes things worse.

Being a huge fan of the Tropico series, I was itching to get Tropico 5.  When  it came on sale, I pounced on the chance to get it.
What to make of this release of the game....
There is a large improvement graphics wise, with the islands and the buildings looking really good.  What is sad is that a lot of the building animations was somehow "cut" from the game. In Tropico 4 if you upgrade any of the buildings with skylights or aircons you could see the building changing with these add-ons.  Animations in the pubs and restaurants was also much better in T4, you could see people entering the building and sitting at the tables.  Largely there are no such small detailed animations on buildings in T5.
There is really a lot to do in the game.  I like the improved economics system, where you can set up trade routes with better pricing for some of your resources and goods.  There is also now a constitution where you can set the type of community that you build.  This is also one of the things that you cannot really see the changes easily, eg. One of the viewable difference is when you select professional military.  Doing that I had all my soldiers abandon their posts in exchange for soldiers with High School training.
The introduction of a timeperiod type of system is nice, but it can at times be a pain especially early in the game.  Especially when you have to please the king with a lot of stuff just so that your reign could be extended for another couple of months.  As soon as you get past this era your are back to elections and keeping your people happy.  Some of the buildings also change according to the timeperiod eg. The docks change the crane and the type of ships that dock.
Another annoying feature in the game is the building/people cards.  In Tropico 4, you could see all the information of the building on the card, even the people visiting the buidling.  The people cards had detailed info on what they needed as well as the tourist cards.  This information is lacking in Tropico 5, sadly...
The campaign part of the game is a 50/50 parcel.  You only play over 2 islands during the campaign.  Each of the missions build on the previous one.  So if you build up a good economy on your island in the previous mission you will carry over that advantage for the next mission in the campaign.  BUT....  You only get to play that island for one mission!!  Beware if you do not spend enough time in building a good economy on both of your islands!!!  You then have to select the poor island for a troublesome mission and it will see you failing that mission over and over.  I ran into that problem to the point of rage quiting in the end.
Having given the multiplayer a try, I can hardly say anything about it.  Still trying to get a game to play with someone else, where the game does not quit because of different versions of the game.  Will have to try it again at some point.
So what is the verdict??   This is a nice looking game, with some nice changes, but I think Kalypso where not quit sure if their were trying to follow the Anno type games or trying to create a different Tropico.  For me Tropico 4 is a way better island gaming experience than Tropico 5.  So if you have never played any of the Tropico franchise and you get this in the bargain bin, give it a try.  If you love the Tropico series, rather stay with Tropico 4.
Special note to the dev's:  I would love to see a new Tropico Pirates Cove, please!!!  Had endless fun with that one!!

It saddens me to see this game get so many terrible reviews solely for the fact that it has dlc on release and "Lacks content". May I remind you that 99% of the dlc is purely cosmetics. SKINS. You can buy these individually or in a bundle for the correlating pattern which is in fact cheaper than buying all of the skins on their own. The other 1% is the season pass; this offers you 4 upcoming hunters and 3 skins for the original launch monsters. Wonderful. So what am I getting at? I'm saying that everyone complaining about dlc is over exaggerating and jumping on the hate wagon of misconception. They say that this game does not nearly have enough content to be $60. Fine, I'll let anyone have their own opinion, but maybe they should look into the overlooked details and facts of the game before stating it so violently.
Let's talk about how much content this game really has. Evolve has a total of 4 classes, and for every class there are 3 characters, which puts us at 12 hunters total. Each character has their own story, personality, unique abilities and play-style (This also goes for the monsters). Every character has individual progression as well. Within this progression there are 3 tiers; each tier having different and more difficult challenges than the last. There are rewards for completing each tier as well. Most of the rewards are little icons you can use to individualize your profile badge. Although, when you complete the 3rd tier you unlock a special skin for that character as well. Not to mention there is an over all leveling system that all of your experience from every hunter/monster goes into. Also, by leveling up you unlock perks for both sides of the fight in which each side (hunter/monster) has 9 perks that have 3 tiers. The progression and rewards for monsters are in the same format as the hunters. So, if you do the math this gives us a total of 15 skins (1 for every playable entity), 45 icons, and 9 perks for each hunter and monster. Oh wait, and don't forget the game modes! There is Hunt, Rescue, Nest, Defend, and evacuate which is a 5 round game which includes all of these game types. I think that is a considerable and reasonable amount of content for launch, but that's just my opinion, remember these things folks! Everything else above that sentence in this paragraph is fact.
I see people commenting on how there are multiplayer bugs and un-stabilized play. I will have you know that I have not experienced any unstable gameplay while playing the game online or offline. I have experienced a few minor bugs, here's the list: un-wanted cursor appearances and disappearances, a small part in the wall on a certain map I cannot jet pack climb on as the hunter, and a small wall that can be jumped over, but cannot be climbed over on monster side. None of these were anything that shortened the length of my hair or had made me contemplate the quality of the end product of this game. I can think of plenty other games where glitches and bugs have been much much worse. I say that all of these things will be fix shortly, for they are certainly easy to spot and reproduce.
Conclusion? I say the amount content is sufficient for release. A big reason why I think people are complaining about content is because they were spoiled from the start. For those who played the game in the alpha and beta stages of the game (especially beta), they were nearly given the whole game on a silver platter! Every single character was available to anyone that pre-ordered the game through steam during the time of the beta. If you didn't preorder you were only missing out on the 3rd character of that particular class! From my knowledge there were not any restrictions on leveling up or character progression. The only thing missing from the game were the individual game modes! And skins.... don't forget the skins. Bottom line is I think everyone needs to see the game for what it is. That it's a really fun and exciting game to play. Whether it's just a game to run around large areas to shoot strange and interesting creatures or an in-depth strategic battle for monster and man alike. Look for yourself! Try to find comments saying that this game is just "straight 2k dumpster baby" or "10/10, uninstall simulator 2015" because I'm sure they aren't there. This game is good fun for everyone.
Danks for reading.

On the one hand, this is a walking simulator: there are no challenges and no meaningful choices. It's far more linear even than Gone Home, which is practically on rails already. I never would have bought this on my own, and, if I'd known anything about it, I probably would have left it on my shelf for all eternity. Games like Dear Esther briefly interested me, but then I realized I could have deeper and more meaningful interactions with movies -- and, indeed, the failures of editing and writing in so many walking sims could never have passed muster in the more rigorous world of filmmaking. So I gave up on the entire genre as a failure: games that aren't actually games, I decided, are bad games.
Fortunately for me, I didn't buy this game, and I didn't know anything about it going in.  (It was a Christmas present, and I deliberately avoided learning anything about it because I was told to avoid spoilers.)
The Beginner's Guide is an affecting meditation on the meaning of games, game design, the creative process, constructive critique, and why we humans do anything (or why we should). The framework is deceptively frank: it's simply a running commentary by Davey Wreden (the creator) on the strange games created by a former friend of his, Coda. Davey walks you through each of Coda's games with a refreshing earnestness, but, as you learn more about Coda through his games, questions begin to arise.
This is a meaningful story that could not have been told in any other way.  It wouldn't make any sense as a movie.  It would be terrible as a more game-y game.  It has to be this.  It's not a thin pile of weirdness pretending to be a deep meditation.  It's not just a bunch of aesthetic choices trying to evoke a certain mood.  It's not a political screed dressed up with the trappings of a story.  It's a walking simulator that is really struggling to think through some challenging personal problems, and invites you to think through them, too. As someone who also creates things (shameless plug: I write for fan audio drama Starship Excelsior), I recognize both Davey and Coda in myself, and I've had some of the same kinds of struggles recently. I'm grateful to Davey for sharing it with us.

On the very surface, this seems like an oldskool sidescrolling shooter like R-type or Parodius. It even has 16-bit graphics and sounds, so it's even more deceptive to write it off as "just another shooter" before you try it.
But there is one very important twist in play: you don't have a ship. Instead, you're some sort of psychich entity that can claim control of nearby ships. This is interesting in different levels:
-a variety of weapons. Each enemy can be braincontrolled (if you aim that braincontrolling option correctly), and each ship handles differently.
-variety in play style. As each ship has limited armor and ammo, you NEED to change ships every so often.
-ties in with the plot seemlessly over the course of 80 levels.
The story deserves credit as well. I generally don't play this sort of game for the story, but it managed to capture me nonetheless. And that's remarkable, seeing how it's "just" shooting enemies. I won't say I get all the details between the humans, the artarus (squids) and the overseer, but...it's certainly miles above the average for shooters. :-)
I'm actually amazed I only played this game for 3 hours. Sure, the levels are short and things can get repetitive outside the boss fights (which are awesome!), but this is the sort of a-few-hours game.
So all in all: I recommend it. :-)

A well made shmup with a unique gameplay mechanic that allows you to take over enemy ships.
The design and the retro-style graphics look great, especially if you are into classic shmups. The chiptune soundtrack is catchy.
The "Enemy Mind" main campaign is quite short and can easily be finished in under 2 hours (it has some additional modes though that provide more to do). Between the levels there are "cut scenes" (text blocks) that tell a story that I personally really didn't care for. The enemy ships look cool and there are many different types to fight and take over.
On the down side there are no power ups or shield upgrades at all and every ship only has a limited amount of ammunition and shield power. This forces the player to use the game's unique mechanic of taking over other ships.
There are also some puzzle stages that require you to switch vessels very strategically. Boss fights are very fun and challenging. Generally the difficulty level is low, so this is nothing for hardcore bullet hell players.

Second Impression (5 hrs in): Something I noticed as I played through this time: I think the narrative changes depending on how you play. I find this to be, on the one hand, fascinating due to the game's simplicity, while, on the other hand, it's incredibly tedious.
See, if the narrative is designed the way that I think it is, then it's almost up to chance on what you'll get. I mean, there's definitely an element of skill to it, but it seems very "hope you know the level design and can plan way ahead."
So that part is a little disappointing. That said, the narrative *is* pretty interesting and it did surprise me when I realzied what exactly was going on. And the story's culmination in the final boss battle was fantastic. It's so simplistic but really rounded out the game in a great way and made it feel complete.
That said, I do have a few other complaints. The last two levels or so seem pretty grueling. There's this part, right before the last boss, that nearly drove me out of my goddamn mind. It was harder than the damn final boss. Some bosses are sort of recycled. I say sort of because their difficulty is ramped up. However, thei reappearance in what is basically a "super" form is disappointing and it diminishes the special feelings of the first enconters.
On balance, this game is an interesting take on the side-scrolling shooter. With an engaging story and fun game mechanics that require the player to adjust as they play, Enemy Mind is sure to leave a positive mark on everybody who plays it.
Initial impression (1.4 hrs in): I dig it. Imagine Gradius had a baby with Kirby and you get Enemy Mind. You, as the player, do not control a single, permanent ship. Instead, you hop around from ship to ship, each with a finite amount of health. Once you run out of bullets for a ship, that's it. There's no ammo pickups or anything. You have to
jump ship and hop into a new one.
Each ship has a different firing mechanism, effectively replacing the traditional "power up" system. So half of the strategy is knowing when's the right time to use particular ships. However, some models clearly stand out from others, and this style of gameplay lends itself to a certain disadvantage on your first runs, as you don't really know what's coming.
In fact, that's primarily where the challenge lies, at least for me. Do I have a ship that's good for the situation? Sometimes I don't and it's not a big deal because I can still concentrate harder and make do. But on a few other occasions I don't and the difficulty escalates much higher because it's simply not a viable choice in the circumstances. This is probably the game's one downside so far: not every ship is viable in every situation. This it what makes particular ships stand out clearly from the rest, because they have versatility in every situation. You'll find yourself looking for those, a la dominant strategy. However, I do not think this detracts from the game's fun all that much.
So far, so good. I look forward to playing more soon.

The Park is a fascinating experience.  You start the game at the entrance of an amusement park, with your child having left behind his teddy bear in the park. When you go to the help desk, your child runs in and you must follow his trail through the park.
I'm actually fine with the concept of an "interactive movie", and I'm particularly open to ones in the horror genre. The Park was more memorable than I had hoped. The early parts can be a bit slow, but the game steadily picks up as you get further along. The game doesn't rely on the creepiness of the park alone. A lot of the game is focused on exploring the psychological state of the mother, and watching her mind unravel the deeper she goes into the park.
While I was satisfied with the overall experience, I do feel that the developers  could've done more in certain areas.  The areas of the park seem bigger than they need to be. Not that I explored every nook and cranny, but I did try to look around, and it seems like there's not usually a reward for going off the beaten path. One of the things I value most in horror games aren't the monsters or the jumpscares, but finding creepy little oddities scattered around the environment. Although "following the trail" is an important theme in the game, I think there could've been a bit more detail for the players who like to explore. Like many horror games, there's a large focus on reading notes. But in many cases, the letters are way too small, and I had to practically press my face against my screen to be able to make out what they said.
The game really has two stories, the history and nature of the park, and exploring the character of the mother. By the end, I felt like one was resolved, and the other wasn't. I've never played The Secret World and I don't know anything about it, and perhaps playing that game would clear up the remaining questions I have, but a spin-off should be able to stand on its own. It seems that a large part of the story is symbolic, but I feel that may have resulted in a somewhat weak ending.
I did have noticeable frame rate issues, but my PC is fairly old by now, and I don't have the technical know-how to say if it's my computer or the game. The indoor areas usually ran fine though.
If you aren't put off by a lack of real gameplay and just want to immerse yourself in the story and the environment, then I would definitely recommend playing through The Park.

I backed this game on Kickstarter, and it's better than I ever could have hoped for.
This game, at its core, is a tokusatsu simulator. What is tokusatsu? It's a style of Japanese live action television featuring transforming super heroes, martial arts, and special effects and stunts.
Let me first say this: don't let the "Inspired by Saban's Power Rangers" throw you or discourage you from buying it. The designers were forced to put that under threat of legal action from Saban, and there are a few subtle digs at Saban throughout the game. Tokusatsu heroes are much bigger than just what came to the West as Power Rangers. In actuality, many countries including Brazil and France got Japanese tokusatsu super heroes in the eighties and nineties before Power Rangers was a "thing", and that is inspired by the full range of Japanese superhero shows. Fans of tokusatsu heroes will spot references not only to classic Super Sentai, but also to Kamen Rider and Metal Hero shows such as Space Sheriff Gavan and Juspion.
There are two main portions to the game: tactical combat and studio management. In the tactical combat portion, you battle "mook" enemies and a "monster of the week" in a format almost identical to Final Fantasy Tactics or Disgaea in an isometric perspective. There are always "objectives" for each episode given by your show director such as performing a certain number of stunts or defeating the enemy in a certain way. Doing so will boost your ratings and improve the show's income.
In the studio management portion, you purchase and set up upgrades for your humble studio, investing in better cameras, hiring big name actors and skilled crew, and upgrading your special effects and costumes. While your costumed heroes may start out with a mop bucket on their head and bicycle pads for armor, with enough positive fan reaction (which you'll see after each episode is filmed via a sampling of tweets about the episode) you might eventually be wearing costumes on the level of a professional production! Additionally, interactions with other companies and fans might affect your production. What will you do when other studios start coming to you with their hands out? Take them to court or give them a cut? What will you do when overseas fansubbers start subbing your show? Let them on the chance it'll increase your merchandising, or drop the hammer on them?
In addition to this, you have a great deal of customization of your show itself. You can name your studio, name your super hero team, and even customize what they say when they transform or do their super attack. Want them to shout out, "Henshin!" when they transform instead of the default? You can do it! Want to pick your own colors instead of the default? You can do it! Want to have an Orange Ranger instead of a Yellow Ranger? Want them ALL to be red heroes? Yes, you can even do that!
This game follows the standard Sentai story elements: heroes battle foot soldier "mooks" on foot in their civilian clothes until they build up enough power (audience approval!) to transform -- and when they do, it boosts your audience approval even more. Once you defeat the monster of the week, of course, as any fan of the shows know, the monster has to grow huge. And what would Sentai be without giant robot battles? Purchase gear and equipment, assemble your giant robot and have a battle on a massive scale.
In addition, there is a motorcycle prop you'll receive later, and an option to shift the show into a "solo mode" featuring a lone motorcycle Rider hero with a flowing scarf that favors jump kicks as his preferred method of defeating monsters. So in case you are curious -- yes, you CAN be a Kamen Rider!
The graphics are 8-bit, but don't let that discourage you. The animations are great, the characters are big and bright with big cutscenes when important events happen. The music is catchy and reminiscent of classic Commodore chiptunes or Nintendo 8-bit sounds with a catchier sound.
Overall, I highly recommend this game. If you're a tokusatsu fan, you definitely will want to play this, but even if you just have a passing interest in superheroes, tactical battle games, or managing a TV studio, the charm and uniqueness of this game will certainly entertain you.

Now that the game is finally done with its Final Wave of beta-testing, the Super Marvelous Super Sentai inspired RPG is in everyone's hands, and it was well worth the wait.
Only vaguely similar in structure to the also wonderful Knights of Pen & Paper (also developered by Behold Studios), the pixelated adventure takes your through the many misadventured of your own custom made team of  Sentai / Power Rangers inspired actors who have abandoned their previous, terrible acting gig to create their own series.
The director? You, of course!
The game is rife with fan service, and if you have any love for the original Sentai series or the Americanised Power Rangers interpretation of the show, you will feel right at home with this game. A great amount of customistation and developement is under your control, from the genders and colours of your team to the overall look of your costumes.
The main game is a RPG treat, bringing you through numerous seasons and many episodes of your own hilariously awkward show. No trope is left untouched as you battle and "chromatze" your way through hoards of enemy lackies and boss monsters in the well designed turned based RPG gameplay. Though the pixel art may not be to everyone's taste, the humour behind the game's inspiration shines through beautifully.
This is a highly recommended game, and one I encourage every Sentai / Power Rangers to check out. If nothing else, its a better Power Rangers game than any official branded has ever been.
P.S. I make absolutely no apologies for the puns used in this review.

I don't believe rating the game poorly for these trivial reasons is very fair to be honest.
Now to the review. The game is pure pick up and play fun, there's alot of nuance to learn but overall you can have some fun stomping around since there is levels to split up experienced players and new players. Obviously right now you have alot of beta players etc.. who actually know the game well and so on so it's a bit skewed.
The hunting, tracking and trapping concept of the game is actually incredibly rewarding once you start to get the hang of it and the combat when coordinated a little is actually quite intriguing in itself. The monster gameplay is also interesting and has alot of nuance to it. Each character plays quite differently as well which means you have a total of 15 characters in the base game at release, 3 in each role.
Playing with bots as well is also of a reasonable level. Learning the game the monster AI will kick your♥♥♥♥♥
This is not your typical fps deathmatch game and treating it as such means you'll lose and not have a good time. This is closer to a strategy game as you track down the monster and try to sneak up on it and engage a successful fight. The slow regen of monster shields means that short skimishes do have some benefit to the outcome of the match even if the monster escapes. The design of the game also tries to avoid anyone having to sit dead for too long unless you really lose a fight badly.
If anything can be said for this game, through all the marketing hype I wonder if enough detailed guidance has been given to how to play the game properly. The ingame tutorial videos and gameplay sections are pretty good at explaining basic stuff but the nuances are quickly required.
Overall I this game has ushered a new era of online gaming as the asymmetrical pvp works very well and demonstrates a good balance. This is how you died.
The entirety of the game is how you died. There is a mystery as to why the zombie outbreak occurred, and you might even find some answers before you die. Ultimately though, Project Zomboid does not represent an against-all-odds struggle where you overcome the undead. Instead, after dying, every subsequent playthrough just lets you survive a little longer, do a little better, and  learn a little more.
Death can come in many, many ways. You have to manage needs, similar to The Sims . You need to eat, sleep, and even need to rest your legs if you're running around too much . You aren't able to see meters that indicate your exact state, but moodlets will appear to let you know exactly what your character is thinking or feeling at any given time. Injuries are common, so if you're scratched or bitten by a zombie, you better tend to them quickly.
The town is populated by other survivors and looters, some just as desperate as you. Everyone is  scared by the thousands of zombies roaming the city, and a looter just might find you and put a shotgun round in your chest as he takes your food and other supplies. Scripted events like this will keep you on your toes, but with every failure comes the chance to prepare a little better for next time.
The zombies themselves are the slow and lumbering kind. You can fairly easily outrun them, but they are legion, and don't easily forget. They are attracted by blood and noise, and all it takes is a single mistake to advertise your location to the horde. You've never had to think in so many different directions and cover your butt in so many different ways before. As a result, every moment is exciting because you never know what lurks around the corner and whether you missed that one thing that will give away your position. Getting into a routine and locking down your safehouse will be just as important as finding food and scavenging for weapons.
Crafting is also a large part of Project Zomboid. At the moment, your character already "knows" the recipes needed to create objects to help him: combining a can opener, a can of soup, and a pot results in a big pot of edible soup, for example. Cooking will eventually be part of the game as well, adding another layer of complexity to basic survival; after all, you don't want to be suffering from food poisoning due to eating undercooked meat if you're being chased down by zombies.
Overall, well worth a buy. It's easy to see that Project Zomboid has potential and lots of merits.

I expected to spend 30 minutes to an hour in this game then forget about it. "Another zombie survival game oh great", How wrong I was. Unlike most games this handles not only physical needs such as food, warmth and water, but tackles the deep down grittiness of the emotional and psychological. 3 zombies lumbering towards you, you WILL panic and this is shown by de-buffs causing your character to swing weapons less accurately in a wild panic or even an angry frenzy if he is hurt. Fall from a second story window fleeing a house invading horde? You'll suffer serious injury and be in agonising pain, slowing you down and affecting your focus and accuracy.
Water supplies and power grids are set to timers as well, spend too long fighting the horde and you may find yourself starving to death or severely dehydrated - I once resorted to having to drink bleach - and thus gaining even more de-buffs. Oh the joys!
Learn to farm for food, forage, hunt or steal for your supper, create the ultimate blockade (with the right tools of course) with the crafting system. Create stronger structures as you read books and progress your handy skills until you can build a fortress fit for the last remnants of humanity.
The game has a fantastic time system, you can set the day length to be a quick 10 minute day, or a full scale real time apocalypse. The seasons change, temperatures alter and even weather patterns will change according to how many days, months or -if your a true survival expert -years. Temperature change can also cause negative affects by the way... to hot? Get a drink ASAP. Too cold? Get indoors or wear more appropriate clothing.
The budding modding and map making community are out to make your experience more difficult with more difficult maps and realistic alterations to existing mechanics or even adding new mechanics -one of my favourite mods adds lock picking and breaking locks to open doors-, the possibilities are truly endless... Just like the horde that will be hunting you down every step you take.
Yes, there are bugs, glitches and the odd infuriating moments. But for an early access release. Damn this game is good.
I would totally recommend it.

Enemy Mind is a 2D sidescrolling shooter with a twist: you don't have a ship of your own. Instead, you control other ships, doing as much damage as you can until you're nearly dead, or out of bullets... then, you just jump out into another ship.
Pretty simple, huh? Well, with a decent variety of enemies, it creates some chaotic situations! It also has an interesting way of telling the story, although it's not very accessible for most people (as it requires you noticing it, and then replaying a lot of it).
I'll say right away that I've had a lot of fun with it! I think it's an unique addition to the genre and certainly worth trying out if you like these kind of games.
There's isn't all that much to say about
. It's clearly inspired by the older 8/16bit era, but it's a modernized version of it, with cool visual effects. It manages to stand on its own and not relying purely on nostalgia to look appealing.
Every ship is distinguishable, which is needed for the player to know who to control at certain times. One problem I had, at times, is the blending between the bullets and the backgrounds. It didn't happen too often, but I did get killed a few times from bullets I couldn't see.
The
was actually pretty awesome! It's also very modern sounding chiptunes. It packs a punch! Definitely get the soundtrack if you can, it's awesome, and adds to the whole atmosphere of the game.
Now, about the game itself, starting with
.
You go through 8 levels, each subdivided into several waves. You have several lives, and you can gain more with combos, but once you deplete them all, you only go back to the beginning of the wave, having the chance to keep going from that point onwards with your score reset to 0.
This makes the game forgiving for those who simply want to beat it, leaving the challenge for the score-attack audience, which is a great way of doing things, in my opinion!
With that said, it still has a few challenging waves, and the game doesn't save your progress regarding the waves. You need to beat each level in one sitting (which isn't really a problem, since the levels aren't very long). At the end of each level, you'll see your place on the Leaderboards, with the surrounding players.
In this case, I want to write about
. Not a very common aspect that I take notice of, especially in an arcade game!
But they've done it in an interesting way, so here it is...
The game has 2 races in war, and you can possess ships from both. At the end of each wave, you'll get a short exposition, from the perspective of the race you're in control of. At the end of the level, the same happens, with a longer exposition.
This means that to uncover the whole story of the game, you can't just go head first and shoot everything. It makes you fit the story pieces together, little by little. There are people on the community hub doing this and taking screenshots of the different plot scenes, if you're interested.
While this is a confusing way of doing story (and will leave you with barely anything if you don't make an effort to uncover it), it's understandable. In this genre, the story isn't very important. Most players will care about beating the levels, not the backstory. However, if you're not like that, you have a little extra! Not caring doesn't diminish your enjoying of the game, but caring does certainly enhance it, so it's great!
Finally, let's talk about the
. There's isn't all that much to say about it, really.
As I said before, you can take control of enemy ships, and you can shoot, and move around. That's pretty much it.
Each ship has very limited ammo, so it constantly keeps you switching around. And each type of ship also has diferent movement/speed, and shooting patterns (some shoot all around, some are stationary turrets, some shoot vertically, some are stuck to the edges/ground, etc.).
It's up to the player to evaluate each wave and act accordingly. It's generally not too difficult, with a few exceptions.
The Boss fights were also a good change of pace, although 2 of them were recycled in a slightly harder version. I won't spoil the last Boss, but I'll say that it was a pretty fun fight!
The downside (for some) is that going through the campaign once will probably not take you longer than 3 hours. But, in addition to the campaign (that you can easily replay, trying out different ships, piecing the story together, etc.) they also provide extra modes that you unlock through the campaign. One is an Arcade Mode, one is Boss Rush, once is a Rock Simulator (yes, you control a meteorite), an early prototype of the game, a flappy bird clone, and the Credits sequence (yes, you can shoot the developers!).
So yeah. If you're into this sort of games, you have my whole-hearted recommendation! I really enjoyed playing through it, and there's certainly more content to keep you entertained, aside from the core campaign.

One of the best games ever I think, I can point out some negative things but they would feel quite forced, most notably low fov, even though there is a fix, and infuriating Little Sister sequence near the end.
My awe for this game is almost like a fanboyism, as its gameplay in my opinion was unfairly criticized, since I find it genius, steadily growing more complex, and actually for the better. It sucked me in like a vortex and never let me go until the end.
Gunplay felt fun, but it was only a small portion of an actual combat, the evergrowing arsenal of plasmids, perks and tools offered varied effects on enemies and security machines, with ability to hack nearly everything- I was able to create my own little strongholds, with its defences constantly clearing or weakening enemies that I could later scavenge. In the middle of battles with my hacked and friendly machines I was able to create tactics and strategies, adjusted to the kinds of enemies I face- electricity, fire, cold, launchpads and bees were all affecting them differently, combined with proper weapons I was able to figure out a position of advantage, and switch between tactics while keeping an eye on my resources.
Resources are gained through scavenging corpses and containers as well as buying them from vending machines [also hackable], levels are vast and offer quite some room for exploration, with secrets scattered around the maps.
Later in game there comes in a crafting system, as well as various junk that now can be used to craft, it's used at the special machines that offer an alternative to regular vending machines, as well as offer different kinds of ammunition, so that you are encouraged to use all of it, to gain most of the potential ammo.
Later on we get chances to upgrade....well practically everything-perks, powers, unlocked slots for both, weapons, health and EVE capacity. Most of it is possible to gain in one playthrough if a player is stubborn, and instead of making him overpowered, it simply gives him more freedom of choice. People usually praise other elements of Bioshock, but for me gameplay is where it shines the brightest.
This does not mean that they are wrong in terms of plot, it's amazing, full of crazy personas, enviromental storytelling, scattered recordings from the past of Rapture, and one of the most memorable plot twists in history of videogames. An Utopia at the bottom of the sea is marvelous, and amazes with its concept and story, I tried to look all around and through the windows, to see the whole of it and experience its beauty. I find it impossible that men from IG were crazy enough to develop such a game, the word ambitious doesn't even begin to cover it, they weren't crushed by the weight of this project and actually made something breathtaking and inspiring. Graphics were stunning and still look good, voice acting is brilliant, story is amazing, and gameplay is superb. I don't know how, but it's there- Bioshock; something that was meant to be a successor to System Shock, and I think there is no shame to actually call it that, while Bioshock is different from it- I might say it even reaches its level of brilliance.

The biggest problem of the game however is its rather unimaginative gameplay. The puzzles are not hard to figure out at all and the items are fairly easy to find. Most of the conversations are just made to further progress in the game and the ones which are not, don't add anything to the game aside from random tidbits of information of the world.

After playing this apparent "tie-in" game, I'm no longer so ambivalent.  I'm now quite willing to give up said life if it's AS ♥♥♥♥ING GOOD as this.  Which I'm pretty confident it WON'T be, but one can only live in hope.
Yes, it's a "walking simulator".  Yes, it won't "challenge" you...well, certainly not on a "gameplay" or "skillz" level.  Yes, it's also not that long, and would henceforth perhaps be asking a bit much in the price department if it wasn't for the fact that it's HANDS-DOWN ONE OF THE BEST WALKING SIMULATORS YOU WILL EVER PLAY.  And one of the absolute creepiest, to boot.
Good story, GREAT storytelling...if you're one of those people who, like me, frequently finds themselves in arguments with less enlightened folk about the "artistry" which is possible in video games, then here's one game which will provide you with plentiful ammunition in taking down your next such opponent.  Games like this are the reason why I virtually never watch horror movies any more, in spite of the fact that I ♥♥♥♥ING LOVE horror movies.
I have seen the future of horror gaming, my friends...and that future is bright.  Truly gorgeous stuff.

Chromatize!!!
Oh, this game is going to stay in my mind when I am thinking about round based strategie right after UFO: Enemy Unkown (sorry - its hard to beat that one)
You play as 5 stunt(wo)men who decide to disobey their director and leave to make a hero-show on their own. Each has a specific role ingame that makes one more awesome than the other.
The plot divides and intertwines between "real-life" and show which leads to funny dialouges between the characters and enemies.
The game itself is NOT a serious simulation and even makes fun of itself. Its mixed with a little bit of income managment and skill editing of the different classes by crafting and/or buying items.
The crafting menu is not complex and not too simple - you get new equipment to buy/craft every "season"(which can be compared to chapters) which require rare materials you can find during an episode(level) or craft/recycle out of lower grade materials.
The gameplay itself can be compared to other RBS - you move your characters a given number of tiles per turn and attack - or use a weapon - or use a skill - or prepare for 'Teamwork' to unleash the super epic ultra finishing move penta deluxe!!!
While gameplay is kept simple the game gives you a number of goals you have to achieve (like: Kill [...] in 2 turns.) in order to gather more audience and get more money and fans for that episode(level) which get harder just like the enemies.
While the enemies are sort of clone troopers its not getting boring since you will encounter a new enemytype or boss almost every level.
The graphics themselves are outstanding (my bar for this one is not set too high) - the looks of the actors are changing with the equipment they are wearing and animations are smooth and flawless. You can see every minute that went into the creation of every art asset in this game.
I'm not quite through with the game but as far as I played I would say that since I saw it on gamescom 2014 it lived up to all my hopes I put in it and didn't waste any of its possible potential. I absolutely fell in love with this game. (Thanks for being with MEGA-BOOTH at gamescom to the devs at this point)
Buy this game if you want a fun ride with awesome ideas/design and changing gameplay.

Edit: This review was done with a key obtained from the developer. Somehow, I missed the disclaimer on this originally.
Not since Darkest Dungeon has an experience hit on as many levels as Chroma Squad has. There is a lot of wonderful design decisions made here, and the attention to detail is what shines here: Every detail seems to be thought out from the wonderful Tactical RPG that involves acrobatics and teamwork, to the detail of the story that plays to the strength of the nostalgia of the old Power Rangers. I had this goofy grin on my face the entire time I was playing the game, and this game is an early contender for Indie game of the year. It's that good.
+:
-Team based combat, especially on hard difficulties, rewards thinking and strategy in its teamwork based combat. Acrobatics (the ability to launch people further then they could run by themselves.
-Strong detail payed attention to the details of each episode within the story, to make it feel like a old Power Rangers episode/series.
-Customization of game takes things to new levels with catchphrases and squad names. Adds a whole level of immersion.
-Little Details make the experience that much more immersive, such as punishing for using a finishing move that doesn't kill a monster. Audience gauge and Director guidelines help add challenge to make the episode more flashy.
-Overall, the nostalgia that the game repeatedly hits works on almost every level, from the 8 bit graphics to the references to the series past. In addition, it's able to mix up the modern day media/internet culture into it as well.
-Studio upgrades leave a lot of different options to play around with. Upgrades, Mech Upgrades, Studio Upgrades, etc.
-:
-Mech battles could be a little bit more challenging.
-Some more information can be provided at times regarding teamwork skills (like the supports healing factor, for example)
-Comes very close to copyright infrigenment in several cases. Worrisome in some cases.

The game starts off relatively nice and easy with broad day light and a mother going to ask for a lost teddy bear. Then her son runs off into The Park and Lorraine, the mother and protagonist, run after him.
This is the point where the excrements hits the fan and you are all of the sudden in an old abandoned amusement park with a life of its own, but what a spectacular amusement park it is.
I was expecting the game to be creepy and keep me on edge at all times. Funcom has attempted to achieve that by using jump scares and a rich athmosphere, both visually and audibly. And the increasingly creepy story they wish to tell in this game just adds to the tension. For my part, the experience was horror and my ticker reached max rate at some points in the game.
However, I found that there were moments of sheer dullness in the game and although it picked up towards the end, they did not end on a "horror"-climax which the game built up to. Instead they had a cinematic ending which was, more or less, lit up and was not notably exciting.
The story element of this game, written by a team of award winning story tellers, is very much playing on strings of the Bonkers-guitar and they want to tell the tale of a very twisted woman. I feel the story line is good, albeit perhaps somewhat thin, but as you progress you get an insight of what's going on inside Lorraine head.
The game play is fairly straight forward and the game rail roads you all the way through the game.
You enter the park. You get on some rides. Along the the way you are narrated by Lorraines inner voice and you find clues, such as reports and notes, providing explanations and feeding you story. And finally you reach the final "attraction" which tries to tie it all together.
There is no "mini games", puzzles, etc - just a story unfolding as you progress through the game.
I think anyone who cares more about the journey, rather than the destination, and who allows him- or herself to be scared and drawn into the game will enjoy The Park.
So I would recommend it for those certain individuals.

This is a wonderful game. I spent many hours playing this game back before it was on steam. Its not finished, and does have some flaws, but if youre willing to look past them *you damn well better be!* you wont be sorry.
The goal here is not to "win" the game, and if you come into it with such an attitude then youre going to be very unhappy.
You are jut trying to survive for as long as you possibly can. You WILL die! But the more you die, the more fun the game is. This is truly a game where you can say to yourself "well if I only did such and such THIS way" or "next time will be different because EXAMPLE" and get to instantly implement your new plan of action and attack.
You start of as an average Joe/Jane. You are not super man, not a bad♥♥♥♥♥MMA fighter, not some elite sharp shooter. You are a block of clay and need to be molded into shape. You cant go toe to toe with zombies and expect to live. You will be bitten, you will die. For my money, this is the most realistic zombie game on the market while still maintaining a level of fun and intertainment.
There is a real sense of loss when you end up as zombie chow. Sometimes I need to walk away from the computer before I jump back in, but the game always compels you to do just that, jump back in. There is so much you can do, so many things you can try. One of my first and most memorable attempts to survive ended when I left a stove on in a house I borded up. I went to the second floor to sleep, and in the morning came down stairs to an inferno. All of the windows and one door I could get to where barricade up and the only other exit was behind a wall of flames, and the house was surrounded by zombies.  I ran back upstairs and to the bed, I was able to make only one small rope from a sheet, but it did not reach the ground *needed 2 to hit the grass* but it was better than burning to death, so with my nail I set the sheet rope up, decended, still caught fire because the building was really burning good, dropped one story to the ground, and as I struggled to get to my feet was set upon by no less than 7 hungry zombies who had a strong craving for survivor flambe!
Have an idea what you would do should the world turn zed over night? Zomboid will let you test your plan.  For $15 bucks you get one hell of a deep and complex crafting system, great RPG elements and total freedom to play as you wish.  The multiplayer is great, and gives you a slightly better chance to live longer. Youtube has some great videos of friends accidentally shooting each other at the same time!
Granted the game is a work in progress, but it already has a wealth of features and ultra fun elements. You would be doing yourself a tragic disservice if you dont pick up this game when you have even the slightest interest in Project Zomboid. Skip fast food for a week and buy this game. You will thank me, you will thank the team, your waste line will thank you, and your significant other and/or boss will curse us all because of the time you will be spending dying!

I think the DLC arguement has clouded people's judgement of the game. Yes it might seem silly but at the end of the day none of the DLC really has an impact on the current game at all, everything that is available to play is in the base game, even if you do have to unlock it through play. I don't believe rating the game poorly for these trivial reasons is very fair to be honest.
Now to the review. The game is pure pick up and play fun, there's alot of nuance to learn but overall you can have some fun stomping around since there is levels to split up experienced players and new players. Obviously right now you have alot of beta players etc.. who actually know the game well and so on so it's a bit skewed.
The hunting, tracking and trapping concept of the game is actually incredibly rewarding once you start to get the hang of it and the combat when coordinated a little is actually quite intriguing in itself. The monster gameplay is also interesting and has alot of nuance to it. Each character plays quite differently as well which means you have a total of 15 characters in the base game at release, 3 in each role.
Playing with bots as well is also of a reasonable level. Learning the game the monster AI will kick your♥♥♥♥♥
This is not your typical fps deathmatch game and treating it as such means you'll lose and not have a good time. This is closer to a strategy game as you track down the monster and try to sneak up on it and engage a successful fight. As the monster you can use stealth and agility to outrun and out maneuver the hunters while trying to evolve, it's actually alot harder than it seems starting out but once you reach level 3 it's insanely fun to stomp on the hunters and the hunters will find it very punishing to fail to shut down the monster early.
The slow regen of monster shields means that short skimishes do have some benefit to the outcome of the match even if the monster escapes. The design of the game also tries to avoid anyone having to sit dead for too long unless you really lose a fight badly.
If anything can be said for this game, through all the marketing hype I wonder if enough detailed guidance has been given to how to play the game properly. The ingame tutorial videos and gameplay sections are pretty good at explaining basic stuff but the nuances are quickly required.
Overall I this game has ushered a new era of online gaming as the asymmetrical pvp works very well and demonstrates a good balance. It may not be the perfect product and live up to the endless hype this game has been given. But I do think it deserves a certain level of applause for bringing a unique and well polished idea to the table and executing it in a way that is both fun, deep and engaging.

Limbo is one of the bigger disappointment I've encountered in my roughy two decades as a video game connoisseur, which is mostly due to realizing that this game could have been so much better. Don't get me wrong, though. There is a lot to like here: the art style is great, the animations are very good, the ambient music is well-done. However, the main gameplay loop is unsatisfying. The problem is that, juding from what I have seen of the game (a little over half, just based on the amount of chapters), the puzzles all have only one solution, which is not something I appreciate in a puzzle game. A much bigger problem, though, is that the pace of the game is so incredibly slugglish. Your avatar walks as if he is geriatric. To add insult to injury, some sections do demand a bit of dexterity, leaving not much room for error. If the controls were tight and responsibe, the occasional trial and error gameplay wouldn't be so bad.
The game being as it is, though, there is plenty of frustration to be had. Due to shortcomings with regards to the controls as well as the design (some puzzles are too much based on trial and error; most gameplay mechanics are introducted in a situation that quickly kills you instead of giving you some room to experiment without any danger), you easily end up dying. For instance, you figure out the solution to a puzzle but misjudge a jump. Thus, you slowly fall to your death. So, you watch the character move in slow-mo, he dies, the game draws out this moment much too long. A cinematic (?) pause has to pass afterwards before you can try again. Just to avoid any misunderstanding: it is not the case that I had been fumbling through half the game and then quit. No, instead I realized that this game is artificially drawn out due to questionable design decisions. With better controls and a faster feedback loop this game would take only about half as long. I couldn't see myself suffering through the rest of the game, so I quit.
(I got Limbo for free during a special promotion on Steam.)

This is my first negative review of any game...so..here goes.
This game retains enjoyment for about 10-15 hours. You end up playing every map the exact same way, because they don't really contribute to the game beyond thematic atmosphere and a few minor obstacles that you will only experience once (then you know where they are). After you've played a map 2-3 times, you will just jetpack/fly/jump/climb past everything without worry..making every arena map functionally the same, essentially just a background change.
There is no player created content like L4D had. No Power Station, Zelda, etc.
All hunters roles have the same final ability, and 3 unique abilities. The 3 monsters you have to choose from when you play, you will only use 1-2 of their 4 ability options unless you are grinding them.
The grindy-unlock system means people in games with you will be spamming one ability to level it up, rather than contribute effectively.
There are also severe problems with the networking in this game. It's very common to be playing with people, and half the team suddenly is flung from the game..replaced by AI that are effectively useless. Or worse, the monster is replaced and just stands there doing nothing, not even fighting back. It just waits while you shoot it slowly to death. This is made worse by the matchmaking taking forever a lot of the time, because when you are excited to finally have a full group to play together...half the game is suddenly gone because of the bad networking, and the game is ruined. Then you have to go back into matchmaking to fill the slots again..
Hopefully they fix the game at some point. Right now it's just not worth it. It feels utterly devoid of content with replayability. Shame because I liked this game at PAX East. I think it had a lot of potential. After 9 hours I was already feeling like there wasn't much left.
