Banished - 10 hours in review
Everything I knew about Banished before playing it sounded familiar. Another city building sim, this time set in a medieval environment. There have been various games that have covered this subject, and inevitably once you make a profit with whatever resource(s) are used to expand your town, you tend to keep doing so.
Banished promised to do something slightly different: population is a resource. They delivered on that promise, and then some. Population is not just a critical resource, it can also be seen as your measure of success. If you are familiar with (medieval) city building sims, Banished won't offer much innovation. If you are unfamiliar with such games, Banished is absolutely a good game to start exploring the genre.
Simulation games inevitably create abstractions to make things playable. Currency or resources are inevitably created ex nihilo in order to keep gameplay going. Mostly, Banished is no exception, and speaking of no exceptions there is one thing medieval building sims tend towards: Nature provides. The amount of resources Banished lets you harvest from forest areas is nothing shy of ridiculous. Incidentally so is the rate at which people age, and children who become adult labourers at the age of 10.
Mostly players skip over these abstractions for the sake of gameplay, and that's fine. Except in Banished, people are so abstract that they have no faces. Zooming in freaked me out the first time. Beyond that singular fact Banished sets itself apart in that it doesn't turn the population factor into an abstract. Most similar games, people just appear. In Banished, they have to be born. They also age, and die, and need to be replaced.
The result is a game that ties the very familiar, with this singular but very critical difference. One of your primary jobs in this game is to get people to breed. You are some kind of god-pimp, and the survival of your town depends on your ability to get people to have sex.
Mostly, this means Banished is a fairly relaxed, easy-going game. Get a decent economy, enough food and some housing and mostly people will breed resulting in a stable population. The environment is not too detailed, clearly a lot of standard objects are used to generate the map, buildings and people, but I never found this too disturbing. You can stress yourself out demanding that you expand and fill the map as rapidly as possible if you seek a more energetic type of gameplay but it's not required. Mostly, Banished is about planning and design.
Even in the realm of mistakes, I found it to be fairly forgiving, and primarily mistakes revolve around its prime resource: population. After fiddling with a town for about an hour learning what buildings do I started my first real attempt at building. As mentioned before, nature provides, so as long as you have people planting trees, harvesting in the forest and chopping trees, you can essentially never run out of basic resources... except population.
After only 10 hours I am not an expert on the population mechanics yet but the gist of it is simple. If you have an eligable bachelor and an eligable bachelorette, and an empty house available, they'll shack up (pun intended) and start breeding the next generation. They and future generations need enough food, all other resources either serve to expand your town or increase health and happyness, factors that make your population more long-living and more productive. Also in the realm of producing offspring, I suppose.
I nearly ruined my first serious attempt by not building enough housing for people to shack up in. The game is a bit weird about families and sex (not that I'd encourage such a thing). People won't shack up and breed in their parent's house, apparently having the elderly about is not conducive to nookie. Primarily this is because families own houses, not individuals, so if the next generation still lives at home, they won't seek another partner, and their brother or sister doesn't qualify as a partner because that'd be wrong. The game conveniently skips over the fact that the entire population of your village (which can reach over 1000 on medium maps) will descend from 4-6 of the originally banished families (roughly 10-20 people). It's okay.
Once I figured out my currently active generation really needed their own places to fornicate in, I set about building such establishments of workforce production and lo and behold, breeding ensued. New children were born slightly faster than my elderly were dying off, though still kudos to the 74 year old grandmother working full-time in my quarry. I suppose with her job being producing stone and the fear of the town dying out, she was caught between a rock and a hard place.
I thought my fledgeling town was saved, albeit with a slight delay... and this is when the tornado hit. I had disasters turned on, because... heck, in other city/village building simulations disasters were annoying but quite managable, you just rebuilt. In Banished however, an unlucky disaster like a tornado will not just wreck your buildings, it'll kill off a significant part of your population, especially once that crosses over your city center like the one in my game did. Most of my population got killed, my storage spaces were demolished so I had an instant famine, and what was left of my population quickly died out. Disaster indeed.
After that it was game over, like I was smacked with the wrath of a god. Must've been 'cause of all the incest.
Next attempt... disasters off.

I love games that change how you think. This is one of them.
Frenic and random it is not.
You are the god among insects, moving just as much as you need to. Step this way to avoid a shotgun blast, step back to dodge a sword strike. Leaving death at every step.
If you can't live up to that make this game will frustrate you. But I was engrossed. I finished the story in one go.

LIMBO,
Starting by the graphics, they are amazing. And by amazing, I'm not saying that they look very real, the quality of the textures are enormous or anything like that. I'm saying that the game looks great. The shades, the monochrome style, the film grain filter, the fact that the scenarios, elements and entities were designed in a sort of chiaroscuro gave the game personality and made it attracting. The look of the game is really different from what you are used to see. And still, it stands out and we have a lot to learn from it.
The sounds and music... are very powerful and fitting. They manage to finish creating the atmosphere of the game. Every time the boy jumps, the footsteps, the gears grinding, the electrified cables, every little detail had a specific, immersive sound. The music kinda made you want to suicide, so it fulfilled its purpose. Dark, extended, haunted and with a little of silent hill. It sounded like you are trapped in a dream with a love-hate relationship towards someone, somebody very harmful, but you still see the hope in his eyes.
Now, leaving the poetry away, the gameplay. Well, it wasn't a challenge. Some puzzles were tricky, but still they are not the kind of puzzles you need to watch a playthrough to know how to solve them. The physic engine was notoriously consistent, and the game squishes the juice out of it the most it can. Finding the eggs was challenging and the reward is quite nice. The difficulty of the puzzles grows linearly and that is a necessary feature in any puzzle based game. Some parts are trial-error, like traps that you don't know they are there, but still you can avoid them next time and plan your strategy to solve the puzzle having that in mind. Sometimes the color palette didn't let me distinguish between some objects I needed to interact, like a branch you have to move in a lake when the spider is chasing you, but it doesn't affect the gameplay at all. The level design was brilliant and felt very polished.
For the final (and my favorite) part: The plot.
I have a love-hate relationship with games in which the plot is a total mistery. There are a lot of theories in forums and blogs, but the real one is the one you want to believe in. The fact that the game doesn't show any significant plot advances until the ending is rare, and the ending being so weird is confusing. But there were a few hints during the whole game that could match the puzzle of the whole plot. The places like the Hotel, the Factory, the Sewers, and the other humans like the ones at the beginning, or the girl which you find at some point of the game and the ending, the brain-controlling worms. We don't know, and the most important thing is
. The fact that there are clues that could be crucial or insignificant keeps it interesting. If Playdead would come out and say "Forget it all, what happened to the boy is this..." it would lose it's touch.
Now, in conclusion, it is not a long game, but every part of it is very enjoyable and if you like platformers and obscure games, you will certainly LOVE LIMBO as much as I do. Great game.

I have to be honest: I mainly bought this game for the visuals and for the sound design. And they are both fantastic. I LOVE the animation. Everything about this game's appearance is amazing. The ragtime and jazz soundtrack is also incredible.
BUT, I don't actually enjoy Cuphead. I played up to the third island and am no longer motivated to pick it up again. It just isn't fun anymore. There are four reasons:
1. My absolute biggest problem with this game is that it NEVER chills the ♥♥♥♥ out and lets me enjoy the visuals! It's such a beautiful game but I never get to look at it because the game is always cranked up to 11! That's just ridiculous.
2. It lacks variety and quickly becomes repetitive. Fight a boss, die, fight it again. Rinse and repeat every minute or so until you win, which might take you up to thirty or forty tries! That stopped being fun after a while. There is no attempt to break up this pattern except for a handful of token platforming sections that only take a few minutes to complete.
3. Related to the first point, your health is so low (3 hits, 4 with a charm that imposes a debilitating attack decrease) that if you take even a single hit in the early stages of a boss you just have to insta-restart. This means that you might be restarting every five to ten seconds until you have the initial stages absolutely down. That is way too much restarting.
4. There is no real impetus in the game. It has basically no story and no cohesive world. Aside from the cartoon aesthetic, the bosses are wildly disconnected from each other. I just don't have a reason to keep banging my head against these bosses.
I want to like this game, but I just don't. It is not the difficulty. I like and play many very challenging games. I just don't like the repetitiveness or the constant restarting. Cuphead fails to break up the difficulty and give you a chance to catch your breath. It also throws away its incredible visual design by never giving you a chance to appreciate it.
All in all, although many do enjoy it - and I get that - I think that this game is overhyped and not really that fun.

If you enjoyed Tropico 4 (which was great if you’ve never played it), you will likely enjoy Tropico 5.  However, as someone who plays a lot of this genre of games, I will say Tropic 5 was the first Tropico where I actually
to become a dictator to survive.  Note I only play on hard mode since I do have a lot of experience with Tropico games.
In every other Tropico game, all you had to do was give the people what they want (housing, food, religion, etc.) and they would vote for you.  I almost never had to issue Martial Law or assassinate someone, unless I just wanted to do it for kicks.  In Tropico 5, the factions have so much more power.  You can have an overall happiness of 80% and an approval rating of 35%, so if you don’t rig the election, you’re going to lose.  For example, if the majority of your population are environmentalists and you build a factory, you will take a huge hit in popularity.
It’s a pleasant surprise because no longer can you easily make huge island decisions and not be punished for it.  If you’ve done mostly communist things for ten years and then all of a sudden become best friends with the USA and make the plebs pay for their own food and medicine, your population will resent you and rebel, even if their overall happiness keeps improving. And hope that those in your military aren’t part of those unhappy factions because even high wages won’t always save you from a coup d’etat.
Wages as they were in Tropico 3 and 4 are gone and have been replaced by something a little different.  I’m not a fan of it because when I’m rolling in the rum and oil dough, I’d like to be able to raise everyone’s wage at the same time and now that can only be done on a per building type basis—and each type of farm is considered a different building, so you can’t even raise all farmers’ wages at the same time, you must go into each type of farm and change it.  They also replaced Penultimo’s voice actor with someone much less annoying, and it bothers me.
Overall, it is definitely a buy if you can get it on sale.  It’s quite different from previous versions but has the same feel-you definitely know you're playing a Tropico game.  As I’ve said though, if you’ve historically been a loving, graceful, democratic leader who would never really use the Secret Police to aid you, this game might force you to change your ways.

Goodbye Deponia is the finale of the Deponia series, and I can only say that the quality of the game just keeps getting better, and that it has left me with many unforgettable moments, namely the ending which almost brought me to tears. I want to say many things about the story and the characters, and the potential that I felt was unfulfilled, yet justifyingly so, but I will try to refrain from writing any spoilers in this review.
As the last game of the series, the puzzles are only getting harder with the addition of managing multiple inventories instead of just one. There were definitely more times where I had to look up a walkthrough to find salvation for my overheating brain than the previous two games, but the challenge definitely makes the game entertaining to play (kudos if you can play through the game without looking up the solutions). Throughout the game you'll find various character references to other games/movies, and you'll have quiite a few giggles interacting with them as the MC. And finally, the adventure was simply beautiful and... magical. I never thought I'd be so emotionally invested in a point-and-click adventure game, but I've never been more glad to be proven wrong.
If it's not clear enough by this point, I am very impressed with the game and would recommend it to those who has already played the previous two games. For those who have not started the series and are looking for a game with a challenging-but-not impossible puzzles, a few good giggles and a great story, then I will say that being able experience the adventures of Deponia is worth every single penny in your wallet. (Maybe not literally, but the retail price is still a decent value ^^)

Highly recommended.

With all the positive reviews for this game floating around I feel I need to add my input. In short, if you enjoy P&C Puzzle games, do not buy this game.
It's quite difficult to find an aspect of it I like- The puzzles were exceptionally poor, lacking in any kind of imagination or ingenuity (Think generic charity shop puzzle-book puzzles and you won't be far off). Where good Point and Click puzzle games move coherently from one puzzle to the next using logical plot points, it feels that the developers simply add arbitrary problems to form a chain of bad puzzles until it is long and bulked out enough to be called a game. This makes the game more of a chore than an enjoyable experience, as there is little in the way of progression or logic. Also, if you don't do the right action in a given time, the main character will explicitly blurt out the solution, cutting all satisfaction from the puzzle-solving experience.
The characters were so one-dimensional it was laughable. Worse, some characters arbitrarily changed their personalities, sometimes hating the main character for no good reason, then in the next moment being overly nice with no explanation. Further, the main character was fundamentally unlikeable (This was not helped by the emotionless mask-like faces the characters have). I also thought the voice acting wasn't up to scratch- is it just me, or does Bwana dip in and out of his accent?
The animation was quite poor, and at times environments looked very rushed and unfinished. The lip-sync was dreadful, and ruined any immersion the cut-scenes might provide.
I also found the game to be completely humourless. The jokes fell so flat it was more of a cringe-worthy experience than a funny one. The only way to get through this game was to laugh at it rather than with.
It was very sad to play this game after seeing comments likening this to greats such as Grim Fandango or Monkey Island (two of my favourite games). It is a husk of a puzzle game, and was genuinely the worst P&C puzzler I have ever played.

In the Journey Down, by SkyGoblin, you will take on the roll of Bwana, a pilot who is scared of heights, and who runs a fuel station on the outskirts of the town St. Armando. He lives with his best friend Kito. It doesn't take long for something mysterious to happen as a professor's assistant shows up looking for an old book. This is where the adventure really starts to begin, and its going to be up to you to escape and save everyone.
Graphically I can definitely feel the African tribal theme showing up in all the character designs. All faces seemed to be modeled after tribal masks, and definitely add something extra to the personalities of the characters that you will encounter. There's also the different area designs, you will of course spend the vast majority of your time around the fuel station, but you will also get to see a cafe, a yacht, and a railway stop. All of these areas have this painted feel to them, but in a crisp way that draws the player into the scenes. As this is a point click and adventure, you will notice that sometimes the items you get to interact with are very obviously placed, and other times you will have to pay attention to your surrounds to find what might be hiding behind a door, on a bookshelf, and a wall, and more.
The music and the voice acting in the game kind of gives me a Rastafarian vibe, with a little twist of African tribal feel. I do think that there are some characters that might be laying it on a bit thick, but for the most part all the voices fit their parts for the game.
The controls in the game are as you might imagine them to do, you are going to move your mouse around the screen, seeing what or who you can interact with, and you are going to click to interact with whatever is currently selected.
This was one of those games that seemed interesting, and that I just had to at least try out, and I'm glad I did. Though the theme and feel of the game was a bit different than I have played, the storyline was definitely something that the further I got in, the more I wanted to know more. That being said there was quite a bit of distraction, as point and clicks usually cause, so that you had to do some puzzle solving, or item combining to complete a goal, or get past an obstacle. I was impressed with the amount of completely different characters you had to deal with, and some of the puzzles that I had to take on. There are some put this here and that will solve the problem puzzles, and there's also those puzzles that you will have to find the solution elsewhere to solve. Now this is only the first chapter, and I have to say that after playing this, and recording the playthrough for it, I am dying to get my hands on chapter 2. I bought this game on sale expecting very little, but looking for the zombie game that really feels like an apocalypse - not a shooting gallery. Surely, I love playing a round of L4D or KF now and then but in truth they are only satisfying for their shooter components, settings, and funny physics.
Project Zomboid is nothing like that.
The first time I fired the game up it told me, "This is the story of how you died." Of course that got the philosopher in me interested. After all, don't you "die" in every video game, but usually with little consequence? Well, that first game, I lasted a mere minutes (4 hours of game time).
From that moment, I realized that there was a lot more to this game than I was expecting, and a lot more than some of the other early access zombie games offer.
Are there still bugs? Yes. Is everything in the game that should be? No.
But what the game does to its player transcends what most games do.
It makes you really care about how you live and die in the zombie apocalypse. And for that, and because it is (in my experience) without any game breaking bugs, this game deserves a 10/10. Someone should have made something like it 10 years ago. I would still be playing it.

I disagree with whatever programming that is used for single player blackjack. What doesn't make since is that shoe play seems to favor the player more than single deck play, which is extraordinarily false in real life. There is no way to be sure the dealer is not simply rearranging the cards at any time to convenience the dealer and screw the player.
Dealer dealt 20 or 21 greater than 50% of the time. Most of your double downs will be dealt a tiny card. Basic strategy is of little use since you will almost always be dealt a 10 with a 12-16 pat hand.
One other thing I noticed. If you bet the smallest amount, you tend to win more than 50% of the time. If you start betting big, you will lose more than 80% of the time. Again, if you bet big, the computer can simply program the deck however it sees fit to win all the time. The programming of this game will just deal the dealer a 21 whenever the player trys to bet large. I've seen the dealer be dealt at least 5 times in a row before. Would never ever happen in real life to the dealer. Because no one would play.
Additionally, at least 30-40% of the time, the dealer will draw to perfectly match your hand or beat your hand by one. while frusterating and not a big deal, it ONLY occcurs when you sway from the basica strategy while trying to mess up the card order so the dealer doesn't auto matically hit to a 21.
Ex: you're dealt a 13 against a dealer up 6. Basica strategy says to stand, however when hitting you will always either be dealt a 10, or if you are dealt a small card, let's say a 4 (to a total of 17) - the dealer will either have an Ace in the hole (17 to push) or will draw perfectly to 18 (not 19-21, only to 1 above your pat hand).
Don't spend really money on this game. It encourages the developers to try and take it even more so by instilling these unfair game mechanics.

There are a lot of reviews for this game that will tell you that the game has a paywall. That the DLC ruins the game. That there isn't enough content.
I am here to tell you that these people are wrong, and judging the game poorly not because it's a bad game (you'll notice that many reviews compliment the gameplay highly), but because /v/ or Reddit told them "DLC is evil" and they parrot it blindly, without regard for facts or context.
So let's start with the facts. The game comes in three editions, offers a Season Pass, and carries with it a load of cosmetic skins. In the future, the game will offer 2 monsters and 6 more hunters. These are all offered at various prices and are, of course, completely optional. Future maps will be offered for free. Most importantly, *none of this DLC - not even the monsters - require you to buy them in order to see them in action.* Turtle Rock has stated plainly that, even if you do not buy the DLC, you will still find yourself fighting the Behemoth in the future, on any of the new maps, alongside any of the new Hunters. The player base of the game will not be fragmented by Haves and Have Nots.
Having said that, let's look at what the game has right now. 12 Hunters, 12 maps, 4 classes, 3 Monsters with a progression based unlock system, matchmaking for the game's 4v1 Hunt mode, Custom games for you and your friends, and Evacuation, a series of 5 matches with using 4 different game modes that features perks based on which side won the previous match. The Monsters are all completely unique from one another, with each one favoring its own style of play. The Hunters are somewhat more homogenous but each Hunter has their own quirks, so that even characters of the same class feel different from one another - the 3 Assaults, for example, are all damage-dealers, but Markov favors ambushes and ranged fighting, Hyde favors distraction and up-close throwdowns, while Parnell has a super mode and covers large areas with explosions. Finally, while the game is multi-player focused, there are dedicated bots for both sides, allowing Solo play in any mode.
All of this adds up to a game where no two matches ever really feel the same. The basic idea is easy to understand, but Evolve succeeds in adding multiple levels of depth to the proceedings. As a Hunter, you not only have to know your class, you have to know how your Hunter's strengths and weaknesses, your teammate's strengths and weaknesses, the monster's strengths and weaknesses, and the layouts of the maps, where to cut off the monster or set up an ambush or where you are at a disadvantage when engaging. As a monster, you have to know the exact opposite of all of that.
Should you buy this game? That depends. If you enjoy working within a team and fighting what amounts to a player-controlled Raid boss across various modes of play, or if you enjoy BEING that Raid boss, if you are willing to put in time to understand how the game actually works, I wholeheartedly recommend it, but it's not an easy game - a Monster is more than a match for any one Hunter, but a good Team will win more often than not. However, if you're more interested in an "evil DLC is evil" punching bag and impressing your internet friends with second hand memes, well, you've already made your choice, haven't you?

This is somewhat personal, but here is my immediate thought after finishing the game: There was a moment, while playing The Beginner's Guide, that I started to deeply regret the time I've spent away from my wife and kids to develop and play video games. I justify it every day by promising myself that I'll have plenty of time to make it up to them, and I have been successful at that lately. The thought wasn't as much about life and death as it sounds, but instead it's about my priorities and what they mean for who I am, and what I'm striving for, as a person. I came to the conclusion while finishing this game that we can't forget our passions, and I like being a father AND a hard working professional. Having one doesn't mean you have to be bad at the other. Sure they can conflict, but video games are my outlet creatively, and developing them puts food on my family's table, and I wasn't this happy with my last four jobs. In fact, I realized that the reason I wasn't happy was because I was focused so hard on becoming what I am now. It was a fleeting regret, but this game made me look at it and accept it in a different way. Thanks Davey.

Enemy Mind is a really fun arcade shooter with updated gameplay. Instead of collecting powerups or collecting weapons you transfer from ship to ship. Each ship has a limited amount of ammo and a few hp requiring you to jump again and again throughout a level if you want to succeed. Each ship has a different weapon, hp, size, and speed making it suitable for different situations.
The game takes place in during a war between humans and an alien race, with you as a psychic presence jumping between each side. Each side has different flavors. There is a small but well written story told between segments of the levels depending on which faction you are possesing.
It has a classic arcade scoring system with fast gameplay that requires you to make strategic descisions on the fly. Its got solid and repsonive gameplay with nice pixel graphics and a good deal of depth to your gameplay choices. Only weakness is that the bosses are kind of weak, interesting and fun but once you're familiar with they can be quite easy. On the whole its an excellent game.

I can't really recommend the game as is, but I'm under the impression that the problem I'm having will be corrected in the future. Time of writing is July 7th 2014, if there have been any patches since then, this review might not be accurate.
So this game is not bad, let's be clear: I simply am not recommending it as a bullet hell/retro shooter enthusiast for the current price. The system seems unpolished: The bounding box, timing, and rules for what bullets collide with what object just don't have the professional intuitive shine that say, Deathsmiles has. I know I'm comparing a company team to an indie developer, but that doesn't make the problems any less noticeable. Other problems: enemy ships can do things you cannot when you possess them (most egregiously: turning around and shooting the other way), and the teleporting beam trajectory could be better (as is it's rather awkward; also it has a charge up time which has absolutely no user feedback).
But this game has a story focus! Pretty rare for this type of game. If the gameplay is just average, how is the story? I'd like to know, too. Thoughout the game you get snippets of story, and it creates a very interesting experience... but I personally think the novelty of the gameplay has an expiration far shorter than the time it would require to go through the game twice (to collect all the snippets of story). However, I never actually finished this game, so I don't know how the story concludes. The difficulty for the entire game is, despite the problems named above, quite easy. Dying is infrequent for those experienced with this genre, and there are no difficulty settings to adjust. The boss fights, once you figure out how to win, are also not hard at all. Then you get to the end of the second to last wave and find that it is near impossible. Brick wall. Not many players will proceed past this point.
I might have kept trying if I could actually get to that segment again quickly. But since it's at the end of the wave, you need to replay the entire wave first. Takes about 5 minutes, and it's patronizingly easy the entire time. Imagine taking a math test and every time you made a mistake on a really hard problem, before trying again you are forced to first to solve 50 basic addition problems (2+3=?). I've poured quite a bit of time in this last wave alone, and I can no longer justify repeating the patronizingly-easy-5-minutes-snooze-fest even one more time just to retry a 10 second difficult segment.
Despite my rant, I'd say those who love this genre should pick it up next sale. But even if I didn't have any trouble completing it, I still feel that this game is a one-and-done deal; you'll play it, you might enjoy it, but once you uninstall it you probably won't be revisiting it.

I must say that when i saw the anoucement trailer a few years back, this game caught my attention immediatly. Not only because of the aestethic, but the frenetic pacing that the gameplay shown had. This was one of the games that i kept repeating in my head "please, don't be♥♥♥♥♥♥quot;. Now that it was released, i'm relived that my prayers were heard. I will refrain from talking about the art direction, because it has all the praise it really deserves. Just look at it. Even if you don't like this art style, you must admit the game looks INCREDIBLE.
So, about the gameplay? Really good, if you like a challenging platformer. You can shoot in most directions, but that doesn't mean you can just fire aimlessly. You still need to time and aim the shots well to kill the smaller minions or to chunk the bigger enemies or the bosses, even with close-range weapons.
The game is made mostly of boss stages, that you need to hit constantly to whittle them down slowly, and the only hint that they are taking damege is the feint glow after every sucessful shot, and the transition to a new stage of the fight. To make the boss hunting a little easier, you can get new weapons and upgrades from the shop, with the coins you collect in the few 'run n gun' stages, that have 5 coins each. Choose your power-us wisely, because you only have few coins to spend.
It is unfair to compare this game to Dark Souls
. I think it is better to call this a refined version of Contra, from the NES. In Contra you run, aim, and shoot, while dodging the enemy fire and getting new weapons. Cuphead has this exact formula, but adds in a Dash, so that you can dodge attacks faster
and a mid-air parry that grants you a power-shot every time you hit a bright-pink enemy projectile
. It becomes incredible the amount of stuff flying on the screen that you have to dodge, but, with enough trial and error, you get to do in a snap of the fingers.
Ok, i praised the game a lot, now lets get to the bad stuff. Not bad as in gamebreaking, but as in "It could have been better". Mind you that i criticise this game after beating it once, mostly single player, and loving every second of those 17 hours:
-Starting off, why in the name of guacamole you can
parry mid-air? I get that you are jumping most of the time, but having to use it as a double tap of the jump button is just odd. Even if the game has platforming challenges built around this particular aspect, i still can't think of a reason to not have a ground parry, even if a delayed one.
-I thought that the lack of a hard mode to challenge the most skilled or avid players being a negative, but the game already has a hard mode. Play it alone. The idea of having a game built for 2 players isn't new, but it feels somewhat incomplete not having a partner all the time, either to save your hide or to whittle the boss faster. It feels like you are trying to drive a car with a flat tire - Technically you can, but it is dangerous and you feel wierd all the time.
-I have a small gripe with the weapons and upgrades. It adapts to the players personal style of playing this type of game, selecting up to two weapons, a power up and one of three Supers. Sounds simple and awesome, but i cannot brush off the feeling that it is somewhat broken. Broken meaning that i used the exact same combo of weapons and powers in almost every non-aerieal boss, including the last one. Peashooter (the standard weapon, mind you), Seeker Shot and Invinsible Dash. Every time i tried a new combination (Spread shot, extra life with less damege, automatic parry), i just felt weaker, even after a lot of tries. I missed the safety of the Invisible Dash, or the practicity of not having to aim a lot using the Seeker Shot. I hope thats just me.
-This game has a lot of trial and error. The boss fights last only about 1~3 minutes, but you die A LOT, sobe prepared to spend some time on every boss, learning its patterns and planning a strategy. I dont think trial and error is a bad thing; it is just a tool of learning and incentiveses you to keep going, knowing that every time you get closer to the end, but don't think you'll just "kill this boss on the first try and move on".
-
One last thing that is not gamebreaking, but might be a bug: In the first stage of the last boss, The Devil, when he uses his head-snake attack, one of the ways to dodge the attack is to run to the opposite side of the room. When he retreats his head, the tongue animation is a little bit off of the hitbox, so when you leave your safety cover you end up getting hit when he  clearly has already retreated.
It may feel that i am criticizing the game a lot, but only because it is easier to list the few bad things i found out about the game than the mountain of praises i can give. Heck, i even sprinkled some fair points and praises in my criticism. Be the beautiful and talented art direction, that captures the magic of a long-gone era of animation, or the fantastic action-packed gameplay, this is the kind of game that just does not age. Simple, effective and just good.

Very late to the party but that's the great thing about having been out of gaming since 2002 - you can just play the cream of the crop and that's definitely where Bioshock is.
The other reviews have covered it well already of course but it bears repeating - Bioshock is a fairly standard FPS with some well implamented RPG elements but in every other way it excells itself - the story, atmosphere, aesthetic, soundtrack, sound design nd graphics (for their time) are top notch all the way through. The story is particuarly lauded and for good reason; rather than focus so much on the characters, Bioshock is fundamentally a story about a place, what it was, what it could have been and the folly that befell it. The dark atmosphere and excellent sound design (eerie ambience, the high pitched whistle of a turret, the demented ramblings of the Splicers etc.) all give the routine parts of the game a suitably nerve racking feel that I found especially absorbing.
Unfortnately the steam Port has a fair amount of bugs in it; most notorious being the sound bug that mutes all the sound after the opening cut scene. There's numerous solutions to this (I found that running in compatibility with XP SP 3 fixed it) but then there are a few weird in game bugs as well, including one that caused me to randomly teleport around the room after examining a splicer and one where an extra Little Sister spawned, netting me not only extra adam but an extra reward teddy as well. During the last boss I was also constantly prompted to do parts of a previous level.
There are some negatives that none of the reviews I;ve skimmed have picked up on - splicers have a nasty habit of spawning right when you've collected an audio log, meaning that you have to constantly replay them. The penultimate level is an exercise in frustration and one of the main factors that makes me hesitant to play Bioshock 2. The screen blur when you get hit is so extreme that if you make a mistake and blunder into an area where you're surrounded then you can waste half your ammo shooting at vague shapes while you're being attacked from all directions and comnstantly discharging lightning. The ending is feeble and anti-climactic as well.
To be honest though these are minor gripes, I play video games for story and atmospere and Bioshock excells here in so many ways; it's exactly what I was promised by my friends and you should absolutely get off the fence and give it your time; all the big bugs can be easilly fixed if you follow the advice on the forums and the other ones, while laughable, are only going to ruin the experience if you're a massive perfectionist.

Goodbye Deponia feels like a collection of rejected story ideas meshed together as a somewhat chaotic adventure game, that somehow acts as the final chapter of the Deponia trilogy. But it’s worth it for the ending alone.
Goodbye Deponia is somewhat of a rehash of the previous episode, Chaos on Deponia, in terms of story structure: yet again one of the main heroes (this time Rufus) is split into three, and you have to complete separate episodes for all of them to eventually progress in the main storyline.
The problem is that these sub-stories feel like reused, underdeveloped ideas from cancelled titles– for example the starting sequence in the hotel feels like if it is set in an entirely different universe. There is little connection between them, they are full of plot holes, and one of them is rendered pointless a minute after it is concluded. Not to mention that Rufus gets an origin story that is questionable at best, midichlorian level unnecessary at worst.
This stands in stark contrast with the last act, where the arcing plot reaches a surprising, clever, and fitting end. This takes up only a fraction of the story, but it is written so well the game is worth for this alone.
The puzzles are closer to the difficulty level of the first game; there is a new element in the form of item swapping between Rufuses (similar to Day of the Tentacle), but it is rarely used. The minigames offer more challenge, but they can be skipped here as well.
In conclusion, Goodbye Deponia cannot live up to the rest of the series, but strangely it provides an adequate conclusion that makes it recommended for anyone who went along for the ride this far.

There are a lot of reviews for this game that will tell you that the game has a paywall. That the DLC ruins the game. That there isn't enough content.
I am here to tell you that these people are wrong, and judging the game poorly not because it's a bad game (you'll notice that many reviews compliment the gameplay highly), but because /v/ or Reddit told them "DLC is evil" and they parrot it blindly, without regard for facts or context.
So let's start with the facts. The game comes in three editions, offers a Season Pass, and carries with it a load of cosmetic skins. In the future, the game will offer 2 monsters and 6 more hunters. These are all offered at various prices and are, of course, completely optional. Future maps will be offered for free. Most importantly, *none of this DLC - not even the monsters - require you to buy them in order to see them in action.* Turtle Rock has stated plainly that, even if you do not buy the DLC, you will still find yourself fighting the Behemoth in the future, on any of the new maps, alongside any of the new Hunters. The player base of the game will not be fragmented by Haves and Have Nots.
Having said that, let's look at what the game has right now. 12 Hunters, 12 maps, 4 classes, 3 Monsters with a progression based unlock system, matchmaking for the game's 4v1 Hunt mode, Custom games for you and your friends, and Evacuation, a series of 5 matches with using 4 different game modes that features perks based on which side won the previous match. The Monsters are all completely unique from one another, with each one favoring its own style of play. The Hunters are somewhat more homogenous but each Hunter has their own quirks, so that even characters of the same class feel different from one another - the 3 Assaults, for example, are all damage-dealers, but Markov favors ambushes and ranged fighting, Hyde favors distraction and up-close throwdowns, while Parnell has a super mode and covers large areas with explosions. Finally, while the game is multi-player focused, there are dedicated bots for both sides, allowing Solo play in any mode.
All of this adds up to a game where no two matches ever really feel the same. The basic idea is easy to understand, but Evolve succeeds in adding multiple levels of depth to the proceedings. As a Hunter, you not only have to know your class, you have to know how your Hunter's strengths and weaknesses, your teammate's strengths and weaknesses, the monster's strengths and weaknesses, and the layouts of the maps, where to cut off the monster or set up an ambush or where you are at a disadvantage when engaging. As a monster, you have to know the exact opposite of all of that.
Should you buy this game? That depends. If you enjoy working within a team and fighting what amounts to a player-controlled Raid boss across various modes of play, or if you enjoy BEING that Raid boss, if you are willing to put in time to understand how the game actually works, I wholeheartedly recommend it, but it's not an easy game - a Monster is more than a match for any one Hunter, but a good Team will win more often than not. However, if you're more interested in an "evil DLC is evil" punching bag and impressing your internet friends with second hand memes, well, you've already made your choice, haven't you?

It is a horror game, but if you're looking for something with more replayability, this game doesn't really provide unless you just really liked the story or environment and wanted to play again.
Worth it for an "experience", but if you're looking or a horror game with more interactive elements such as stealth and combat, you could probably get something else great at the same price instead.
Very simply put, you play as a mother looking for her child in an amusement park. However, things aren't what they seem on the surface, as the park turns nightmare-ish, and you're not sure if you're in the present time, or in reality. I would say that the game starts to pick up around the third ride or so, as you start finding notes that hint at the park's past. As the game progresses, you also start to find out secrets and mysteries of your own past, and of your relationship with family and son.
I felt that the game, while very slow in the beginning, really picked up in the second half. The ending left me pondering, the story made me debate and sympathize with some more heavy subject matter the game brought up. The characters are very human, and possibly even people that you could meet and see around in real life, and putting myself in her shoes was definitely a wild and dark roller-coaster ride (no pun intended).
I feel that that some aspects could be improved, for example the pacing in the beginning, or perhaps fleshing out the story a bit more. I knew enough to piece together things in my mind, and definitely don't mind ambiguity and intrigue, but some parts were definitely not really linked together. (Perhaps there was some reference to The Secret World that I didn't get, but I played TSW for some time and there was no info that I really understood to patch up those missing links. If you have info, please don't hesitate to let me know!)
The game is in first person perspective, and you can toggle running or walking. The menu has enough graphics options including field of view (important to me!). Mostly you try to follow your son's voice, and there are cutscenes triggered at each location, that convey story and atmosphere. The initial locations are more cutscene oriented, but in the second half, especially in a good part of the game, you have more interactivity. I found that this suited the game to convey this story - it's not survival and there's no combat.
One big thing I hope that can be improved, is the size of writing on the notes you pick up throughout the game. The writing is unproportionally small so may be really difficult to read on smaller screens.
I got the game at launch, which was $7.55 Canadian $. For an "experience" game, I felt it was worth it, like how I would pay $10+ for a movie at the theatre. The story was good and I felt I got what I was looking for, psychologically.

Here's the thing: Limbo is essentially a puzzle/platformer. As a puzzle/platformer it really really sucks. Like it's terrible. Pretty much all the puzzles can be solved by looking at them for two seconds, or they can't be understood because you're missing a piece. Now, retracting a piece is definetley a fair thing to do in puzzle games, I have no problem with that, my problem comes with the fact that you don't proceed to search around for the missing piece, you just walk backwards until you go, "Ohhhhh I was suppossed to take the box with me ohhhh, OHHH that's fun I'm glad." I recommend this game with a few reservations and qualifying statements.
For me, the ultimate survival horror experience of my life was watching The Road, with Viggo Mortensen and his son going up against a twisted post-apocalyptic world full of very human monsters, the hard hitting scenes and striking cinematography made it a terrifying experience which I won't soon forget.
As far as I'm concerned survival horror - or even simply survival - games need something of the ingredients that made The Road so impactful for me. It needs atmosphere, it needs a huge and hugely evocative landscape, it needs myriad foes, it needs mighty expanses of silence for the player to wander, pondering, through snow drifts, and finally - perhaps most importantly - it does need some kind of direction.
And that is where The Long Dark has, at least for the time being, failed me. You could say that to a certain extent each of those requirements but the last has been satisfied by this game - though that is not an entirely fair statement, since this is something of an open BETA of the game and the finished title - should it ever come out - will presumably feature a story (this of course would not instantly render the game a perfect survival/survival-horror title, because there are stories and stories)
The game doesn't score big on too many categories. Firstly, the graphics are not entirely immersive, effects like fog seem like they were lifted from xbox/ps2/GCN titles and the rifle, especially, looks like it came from a 1990s dear hunting simulator. The environments are similarly restrained - the broad reaches of the maps you are free to stumble across lose something of their appeal when you realize that there is very little scope for Easter eggs or reveals (discovering precious mysteries a la Skyrim) in a world that has been painted with very few brush strokes. Of course, again, this may be resolved in the final build of the game.
The enemies, well they are pretty good, but the combat is not resolved enough, and the foes not scary enough, to really keep me on the edge of my seat.
Indeed, the scariest part of the game for me is the mundane task of making sure you have enough food, water, and body warmth to keep going. This is where the game finally allows you to fill in the blanks with your imagination successfully - there are the cold mechanics of the central game, there is the mathematical reward of the various actions you can take to address your problems, but then there is the human element of attention span, creativity, and problem solving that adds just enough of a Z-Axis to your emotional experience to make that part of the game truly reactive and thrilling.
Very little of the rest of the game did that for me. Perhaps that's just my personality talking.
This is a lovely, lightweight game. When the final build comes out and the game is, ideally, almost as chock full of intrigue as a Skyrim or somesuch (a tall order, I know) then this may justs end up being an utterly enthralling title, but as it stands once my guy had survived a week or so I felt I had done all there was to do, and haven't touched the title since. Get it on sale.
7/10 (yeah, number ratings, why not? I employ them in conjunction with my review to round off a leaning I've been trying to articulate)

Ingredients
2 large eggs
Salt and pepper
2 to 3 tablespoons shredded cheese (optional)
1/4 to 1/2 cup filling, pre-cooked if necessary (optional)
2 teaspoons unsalted butter
Minced parsley, to garnish (optional)
Equipment
Mixing bowl
Whisk
8-inch nonstick skillet
Spatula
Dinner plate
Instructions
1. Whisk the eggs: Crack both eggs into a mixing bowl. Whisk the eggs until completely combined, and season with salt and pepper. If you\'re adding cheese or other fillings, make sure they are prepped and nearby.
2. Warm the skillet and melt the butter: Place an 8-inch skillet over medium-high heat and melt the butter. Tilt the skillet as the butter melts to evenly coat the bottom. When the butter stops sizzling, the pan is heated and ready.
3. Pour the eggs into the skillet: Pour the whisked eggs into the skillet. Immediately tilt the pan so the eggs coat the entire bottom. The eggs should sizzle on contact; if not, continue cooking, but remember to heat the pan a little longer next time.
4. Drag and push the eggs to form waves: Use a spatula to gently drag and push the cooked eggs from the edges toward the center of the pan, making space for the uncooked eggs and forming waves in the omelette. Tilt the skillet so that the uncooked eggs flow into the open spaces.
5. Cook the omelette for 1 to 2 minutes: The omelette will finish cooking in 1 to 2 minutes. When done, the bottom will be set and the edges will look crisp. The top of the omelette should still look fairly wet and uncooked, but there will no longer be any loose, easily flowing liquid egg — the omelette will continue cooking off the heat, so finish when you think the top still seems a bit underdone.
6. Top with cheese and fillings: If using, sprinkle the cheese and fillings down the center of the omelette.
7. Fold the omelette: Fold the bottom third of the omelette over the center, and then fold the top third down. Alternatively, fold the omelette in half.
8. Slide the omelette onto a plate: Gently slide the omelette onto a plate and garnish with parsley. Eat right away while still hot.

This is the third and final installment in the Deponia series. You need to play the other games for this one to make any sense, as it is a direct continuation of the story.
The main plot (while as convoluted as ever) does a good job of wrapping up all the loose ends, and it fills in all of the backstory question marks. I thought the ending was cheap and unsatisfying, though.
The puzzles were on par with the first two games, although this chapter throws in a new multi-inventory system that adds an extra layer of complexity. There is also a heavier reliance on needing to perform actions in a particular order.
I liked, or at least tolerated, most of the mini-games in this one. There were no hair-pulling sequences like Platypus Bataka, and it was easy to get all of the achievements.
Goodbye Deponia contains an array of new locations, but brings back most of the side characters from the first two games. You also eventually gain the ability to switch back and forth between multiple parallel story-lines.
The pacing is better than in the second game, but it still feels like a slog. I think by the third game, I just got sick of taking twelve steps backward for every one step forward. It would have been nice, for once, to feel like I was actually working towards an end-goal, instead of spending all my time band-aiding the problems caused by Rufus's idiocy and recklessness. I think if you combine Roger from Space Quest's bad judgement, Leisure Suit Larry's sexism, Urkel from Family Matters' accidental destruction, Mayhem from the Allstate commercials' intentional malevolence, and the cast of Seinfeld's problem-solving skills, you might get something approximating the experience of controlling Rufus.
In general, I felt there was a tonal shift from "generally funny with occasional dark humor" to "everything is awful and every joke is at someone's expense." Chaos on Deponia had its own morbid and uncomfortable moments, but Goodbye Deponia purposely goes out of its way to make Rufus as irredeemable and disgusting as possible. While it makes sense in retrospect, it is difficult to play through. I missed the comedy that made the earlier games palatable.
[Major trigger warning: the content of this game contains images and dialogue related to depression and suicidal thoughts]
What can I say? This is an irksome and doleful game that happens to have high production values and decent point-and-click puzzles. While it is a fitting end to the series, I don't think it was necessarily the right end. I give it a 6/10.

Picked it up primarily because the art and music reminded me a bit of Grim Fandango. The storyline has some sparse similarities to GF, but is original in its own right and I loved the Afro-Caribbean flair; coupled with the graphics, which were kind of a cartoonish noir, and it was really enjoyable. I thought the dialogue was a little tacky at points, but that really didn't detract from the humor or the overall quality of the game. A bit more difficult than I expected it to be, which was a pleasant surprise; it mixes traditional puzzle-solving with the usual point-and-click puzzles, which was pretty refreshing. It's a bit on the short side, but hey, it's only the first chapter--and seven bucks is a fair price.
When you beat the chapter, some bonus behind-the-scenes material is revealed, which I personally loved because I like seeing the creative process for games. Planning on playing chapter two when my next paycheck comes in, and I would definitely recommend this game to anyone who wants a light, fun point-and-click experience.

Short review:
Recommended in every sense of the word. Great game, great concept, great realism (as it can be for a fictional idea such as zombies and [fictional, as of now] the apocalypse). And it can even run well on your mother's PC. And I wish they keep it that way, or at least provide an option to run the game on lower settings if they upgrade as it's stated in their intended plans, as my PC is not unlike my mother's. At any rate, try the demo to ensure compatibility before considering a purchase.
An early access, unfinished game, you'd buy. But the game's in great playable shape as it is, with multiplayer as well as single player capabilities. And the developer's provide weekly updates, 'Mondoids', which can be viewed online by those who have and even those who haven't purchased the game. They seem to be pretty consistent, and determined to reach their goal of a 1.0 game. They also seem to be determined to make it a quality release by taking their time to produce updates with noticable differences from previous versions of the game.
I've owned this game less than a month I think, and already the user-interface has become more friendly through an update, as well as an attempted fix at multiplayer lag issues. All in one update.
You make your decision on buying this game. I'm happy with my decision, especially at the affordable sale price of around eight USD. The original price of around fifteen USD even seems justified. Though, with my budget, I'm not sure I would've done that for money reasons.
Thanks for reading.

Every level in Superhot is an exciting, self-contained, time-bending puzzle that turns typical fast-paced first-person shooter mechanics on their head. Every time you move, your enemies and their bullets do, too – but if you stand still, so will time. It’s a unique idea that creates a smart, tense puzzles where, in between reloading and lining up a shot, you can sometimes dodge every individual bullet in the spray of a burst rifle by moving one small step - and therefore a fraction of a second.
Even as you learn that painful lesson, near-instant respawns keep Superhot’s pace feeling addictive, rather than frustrating. The levels are also designed in a way that compliments both replayability and trial and error: they’re small, self-contained combat instances that would be a tiny part of a level in most games. The real-time playback you get when you complete a level might only be five seconds long, but Superhot’s real gameplay exists in those moments where time has stopped and you have to carefully calculate your next movement based on a heightened situational awareness of what the enemies around you are likely to do while they can move, too.
Tough decisions happen in those moments: Is it worth picking up that object to throw, knowing that picking something up is the most time-consuming action you can take, and your enemy might have moved three feet to the left by the time it lands? Something that an action hero would have to do by instinct in a split second is, in Superhot, a carefully thought-out move.

While the difficulty does increase throughout the 32 levels by introducing environments with less cover to hide behind, multiple entry points for enemies, and usually a lot more enemies armed with shotguns and rifles instead of clubs or pistols (just like other shooters), Superhot also presents scenarios that would likely be impossible without the ability to slow time. One of the later levels, for example, has you standing unarmed in a small room with three armed enemies. You’re not Batman - there aren’t any fancy takedown moves, so you have a few intense seconds to rely on your own attention to detail, and take tiny steps that let you see which enemy might raise their gun first, whether one of their bullets will be inside your head in the next second, or whether the one you just disarmed has recovered behind you and is ready to punch you out before you can shoot the others.
None of my deaths in Superhot felt unfair, though - with white, plain environments that starkly contrast with glowing red enemies that shatter when they’re dead, with a sound effect that makes sure you know they’re out of the picture, every aspect of its visual design is catered to your success, so long as you’re meticulous.

But while every scenario offers a unique challenge, and every level is wholly worth playing, there’s a very significant lack of them - Superhot only takes around four hours to finish, and never significantly evolves its concept in that amount of time. Unlike a puzzle game like Portal or Braid, which constantly introduce new spins on their novelty mechanics, Superhot always functions based on the same time-stopping principle, just in different environments. It doesn’t bother to introduce new weapons or effects to master, except for a ‘possession’ style action that you’re never overtly prompted to use because no levels are designed around it. In its lack of variety and brief length, Superhot feels underdeveloped – a good first step toward a great game, but not quite there yet.
Finishing the main story will unlock some very basic challenge modes in the same levels, but also an ‘endless’ mode that’s fairly addictive in its near-ridiculous difficulty. Hopefully we’ll eventually see some leaderboards, but they weren’t available at the time of review - the difficult-to-decipher menu is actually full of holes and links that lead to nothing, or things that aren’t explained well.
That’s if you can manage to get through the story without wanting to quit, though - what starts out as a laughably cheesy 90s-style hacker story turns into an annoyingly corny roadblock in between the enjoyable gameplay. While it uses its premise in some creative ways - like telling you to quit but rendering your ‘esc’ button useless - it’s largely just nonsensical in its ridiculous hacker hyperbole, like telling you your body is disposable, and you should submit to the software. The entire experience also feels very skewed towards the upcoming VR headsets, as opposed to the 2D screens it’s playable on right now, and while it’s easy to imagine playing these levels and experiencing some of the pixelated software-inspired cutscenes in VR, I doubt it would make the story any more impactful or intelligent.
Superhot’s clever time-manipulation idea delivers consistently fulfilling challenges by turning blink-of-an-eye action into carefully considered and cautious tactical decisions. It avoids potential one-hit death frustration with quick respawns and deaths that always feel earned and avoidable in hindsight. Its unique brand of puzzles are complemented by simplistic but helpfully high-contrast art and sound design, yet undermined by a tedious, intrusive story and a reluctance to put new game-changing spins on its ideas to extend their lives.

Ingredients
2 large eggs
Salt and pepper
2 to 3 tablespoons shredded cheese (optional)
1/4 to 1/2 cup filling, pre-cooked if necessary (optional)
2 teaspoons unsalted butter
Minced parsley, to garnish (optional)
Equipment
Mixing bowl
Whisk
8-inch nonstick skillet
Spatula
Dinner plate
Instructions
1. Whisk the eggs: Crack both eggs into a mixing bowl. Whisk the eggs until completely combined, and season with salt and pepper. If you\'re adding cheese or other fillings, make sure they are prepped and nearby.
2. Warm the skillet and melt the butter: Place an 8-inch skillet over medium-high heat and melt the butter. Tilt the skillet as the butter melts to evenly coat the bottom. When the butter stops sizzling, the pan is heated and ready.
3. Pour the eggs into the skillet: Pour the whisked eggs into the skillet. Immediately tilt the pan so the eggs coat the entire bottom. The eggs should sizzle on contact; if not, continue cooking, but remember to heat the pan a little longer next time.
4. Drag and push the eggs to form waves: Use a spatula to gently drag and push the cooked eggs from the edges toward the center of the pan, making space for the uncooked eggs and forming waves in the omelette. Tilt the skillet so that the uncooked eggs flow into the open spaces.
5. Cook the omelette for 1 to 2 minutes: The omelette will finish cooking in 1 to 2 minutes. When done, the bottom will be set and the edges will look crisp. The top of the omelette should still look fairly wet and uncooked, but there will no longer be any loose, easily flowing liquid egg — the omelette will continue cooking off the heat, so finish when you think the top still seems a bit underdone.
6. Top with cheese and fillings: If using, sprinkle the cheese and fillings down the center of the omelette.
7. Fold the omelette: Fold the bottom third of the omelette over the center, and then fold the top third down. Alternatively, fold the omelette in half.
8. Slide the omelette onto a plate: Gently slide the omelette onto a plate and garnish with parsley. Eat right away while still hot.

Bioshock gets my recommendation on the overall presentation rather than the combat.  I've played it many times over the years and my thoughts are below....
The Good:
1.  The setting is awesome, and the overall level design is great.  All the music, sound, and voice overs feel like they are from the proper era
2.  The characters and storyline are interesting and well acted/voiced
3.  The weapons and upgrades are, in many ways, better than a lot of FPS's out there
4.  You get your money's worth - it's not a short game
5.  The plasmids add unique combat elements to the game
The Bad:
1.  I'm tired of message logs and getting door codes from them
2,  There is little to no puzzle solving elements
3.  Being led thru the game by a voice on a radio has been done countless times
4.  The plot elements have been done before
The Ugly:
1. The combat is very clunky and just messy.  There is so much crap that gets in the way, and the randomness of splicers coming and going gets to be a pain after awhile.
2.  The sound drops out a lot, especially when using the Tommy Gun
3.  There's a turning point in the story late in the game that you will see coming from a mile away
4.  The map totally sucks

Update:
6 months have passed since I wrote this review.
The roadmap has been public for almost 8 months now and 23 of the 27 items in the "1 - 6 Month" category are still "not ready yet".
A new update is mentioned that should be released soon and contain the clothing update.
Maybe it will also contain the Steam Trading Cards that should have been released two updates ago. Maybe it won't.
A very generous summary of the "progress" would be about 9 months for about a third of the things they wanted to address in 6 months and this describes pretty well the discrepancy between what Hinterlands keeps telling and what they keep delivering.
Yes, they are still delivering updates.
But at this pace all those things that were supposed to take "1 - 6 Months" won't be done before 2018.
Original:
I bought The Long Dark as an Early Access title in December 2014, because I liked the overall setting (Winter, Single-Player, Survival), the independent developer Hinterland introduced themselves as experienced game developers ("veterans of the industry", "AAA titles") and the goal was to develop the first episode of a narrative story in about 3 months time, while offering a Sandbox as a playable testing environment in the meantime.
The atmosphere and setting of the game are really great. The artistic style is consistent, fitting and most of all very pleasing. Hinterland have taken some liberties in portraying wildlife and occasionally favored game design over realism, which I find is nothing to complain about.
But 18 months and three failed release dates later it is still in Early Access and without any released episodes of the announced Story Mode. It's difficult to tell how long it'll be until Story Mode is completed because Hinterland have stopped giving new release dates and engaged in a rigorous "it's done when it's done" approach.
There are quite a lot of people who seem to be fine with playing just the Sandbox for all this time, stating that they don't want or care for the Story Mode. However, I actually bought this for the narrative story and Sandbox simply doesn't hold any interest for me anymore. You can't actually do that many different things in the current game and just trying to survive for one more day without achieving anything else than surviving for one more day is simply not my cup of tea. This is especially true since many of the in-game activities are represented by abstract progress bars that simly show the passage of time. You never actually see your character repairing, crafting, eating, harvesting or cooking. The maps are also static, so after some time you know the environment like the back of your hand.
After having failed the most recent release window Hinterland published a roadmap for the future development in April 2016, containing development items categorized into "0 - 6 months", "6 - 12 months" and "12+ months".
Unfortunately, Story Mode is not a part of that roadmap.
The roadmap was recently updated, after 2 months had passed. It seems they are trying to put 4 of 27 items of the "0 - 6 months" category into the June update. The remaining items are in the same category as in April, meaning what was thought to be 6 months away in April is still 6 months away in June.
So instead of one big change to the anticipated release date once a year, there are now several small ones. It might look better because instead of announcing a change to the planned release date, they are simply not updating the planned duration until completion, but the effect is still the same. With this approach I'm afraid the roadmap will take years to reach anything close to completion and Story Mode may not be coming for quite some time.
While it might sound great that a developer is actually delaying a product because "it's not ready yet", I cannot recommend an Early Access title that keeps postponing its release on the sole premise of always needing more time.
Sadly, it seems The Long Dark is following the poor tradition of broken promises and seemingly endless development phases that plague Early Access.

This is the first Tropico game I haven't enjoyed. You seem to spend the entre game fire fighting and the campaign is just freaking annoying. I'd rather have realistic economic goals for my island than some far fetched plot about the end of the world. You end up just not caring. It of course retains it's typical humour but really goes overkill to a point that any characters in the games are incredibly unlikable. Even your own president.
There's a wide array of buildings to choose from and I really liked the progression through the era's Colonial through to Present day but the games campaign revovles around heavy military usage yet you once again lack real control over your troops. It's highly annoying to watch them act consistently like brainless turds during an invasion or rebel uprising.
Futhermore the game has issues with the staffing of your buildings, as your island becomes ever more populous people seem unwilling to ever work in your manufacturing plants meaning they stand there empty most of the time. Frustrating is not the word. Not to mention that mining resources run out far too quickly meaning you can miss targets in game since you son't actually have anymore of that resource to mine.
And finally the targets are boring as hell. Given that there's now 5 countries (Yes Europe isnt a country but whatever) you can negiotate with, why do they want the same things all of the time.
I did enjoy playing Tropico at times, but it is a seriously lazy game. If the developers had spent more time balancing the above issues and ditching the cheesey puns that occur every 5 seconds then maybe just maybe i'd recommend it to you. Only ever buy on a Sale at a very generous rate.

Seriously, though, between all of the games, the beautiful environment, the character creation tools, and the people around you keeping it all lively, there is no better casino that won't make you mortgage your house, or the company payroll and riding it on black.

Think traditional Sim City but with a twist. This game is a midieval-esque city/citizen management game. The story line of the game is that you control a group of citizens that were banished from somewhere. That's it. Your goal is whatever you want it to be. You can thrive and grow, survive or starve to death.
The tutorial only covers the basics and gives no insight into how to grow your city. Be prepared to be frustrated at times, your your city needs outpaces citizen growth, or when citizen growth outpaces your food/housing production. That being said, there-in lies the challenge and fun of the game. These problems and the varying starting conditions allows for a lot of replayability. The game is neither an idle nor active game, making it great for playing when you have an environment that creates multiple interruptions.
One frustrating aspect is that merchants seem to have a random pattern of arrival. Often, I am limited on growth that I want to take because I am unable to diversify my food production.
The user interface isn't 100% clear, but highly customizable regarding which screens are presented as well as their location.
I would recommend this game. A simple, bug-free, polished and enjoyable game!

I've read the good and the bad reviews, and ultimately a game like 'The Park' will be polarizing. On one hand the story, being widely open to interpretation, will leave some unsatisfied and wanting a clearer explanation. On the other hand, there are those like me who don't mind filling in the blanks with my imagination and taking in the atmosphere.
The game, for the most part, falls just short of scary, the focus being more on the the protagonist's increasing panic at the thought of losing her child than the cheap jump scares and monsters we're so used to encountering in modern horror titles. It is a descent into horror rather than a trip through it. It starts 'Ether One,' takes a turn into a 'Silent Hill' atmosphere, then makes a very smooth transition to the psychological horrors of titles such as 'PT' and 'Layers of Fear.'
I loved this game. It was just the right length to match the pacing of the increased intensity and it left me wanting more. I will definitely be trying out TSW now, knowing that this game weaves into the lore of that title.
One issue and it seems to be a common one. I had huge frame rate problems on any settings above high with 2X AA. That seems to be the magic combination of settings in case anyone else is having these issues.

Ingredients
2 large eggs
Salt and pepper
2 to 3 tablespoons shredded cheese (optional)
1/4 to 1/2 cup filling, pre-cooked if necessary (optional)
2 teaspoons unsalted butter
Minced parsley, to garnish (optional)
Equipment
Mixing bowl
Whisk
8-inch nonstick skillet
Spatula
Dinner plate
Instructions
1. Whisk the eggs: Crack both eggs into a mixing bowl. Whisk the eggs until completely combined, and season with salt and pepper. If you\'re adding cheese or other fillings, make sure they are prepped and nearby.
2. Warm the skillet and melt the butter: Place an 8-inch skillet over medium-high heat and melt the butter. Tilt the skillet as the butter melts to evenly coat the bottom. When the butter stops sizzling, the pan is heated and ready.
3. Pour the eggs into the skillet: Pour the whisked eggs into the skillet. Immediately tilt the pan so the eggs coat the entire bottom. The eggs should sizzle on contact; if not, continue cooking, but remember to heat the pan a little longer next time.
4. Drag and push the eggs to form waves: Use a spatula to gently drag and push the cooked eggs from the edges toward the center of the pan, making space for the uncooked eggs and forming waves in the omelette. Tilt the skillet so that the uncooked eggs flow into the open spaces.
5. Cook the omelette for 1 to 2 minutes: The omelette will finish cooking in 1 to 2 minutes. When done, the bottom will be set and the edges will look crisp. The top of the omelette should still look fairly wet and uncooked, but there will no longer be any loose, easily flowing liquid egg — the omelette will continue cooking off the heat, so finish when you think the top still seems a bit underdone.
6. Top with cheese and fillings: If using, sprinkle the cheese and fillings down the center of the omelette.
7. Fold the omelette: Fold the bottom third of the omelette over the center, and then fold the top third down. Alternatively, fold the omelette in half.
8. Slide the omelette onto a plate: Gently slide the omelette onto a plate and garnish with parsley. Eat right away while still hot.

The third installment of the tale of Rufus and Goal brings to its final conclusion a story about the survival of the fittest at the expense of the weak, the personal drama of an anti - hero who tries to make amends for his mistakes though he never learns from them, and a vortex of explosions, disasters and failed stratagems that began with the first game in the series. Although it falls somewhat short compared to the superb Deponia (1) and despite some flaws in its execution, this 18-hour long game that features a solid allegorical background and great puzzles is anything but a failure.

SUMMARY
The gameplay is tight and smooth, evocative of favorites like Mega Man or Metal Slug. It feels like more could have been done with level design and platforming; it's pretty much all bosses, but there's more than enough challenge, variety and gorgeous artowork to pick this one up for full price. There are glitches, but what did you expect from the Unity engine?
IN-DEPTH
CupHead is a damn fine labor of love that is bursting with tributes to some of the greatest run and gun games ever created, including but not limited to: Mega Man, Metal Slug, Gunstar Heroes, Kid Icarus, Contra, Batman & Robin for Genesis, Final Fantasy 6(!!) and arguably Street Fighter II.  For cartoon lovers like me, you'll find omage to Tom & Jerry, Fantasia, Woody Woodpecker, Betty Boop, Popeye and even The Pixel Prince Paul Robertson. It's wonderful, a constant joy and a merciless challenge members of my generation will find a welcome change from the same old thing (and I don't intend that ironically). Every moment something amazes and impresses! It's non-stop fun in every way.
Negatives: Some game breaking glitches and a couple of attacks which are literally unavoidable because of said glitches. The bulk of the power ups are useless, I actually didn't get any my second playthrough and it was easier because the Supers are more trouble than solution.
TIP:  If you're Using an XBox Controller, First Thing: Change your EX Shot to Left Trigger.
