The Park is a short bite sized nugget of terror. Giving you a glimpse into madness itself using the whimsy and charm of an amusement park from hell. You will guide a young mother as she searches for her son Callum. Along the way you begin to unravel the mystery of the park and learn more about Lorraine. While I enjoyed the game cinematically, there are times the game takes your out of the action and lets you just watch. Which is fine but I never felt like I was in any real danger. For the most part The Park does rely on jump scares to get you. There are moments of intensity and dread but low on the actual scare factor.(Atleast for me) As for the story of The Park, to really understand it or enjoy it is a matter of interpretation and plenty of reading. Scraps of paper and notes are strewn about the game and give you a glimpse into the backstory of the world. By the end though you are still left with more questions then answers. I think this was done purposefully though. Something that buyers should beware is that the game does have some glitches. The game crashed once on initial start up and I had to restart after Callum got scared of escalators and prevented me from moving further. Despite these minor hiccups, I did really enjoy the somber story of The Park. The ending is quite shocking and leaves you with your mouth open. The only gripe I have is that certain pieces of backstory are connected to another game. Which I haven't played. The connected stories are rather loose and doesn't necessarily prevent you from enjoying The Park but those looking to really dig into the lore and story will need to venture further onto message boards and wikis. In all it is a well defined story and had me intrigued to the very last minute.

Day 1
My first in-game day was spent wandering around and trying to figure out the controls. I picked up some food and a baseball bat and ran around smashing windows, climbing inside people's houses and looting. After caving in a few Z-heads I was told I was thirsty. I drank some water from a toilet and all was well. I was then told I was hungry. Searching in a house I found a "TV Dinner", which sounded perfect. I walked over and put it in the oven. While I was waiting for it to cook I read a book. A short time later I came over to the oven only to find I had burnt my TV dinner. The game told me I would get depressed and unhappy should I eat it. I did. I was instantly overwhelmed with depression and told I was tired. I went to sleep on the couch.
Day 2
The next morning I awoke in an unhappy mood. I was playing about with the controls and somehow managed to accelerate time at an alarming rate. After smashing some keys I finally got it back to normal. My character was hungry, thirsty, bored, depressed and tired now. O goodie.
I found a steak and slung it in the oven to cook. I was not going to let this meal burn, so I stood there watching it cook. The instant it was finished I grabbed it and scoffed the whole thing. As is tradition, I washed it down with some toilet water. I was told my character was going to collapse (presumably because he had been awake for about 2 days solid due to the time accelerating-issue). I curled up on the sofa and went to sleep.
Day 4?
I woke up in the middle of the night and could not see a thing. I thought it best I continue with my book in the pitch black, so began reading for a bit. Morning came and I was hungry and thirsty. I searched around the neighbourhood for supplies and came across a packet of cigarettes and some peanut butter. I ate the cigarettes and the peanut butter and sipped some more toilet water. I also found a backpack and various other supplies. I went on a journey north. My mood seemed to change as I smashed Z after Z' head in. My depression lifted and I found new vigour. As the day went on I looted a liquor shop for crisps and ice-cream and broke into a farm house to steal a hammer and nails.
....that's pretty much how my game went so far.

I’ve always thought things like urban exploring were super cool. I used to work for a certain media giant and its theme parks and exploring the abandoned and left to rot secrets there were some of the most thrilling experiences I’ve had in my life. So when I started seeing The Park in my recommended titles I knew it was for me. A horror walking simulator in an abandoned theme park? Sounds awesome. I have never played or even heard of The Secret World prior to playing this.
The Park creates an awesome atmosphere through great graphics and narrative story telling. The narration is well voice acted and the monologue does well progressing the story. Each ride felt pretty real and I loved that they weren’t cut scenes and that you had full control of the camera on each ride. The climax of the game was super creepy and really tense. The way the notes are scattered and written is great too. If you take the time to read them you’ll have some idea what’s going on. If you don’t read any of them you’ll have no idea what’s happening. I like that in this type of game. It provides incentive. At the end of the game I was really enjoying myself. I was creeped out and trying to piece together what exactly was going on. Then, sadly, they completely ruined the atmosphere that they had set up and ended the game with a third person cut scene. They give you full control over your character for the entire game and then take it away from you for the ending. I have no idea why someone thought that was a good idea. Yes the game is short, but it isn’t a full retail priced game and the atmosphere is great. Gamers need to stop being brats and expecting 50 hour games for $10. I was definitely willing to purchase additional content for the game, to get more of a picture of what was going on and I was sort of hoping that there would be additional content to do that, but after the ending I’m hesitant and kind of turned off to the story. I enjoyed the game, it’s a good buy for $10 especially since I played through most of it on Halloween but the ending leaves a very bad taste in my mouth.
I’ll probably play through one more time to really soak in the atmosphere and get the achievements that I missed but I probably won’t touch it again otherwise. Other horror games like this have been known to follow up with free updates with additional content or maybe even a reasonably priced expansion. Those might get me to come back for another couple of hours but otherwise this is a 10ish dollar one time play through experience. Get it for $10 instead of renting an HD horror movie. Sort of recommend.

You won't be able to last too long tucked away inside an abandoned house though, because you'll inevitably run out of food and resources.
It's more a simulation of the actual zombie apocalypse to test all those theories you've ever had about how it would go down. What it isn't is just another arcade-style shootemup zombie video-game. I recommend it for anyone who wants to experience the zombie apocolypse but who doesn't have the gusto to take over a CDC headquarters and let loose a deadly virus in real life.

TL/DR? Here's the short version:
- Nice and detailed survival simulation
- Graphical style helps build an atmosphere of isolation and tension
- "Proper" zombies, but with options to set them the way you want them in Sandbox Mode
- Building & Crafting. Build your own fortress against the zombie hordes
- It's really good. Buy it.
This could very well the pinnacle of the Zombie Survival generation.
With a market that's been flooded with zombies over the last decade, Project Zomboid is offering a world that is just as dangerous as the shambling hordes we've come to take for granted. Heat, cold, hunger, and even wetness are all things you have to deal with in order to survive. And that's just the physical side of survival. Boredon, panic depression... all the hallmarks of isolated survival are there.
From a graphics point of view, it might look like a 90's throwback, but the isometric view combines with the lighting and line of sight mechanics make for an incredibly unnerving experience. You might be able to see your surroundings, but you won't see zombies shambling up from behind until you turn around. The graphics might seem tedious and repetitive, but this somehow just nails down the feeling of underlying hopelessness of your situation.
It's nice to see an implementation of Max Brooks' "proper" zombies. But of course the developers realise the power of choice, and offer a variety of setting to alter the zombie behaviour, allowing you to experience the end of the world the way you want to.
Apart from a few minor glitches relating to character positioning when interacting with objects (most notably looting closets/cupboards places next to each other), there is nothing I can find to complain about in this game. And with more content coming with updates, this is definitely one I'm glad to have picked up and can comfortably recommend to anyone looking for a detailed survival game, even if you are as "zombied-out" as many people are by now.

When I managed to nab a copy of this, admittedly from a live streamer (from who I am eternally grateful for, if only for giving me a free copy of a hidden gem) , I was a bit skeptical as to how much I'd enjoy it. And yet, despite everything the system of leveling up in different categories, fighting through hordes of enemies and watching unique cutscenes for each character makes it a very fun co-op experience.
So yes... Grab this game as soon as you can, it's worth every penny, especially if you're playing with a friend.

I initially tried to play Scourge Project 1&2 and failed, mostly because the screen resolution was desperately set to "lowest". It was a blast to play Doom like this, but in full 3D, you just feel visually impaired. Anyhow, Scourge : Outbreak solved this problem, so I finally was able to play it.
Aside Left 4 Dead, it was the second time I played a "third person / team based / tactical fps" but since I love real-time party-RPGs like Dungeon Siege, or turn-by-turn tactical RPGs like FallOut Tactics, this one sounded engaging.
The gameplay is pretty straightforward : choose one of the 4 characters, use a tutorial if you need and get some backstory (nice addition), then run into action with your fellow heavily armored buddies, receiving mission updates along the way.
It seems that the game makes a good use of modern FPS tropes like choose-2-weapons-to-carry and glue-yourself-behind-boxes. The orders you can give are contextualized : depending on where, who or what you are targeting, you can have the closer team member take cover, focus on an enemy, open a door, use a turret, revive another team member ; without losing the pace of the fight which is great. Overall, each team member is a decent shooter and never forgives to save you even under heavy fire.
The special abilities are kinda neat, but for me, the real pleasure of the game was to consider each confrontation as a puzzle : where should I position each team member in order to assault or defend? Sometimes an sub-optimal line of sight could cost your team frequent death/revive cycles.
The enemies are challenging enough, even in beginner more. Soldiers can take advantage of the level and bosses requires some strategic planning. But the strange design decision of infinite critters that mysteriously vanish when you reach the next checkpoint somewhat disrupted the experience.
Since the storyline is purely functional and the characters kinda stereotypical, playing solely for the story won't reward you. It seems that there is a leveling mechanic, granting you points in different categories like "short range kill", "head shot", "assistance" but I don't know if it grants you with bonuses except for the powers.
To wrap it up, Scourge Outbreak is a decent team-based shooter, with a nice game flow, and correct level design. Nothing truly memorable though, so it feels more like a filler.

This game is one of the most realistic and intense games i have played, great if you play games like Verdun where you die more times that you can count, have to actually use you brain and not just twitch shoot, and often dont even know where you are being shot at from. It also has a similar feel to Insurgency in that you weapon is never centred so hipfiring is woefully inaccurate, with a mosin (oh, on this game, on fuller maps the sniper, SMG, MG or semiautomatic rifle classes will be taken so you have to become pretty good with the humble mosin/Kar98) you cant hit anything over 3 meters (not an overstatment unless you are a boss) with a rifle hipfiring.  This game has very few cons and these can be overlooked such as the small community meaning you dont often get to play on the map you want as it may only have 12 player (this sounds like enought for COD players but the maps are so large you need at least 40), the graphics arent amazing and the map load times are rediculous (that my just be me however). Other than that there are just pros: gritty and realistc play, team based objecitve missions, a very good supression system where you accuracy gets affected, map sizes make it feel like a full scale battle and not a quick COD stlye skirmish and finally the general feel of war and hardship in the game. Every once in a while you stumble into a game that is just a pearl. With The Long Dark I struck gold and got 100% my cup of tea. I love survival and exploring games, making a base or in this case hoarding/starving simulator go apesh!t, I'm loving it. And the style is really special in breathtaking in my opinion.
So you have your first try on the hardest setting with the "bring it on I'm made for this game" attitude, dying within the first 24 hours of hypothermia... Learning the game mechanics and the layout of the 1st map I made it a little further each try. Fist 2 days, then 5, then 11.
I thought I had my act together then, at day 11. I found a preppers cache with food, made my base at camp office at the lake. Had a hunting rifle with ample of ammunition, axe, hunting knife etc. enough wood at the base, water, food, plenty stored for days to come. Went on a hunting trip, shot a dear, was going to skin it, not a care in the world, BLIZZARD! omfg I'm freezing and exhausted becuase of it. Collapsed about 30 meters from the camp office,... faded into the long dark.
So I learned my lesson and now I make a campfire if I have to skin and gut something.
My try after that was my best try after that. Same story, great gear, but I ran out of food and was beginning to starve. No Deer to be found where I usually found them for 3 days in a row so I went on for fishing. On my way to the fishing hut a wolf showed up between me and the hut, charging towards me lit flare to make the wolf stop hopefully. "Well, I guess wolf is back on the menu". Crouched for a better angle, aimed my rifle !BAM! and... missed! as the wolf went for my throat. "O crap get it off get it off get it oooooff nooooo my clothes. aaaaaaah it bit me crap that hurt bad omfg I didn't know they could huuuurt you sooo bad!!!!!!"
"I'm not sure if I'm going to make it" my character gasped" Bleeding bad I took care of the wounds at the spot and stumbled back to the camp office. I needed to rest, I needed calories to recuperate while I rested or I'd never wake up. Then I realized I still had some tea left!!!
Down to 3% before passing out//dying.I grabbed my lantern "out of fuel"... Looked in my inventory to refuel it, no fuel left,... Lit another flare. Couldn't nearly see anything as I was close to death and walking and stopping at a spot was a great challenge. When I finally ended up in front of the fireplace I see I'm down TO MY LAST MATCH. This better work! "Come on little fire!" YES, the fire is burning and I'm making tea, 3 whole cups, 300 calories! Now to rest, I fire up another flare and stumble my way upstairs leaning to the left wall to not go all over the place. I rested, for like 2-3 hours if I remember correct. Just so the calories and the rest would patch me up a bit and I'd have a chance to get to the fishing hut. If I'd rested too long the starvation would kick in again and would kill me for sure! I was back up to 6%! I had a fighting change!
I lit a flare, made my way downstairs, exit the camp office. I'm not sure if there was mist or I was just nearly completely blind of being nearly dead, but I could not see crap. Going from left to right as walking in a straight line was not possible in my current state. I walked around till my flare burnt up, lit my last flare and still could not find a friggin fishing hut, my last and only hope.
Then an achievement popped up "You prep the preppers" I made it to live 30 days!! Tea ftw! As I walked on with my last strength I see the lake cabins. I already looted that place so no food in there for sure, but maybe if I just rest for one hour... and if I don't wake up, at least I did not die outside in the cold but in a warm bed. As I lay my tired and starving body down on the bed I set myself to sleep for one hour as I fade into the long dark.

Limbo started off as an experience. Similar to what you'd expect when seeing the trailer for it: an intriguing and relaxing theme of soft mystery through a peaceful environment. Distinctly stylistic, mostly lush and natural, industrial bits sometimes in moderation. Light puzzles are sprinkled in here and there. Nothing complex enough to ruin the experience or slow the progression.
Then the puzzles get complex. Water puzzles. Gravity puzzles. Magnet puzzles. Speed puzzles. Timing puzzles. The only good thing I can say about them is it'll start you right back in front of the puzzle you failed instead of make you do an entire segment over like most games.
LIMBO loses it's magic as the difficulty increases. It became just another puzzle game by the end. The lush relaxing environments largely became plain beam platforms and simple straight angle rooms. The magical relaxing nature disappeared because of the difficulty spike. The world's mystery theme vanishes entirely as though the story was only early bait made specifically for the trailer.
I honestly feel a little let down. This game had a magical feel for half of it. Then the second half dropped that. I wouldn't be surprised if two different people designed separate halves of the game.

From the brilliantly twisted mind of Scott Cawthon comes an indie horror game that, from the surface, appears to be nothing but jump-scare fueled nightmares, but in fact, it is so much more.
You play as the newly-hired security guard, Mike Schmidt, whose job it is to observe the overnight goings-on of Freddy Fazbear's Pizza, a family-friendly pizzeria that has fallen upon hard times since an incident known as the "Bite of '87." But beware, as the restaurant is filled with animatronic anthropomorphic characters that roam the halls at night and are itching to send you to an early grave!
For 5 nights from 12:00am to 6:00am, you must observe your cameras and listen closely as Freddy and his friends pace up and down the halls and in and out of rooms causing disturbances wherever they go, but in doing so, you must also learn to conserve your battery power as flicking on lights and closing doors can cause a power outage, leaving you vulnerable.
Each night becomes increasingly more challenging, with the animatronics moving faster in pace and awakening other horrors that will leave you wondering if it is just Mike's imagination or something more, and upon completion of the game, you will unlock other challenging modes.
Those apt to pay attention to a game's surrounding will notice subtle changes in the environment as they check each room. Keep these in mind, for they become of great importance going forward in the series and serve as clues to uncover the terrifying mystery Cawthon has weaved throughout each installment.
The fourth title in the series is due out October 2015.

The Park is officially designated as a first-person psychological horror adventure. Already I am at odds with the game, as adventure implies exploration, or a puzzle element, and horror implies the need for survival against something that is trying to kill you. The actual exploration in this game is limited to looking for your child, which is the whole point of the game, and there are no puzzles that you have to solve in order to continue. As to horror, the gameplay did nothing to add a feeling of doom, or threat to the character, out side of the story. There is no gameplay, no stealth, no challenge as to how to progress to the next zone, only the need to keep walking and get there. If anything, I would classify this game as a walking simulator with a spooky mentality.
The strongest element is the story, with an immersive environment and a captivating, emotional lead character that draws you into the story. You are pulled into this dark, haunted, confusing theme park as you look for your child. One thing that takes away from the story is that you have to get on the various theme park rides; not because you think your child is on them, or because it is part of the story, but more because you feel you have to in order to collect some lore, and because the developers want you to experience the ride.
The game is short (1-2 hours long) for price they are asking, I feel it needs more than just a really good story. I am conflicted about this game; the story was really good, but the gameplay was atrocious, with little interaction and no adventure element, or choice. For the story, I would recommend you watching a 'Let's Play' from a player you enjoy.

I'm in love this game. I've always loved vehicular combat games like Twisted Metal, Vigilante 8, and Destruction Derby. Sadly, while I've heard good things about the original Carmageddon, I never played them as I was a console gamer at the time. Well, if this game is somewhat indicative of past games in the series, I should probably explore others. That said, by no means is this game perfect. It actually has a few glaring flaws. But overall, it's awesome. When I was a teenager, I poured hours into Twisted Metal on the PSX. It was my go-to multiplayer, and just oozed attitude. It was also the game that showed me the potential of the 32-bit era, as my Sega Genesis couldn't touch a game like Twisted Metal. Well, I get the same feelings with Carmageddon: Max Damage. I can't imagine older consoles being up to snuff for a game like this. It's not the graphics, but the sheer largesse of the maps. There's just so much to do in Carmageddon. Sure, you can hit all the check points, but you can also hunt down opponents, or mow down poor pedestrians (peds). There's so much to explore in Carmageddon, and the game rewards you for being curious. The graphics didn't wow me, but it looks decent and has a steady framerate. What makes me scratch my head is why the draw distance seems so short. But the draw distance of the horizon isn't the reason to play the game. You play it to crash cars and mow down peds. And on that account, it delivers. There's lots of blood and wreckage. What amuses me is how, when you're repairing your car, the parts that have fallen off magically fly back to your vehicle and become intact. That's a nice touch. Sound is a highlight for Carmageddon. It's got a killer soundtrack. Even if you don't like that genre of music, you can appreciate how it contributes to the game's ambience. The sound effects are likewise nice. When you move down peds, the sound of the blood flicking everywhere is so satisfying. Ditto when you throw a mortar shell at another vehicle. Special kudos to the announcer who really makes everything sound like a circus. And here's why the game is good but not a classic. The steering seems like it's out of Grand Theft Auto. Sure, that's fine if you're playing a pure sandbox game, but as this is an arcade game at heart, it needs to be more razor focused. The hand brake often seems useless. In other games, this gives you opportunities to drift, but I find myself just taking my foot off the gas if I want to go from A to B. The worst problem with control is that, when I press the "A" or "Y" buttons, Carmageddon seems to think I'm pressing "X". This means that when I have an enemy on sights, and I'm so close to closing the deal by throwing a mortar shell, I instead "recover" and I'm docked thousands of dollars. When this happens, I get annoyed as hell.

Hardware

My gaming PC hosts an i7 processor, 16GB of RAM, and a GTX 1050 Ti. This is more than capable of running Carmageddon. Yet, when I sometimes abort an event, Carmageddon either crashes or causes my entire PC to freeze. This only happens when I'm aborting the event. Otherwise the game runs fine. I also wonder about the lack of optimization for laptops. Why aren't laptop graphics cards officially supported? Seems like the developers cut corners here. It might seem like I'm being harsh here, but I actually do like this game. If the developers fix the obvious bugs, I would consider this a future classic. I right this as Project Zomboid is in Early Access. Nevermind that the game is unfinished, because playing it would convince you that it is already complete.
The amount of content and detail already in the game is amazing. With workable multiplayer you have a cornucopia of options for gameplay. You can start your own survival game, where you explore deserted towns in hopes of avoiding or hunting the undead; you can start a sandbox game, where you pick and choose the details of the virus, it's qualities, as well as the environment around you; You can also hope onto a server, many of which are filled with efficient role-players for a more cooperative and tense experience.
So far, the developers have thought a lot of things through. Power and water utilities die over time. Food rots. Food burns. Weapons break down. Crops dry up. You can get sick. You can wound yourself by crawling through a broken window, which may have caused an alarm. You have traits and skills, as does everyone. You can choose to play in real time or at an accelerated pace. In addition to hunger and thirst, your character demands comfort, destressing, and sanctuary.
This game is brilliant, but not without flaws.
There is no campaign, leaving it a true sandbox experience. This, I know, may be a major turn off for some gamers.
It is an Early Access game, still incomplete. I understand there will be at some point an introduction of vehicles and NPCs.
Fortunately, the developer(s) are constantly fine-tuning the experience and adding new content, so even those who play it religiously will still find interesting things being introduced into the game without getting too bored with it.
I'd recommend this to anybody with a fondness for survival or simulation games.

Overall I liked quite a few things about Rise: Battle Lines.
I really liked the idea behind both players making their moves at the same. This mechanic has a lot of potential and makes you think more about what you think your opponent is going to do rather than what you want to do on your turn.
Rise: Battle Lines also thrives on being simple to learn and quick to play. You can learn the game in minutes and you can finish a match in 10-15 minutes. If you are looking for a highly strategic game you are going to be disappointed. If you are looking for a quick pick up and play game that has just enough strategy I think you could have some fun with Rise: Battle Lines.

I do have two issues with Rise: Battle Lines though.
First I wish the game had some more variety. The game only has six different types of units and I kind of wish the game would add a couple more. With only six different types of units I think the game could get repetitive kind of quickly. After extended plays it might feel like you are fighting the same battles over and over again.
Second I wish there was a little more strategy and a little less guessing in the game. Being able to guess what the other player is going to do on their turn seems to be the most important thing in Rise: Battle Lines. If you guess well you are much more likely to beat your opponent rather than having a good strategy.
Overall Rise: Battle Lines has the foundation to be a good game. If the game can add a little more variety it could be a good game. If the idea of a simpler quick turned based strategy game appeals to you, I think you could enjoy Rise: Battle Lines.

Note: I received a free review copy of the game from the developer.

Scourge Outbreak is basically a 4 player buddy 3rd person shooter in a sci-fi motif, that goes for the fast and furious instead of any precision. There's this long story about how this Merc squad that goes by call sign "Echo Squad" was working for this "Tarn Initiative" which is some sort of secret org out to break the monopoly of Noguri Corporation, and each of the 4 members have a personal reason against this monolith. And there are signs that the Noguri Corp is using some sort of xeno material they got from an asteroid for something really sinister...
In practice, this game is a mix of corridor crawl with a good dose of run-and-gun that's reminiscent of CODMW or Counterstrike levels, albeit not as many alternate paths. You can only carry two weapons at a time, and you can choose any of the 4 classes available, and choose a special "perk" that gives you a bonus. So choose your weapons carefully depending on ammo available. The best gun you have may not be the one with the most ammo.
This game gives a good variation on the guns though, as each type of gun (assault rifle, SMG, pistol, shotgun... ) can be of one of several variants, or just plain. Variants can have increased accuracy, faster reload, increased damage, better stability, even grenade launcher, depending on the weapon. This makes the game less monotonous without going into "which gun is better" bazillion variants like Borderlands series.
In practice, the guns do feel powerful enough, and sounds okay. The heavy weapons like mini-gatling sound serious, but the plasma gun seem to be quite undersized. There's a full cover system, where you can even blind-fire from cover.
The game gave each character two special skills... With enough "ambrosia" energy, each character to either generate a temporary forcefield for protection, or cause an energy smash to zap all enemies nearby. There are two versions of the shield (static vs. dynamic) and two versions of the energy smash (again, static or dynamic) for 4 variations (one for each class of characters).  On easy you may rarely use the shield, or smash, but on higher levels it may be the only way to survive when you get swarmed by enemies.
The graphics are quite good but not extraordinary. The character models have the right poly count to look detailed enough. However, the voices are not very distintive, esp. for the 'soldier' guy. Weapons sound and music are okay.
The writing seems to be above average, as the game really does start on a bang. When sent to infiltrate the enemy facility, your drop pod was hit (by what?) before you even hit the ground and you lost most of your weapons. Can you survive until you find something? You are helped by a guy on the radio, as you try to chase down the traitors that got you shot down, but is that what's really going on, or are you being played for some alternate purpose? As you fight through the levels, you discover clues that perhaps, things are not quite what they seem, but you're already committed...
The AI is actually quite decent. If you "fall" your 3 AI buddies will do their best (even raise their shields) to gain some time to revive you (and you're supposed to revive them too if they fall). Obviously if you fall in the middle of an enemy horde, you may bleed out before they get to you. And if all of them got incapacitated it's game over, man.  Besides that, AI buddies will take cover, shoot, protect certain spots, etc. They will even take orders from you to go somewhere, get on certain trurrets, and so on.
The bosses are pretty good. So far I've killed 5 bosses and they all involve different methods. Enemy gunship requires sticky grenades... or environmental trap. Level end boss are sufficiently tough to be challenging but not impossible, if you figure out the problem. Else, you'll waste ammo and curse.
One weird part about this game is there is no save function, only checkpoints that save automatically, and it seems it's MOSTLY at the right places.
All in all, Scourge is basically an attempt to redefine the SciFi 3rd person shooter, and this one is actually quite good despite its lack of big-name publisher. If you like this genre, give it a try.

Having grown up making my own video games and swapping EXEs with a childhood coder buddy on a regular basis, the idea of a game being a dedication to a friend's unappreciated work is captivating.  And for the first few levels, that's exactly what I felt from The Beginner's Guide: pure, giddy captivation.
It's a shame then that the game devolves into an over-dramatized, self-indulgent narrative that takes it's own liberties with the supposed source material all to convey an IRL message that seemed more forced than sincere.  While going for feels, the game would rather misuse another's work than be a guided tour of appreciation, all the while leaving a bitter taste in my mouth.
Had this only been a game about "Look at what my friend has made over the years, aren't these amazing ideas!", I would be raving about how wonderfully unique it is and how its an empathetic preservation of a swansong.  But that's not what I got here.  The Beginner's Guide is a fantastic idea sullied by too much drama.

Every once in a while you stumble into a game that is just a pearl. With The Long Dark I struck gold and got 100% my cup of tea. I love survival and exploring games, making a base or in this case hoarding/starving simulator go apesh!t, I'm loving it. And the style is really special in breathtaking in my opinion.
So you have your first try on the hardest setting with the "bring it on I'm made for this game" attitude, dying within the first 24 hours of hypothermia... Learning the game mechanics and the layout of the 1st map I made it a little further each try. Fist 2 days, then 5, then 11.
I thought I had my act together then, at day 11. I found a preppers cache with food, made my base at camp office at the lake. Had a hunting rifle with ample of ammunition, axe, hunting knife etc. enough wood at the base, water, food, plenty stored for days to come. Went on a hunting trip, shot a dear, was going to skin it, not a care in the world, BLIZZARD! omfg I'm freezing and exhausted becuase of it. Collapsed about 30 meters from the camp office,... faded into the long dark.
So I learned my lesson and now I make a campfire if I have to skin and gut something.
My try after that was my best try after that. Same story, great gear, but I ran out of food and was beginning to starve. No Deer to be found where I usually found them for 3 days in a row so I went on for fishing. On my way to the fishing hut a wolf showed up between me and the hut, charging towards me lit flare to make the wolf stop hopefully. "Well, I guess wolf is back on the menu". Crouched for a better angle, aimed my rifle !BAM! and... missed! as the wolf went for my throat. "O crap get it off get it off get it oooooff nooooo my clothes. aaaaaaah it bit me crap that hurt bad omfg I didn't know they could huuuurt you sooo bad!!!!!!"
"I'm not sure if I'm going to make it" my character gasped" Bleeding bad I took care of the wounds at the spot and stumbled back to the camp office. I needed to rest, I needed calories to recuperate while I rested or I'd never wake up. Then I realized I still had some tea left!!!
Down to 3% before passing out//dying.I grabbed my lantern "out of fuel"... Looked in my inventory to refuel it, no fuel left,... Lit another flare. Couldn't nearly see anything as I was close to death and walking and stopping at a spot was a great challenge. When I finally ended up in front of the fireplace I see I'm down TO MY LAST MATCH. This better work! "Come on little fire!" YES, the fire is burning and I'm making tea, 3 whole cups, 300 calories! Now to rest, I fire up another flare and stumble my way upstairs leaning to the left wall to not go all over the place. I rested, for like 2-3 hours if I remember correct. Just so the calories and the rest would patch me up a bit and I'd have a chance to get to the fishing hut. If I'd rested too long the starvation would kick in again and would kill me for sure! I was back up to 6%! I had a fighting change!
I lit a flare, made my way downstairs, exit the camp office. I'm not sure if there was mist or I was just nearly completely blind of being nearly dead, but I could not see crap. Going from left to right as walking in a straight line was not possible in my current state. I walked around till my flare burnt up, lit my last flare and still could not find a friggin fishing hut, my last and only hope.
Then an achievement popped up "You prep the preppers" I made it to live 30 days!! Tea ftw! As I walked on with my last strength I see the lake cabins. I already looted that place so no food in there for sure, but maybe if I just rest for one hour... and if I don't wake up, at least I did not die outside in the cold but in a warm bed. As I lay my tired and starving body down on the bed I set myself to sleep for one hour as I fade into the long dark.

I had no interest in Evolve.
I'm not into PvP really. I like games with a rich story and long single-player campaign. I wasn't going to buy it or even try it.
So when I got into the Evolve Alpha, I wasn't even going to play it. But some of my friends were coo-coo for it and talked me into trying it. So when I say this game is FREAKING INCREDIBLE, don't take that lightly.
The first time I played it, I had problems with it. Mostly because the graphics are pretty detailed and I ran it at higher than recommended settings, which rendered it was unplayable. But since then I've purchased a new gaming PC that runs it smooth as silk. After those initial problems I think I played it for several hours straight. Then when I came home from work the following day, I hopped right back ingame.
---- SO WHAT'S GOOD ABOUT IT? ----
Where do I begin?
* BALANCE - At first glance the most obvious plus is the graphics, but after several hours of playing, the graphics just aid in the immersion, and the thing that really sticks out is the asymmetrical gameplay still strikes an incredible balance.
* GAMEPLAY - Tight and responsive controls. Although that's hardly a feat for a modern AAA+ FPS. Evolve does a good job of making the controls transparent between the user and the game. Other gameplay-related plusses would be the very different classes, and how they were clearly well-considered and designed to be played differently. Each has very specific strengths, and even the guns and tools for each class are useful, original, and futher the character's role. The addition of fantastic character mobility: humans in the form of jetpacks (which are tons of fun!) and the monster(s) in the form of powerful lunging and climbing abilities, it gives map traversal more of a "parkour" feeling, with the monster trying to get some distance so he can grab a snack, and the humans trying to catch up.
* GRAPHICS & ART - Ok, ok I had to say it. The graphics are among the best of any game.  Levels are interesting. Character designs are interesting. Monsters are VERY interesting.
* INTUITIVE - So... the very-first game I played I wasn't useful (due to my framerate being about 2), but the first game that I was able to control, I was also able to contribute. The controls, weapons, and tools are very intuitive, and the details are covered in helpful (and gorgeously rendered) instructional videos prior to using each class for the first time. The result is a great "easy-to-use, difficult-to-master" dynamic for each class and tool-weapon.
* ORIGINALITY - yeah its like Predator-Prey, if you ever played that as a kid. And while I'm sure someone sometime has made a digital multiplayer game out of it, its never been so high-profile with space technology and Cthulu monosters. Everyone else is doing L4D clones for their co-op multiplayer games, and I need to give Evolve props for really doing something new.
* ADDICTIVE - Tons of fun and keeps you coming back.
* AUDIENCE(?) - This is maybe less of a plus for the game as a plus for the people who play it, but... I haven't had any jerks sabotage the game or otherwise be total butts in alpha or beta. Maybe that will change for general-release, but I hope not.
---- IS THERE ANYTHING BAD ABOUT IT? ----
Yes, of course. Nothing is perfect.
* THE CHASE - You end up spending a lot of time just running. At first this is kinda fun, but after awhile it gets monotonous. You will spend about 80% of your game time just running. While parkour-y jetpack running is fun, even that gets tiresome after a few games, and you end up craving the action more and more.
* BEING THE MONSTER IS LONELY - while it seems like a great selling point (everybody fantasizes about being a huge powerful pseudo-god Cthulu monster, right?), its hard to feel good about all the other players ganging up on you, using their numerous abilities to slow you down and otherwise nerf your monster-powers to make you easier to kill. The result is that being the monster is frustrating and lonely, and I don't think I'm the only one who feels this way: In the games that I played, everybody set Monster as their least-favorite class, and so everybody eventually ended up playing Monster.
* DAISY AND DETECTORS - There's one class who's job it is to find the monster and "trap" it so the other humans can injure it. One hunter is able to put up motion sensors, but they seem like they're one-time-use. Not terribly useful. Daisy is a little better (she's a dog-thing that tracks the monster's scent) especially due to her healing ability. However, she's really REALLY slow compared to the monster, and so the tactic of "following daisy" usually doesn't work out so well. And yet - you inevitably end up following the Hunter and their tracking method, because nobody else has an effective one.
* 3RD PARTY DRM - I didn't have to sign up during alpha, but when I got closed beta access, I had to create an account in order to play. The account signup was very buggy, but with some persistence, was able to register. So far they've not sent me any ads or anything.
* WILDLIFE - the animals and carnivorous plants in this game take away quite a bit from the enjoyment. Its hard enough to track the Monster long enough to catch him a few times before level3 without getting trapped by carnivorous plants, eaten by crocodiles, and otherwise interrupted by giant... things. I can't help but conclude that this game would have been better with strictly herbavorial wildlife for the monster to eat and to occasionally attract the attention of humans, but all the others kinda clutter up the experience. I can see that maybe they're trying to break up the tracking monotony, and perhaps it would have succeeded - if only for the fact that as soon as you have one of these encounters, all you want to do is get away because the monster is evolving! If fighting animals did more good than just a one-off powerup, maybe this game mechanic wouldn't feel quite as useless.
*SINGLE PLAYER? - I am adding a question mark to this because I don't know if there will be a decent single player campaign or not. If there is, I will move this to the plus side. In the alpha there was no single player, but the beta had single player missions that acted as a tutorial and introduced each character, but didn't do much more. I am hoping that the final release will have a story mode in addition to the excellent multiplayer. The characters are too interesting for game-makers not to develop their backstory, and also: I want to know where the monsters came from! Its an opportunity for game-makers to enrich this new franchise, and I hope they don't pass it up.
---- CONCLUSION ----
The negatives are all rather-minor petty annoyances, vastly overshadowed by the incredible positives of this game. I highly recommend it.

I'll be honest, the presence of an "Evolve Shop" with overpriced skins on launch was a shockingly dumb mistake on 2K's part. Treating the customer like a sap willing to pay for anything, after spending AAA money on a title is a really stupid thing to do and 2K should apologise and withdraw this stuff now. However, I cannot let that interfere with my review of the game itself.
It's a blast to play, especially with friends (which is also conducive seeing as how communication is VITAL to the Hunters' success) but solo as a Hunter or Monster is also extremely satisfying. There are few things more satisfying than landing that killing blow on a Stage 3 after a long, bloody fight or pouncing on that last helpless Hunter and laughing as they scream and die underneath you.
The different Hunters and Monsters aren't just for show, they each have their own unique personality and playstyle (EVERYBODY loves Bucket). With (at time of writing) 3 Hunters per class for a total of 12 Hunters and 3 Monsters there's a fair amount of variety on show, with different combinations of Hunters yielding different results and dialogue (although the ambient dialogue is a little sparse and repetitive, they could have worked more on that). The different Monsters. however are VASTLY different from each other in both how you play them and how you tackle them. For example, the Goliath is a plain brute, got plenty of health and armour and does heavy damage at close range, whereas the Kraken is a flying monster who can devastate the Hunters at range but has weaker armour and health. They are almost diametrically opposed in how the player would play as them, and the Hunters have to adopt very different strategies to take them down.
Visually this game is stunning, as one might expect given that it uses CryEngine. This does mean that lower-mid to lower range systems are going to suffer, especially on denser maps. I myself had to downscale to 1600 x 900 to run this smoothly enough. One complaint I might have is that while the varying maps may look different, from a design perspective they aren't particularly distinguishable from one another.
At current there are two distinct game modes, Skirmish and Evacuation. Those who played Big Alpha and the Beta will know Skirmish as single rounds of Hunt where the Hunters and Monster duke it out until the other dies, or the Monster destroys the power relay. Evacuation on the other hand is a 5 round based gamemode, starting with a Hunt round, leading onto a choice between three game modes on 3 maps of the players' choosing (there is a vote before each round). These are the familiar Hunt mode, Nest mode and Rescue mode. In Nest, the Monster must defend various eggs scattered throughout the map while the Hunters must destroy them. The Monster can hatch an egg to spawn a Goliath minion, which will seek out and attack the Hunters although it is weak by itself and if it dies will count as the egg it hatched from being destroyed. In Rescue, the Monster must find and kill bot-controlled Survivors around the map, one group at a time. They spawn incapacitated, and the Survivors must rescue them and bring them to an evac point to be extracted to a drop ship. If the Monster kills a certain number of them, or all the Hunters, it wins. If it fails to do so, the Hunters win. The fifth and final round is called Defend, and involves a Stage 3 Monster and a stream of Goliath minions who must destroy a series of power generators. What makes Evacuation interesting is that for each round, the outcome will affect the next round, such as the Monster winning a round resulting in more powerful and hostile wildlife for the next round, making it harder for the Hunters, or the Hunters winning and a series of MedBays will be in the next map, which can heal and even remove strikes from Hunters. This makes each Evacuation different from another, with little chance of true repetition (although I would argue the differences are subtle).
All in all, despite 2K's serious faux pas on launch, Turtle Rock have made a very fun game here and if you've the money I would recommend buying this game, just don't give 2K any of your money for the skins, I think it's safe to say a boycott on those is necessary.

You'll note my hours as of this review; 6.3 hours on record since I bought this game, and not a single hour do I regret. I'm writing this early review because this game is wonderfully easy to get into. The tutorial is simple and straight to the point and probably within ten to twenty minutes, you've got the basics! I call that a plus in my book.
I've gone through two towns so far. You'll do it too, but wait before you make a decision based on what I said! Even when I did lose focus or forget something, it was because I didn't understand what needed to be placed where. I know I said the tutorial goes over what you need to do - and it does! - but it also intentionally leaves some of the advanced stuff out. There's a reason for that. I've found that reason is to help you learn as you go through your towns, to discover what works and what doesn't. To have that, "Oh! So that was what I was supposed to do!" moments. I'll share mine.
My moment was when I realized the game had a stone quarry. I already knew it had an iron mine, eventually finding out that you could mine coal from the same iron mine, but I always sent my extra farmers out during winter to collect stone. Eventually I kept running out of stone - there's only so much in a given area! - and before one brutal winter I decided to upgrade my citizens homes to stone. It started fresh, but soon I realized I was running out of stone, and before I knew it I had allocated the wrong amount to recovery and my people were starving to death. Boom, death.
Move to second attempt. I built the quarry, then realized under the homes tab they actually had one of those homeless houses for citizens without homes. I got the idea then. So I built the shelter first then, as I upgraded the homes, the displaced citizens could reside there as I sent more to the quarry to gather the stone. Eventually my ultimate plan of upgrading my town was complete, all thanks to me investigating on my own what worked!
See, that's the beauty of this game. It makes you feel like you're leading these people and it encourages trail and error. When you do wrong, you're brutally punished. Forethought and planning is greatly rewarded (building storage barns before the barns are full, for example!). That's what I love about this game. That and it's really relaxing; I simply love the music and relaxing atmosphere!
It's worth the price and you should buy it, if just only to have something to relax to!

I didn't think I'd be scared of animatronics, but there I was,♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥my pants on night one because Foxy jumped me since I was too stupid and afraid to do anything. Now I can say I'm pretty scared of animatronics. This game is great, not perfect, but it's definitely a satisfying and refreshing take on the horror genre. The controls and gameplay are simple, but it does such a good job at instilling sheer panic and paranoia, that it becomes much harder than it seems. You are forced to fight against your own sense of fear and vulnerabilty in order to save power. The story too is actually very interesting and haunting in itself, especially once you play the later games (fnaf 2/3) as well.
Only 'issue' really is that it doesn't take long to learn the patterns and behaviors of the animatronics, meaning the game becomes more predictable and less scary. It's not too hard to develop a strategy to easily make it through all six nights. However, after all six nights, the game does offer a custom night mode, where you can take on the dreaded 4/20 mode if you dare. It's great because, although it is very challenging and frustrating, it adds replayability of the game and it's very rewarding once you get your strategy down and beat it.
All-in-all this game is solid and I definitely recommend it. Well done Scott!

This was a hugely disappointing conclusion to the amazing Deponia series. Not just because of the lacklustre ending to the plot, but also because of the ugly nature of many of the acts of Rufus. In previous games he was a crazy but lovable hero, whereas in Goodbye Deponia, he is responsible for selling a black woman into slavery to a monkey who forces her to dance in a skimpy outfit, whilst you feed her boyfriend to some sort of mutant parasitic monster burrito vendor. He also is responsible for the deaths of a group of orphan children that he comes across, and feeding a baby an entire bottle of anti-depressant drugs. At the end he is also finally responsible for the death of his biggest fan, who jumps off the Highboat when Rufus falls.
Overall, this game was a massive let down, and the ending to the plot made it even more of a waste of time, as the eventual result could have been achieved by just letting Cletus and Goal return to Elysium in the very first game, but many more lives would have been saved in the process.
If you love the Deponia series - Do. Not. Play. This. Game.

This game is a beautifully executed insult to all humanity.
In this last installment, the protagonist Rufus reaches levels of anti-heroism that are no longer funny-awkward, but plain "dafuq I'm gonna stop playing right now" despicable. The game had a pretty interesting plot point in the middle, which could have been a turning point in character development, but they blew it for laughs. And those aren't really laughs either, just "oh noes" moments.
(For example... Rufus finds some orphans, whom, in order to advance the game, you first have to send into the van of a paedophile, and then feed to a monster... I have no idea if there was a time and location where that counted as "funny", but it sure isn't now.)
Really. The writing is a serious mess. The jokes are unfunny and sometimes downright insulting. And if you think "well Deponia is supposed to be like that", this game is totally nothing like the earlier ones. Really. Those were funny, most of the time. This is just, well, cringy. And the finale is completely off the bat, and does nothing to redeem Rufus, OR the writer.

First of all, Project Zomboid is a Survival game that is based around survival in the zombie apocalypse. This also has rougelike properties such as one life system and choosing traits or perks and having to balance good traits with bad traits such as Cataclysm. (The Zombie Rougelike Not WoW) I would say it’s realistic for what it is, Such as that you’re not the hero of the world in this game, you’re just a normal person trying to survive. But mainly that you have to deal with a lot of things such as hunger, sleep, thirst, depression, anxiety, and of course zombies. Sadly, since this game is in early access it seems like a lot of these things you have to deal with do not affect your game play that much. You just have to deal with hunger, thirst and sleep. That’s about it, everything else do not really affect your character in anyway besides sickness and panic. But those are so minor, but if you get sick you are most likely infected and your dead anyways. But it seems like from the 204 hours I played of the game you would imagine that would I get sick at least once right? I never got the flu or a normal sickness even with the perk that makes it so I can catch sickness easier than the normal player. And panic doesn’t really effect you as in you can be freaking the hell out but it doesn’t matter since you can shoot and smash and cut zombies pretty much the same as if you were not panicked. So it seems like a major part of the game is kind of missing with the moodles since half of them don’t affect you in anyway. The game does have a rather high learning curve, as in you would  think first off by just starting to play the game the zombies aren’t a threat *COUGH COUGH DAYZ COUGH COUGH* but that’s sort of true. Once you have the combat down the zombies become an annoyance more so then a threat. This also is backed up as soon as you find a baseball bat or a pan or an axe or something you’re pretty much good as long as you’re careful. But that doesn’t mean zombies are just silly, they can and will kill you if you’re not careful. But if you’re just starting out it might be a little awkward with the holding down ctrl and left clicking stuff. But it just seems like the weapons you can choose from that are worth a damn are a hammer, pan, baseball bat, and axe. Everything else is just complete garbage. What about guns, well if you are going to go into a street full of zombies with your whole 15 bullets that’s not a very good idea. Your character has apparently never had any kind of gun interaction in this new update that using a pistol or anything else but a shotgun is horrible and you just miss pretty much every other shot and next thing you know you have 100 zombies on your♥♥♥♥♥ Which is pretty true that a lot of people haven’t shot or handled guns in their life, but I mean it seems sort of silly that you can’t hit a zombie less than five feet away from you with a pistol.  So basically you’re out of the gun choice if you have a♥♥♥♥♥♥ton of ammo or you just want to die.  Now food isn’t really a problem with me as that you just take all the canned food and chips and what not, all the nonperishable food and you stick in your house or gun store or whatever you have as a base and you just collect it. It’s not like you’re going to eat all of that food before you die but might as well right? Farming and Carpentry are pretty hard to do and farming isn’t a really reliable way of getting food as it takes time and apparently you can die in one day from not drinking or eating. Depending on the perks you have of course. But Carpentry takes a long♥♥♥♥♥time to level up and have anything decent to build even with the books, and I found myself un-boarding and boarding up windows just to level my skill up so that I  can build stuff. That looks nice anyways. The Level one and two buildings look like♥♥♥♥♥♥in my opinion. But as soon as you go out of your house, you turn into either a hoarder that just sets up at a house and just collects everything that might or is useful from all the houses nearby, or you’ll be a nomad and just go around killing zombies and just wondering around. Which both play styles are pretty fun but the game loses its touch after like a month in game cause now you have a♥♥♥♥♥♥ton of stuff and your just thinking what you can do with your house or your still just wondering and killing zombies. But I think the nomad play style goes into the hoarding eventually that you find a nice place you like and there you go. To be honest I have never used farming to get any food in this game. Hmm, I'm going to try not to spoil the plot while still giving some impression of the game...
Basically, it's a series of ... unusual maps designed in the source engine.  Gameplay wise, you mostly have to walk through and occasionally complete simple tasks or choose dialogue options.  No combat or puzzles or anything like that, it's only for the aesthetics.  The main point of the game is the narration that accompanies the walkthrough.  It explains the narrator's relationship with the mapmaker.
It's not poorly made or anything, but ultimately I feel the plot is a bit meh.  It's predictable for the most part, and while it does get you thinking, I ultimately didn't feel that all that touched by it.  My main interest after playing through the game was to find out how much of it is a true story and how much isn't.
Gameplay-wise you can expect about 2-3 hours for a playthrough if you are quite thorough about it. Otherwise it might only take you less than 2 hours.
Final verdict:
I really liked some of the aesthetics but didn't find the plot all that compelling.
If you are a source engine mapper, I can suggest it just for the aesthetics, but otherwise I would only suggest playing it if you are specifically interested in this type of game.  Certainly don't buy it if it is not on sale.  2 hours of gameplay simplay don't justify the full price.

Scourge: Outbreak is a headache-inducing third-person co-op shooter designed for four players. The game features terrible gun-play, poorly implemented powers, terrible game-play mechanics, bad voice acting, and strange level designs.
Being a shooter, the game revolves heavily around gun play, its a shame than that this game falls short on pretty much every aspect of the gun play. The game has plenty of guns to offer, but due to every enemy essentially being a bullet sponge, including the very first grunts of the game, most weapons are either useless or only useful in set situations. Limiting players to only two guns at a time discourages experimentation since the risk of doing so is punished by encountering bullet-sponge enemies. Shotguns have an astoundingly short range and snipers cannot kill anything in one hit by the time you get them which makes the shotgun highly situational and the sniper essentially useless. Grenades have no throwing arc and the result is guess work when trying to hit specific targets at any distance, a tedious affair when grenades are required to kill something. One of the essential parts of being a shooter, the placing of bullets into enemies, is one of this game's weakest attributes.
The powers that the four main characters receive in the game end up feeling more than a little disappointing when you get them, primarily due to an antagonist's teleportation powers being the teaser to your personal powers. Each person is supposed to end up with different powers, according to the voice over, but what ends up happening is that each character has different versions of ground blast and shield. Ground blast is only useful near enemies, with the exception of Amp who can somehow throw her blasts like magic grenades, and shield is fantastic since it lets you not die when reviving allies that will inevitable fall due to lack of cover or the AI running into the open. All of this is only possible if you have enough Ambrosia, which you only get from green barrels of goo that explode if shot, meaning you could end up without a source of energy and as a result, no powers. Overall the powers are neat in concept, but you likely wouldn't miss them if they were removed.
The mechanics and concepts in the game show that inspiration has been taken from several shooters, most notably the cover system taken straight from Gears of War. A problem that arises from this is the implementation of most of these ideas are done terribly or simply aren't designed well. The cover system doesn't work well if you don't include the cover to go with it, or the ability to use your guns properly from cover. The result is that most enemies behave in such a way that locking to cover is detrimental to the game-play experience and likely to get you killed unless there is no way to be flanked. Worse is the alien enemies that have to melee you to hurt you, making cover a dangerous affair. It is strange then that the aliens are introduced in a cramped corridor with nearly infinite amounts until you kill the lead aliens. For a single player this section is virtually impassable as the AI can't cope with the amount of enemies and reviving the player at the same time. The strangest part of the introductory area of the aliens belongs to the end of it, where you have to defend against a rush of them while a door is on a timer to open. During the defense there are defenses on the wall helping you hold them off, giving you time to fight the aliens without getting swarmed while still feeling as if you will. These strange decisions continue to appear in later stages, such as a boss you can't kill unless you remove barrels of Ambrosia that are healing him after a certain damage threshold. Those are the very same barrels used to regenerate your own powers so by destroying them, you lose your powers shortly after receiving them. Another boss requires you to throw grenades at specific parts from a distance, which is immensely tedious without a throwing arc and should not have been included without a useful launcher of some kind. The game could have benefited greatly with fewer but more focused mechanics, but opted for more is greater.
The voice acting in Scourge: Outbreak is not so much terrible as it is inconsistent, such as the lead character having an accent constantly change from sentence to sentence and occasionally in the middle of speaking. It sounds like they had multiple voice actors and forgot to decide on a specific actor. Other examples are lines delivered from antagonist's that often sound unrehearsed or as if the reader is perplexed by the writing. The result is an inconsistent delivery of vocal work that ends up jarring and pulls you out of the games world.
The level designs used in this game seemed to vary between corridors and big open rooms, with corridors taking the stage the majority of the time. One area of the game has you wait in a corridor while the game scans the protagonists, the door than opens to another corridor that leads to a cut-scene.  Corridors leading into corridors appears to be their way of slowing the pace down after combat; it's a poor method since there is no sense of progression, just going from fight to fight. Some sections have what appears to be water slowing you down, though as it is walked through, it moves away from the player as if jumping in a gelatinous substance. Having the character slow down in water is unnecessary, especially in rooms that have nothing in them which is always the case. Sadly most levels are poorly designed, either with too much cover, making it detrimental in the search of enemies, or too little cover, making it hard to survive the enemy's onslaught.
This game is not recommended, even on a budget due to many frustrating moments and poor enemy design. The game is pretty much unplayable alone and renders you powerless when in a group since there is a lack of Ambrosia. I recommend not buying this game at any price.

Evolve has a few different game modes, I will keep it simple.
Hunter - Hunters must kill the Monster before it destroys an objective.
Rescue - Hunters must find and rescue downed survivors, the Monster must kill survivors before they are extracted.
Egg Hunt - Hunters must find and destroy eggs around the map, the Monster must defend them.
Defend - A MOBA type game where the Monster has Minions that are sent to kill an Objective, the Hunters must defend this and deal with both Minions and the Monster.
The team of 4 each play a set class as follows:
- Assault
- Tracker/Huner
- Medic
- Support
Each role has unique abilities that compliments a team with good communication and teamwork.
But what if 3 people want to play Medic?
The game allows you to rank each class from 1-5 where 1 is most desired and 5 is least.
It will then try to match you into games where you 'fit in' and are fairly close in level where possible.
If you are all friends and everyone chooses Monster, one person will get it randomly, then the rest will be allocated via their ranks, and once again if 2 people want Support one person will get it the other will be put in for their next pick and so on..
Progression in the game is handled via 'Levels' and also 'Mastery'.
Levels are earned by doing what you are mean to do, using abilities correct etc.
As you level up you unlock Perks which you can pick at the start of each round to apply a perma buff to your character.
Mastery is earned in a similar way, but to progress up the Mastery tree you may need to focus on certain tools/weapons to unlock your 'Next tier' by doing X total accumulative damage with weapon Y.
As you progress in Mastery you get bonuses to they tools/weapons you use and it can unlock other characters and skins.
There is some complaining about Day 1 DLC which are SKINS.... these do not impact on the players performance thus really should not be as big of an issue as people make it out to be, there are plenty of games out there that do Cosmetic DLCs, people just need to open their eyes.
All in all the game is fun to play once you get your head around it.
It is a little on the 'deep end' with no Tutorial at the main menu, rather you need to watch a video prior to a round if it is your first time playing a class.
A lot of pressure is placed on being the Monster, being alone and knowing you are being hunted it is important to keep on the move while constantly feeding to strengthen yourself and replenish your armour.
If you love team orientated games that require you to think quick and work together then this is a great game!
If the 4 hunters do not work together, even a average skilled Monster could very easily devour them early on.
For those with that like Match 3 gem type games, there is a game called Evolve : Hunters Quest you can get for Android, iOS and Windows Phone, playing this unlocks Badges in the main game and also provides a 50% boost to Mastery.

Seemingly infinite spawning enemies coupled together with dumb AI make this Gears of War style game boring and tedious to play. I've had instances of AI companions trying to heal me by running in front of an enemy turret. Enemies are made to soak up bullets making for unsatisfying gunplay and have the added bonus of infinite grenade spam. Pouring thirty rounds into an enemy only to see it jump and incapacitate my character left me unimpressed. In some cases I could fire 200 rounds into an enemy and not kill it. Possibly, that specific enemy is headshot only.
This game also has weird balance issues and a lot of jankiness to it. Some of it looks genuinely hilarious like vaulting over cover or the sprinting animation. The balance issues are more frustrating though. The AI has the benefit of having infinite or some regenerating Ambrosia (the stuff for your powers) while players need to stand next to barrels of the liquid. Those barrels can be destroyed, deliberately or on accident which is less than ideal and also less fun.
There was also this one fight with a second plane where you had to stick grenades to it, but the lack of grenade arcs makes the it frustrating; my friend and I spent a good fifteen minutes just lobbing sticky grenades and sometimes they would make it.
I can't recommend this game for a single player experience. Maybe try the Resident Evils, Just Cause 2, Hitman: Blood Money, Tomb Raider 2013, Sleeping Dogs, the GTAs, or Saints Row IV for a third-person experience. I suppose you could look into Spec Ops: The Line, Binary Domain (some rough boss fights), Inversion (no co-op, possibly bad), or even Dizzel (f2p Early Access multiplayer game) for that more GoW feel.
Otherwise, have friends for Scourge. Do not rely solely on this game's AI. I tried it single player and my team mate's behavior is a constant crap shoot. I highly recommend bringing in at least one friend if you going to play this game. That way, the AI can go around using their infinite ammo and powers while you two actually complete goals. Play with a human, please.

This series (it is a series, so if you're reading this and looking to buy it, then you should get all 3 games) is the closest I have come to filling a void left by the disappearance of a great genre from gaming. In fact, this game didn't just come close, it did the job perfectly. If you too played some of that last generation of 90s point-and-click games (Curse of Monkey Island, Toonstruck, Discworld) and want something that matches up to that greatness, then this game is it!
Sure, it has a few tiny issues (mostly translation issues from German to English), but these can be very easily forgiven since Daedalic got the mix of funny cynical charaters, story, puzzles, dialogue and story just right, picking up where these great games left off and drawing on everything that there is to be learned from them. If you like classic point-and-click game you WILL NOT be disappointed. They haven't fiddled with the genre or tried to bring it to thr touch screen like certain other devs have - they left perfection as it was, focussing instead on what matters in these kinds of games instead of trying to re-invent a genre which doesn't need to be re-invented.
Perhaps the only thing I am annoyed with is no native Linux support and wished the devs would port this like they have with some of their other games. If you do use Linux, all three games run well on Wine - but obviously there is no guarantee or oficial support, so I would wait for a native version.

In many ways, I am extremely disappointed that this series had not reached what I felt was a higher potential, but it also delivers a frantically great experience that will have you entirely immersed in the fascinating world it presents.
Throughout much of the game, the humor that was once so charming crosses partly over to being crude as well as insensitive. And, the opportunities they had to develop these characters more, for us to see them thrive and gain more through their experiences, to grasp the reality of their situation, then to grow wiser as a result, was all missed. At its core, all the characters are static. Rather than growing and being the preferable dynamic characters they should have been, they learn nothing and remain the same. It really is a shame, because all these characters are so likable and interesting. Instead of development, we had been given an abrupt ending that very poorly tried to end the series with an open note, but absolutely failed to do so.
The gameplay is improved, however. The first section is very well-done, and I found myself enjoying it far more than any other part of the series thus far. As the game went on, it became progressively more cryptic and difficult, but still managed to maintain a somewhat fresh twist on the point-and-click formula. The settings and environments remain beautiful, and the animation never failed to impress.
The Deponia series, despite its shortcomings, proved to be a very memorable trilogy of games filled to the brim with a sense of wild imagination that spurred my mind alive. It possessed additional potential that could have propelled it to become a true classic, but as it stands, I feel it is still well-worth your time if you're even remotely interested in this type of genre.

Soooooooo... Having liked both previous game (the second less than I would have hoped, but still), I read many reviews before starting this one and when I saw the four major complaints (which I will explicit afterwards), I was scared of being utterly disappointed. Well, that would have been a mistake.
. I still prefer the first one, but this one is arguably better constructed/paced, funnier and ultimately more enjoyable. Now for the complaints (spoiler free-ish):
The puzzles are bad: The main issue with the second game was that it was damn near impossible to complete it with the sole hints the game provided. While playing the first act (which is moreover badly designed), my fears came true. You don't know what to do, how to do it and why you have to do it. At one point, the game even mocks you so, telling you that the solution is the least obvious one. Well, I insisted, took a walkthrough and moved on. Then, starting with act two (
), it got better and the puzzles, while more complex, were better designed and explained.
There is a racist segment about slavery: Yes, it exists. No, I didn't find it funny. No, it is not as bad as it seems. Rufus is a prick (sometimes a lovable prick, but still), it is explained why (not excused, far from it), so he does something horrible without thinking of the consequences and he's a d**k about it afterwards. If you exhaust every dialog option, you'll see that everything is not black or white (sorry for that one, but I had to)
There is a child molester: Yes, and Rufus tells some kids that it is okay to go into stranger's vans. As it happens, the children never go in, as they know better (morality is saved, yeahh). Afterwards, the joke (still not funny, I agree) is at Rufus' expense.

I'm recommending this game for one reason: Multiplayer
Tropico 5 nailed the multiplayer aspect.
Being able to play alongside my friends is the reason I love this game.
It's the best multiplayer city building game out there. I have not come across any other like this.
Tropico 5 lets you build next to players or with them. Cooperative or Competive, whichever you prefer.
SimCity can hardly compete since you don't build together, you build in seperate regions.
Cities: Skylines is the best city building game on the market hands down, but no multiplayer.
During a multiplayer game you can share money, roads, utilities and military forces.
It's very satisfying to share the love of these games alongside people who also love it.
There are a lot of hilarious moments, especially if you're playing with friends.
The rebels have basically become a meme among my friends because they're idiotic and easy to joke about.
The only downside is being forced to send backup when a friend is attacked. If you get attacked while your troops are in a friend's city, all you can do is pray. Also, mandate is bs.
The game could give all the mandate to one player but not the other.
Don't even get me started on roads. Roads suck. They're horrible.
The multiplayer is great and I hope it sets the foundation for future games.
The dream would be this multiplayer on Tropico 4, Cities: Skylines or SimCity.
I personally feel like it still capted the same feel as Tropico 4, except it was watered down and made much more difficult.
You will never truly defeat the rebels or please everyone, this game is best played as a warmongering oppressive dictatorship. It will give you the most satisfaction since your prize is blood and trust me, there's plenty so you might as well enjoy it.
TLDR: Multiplayer mechanics are great, game is a downgrade, still enjoyable.
Advice: Spam sugar plantations and rum distillaries.

The Beginners Guide is unlike anything I've ever played before for a very interesting reason, in that its extremely personal. It's very unconventional in that it delves into the relationship of two real people, "Davey Wreden" and a game developer friend of his named, "Coda."
The Beginners Guide plays like the Stanley Parable, (also made by Wreden if you did not know) you and Wreden who serves as the games narrator play through a series of games made by Coda. As you play through them Wreden discusses the meaning he interpreted from that particular game as well as giving insights into Coda. I can't really say more about it than that without going into spoiler territory but it was a very interesting journey to go through.
I recommend this game very highly, it has a lot you can infer about many things. The very intimate and personal journey you go through with Wreden is emotional and unlike anything I've really seen in video games. Another thing I loved about this as well is you can clearly see the impact Coda's games had on Wreden when you compare Coda's material to Wreden's, "Stanley Parable."
I'm going to stick my neck out here and give it a 10/10 FOR WHAT THIS GAME IS. It's an experience unlike anything I've seen before and I will be thinking about this game for a long time.
