December 2016 expanded edit:
I still love this game, and it's nice to chill out in. It's really worth a try, especially if you like Poker and Blackjack. There is an active playerbase, a friend system, and always people running around the Casino to interact with.
Card decks in this game are simulated realistically. If you use perfect strategy in multi-deck blackjack (or share info with your sneaky friends in VIP single-deck), you can effectively count cards like is possible in real life, minus the pit boss kicking you out of the casino. You can even watch other people playing and sit down at the table when you think the deck is "hot", but be careful because if someone else gets up the dealer will shuffle!
What people don't realize, and why many reviews are negative, is that losing streaks are naturally much more common than people think. Things will happen like the dealer gets blackjack 2 or 3 times in a row and people will yell RIGGED!!! But if you play enough it is bound to happen in every game. People focus on the negatives, and when they win big they bet more and lose it quicker than they won it. All games have a house edge you won't win against in the long run, unless you count cards masterfully or play vs other players in Poker.
I've gone broke dozens of times. When you go broke, every 15 minutes you can collect a little money from change machines. When waiting for this time to pass, the best thing to do is bother other players by humping them with your "awkward dance". The best players to do this to are the ones that have fallen asleep idling next to the change machines waiting for free money. You can also play bingo for free about once an hour, and poker once a day at a separate table for free money. There is also a little free daily money on top of this. It sounds easy, but earning a lot is a challenge.
Once you have successfully clawed your way out of the loser salt mines, there is $5000 poker, and the elite "VIP" status can play $25000-entry poker. To reach VIP status, you have to earn enough "Rep" in one month. "Rep" is experience points you get from winning. You can use rep to unlock fancy clothes, effects, dances, pets, emotes, etc. VIP status gets you into the back room of high stakes tables, poker, and even fancier items! This way even though the house has an edge over you in probability, you can still progress in the game and can always dream of having a good enough run to make VIP. Other VIP's can give you temporary passes to get in as well.
You can resurrect your empty bank account by paying real money if you want a quick escape from the salt mines, but it is not necessary. As a free-player I hit VIP the first month I tried, mostly through Poker wins. The Rep you earn can buy most of the vanity items you want if you don't mind waiting, and humping is free anyway.

A solid attempt to recreate the fun of the original that fails utterly.
From the car design to the music to the map design, the creators have tried to hearken back to the splatter-tastic turbo charged gritty fun of the original, however relentless nickel and dime opponents, a tin foil car, insane repair frees, no failure option and a shallow, performance linked upgrades and unforgiving vehicle physics make it more painful for you to play than the peds you crush - at least it is over for them in a split second.
Starting off, the recreation of the original first level and original opponents is fun ... especially since, even after all this time, I remember where a lot of the powerups are. It was fun thrashing my opponents. Then, I tried to do a regular checkpoint race .. and the pain began.
Every opponent is out to get YOU. They aren't out to win, they aren't out to trash each other. They want YOUR blood. If they are halfway across the map, they will continue to run checkpoints until they get close, then it is open season on your bumper. This means you can not play this as a normal race, especially if winnig by trashing the opponents is a victory condition. They will ignore everything else. I once had a field of four enemies, and a cop car, continually focusing me so much they starting ramming each other just to get to me ... one actually wrecked another, and none of them cared. This becomes incredibly frustring incredibly quickly especially with the damage model and driving physics.
You will run forward, do a 180, and by the time you get to about 10 miles an hour your opponent is barreling down on you at insane speed since pretty much all the cars are faster than yours at the start. The damage model is also incredibly unrealistic. In order to damage you, all the opponents need to do is gently back in to you, or turn in to you from a foot away, and you can lose a wheel. Repariing even green basic damage to your car's body can cost upward of 1300 credits, with a cash barrel giving you about 200 and a checkpoint about 1000. This means if an enemy taps you .. at all.. you need to run down 5 or so cash barrels, make the next checkpoint (with everyone on your tail, and they are faster than you) or slam through a crowd of peds to make up repair cash.
All the opponents have the same AI regardless of their vehicle capabilities. They all will turn as fast as they can in to you and burn full speed at you. This causes some vehicles with bad handling and high acceleration to spin all over the map, vehicle with good handling and slow speed to turn constantly in circles, but small, light vehicles with good handling and middling speed will be the bane of your existence. They will get right on you and constantly turn in you. Since they turn faster, you can't outturn them. Since everyone is faster, you can't outrun them. They will push their doors against yours and with a car that weighs half of what yours weighs and using no speed or ramming, will reduce you to a flaming pile of rubble.
Getting upgrades means getting upgrade tokens. Once you find them tucked away on a map, actually USING them requires you to meet certain race and area goals. So if you just can't beat a map or a certain race .. well.. too bad. You can't upgrade.
I can see the developers really tried to recreate the original, but I don't think they ever played it. It is if they had the source code and original assets and were asked to just duplicate it with upgraded textures and polygons ... and did that. I'm not sure they played the original game or this one.

Firstly, I played C1 and C2 to death back in the days. I loved those bloody games.
Then I saw the Kickstarter for what was then Carmageddon Reincarnation. I was intrigued, but didn't back it -- I was perfectly content with playing C2 and needless to say that that the horrible TDR 2000 had left an awful taste in my mouth.
So I eventually saw C: MD for 20 quid, and I finally decided to pull the trigger. And I have to say, I am NOT disappointed! C: MD takes what was great about C1 and C2 and throws it into the blender to create a very satisfying modern twist on some classic games. Having both the C1 and C2 Hawk/Eagle is really nice, and it's also great to see some familiar faces from both C1 and C2 returning. I remember hearing about stability issues back in the Reincarnation days, and I'm pleased to say I have encountered none of those with C: MD -- the game runs silky smooth and has never crashed on me. Which is a refreshing change as I had accepted random crashes as a reality of C2.
I am not a big fan of the Ped Race, lap race events and such, so I just skip them, and it doesn't hinder my progression, which is really nice -- TDR 2000's "race mission race mission race mission" system really♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥me off.
I like the variety in the pedestrians -- old people with walking frames, fat people, people in wheelchairs, ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s, cheerleaders/american football players (and as a nice nod to C1 you can run in on the field and squash them), animals -- everyone is fair game and I bloody love it!
Soundtrack is a bit meh -- not bad, but I miss the days of Fear Factory and even Iron Maiden. Otherwise, this is the good old Carmageddon we so dearly love. Anyone who has enjoyed C1 and C2, C: MD or Carmageddon 3 as I call it, is well worth a purchase and your time. It is a hell of a lot of fun, and had I knew back in the day how much fun the game would have turned out to be, I would have backed it on KS.

The Long Dark is one of the more well done games in the Survival genre.
The artistic visuals are very pleasant to the eyes, and the sounds/music is atmospheric enough to wrap you up in the landscape that is the environment.  While not the most realistic game ever to grace the genre, what it does, it does extremely well.
Crafting is satisfying without being overly complicated or too simplistic.
If I had one small complaint about the game, it would be the size of the map.  While it's not tiny, it's small enough to revisit areas that you've already been through.  In certain instances, that could be a boon though.
All in all, it's clear that the dev(s) care about their product and continue to work on it.  That being the case, I have no problem supporting them in this endeavour.

The game is surprisingly balanced still (mostly 50% win percentages swinging either way for either the hunters or the monsters), and it feels like the game is very well optimized, being able to run everything on ultra and still hitting a smooth 60FPS (running a GTX970 sure but I still have to tone down the settings on things like Far Cry 3 or else things start to stutter). If you liked the Left 4 Dead series, I'm more then certain you'd enjoy Evolve, the devs did a great job with something new and giving the whole hunting scenario a nice new touch.

I'm not gonna comment on the DLC stuff since other people wrote enough about that. (Don't really agree with the heap of DLC though... it's getting silly, if not sinister.)
What I'm gonna comment about is the game itself.
This... is a 6/10 or 7/10 game (not using the IGN scale here - aka <6/10 worse than Satan). Fun but flawed. Gem in the rough... for fans of the genre, innovation not enough polish. That kind of game.
I love this kind of game... just not for 60 bucks.
When the gameplay "clicks" it feels amazing, there's nothing quite like this out right now. But it doesn't "click" often. Most of the time it's boring and tedious, some of the time it's frustrating and some of the time it's really fun.
The progression system feels like it's there just for the sake of being there. "What? A multiplayer PvP shooter without a progression system?! Surely you jest!" So the already monotonous gameplay gets additional grind element put on top of it.
Not to mention that the progression system promotes some seriously selfish gameplay. Case in point is the Markov's "cause damage by mines" requirement. Good monster will pretty much never step on a mine (and the number required is pretty high)... so to clear this you'll be compelled to run around with mines instead of actually helping your team. And there are many things like this in this system.
Even when you unlock new characters very little changes. Playing this game was a rollercoaster of excitement and then "wait... that's it?" kind of feeling. So I know for a fact that new hunters/monsters can only do so much to keep the game fresh.
The maps... are mediocre. Feel a bit too small, but then again they are big enough for a good monster to avoid you forever. None of them feel memorable (at least in the actual layout) or interesting... it's just a backdrop for the gameplay... competent if uninteresting.
This is based on both betas and roughly 50 hours of playtime. So take it for what it is.
To finish off... I said that it's 6/10 kind of game, so why am I giving it a thumb down (since above 5 is still positive right?). Well, this is a store and so the question is: "Should I spend my 60 (presumably) hard earned bucks for this game?" And for me the answer is "No". I might change this review accordingly based on how this game develops over time.
I can't really hate this game (have no problem hating 2K though :P)... but I can't really love it either. Bit above meh. Just wanted to present a (negative) review that is not just about the DLC.

Firstly, yes, of course it's good, it's Bioshock.
Why is it good, though? That's what's hard to explain.
Firstly, it's incredibly atmospheric and immersive. Rapture is a city with amazing architecture, as well as suprisingly talkitive and lively inhabitants who feel like they all have their own definitive personalities, even when it comes to the mobs you fight so routinely. The gameplay is also amazing, with an ingenious fusion of survival-horror, fps, and rps elements at work, all making sure you'll never get bored with any one aspect of the game. The story is also rather good in a Dishonored sort of way, where you always have a good idea as to what's going on, but if you want the meaty details, you have to go seek them out for yourself, so regardless of whether or not you like a story-focused experience, you'll like Bioshock.
The game isn't without its flaws, though. There is an awful lot of backtracking in some sections, which gets rather annoying, because whilst exploring an incredibly depressing and murky city is fun when the scenery is kept new and refreshing, being kept in the same place and walking through the same halls until you can draw a map of the place becomes maddeningly annoying. That only happens once or twice during the whole 7ish hour game, though, so that can be overlooked. Speaking of maps, the menus, including the map, are all either stupidly simple or needlessly complicated, with no in-between, which becomes annoying when you get lost and end up spending a little longer than you need to figuring out what the ♥♥♥♥ the map means when it shows an arrow connecting two sections of a building that look way further apart than they actually are. The jumping mechanics are also likely designed by a descendant of Adolf himself, which can be overlooked until you start having to do precision jumping to avoid electric wires so as to get to rewards that you can't realistically continue without.
Despite all these nitpicks, Bioshock still remains to be a good game, and still holds up to, if not exceeds the expectations of AAA games nowadays. If you haven't already, I highly recommend you at the very least try this game. If you like it, you might even get interestsed in the rest of the games in the series. Bioshock 2 is still♥♥♥♥♥♥ though.

It's just like Carmageddon 1 but with better graphics and more stuff. The handling is as terrible as you remember from the first game but it does convey serious weight to the cars. The sound of hitting a pedestrian is really satisfying. the graphics aren't anything special but they look alright, and with upwards of 700 NPCs on the map I can forgive them for not being super detailed. Most importantly, the game runs perfectly smoothly on my PC no matter what's happening. If you've never played Carmageddon before I do recommend this game, just don't expect it to have any focus on actual racing - you can't really pull "sick drifts" or anything, the car is more like a weapon than a vehicle.
There's some stuff that's new to this version (compared to Carma1) - cars can be painted in a fairly decent selection of alternate colours. There's some new cars, powerups, and maps. Many powerups can be picked up and activated by player choice, as opposed to Carma1 where every powerup just had a passive effect for a certain amount of time. The damage is a lot more detailed - you can lose wheels, and the car can be cut in half, along with all the different parts and bodywork. The soundtrack is a bit more dubsteppy now, which I like, although I'm pretty sure the classic music is still in there as well.
So yeah, this is definitely worth $20 if you were a big fan of the classic Carmageddon games. If you never played Carmageddon before I think there's a free demo of the original on ios.

If you have never heard of or played The Secret World, you will not really "get" this game.  Most of the game will seem arbitrary, dissonant in tone, and nonsensical.
However, if you understand where "Kingsmouth" is, have completed "The Seven Silences" quest and know who Carrie Killian is... this game is fantastic and chances are, you've already bought it.
I can't outright recommend this game otherwise, you probably won't enjoy it.  There aren't enough "jump-scares" to fill a proper "watch me shriek" YouTube "let's play," and a lot of the story is delivered through inner monologue and visual imagery that won't make much sense to you without the greater context.
I'm giving this a thumbs-up however, because if you love The Secret World and Tørnquist's unique neo-Cthulhu stylings, then you'll get exactly what was intended out of this game.

It's short.  That's not a complaint, that's just re-stating what the developers said all along, since I've seen many people complaining about it.  And for those complaining about the cost, think of the it as the price of admission to a movie.  It lasts about as long as a long movie, and tells a good story that you get to participate in, which some people do in the theaters; but in this case, you are supposed to.
I really enjoyed the game.  I took it slow and participated in the ambiance.  That's what makes this an engrossing game.  I am slightly biased, as the sinister carnival scenario is my favorite theme (which is why I really like the amusement park area in Secret World).
If you are looking for a fast paced game, skip this one.  It is intentionally slow paced.  It is linear, but that is necessary to make sure the story unfolds as it should, and doesn't detract from the game; it didn't feel forced to me.
I liked the fact that it was psychological horror, and not just full of jump scares (there were almost no jump scares, but I'm not telling where the couple that are there are located...).
I did like the ending as it was, to me, somewhat ambiguous, leaving a lot of room to think about the game and the journey there instead of having things spoon fed to me.
It's a lovely homage to Lovecraft, which is also another of my favorites.  There was obvious influence from Silent Hill; again one of my favorites.  So all in all a nice mixup of goodness.
The only real complaint I have is that Lorraine's wrists really creep me out; the model bends all wrong.  :)
I would like to see more stories presented this way.  No guns or fights; just good story telling.
Kudos to Funcom for stepping outside the mold.
It is definitely worth taking a trip through.

The Park was definitely worth my time and money, and the following is a list of pros and cons that fit in accurately describing this atmospheric game.
PROS
- Graphics are very well done
- Story is linear, which is important for a horror genre
- Cutscenes are well placed and not to frequent
- Audio isn't overpowering but is quite accurate in representing the mood
- Gameplay was smooth, not too many controls
- Dialogue between mother and son throughout the game was AWESOME
- Twist on the hansel and gretel story
- Getting jumpscared by a chipmunk!
- Rollercoaster ride flashbacks were excellent!
CONS
- Story was very short, playthrough with as much exploration possible took about an hour
- Some visual effects were annoying
- Wanted to see the Chipmunk more!
Overall a great game, and hope to see more intriguing titles like this from Funcom, am definitely now a fan!

This is the first Tropico game I've played.  The concept is cool and really refreshing.  It has a great level of detail and the there is so much depth to this game (actually, almost too much).  It has a lot of potential to be fun, but there area few problems that took away my recommendation.
As a newbie, I don't know what I'm doing.  If it weren't for SimCity, I'd be completely lost (and yes, I tried the tutorial).  I play on all medium difficulty settings and I'm finding myself struggling to get an approval rating above 50%.  I give the people everything I can give them and yet they're still unhappy.  Many of them claim to be bored, but I can't build anything except taverns.  They whine about how boring the house is, but all I can build are country houses and mansions (and I'm not buying a mansion for a farmer).  So you could say "why not lower the difficulty?" but then the game becomes boring.  I want a challenge, not an impossibility.  When you rely on approval ratings and the people hate you for reasons outside of your control, that's not fun.  You could say "so just become a dictator" but that defeats the purpose of having a choice in the way you play.
The game is also a little overwhelming when it comes to management.  Just too much stuff that no president/governor actually does.  They might be cool features to some degree and they could be why I failed the first level, but it's just a little too much to juggle.  It'd be nice if it were more similar to SimCity, where you just zone areas and have the people figure things themselves.  I see no problem with having the *option* to intervene, but this game *requires* it, and I consider that more tedious than fun.

It's a game about banished townsfolk who asked too many questions. Which resulted in their timely departure from the town they once came from. Now they must start anew; make food, chop wood and sell wool coats - all of this while a tornado or a wild fire takes out only 12% of the population. Diseases can be a mixed bag at times and food production can starve people to death if improper rotations are met.
The atmosphere of the game is relaxing and peaceful, falling asleep to the music is sometimes a much needed plus.
As a side note, the steam workshop has a spectacular amount of mods that add layers to the game if you want to challenge yourself further.
The game itself has no real endgame as it continues till you stop playing, more over the style and means of having a thriving community is entirely up to you - there is a map seed to generate each map for mountain terrain or rolling hills and valleys.
For the builders of cities or the city management genre this game stands alone in the hybrid sense as it caters to both seamlessly. If your interests lay in roller coaster tycoon-like games or city management games like sim city. You'll be pleasantly surprised by this game. How far will you go for world domination - I mean apples.

I enjoyed Tropico 5 quite a bit. It's a bit different than CIties skylines but I would say that for me it has atleast the same entertainment value if not better. Tropico 5 was definitely better than EA's simcity. Nevertheless, I think Tropico 5 (or 4, more on that on the end of the review) is a must buy for everyone who like building games or economic games in general.
I must add that Tropico 5 is more difficult, atleast I found myself struggling with economy on my first two runs. This is because you rarely receive constant income like in other city building games, but instead you receive money when trade ships show up and buy your resources, and the income you get from a single ship is very irregular. For example one day you might receive 1k for selling bananas and weeks or months later when next ship arrives 10k for jewelry. And meanwhile you are constantly losing money to upkeep your production facilities.
Tropico 5 is quite solid actually, no bugs or anything that I've experienced. Only thing I was a bit annoyed about was that everytime autosave happened my game went to a loading screen and after that for some reason wanted to change my dynastys name, so I had to press cancel and second loading screen followed. But that can be avoided by reducing or disabling autosaves in options. Loading screens were also fairly short so I wasn't too bothered really.
It is quite common that Tropico 5 can be bought at discount, especially outside steam, but I can recommend it for full price as well if you like building games like I do. Many reviewers seem to say that Tropico4 is better, so check that out before you buy and make your own conclusions.

Day 1 - We deployed to the Eastern Front a week ago. Heinrich took some shrapnel in his arm, but he'll be alright. He got sent home. Progress is fast. We're pushing out the Bolsheviks at a large rate. We're at the gates of Stalingrad.
Day 4 - We've pushed past the defenses. Casualties were high... Johann didn't make it. Neither did Albert. Johann got shot by one of their sharpshooters. None of us were able to get to him. He bled to death... Albert got killed by a grenade. At least his death was quicker and more merciful.
Day 5 - Got a letter from my mother back home. Heinrich is recovering well, but will not be returning. The shrapnel severed ligaments in his arm. The men are glad to hear that he doesn't have to come back. This place is really going to hell very quickly...
Day 13 12:00 - We were ordered to take a train station yesterday. Close quarters fight. Very nasty. Albrecht got his skull crushed by a Soviet using his rifle as a club. Saw another boy, no older than 19, gutted with one of their spike bayonets. He lied there on the floor crying for his mother as his intestines were spilling out.
....what are we even doing here?
Day 13 17:21 - Soviet counter-attack. Three more of the original squad died today in an artillery bombardment. Two died from more close quarters brawls. We repelled the attack... but at too high of a cost, in my opinion. I would suggest that we destroy the tracks at multiple points and abandon the area... it holds no real tactical value anyway. Operative word being "would." I'd rather not get shot by "Herr General" for "cowardice, defeatism, and insubordination."
Day 21 - Replacements finally arrived. Is it just me, or are they accepting them younger? We were pushed out of the train station. We have no plans to take it back... yet.
Day 22 - Tomorrow we're supposed to attack somewhere... they didn't tell us where yet.
Day 23 - We took the hill called "Mamayev Kurgan." This place holds no strategic value at all... why did we take it? "Because we can."
...No members of the original squad are left except for myself and Karl. I had a grenade explode no more than 5 feet away from me. How am I still alive? I'm getting tired.
Day 26 - More replacements have shown up. I'm not even going to bother to learn their names anymore. They just get killed... The Soviets across the park keep playing their anthem over loud speakers. The ones that are closer to us are yelling at us, presumably insults. We insult back.
Day 29 - We're holed up in an abandoned, bombed out, apartment building.
Day 30 08:16- I saw the funniest thing. Last night, a Soviet was trying to sneak a teenage girl into where they were hiding out. Don't want to think about why. They came under machinegun fire from their own men, who thought they were some of us trying to scout their position. They were both killed.
...It looked like they were dancing when they were getting shot at. Not actual dancing, but like when one of those cartoon characters "dance" when shot at.
Day 30 19:07 - I take it back. The funniest thing I've seen today is a dead horse. I don't know why I found it funny... but I laughed.
Day 31 - I want to go home...

Hard as nails game but the best WW2 shooter out there but only if you like semi realism and steep difficulty in your shooters! There's no pay to win crap like Heroes & Generals and no arcade mode like Call of Duty. If your good with tactical thinking ie know when to flank or when to camp, have quick reactions and work as a team you'll do well, if you want to get the most kills and love K:D this isn't for you trust me. Theres not many unlocks or level ups so Call of Duty fan boys may not like it plus the rifles really do take skill to use at range. Focus is on game play in RO2 and not levelling and getting new gear.
RO2 rewards team play and cooperation with your fellow players. More often or not the team with the worse squad leaders and sniper fan boys lose. Commanders and squad leaders must do their jobs with supplies and arty strikes to win and normal players must stay alive and not waste re-spawn points making stupid decisions going for kills. I love the very steep learning curve and some games end in total annihilation. The satisfaction of winning a long battle is great though and you can fully appreciate a good squad leader who knows when to attack or defend.
What I really like about RO2 that some players won't is its a squad and solider based shooter not dominated by tanks and planes. If you want tanks and planes I suggest Battlefield there are some in RO2 but they don't decide battles all the time. The focus is pure man vs man combat with guns and controlling points and areas of maps to win.
If this game was updated to have terrain or building destruction it would be perfect, however this doesn't ruin the game experience. 32v32 matches are full of explosions, death and chaos! there's smaller matches and non hardcore for new players, I suggest 12v12 servers whilst you learn the maps but please man up and play hardcore mode :-D
This game will take you 10-15 hours to learn and develop any decent skill cap. The best players fully understand how mistakes and running around headless are punishing casual shooter players will get frustrated with fighting over the same building for long periods.
Everyone will get frustrated, angry and ragey but that just adds to the pure enjoyment when you finally win. This is a proper mans shooter........................
My only real complaint is the German weapons seem a bit better until you get unlocks with Russians or Americas (if you own the expansion you get the US) and the engine could at times do with a bit of tweaking and better optimization but lag isn't too bad.
Seriously though if you want the best WW2 shooter experience and immersion this is the game. I really like the campaign multiplayer where you fight to capture maps until one side loses all the territory.... best played like most modern games in a group on Team Speak or Skype with friends.

Any power, any hero, any team you want can be made in this game. If you don't mind a distanced perspective, there isn't a more complete super-hero experience. Doesn't change too much from the original game.
I would say that the original has a slightly better storyline (but it isn't bad at all), and I miss the ability to "hold back" ability strength in favor of not using as much energy, but overall it is definitely still Freedom Force!
Core gameplay is fairly simple:
1. Choose 4 characters to form a squad.
2. Tackle objectives in moderately sized maps that offer collectible power ups, bonus XP, and "prestige" to recruit more characters to your team roster. I have found that no particular set of four heros is perfect, but certain characters handle a wider variety of situations easier than the others.
3. Completing any objective rewards you with more prestige.
4. Once you have enough prestige, you can create a custom hero with almost anything you want, breaking the game, or just recruit the entire Freedom Force roster  if you like.
Replayability is there too, since there are so many heros available to you, and many characters have crazy abilities that can combo with others so well. If you like experimenting with team composition, there is a lot to like here.
Grab both games while they're on sale fast! Dozens of hours of super-hero fun at a bargain.

BioShock is a beautifully atmospheric game, with an excellent 60’s art deco style. The main selling point is the story, which is pretty damn great, and the world of BioShock is developed through Audio Logs and brilliant set piece moments. The guns are the standard setup of Melee, Pistol, Machine Gun, Shotgun, Grenade Launcher, Crossbow and the special weapon this time, the Chemical Thrower. Each of these weapons has 3 ammo types, standard ammo, Armour-Piercing and Anti-Personnel. In the supporting cast are ‘Plasmids’, powers such as Electro-Bolt, Incinerate! and Insect Swarm to name a few, powered by EVE.  Also, for some RPG-esq customization, they’re ‘Gene Tonics’, which you can equip, chop and change to your heart’s content. There’s a reasonable selection of dudes to fight, Melee, Gun wielding, Grenadiers and Spidery ones. The creepy Little Sisters wonder around BioShock, and gather ADAM, a wonder substance used for creating Plasmids and drugged up most of the people in the game. In Game, ADAM is used to buy and upgrade Plasmids/Gene Tonics, and presents the moral choice BioShock has. But first you have to fight Big Daddies, which at first is a big challenge, but then later is too much trouble.
However, it’s not without problems. BioShock is in no way challenging, and you get showered with Health Kits and items to recharge your EVE, and ammo. I didn’t really bother with the alternate ammo types, the regular types were just fine. I did go to the maximum slots for Plasmids and Gene Tonics, but I also found I was only using 3 Plasmids and about 4 Gene Tonics in each of the three categories. On the note of Gene Tonics, certain combinations are gross. For example, I was doing increased Wrench Damage, had silent footstep, received 25% less damage from most sources, 100% less damage taken from electricity while dishing out an additional 60%, and I did electrical damage whenever I got hit by a melee enemy. And that was only in combat! I had easier hacking, plus I received additional health from health kits, and an increased to both Health and EVE. ADAM simply isn’t as important as the game would have you believe, especially since how much of an effort it is to fight Big Daddies.
The Vending machines for ammo and general items were largely untouched by me, mainly for the reason that I didn’t need them, along with the half-arsed crafting system. I was only making Auto-Hack tools in the end, which brings us onto Hacking. Hacking is bloody awful, as you have to play Pipe Dreams to hack a system. In the end, I was just buying out or auto-hacking systems, as money was largely useless and I really couldn’t be arsed. A lack of inventory is also strange, so you eat food straight away as you pick it up, you never know how much of a weird item you’re carrying for crafting, and not being able to dual-wield Plasmids and a gun is really, really annoying, especially since you have to swap with right click.
Oh, and the final boss fight is awful.
Overall though, I really enjoyed BioShock, and would greatly recommend it, as all the problems I cited are largely insignificant in the grand scheme. As a final note, the whole 'Moral Choice' is a bit too Black and White, and something in the middle would have been much better.

"Outlast"
Horror is a tough genre to tackle nowadays, however, one indie studio have managed to revive what we all crave - A blood-curdling, heart-racing, breath-taking horror experience that has all the elements we haven't seemed to find in a lot of horror games these days.
"Outlast", set in the mountains of Colorado, sees Mount Massive Asylum ravaged by someone or something that has left the place overrun with free-to-roam psychopathic patients that just want to rip your head off.
The game has it's fair share of terrifying chases and atmospheric tension, accompanied by a thrilling soundtrack from Samuel Laflamme who got it just right. It's pros are endless, and it's cons are few - One to mention, the story is ever so slightly repetetive, but kept me on the edge of my seat!
"Outlast 2" (stylised as Outlast II) was announced in October 2015, and has since shown a full demo and screenshots (and we're sure there are more to come before it's release!).

With the rave reviews coming out for Inside, I thought I'd go and wrap up puzzle platformer Limbo, their previous game. I had gotten through 75% of it on the Xbox 360, so there weren't so many surprises in finishing it here on Steam.
Overall, Limbo is best known for its grim, moody aesthetics and gruesome deaths, that while not gory, still manage a certain grotesquerie to them. Part of it is the imagination running away and part of it the child protagonist. If you're offended by seeing a child die - and die over and over and over - you'll want to turn back now. Still, even through it's been a half-decaded since its release, the music and visuals remain striking.
The gameplay is more good to above-average, relying a lot on trial and error often to solve issues. At its best, the puzzles work organically and obviously, and generally none of them are massively taxing, but the later puzzles lean too heavily on working split-second timing more than your brain. The first half of the game is the strongest, dealing with alien creatures and hostile people, but the latter half seems to run out of ideas somewhat and falls back on puzzle platformer tropes like navigating moving gears, sliding boxes onto switches, and gravity flips. Still, it makes a habit of not repeating itself, which leads to its relatively brief length. There isn't a lot new here if you're played a lot of puzzle platformers, but does have a grim charm about it.
In general, Limbo is worth giving a whirl if you like the aesthetic. The mood is much of the game's appeal, and it won't take you long to tear through it. While it's not going to have the impact it did at release when atmospheric, artsy platformers were still a novelty, it does hold up pretty well.

Them - The Summoning is the first chapter of a more complex story - I didn't check if it was the only game or if there are more. Anyway, there are several twists in the story.
The gameplay is purely an hidden object game, with an inventory to complete items or to find others. In other words, you will be given a list of items to find. Some of them are hidden in drawers but they're not signaled. And if you want to unlock the extras, you have to find 10 bonus objects. You don't know what they are, in other words, click randomly to find them. And to top that, the items are very very small or sometimes, you're asking yourself if it was really visible. If you play in Standard, you don't have any chance to have an hint. In Easy, at least, after some minutes, it's blinking or being shown. And the HUD is also on hidden objects by moments. You're not really enjoying the hidden objects scenes. The puzzles are just anecdotic.
The graphics are acceptable, however, the HUD isn't making justice to the them and is completely impersonal. The drawings in the custscenes are also very good. The soundtrack is also good. But it's not really enough. When you see the menu, the old school buttons don't give you any envy.
In other words, Them - The Summoning isn't that bad. However, I didn't really enjoy the hidden objects scenes. I'm convinced by the story but as it's disserved by many problems... My conclusion is that Them - The Summoning cannot be recommended unless you're an hardcore hidden object gamer.

An uneven hidden object game that largely removes everything apart from the hidden object scenes (there are a handful of inventory items but they are picked up during the HOG scenes, and a couple of spot the difference puzzles).
The story is okay with a few oddities such as in the policemans office, and when you start hammering walls when the police are searching the building for you, but the story is not really going to be why you would play this (especially as being part one of a planned three episodes of which the others don't seem to exist yet).
The game also isn't very long (1-2 hours depending on how much you want to resort to the hint button probably) and like most HOGs isn't particularly replayable. Still it can be picked up pretty cheap, so that isn't necessarily
So it all comes down to the hidden object scenes. Firstly the scenes are reasonably clear and the graphics are good enough, and most of the hidden items are decently placed, so the game is playable enough, but there are a fair amounts of weak links here - there aren't many misnamed objects (the bane of HOG games), but there seemed to be a few with dodgy hit boxes, a fair amount of silly places (pumpkin, stuff silhouetted in the sky, the letter E type stuff). A major negative for me was some of the openable objects, some of which were completely nonobvious that you could interact with them (the mirror for example), where others like pillows would "open" any time you moused over them (but in other scenes pillows were immobile). There are also quite a few places where you are searching for an item that has several matches ("plant" when in a garden setting!), but only one is correct, which isn't great.
In terms of specific scenes the two screen pannable scene outside the church was an interesting idea, but I found it annoying once most of the items were found as you couldn't even be sure what you were searching for was on screen. Also it and the scene before had an annoying "wind" effect constantly obscuring the view. The UV filter bit was also an interesting variation, although all the animals looked about the same to me.
Finally we have the bonus items - this seemed a bit tacked on and very variable in difficult (marbles, coins, mice were easy, whereas knives, snails and darts were very difficult to find the last few, etc.
Overall then an okay HOG with a few flaws, with nothing exceptional about it good or bad. There are plenty of better options out there in the genre, but it is playable enough especially if you are paying less than a pound for it.

This game will get you, it is not a matter of if, only a matter of when....
Day 27.
Close call. My starvation had gotten the better of me, I needed food soon or else I would pass out and possibly never wake up. I had taken residence in a lake side cottage some 15 days before, it had, at the time, been a god-send. Food, water, shelter, and plenty of chairs and shelves to break down for wood, I had made it. Now the food was all but gone, my cottage ran cold most nights, and without the ability to distill water (lack of feul; aka chairs) I had a verrrrrry serious risk of disease from drinking the water that, at this point, probably contained some kind of stool. I was nearing the breaking point, but I had just enough supplies to go reset my traps and possibly live throughout the night to try and catch something, it was all or nothing. I wake up on the 27th day, and the wind is howling, I look outside and it seems as though I am staring at a blank peice of paper. Great. Here I go to die.
I decide that I would rather die frozen in the ground somewhere ( I could be one of those people in someone elses game perhaps) than starving to death in a shadowed cottage so, I take my chances. The long trek begins, I set off across the frozen lake to the spot I had designated for traps when I had first arrived in the area. I am bundled up with the best clothes that frozen people can buy (very comforting when you are trying not to freeze), and set off, resiliently into the morning (or night, honestly couldnt tell it was such a storm). I make my way slowly through the howling winds, unable to detect any landmarks on the edge of the lake, and am effectively, lost. Finally I spot a small island that I had seen days earlier in the middle of the large lake. Great, I am halfway there. I was numb before I left the cottage in the first place so, at this point, I would be lucky to be able to count my toes on one hand (depending if I had fingers either). Finally I limp through the cold to an outcropping off the lake bed, and I see three rabbits frolicking through what must be 2 feet of snow that has fallen within a few hours. Three small, little, tasty, little, small rabbits. In a fit of anger I run after them, I would just eat them raw if need be, im sure cold raw rabbit meat is super tasty anyways. I run out of breath in about two seconds and am forced into the realization that I still need to set my traps, and that this stranded experience has neither turned me into Usain Bolt, or an experienced, versatile hunter. I set three traps, one for each rabbit I was so longengly looking after, and set off back across the frozen tundra. This was a short lived task however, I hear a howl through the wind, but a different kind of howl. This was not wind, this was the hunting pack. I had seen them skulking around the lakes beaches a few days before, and now they had found their chance to take on little old feeble me. All I could think was, "I walk through the shadow of the valley of death, and I am definitely F****** afraid of this evil". I took off, well as fast as my ice blocks of legs could carry me. I had the general direction of a cottage I had seen a few days ago eariler, in relations to my trapping ground. Luckily for me this hunch was correct, I came upon a small abandoned house with the wolf pack in hot pursuit, and slammed the door in their face. Great! Then I realized that I had a grand total of an axe and a flair in my pack, as well as some currently useless medical supplies and about half a slatine cracker. You better believe that was the best damn cracker I have ever had. I had to wait, the wolves were at the door and there was no where to go. I contemplated my options: 1) Die inside 2) Die outside 3) Chop off arm, give to wolves, then die.
Well I went with numbero dos on this one. I ran outside, straight into a wolf. He was one of the ones from the pack but had strayed a bit from them and was more or less on his own. He saw me as easy prey and charged. I fumbled around in my pack for the last flare I had found and chucked it at him right as he was bearing down upon me. Smacked him across the top of the head and scared him off, only he wasnt the only one. Guess who was back. His friends. Well now I am a nice refrigerated raw meat sack to them, and I just♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off one of their buddies, so they were slightly aggravated. I took off across the lake (I could kind of see now, the blizzard had gone from blank page white to more of a constant blast of confetti to the face) and headed for the woods to try and lose them. They slowed but didnt stop giving chase and forced me to look for a quick fix to the situation. As I wheezed my way through the forest, being stalked by the two wolves that were still interested in this easy meal, I finally came upon train tracks of some kind. I saw a derailed train covered in feet of snow and decided to hunker down in that as night was falling. By the time I had pulled myself up and into the train car it was pitch black and I couldnt see my hand in front of my face. I rolled out my sleeping bag that I had luckily brought with me and tried to not freeze to death in the process of sleeping. I woke up at the crack of dawn, essentially dead in every way but spirit. My core body temperature was probably colder than the ice I had slept on. I was, as always, close to starvation and exceedingly dehydrated. I decide to look around this abandoned train car and see if I can somehow survive this disasterous situation.
There it is. The one thing that could have saved me. I had on and off been looking for this singular item since the game began. It is the rifle (now for people who have never played this game, the moment you find a firearm is about on par with winning the super bowl 15 times in a row, 20 if it has ammo) and guess what, it has ammo. (I can see the super bowl rings now....) I feel a type of elation that is impossible to describe. I MAY JUST LIVE. Now comes the trying to live part. I make my way down the tracks as I remember my cottage being relatively close to a set of tracks, whethere these were those, I was completely unsure, but its all I had to go on. Then the second best feeling ever in this game, I saw a red flag flapping against the white nothingness of the crisp air and snow, the flag that adorned the top, of a small shadowed cabin I called home.
10/10 You feel as though you are the character (minus the frostbite)

I'll finally post my review of Tropico 5, sort of as my swan song to my long history with a game I've come back to countless times since it was released back in 2014. Back then I bought at full price, same for the two extensions (Waterborne and Espionage), and many of the DLCs (mostly to get my hands on new maps). I've not regretted a cent of that cumulative purchase price; it's come out to about $1 for 10 hours of pure play time. I spend $3 every day for my morning coffee, and about 6 bucks to throw a dart at a balloon at the county fair to win a pink elephant which I couldn't even convince my girlfriend to carry. If you niggle about a dollar or two more or less for this much value that you get with Tropico 5, there's something wrong with you. If you still haven't purchased it (either you've lived behind the moon or you just took up strategy gaming), it's so cheap now for what you get, just buy it. End of THAT discussion.
I'm finally posting a review also to counter the many posts from the good people who love their Tropico 4, and post negative reviews on this board. It's a blessing and a curse for any creative to create something that is so strongly adopted by many. You may have followed the saga of the unfortunate Alden Ehrenreich, who Disney cast to be the young Han Solo in new episodes of the Star Wars franchise. Mr. Ehrenreich will not live another happy day on social media because the die hard, self appointed guardians of the Star Wars fantasy galaxy will rather have a septuagenarian Harrison Ford act out a young Han Solo than - heresy - a young and fairly unknown Mr. Ehrenreich. Something similar seems to be going on with Tropico 4 and now Tropico 5. Tropico 4 created a unique world that sucked people in, and with which they became so familiar that anything that breaks with tradition becomes a bridge too far for some. But to continue a successful franchise means sometimes having to take things into a new direction. Tropico 4 already got cluttered, and its graphics and tool tips and drop down menus betrayed its origin in the age of desktop computers running Win XP Pro with a middling graphics card. At a certain point, the economics of game development are inescapable: you have to be able to address a user base beyond your hard core niche players (who aren't getting any younger either), and open up to new systems (consoles). Firaxis did the jump with going to Civ 5 from Civ 4, and the reactions were similar. In the end, I've logged many, many hours on Civ 5, seen the modders base for that game grow exponentially and churn out awesome free mod products, and wonder with hindsight what the heck all the fuss was about in the first place. Same with Tropico 5. The devs had to break with some traditions, and what we got - and what you should get - is a game with beautiful graphics (don't buy this with a marginal graphics card, you want to run this on max resolution with all effects and all texturization turned on) and wonderful replayability.
This is personal, and may not apply to you, but I found a few decisions the devs took unfortunate. For example, they lost me from ever playing their campaign again when they force you - warning: spoiler -  to switch islands right at the start. There's no rational reason, no macguffin brilliant enough to somehow explain that story-wise, so the devs didn't even try. They just send you on another island. That took me completely out of my little world they had me in, and I never touched their campaign again. You may also find that the wit of the base series is lacking from the DLCs, which veer into slapstick and - again for me personally - made them too silly for me to care. I did wholeheartedly adopt Sandbox mode, in which I think Tropico 5 truly shines. Again, it's a special beast: those who wish for a city builder a la the old Sim City franchise before EA inexplicably decided to drive that against the wall, or the more recent Cities:Skyline, will find Tropico 5 odd in some aspects. You have to put up with the silly story lines and some extreme abstraction in some aspects of gameplay. The amount of information available to El Presidente is also somewhat limited (but then, you can always just consult the T5 Wiki). But Tropico 5 has something that makes it addicting: personality. If I build a perfect city in a city builder, fine. Yawn, eventually. But with Tropico 5, I found I can build cities, like real cities. With slums. Traffic jams. Political shenanigans and NIMBYs you just can NOT get along with. And you know what? You won't have to. Just have them come out on the street, then roll over them with your tank. And after the mayham of another revolution put down, sit back in your presidential lawn chair on your presidential lawn with your presidentially strong pina colada in hand, and look from atop high out over your sprawling, smelling, living, breathing, but strangely beautiful city, and take in that gorgeous sunset painting the sky behind all those houses in the most magnificant colors any citybuilder will give you. That's Tropico 5 to me, and that's what made all those hours I played it time well spent.

The tutorial for the game is terrible.  It spends more time talking about basic building mechanics than explaining how any of the metrics of citizen happiness and values work.   It basically just mentions that they exist and that they affect your popularity with the citizens. It doesn't explain how far the numerous "nearby" bonuses extend, It doesn't explain how to get useful information from the statistic tracking almanac.  Most of what I know of the mechanics of the game I got from reading guides.
The other main issue is that the citizen AI makes almost no sense whatsoever in its decision making.
My current island has 100s of homeless and jobless people despite there being more than enough houses and jobs for everyone.  I have homeless people who work in the nuclear power plant and jobless people who live, also homeless, next to open entry level jobs.  I have open college and high school level jobs and virtually nobody in either school.  I have dozens of farms and several food imports but citizens starving regularily.   I have quadrupled the number of couriers in the city but I still dont have materials and goods moving anywhere.
These issues and the happiness meters they reflect upon are so nonsensicle that I am convinced they have a randomized element to them.
I have heard that these issues are almost entirely fixed in one of the DLCs but that's arguably even worse because it means that they are effectively holding the functional game hostage for another $5.

While I missed Carma: Reincarnation, after playing this I understood that I didn't miss out on that much, and that this version is kind of superior.
Let me begin by saying that I love this game.
And here are my reasons why:
1. It's a game mainly about just having fun.
It's self aware, I like that in a game. Powerups and "Powerdowns" are funny and annoying at the same time, but that just adds to the game.
2. It's very arcadey
I really like the chapter system they got going on, with a variety of events that you can play against the AI.
Usually consisting of a "classic carma" event where you can do things at your own pace and other events that are more competitive, which is my favourite thing about this game! I mean, I still end up unlocking chapters way too fast because I guess I'm too good at ♥♥♥♥ing around in classic carma? But that's not too big of an issue to me.
My main issue with Carma 1 and Carma 2 is that there objectives were too broad or too strict as in.. In carma 1 all you could do is ♥♥♥♥ around, and in carma 2 you have events where you ♥♥♥♥ around for ages until there is an unskippable mission that is usually an annoying time trial.
Don't get me wrong, they're stellar games and I loved every hour I spent trying to complete them, but this game is by far my favourite game in the series and while I've not 100%ed this game yet, I am certainly gonna try.
3. I like the car handling
I know some people won't agree with me on this but I found the handling in general to be easy to get used to and it feels just right, plus the cars no longer feel like they're on the moon.
4. THEY MADE UPGRADES ESSENTIAL!
This. This is good. Normally in Carmageddon, once you got a bunch of upgrades, you essentially become unstoppable and the game becomes too easy, like in Carma 1 usually opponents just end up wasting themselves by trying to attack me while I'm just ♥♥♥♥ing around.
You are limited to how many upgrades you can get, and even getting them isn't all too easy, since you have to collect upgrade tokens, which is just.. the most arcadey thing ever, and I love it.
Basically, difficulty is real in this game and it makes me so happy to have a game that is challenging throughout.
5. Achievements are actual achievements, instead of boring, mundane♥♥♥♥♥♥that you do all the time (cough cough kf2 does this)
While I love this game, I do have a bit of issues with it.
1. There aren't enough maps.
There are quite a few maps which are huge and fun to explore, my favourite being the city maps.
But I think that it could use more, why not bring back that Ski Resort map from Carma 1? I mean this is a remake, isn't it?
2. The cars that you knew are good stay good.
This is kind of a mixed bag since your favourite car from the original is just as good or better than it was in Carma 1.
My point is that there aren't a lot of "new" cars which are good to drive. There is only one "totally new" car that is worth driving at all, and that's the Crazor. Looks good, handles good and is fun to race around in.
I mean, gimmicky cars are a staple of this game, every car feels different and that's fine, I mean, look at the Annhiliator, the literal gimmick of a car, made for fun.
But I never felt compelled to drive the Snaky ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ or the Tropikill since, if the AI suck with them, how am I gonna make use of them at all?
That's about all my thoughts on this game. Loved it to bits. The stupid puns, the music.. Favourite Carma game to date.

I liked this game and it is thrilling to experience how developers still manage to make good stories. We see the history through the protagonists eyes. Lorraine lost her son a the amusement park and starts searching after him. In the coming sequences we see odd things, experience paranormal things and the context is puzzling. The last scene is surely the climax of the whole story, Lorraines story.
As I see it she was not only depressed but seems to have a traumatic story. Just think, early attachment problems, a mother who rejects her and accusing her for having abandoned her by running away with the father. Then father is gone and her relatives dont want to share the insurance amount with her. There she stands alone before she meets a man and happiness is back in her life. But not for so long. The man dies and she becomes a single mother with a low-paId job. She also had post-partum depression for which she also was hospitalized and medicated for. I interpret the park as the conscious level and the grottos and the stairs in the last part as the sub-consciuos levels. As she walk through the rooms several times she relives the trauma again and again. Slowly the repressed memories comes to a consciuos level but she actively tries to repress them. The final scene where she stabs her son seems to me to be a try to get rid of the alien part of the self. I think that her son is in custody and that Lorraine seems to be psychotic.
Overall I liked the game as mentioned earlier. There are some cons though. Gameplay is a little bad mechanised and there should have been icons popping up when reading a note and alike. Walking is too slow and I finished the game by running. The game is a little too short and could have been longer.
I recommend this game for those who fancy psycology and ambient soundtrack.

If you like highly realistic shooters, then you should definitely check this game out. There's singleplayer and multiplayer, but multiplayer is where the game really shines. The bot AI in this game is really bad, so if you are looking for a singleplayer experience, i can't really recommend this game fot you. If you want to play online, then i suggest watching a couple of reviews and gameplays of the game, because the realism might not appeal to everyone. it's a really unforgiving game, especially in hardcore mode servers. You die from 1-2 bullets, you get no kill cam, you have no crosshair, your soldier gets tired from running really fast, your vision gets blurred from explosions and supression fire very easily and snipers will kill you very often if you are not careful. There are many more things that make this game difficult and realistic, but i'll let you discover them. The game is meant to be played on hardcore mode, so i recomment atleast trying a few matches. It can be extremely fun and satisfying when you are winning, but it can also be very frustrating if you are losing. In order to win a match, a team must play together and have a good communication. It's also very important to have good and experienced player in key roles (commander, squad leader, Machine gunner, etc.) If a team fails to do these things, it is destined to lose, except if the enemy team is even worse in that regard. I also must point out that if you are planning on acting like Rambo- not using any cover, rushing and gunning down everyone, you will be killed countless times by snipers and you won't even get close to the enemy.
All in all, I definitely recomment this game, but before you purchase it, again I suggest watching gameplays and read better and more professional reviews than mine. This is game that many people might not like.

The game has it's problems. For example they use both a number system and a moodles system and it gets confusing. I don't mind the moodles system, in fact I admire the originality but I would say make the number stats system visible too.
On the whole I really appreciate the game, it has brilliant developers, posting the oh-so amazing mondoids and with a sense of humor anyone'd die for.  Keep up the good work, dev team if you're reading this, and if you're thinking of buying the game, I say go for it as long as you don't mind a bit of hardcore. Meticulous pixel hunting in overdrive with a good plot and a plethora of beginner developer/writer mistakes.
Them, Chapter 1 was the first and the last game of the indie company Gamatic (game + fanatic), and it’s obvious that it was created by a really ambitious aspiring writer. It revolves around a single plot idea– a conspiracy thriller with some supernatural elements– but the dialogues are really clumsy, and due to the three-game structure it ends in a cliffhanger that never gets a proper resolution.
The game itself is a series of photograph-based hidden object scenes, each crammed full of the tiniest object possible, turning it into a never ending series of pixel hunting, where finding anything is more of a question of luck, not skill or sight. The hit detection is also a slightly off sometimes. But on the really positive side, the soundtrack is nice.
I wish Steam had a middle option, because it’s not a terrible game, but since I can’t recommend it at full price to anyone, I have to use the ‘not recommended’ tag on this one.

I was very pleased to find that even my very basic laptop was able to run this game at pretty solid FPS (mid to high 30s, at about medium settings). Though not on the highest graphic setting, the visuals are still very impressive and you really don't lose much in the beauty of this game.
I think my favorite part of this game is that it is a game that is great at doing what it was made to do. By this I mean this is a game billed as a survival game, and that is what you do, everything in your power to survive! This game is one of the first to scare me, not because of monsters or jump scares but because you really feel out there and exposed. When you are wandering through the trees and suddenly you hear the growl of a wolf, or when you come around that corner and are face to face with a huge bear, but more so when you are in the middle of no where with no place to hide and  blizzard suddenly pops up out of the blue. This game pulls all the punches, and really makes you work, and no two games are ever alike, which is incredible.
I have only logged 40 or so hours thus far, but I have palyed many games, because until you get the main mechanics down you will lose, A LOT!! But once you learn how to balance traveling and looting and keeping all of your meters taken care of you learn how to last. This is truly a survival game like no other survival game, and I look forward to everything that is to come, I will continue to recomend this game to all my gamer friends!

Hi, today I'll talk about the second expansion of Half-Life, Half-Life: Blue Shift. This is probably the weakest entry of the initial trio because the lack of new elements hold it back from being as innovative and fresh as the first two games. Nevertheless that doesn't mean that Blue Shift is a bad game. Personally, I liked it because I could experience yet another perspective of the great Black Mesa incident and the birth of a character of great importance in the Half-Life universe.
The plot of Blue Shift has a more personal twist compared to the other two previous games. The protagonist, Barney Calhoun, doesn't have the mission to stop an alien invasion nor nothing of the sort, all he wants to do is to escape from such dangerous place. Personally I like the idea that not everyone acts the same in a situation like that. Some poeple want to see for their own life.
Beyond that the story of Blue Shift doesn't have any interesting elements. In fact, this is referred to at the end of the game, since there is a big difference in the endings of the first two games and this one.
The gameplay is practically the same as the first Half-Life. The movement, the weapons, the enemies, everything is great. The mechanics are fluid and responsive. I think that this point is negatively affected by the lack of new elements or mechanics. There are no new weapons or enemies so it can feel a little repetitve, especially after playing the first two games.
The same as the first game, although with a slightly greater amount of details. The graphics for its time were pretty good. The FPS' were still developing aesthetically and Half-Life was a step forward without a doubt. It's obvious that by today's standards it isn't impressive. However for me the visuals of this game are a classic, a stamp that was won over the years product of the nostalgia of players like me.
It's the same as the original game so it inherits all the good elements of it. There's also some new music although it isn't as great as the original. I think it could have been used better, there were moments when it simply stopped suddenly or didn't really match the mood. As for the SFX it seems to me they reused most of it from the original game, which is fine. The voice acting is good, and I really like how they choose a different voice actor for Dr. Rosenberg.
In conclusion, Half-Life: Blue Shift is an OK expansion. It lacks new elements and mechanics compared to the first two games but still is an enjoyable game. I recommend that you play this if you are a fan of the Half-Life series, or if you want to try all the games of the series.

Right, let me preface this by saying two things, first off, I got this as part of the Humble Bundle "Freedom Bundle", so I did not pay full price. Second, I am not an artistic man, and have been known to say 'artsy fartsy' unironically. That being said, I went into this game knowing nothing about it, and with a relatively open mind. Now clearly I didn't care for it, but let's break down the good and bad anyways.
The Good
- There is a fairly constant feeling of mystery in this game, and the armosphere is well done for how little there really is to this game. There isn't much in the way of sound, but it is used to a somewhat decent degree.
- The simple polygonal art style serves the game well by adding to the mystery.
- The game is mercifully short.
- There is a story here, even if it's not a good one.
The Bad
- This game is incredibly short. Yes, this is good and bad.
- The controls are awful. You control your character by dragging the camera with your mouse, and clicking on objects and floating arrows that control your actual movement. It's over-sensitive, and really tedious, especially if you have to walk alot to solve a puzzle.
- The puzzles (the only real interactive gameplay) are either easy, or tedious and easy. They serve a distraction to pad out the already short game, and won't take most people very long to solve at all.
- The story of the game, whilst shrouded in a veil of mystery, is just kind of stupid. I'll mention it in the overview, so skip that if you don't want spoilers.
- I hope you like the same humming noise for most of the game.
Overview
Rituals is an art "game" in which you stop a big company from using nature as a massive drug trip and it's bloody awful. It controls like crap, its story is stupid (yes, that is the best word to describe it), and it's simply not fun to play. This game isn't even worth the time, let alone the five dollar entry fee. The few things it does right are undone by the everything else it does wrong. This game is not worth the purchase.
Tl;dr: Don't buy this game. You're better than this.

All I could think about when running that series of quests is that I wanted a better, more in depth look at the park, and this game delivers the content I was looking for.
If you have not played through the story in The Secret World, much of this game will seem linear and boring.  It expands on what we learn and gives us another taste of the darkness that stood out in my first playthrough.  As TSW is broken up into sections and areas, you have to leave that section to further advance your character.  Having a short reprise, for me at least, was a nice throwback.  If they make more games like this, based on the other sections of the game, I will probably buy them as well.
I honestly think this is a good start in a new direction for FunCom, and that more of these games, with larger and further developed storylines will be worth the playtime.
I feel like they made this game for me.  Thank you FunCom.

There's not a lot going for this game other than being short. It's just an unfortunate combination of rotten controls, fairly pedestrian puzzles and a sorta pretentious story.
To describe the controls, imagine Myst where you can freelook in a low-polygon environment. It sounds fine in theory, but the mouse must be used both for looking and for clicking on stuff. Switching between those modes requires holding a mouse button to look. The camera remains stuck wherever you release the button. Sometimes the camera is readjusted when you click on something interesting, but normally you are looking at some random place when you move from one location to another. The whole scheme seems ripped out of the original System Shock, which hadn't figured out how to navigate a 3D environment. Not sure how this could be fixed, but it would have helped if the camera were adjusted in the direction of travel.
The puzzles are maze- and item-based. I'm afraid the are typically either insultingly easy or annoyingly obtuse. There's an alligator puzzle that's mildly interesting.
Now the game would be rescued if it had a clever story or engaging atmosphere. But this is no Thirty Flights of Loving. The short, disjointed story seems to be trying to say something about death, religion, environmentalism, corporate greed and the tedium of working life. It's not very cohesive. It feels like the game designers had an idea of what they wanted to say, but weren't able to pull it off.
I don't hate the game, but Rituals isn't something I'd recommend spending time on.

To say it briefly, Carmageddon: Max Damage is a fun and endlessly entertaining game. If you like destruction derby games or just plain mayhem, you will probably get hours of entertainment out of this game.
Quality graphics and destruction physics plus, in what feels like a first for a Carmageddon game, decent handling of vehicles. The game isn't without flaws, but the amount of features and game tweaks is impressive and really well thought out by the developers. Attention to detail continues throughout the game as you find subtleties in the UI and fun features like looking up close at the damage you've done to the other cars after the race and watching full race replays. There are lots of adrenaline-pumping moments and going back afterwards to watch it again and again from different angles is superfluous but very statisfying. If you've played the Carmageddon games before you'll feel right at home but there's lots of new features to enjoy. Plus you can mod the game to your heart's content.
Vehicle handling has improved drasticly since playing keyboard-only back in the 90's, but sometimes it feels like I'm piloting a buttership across a hot skillet. Your vehicle will handle different on different terrains but the effect subtle and the accelerator spins up your tires fast so it's difficult to control the car precicely.
Honestly, though, you aren't playing this game because it has magnificent car physics, you're playing because it has magnificent destruction physics. Car models get crumpled and ripped in half while the driver gets thrown out the windshield. Maps are large and full of funny peds, jokes, and gags. Weapons and powerups add more mayhem. And of course, gore galore.  If you want some crazy action with no real purpose then you can't go wrong with this game.

I'll be honest and say I played for all of five minutes. The controls are just something I don't want to deal with. I like walking simulators, I like slow moving games that make you think, and I don't mind wandering around for a bit before I know what I'm doing. However the control scheme here is a massive mistake. You click on arrows to move in chucks, like the old myst games, except unlike those games you have to constantly drag the mouse around to re-orient your view. It makes simple navigation even through straight corridors absolutely tedious.
I got to a locked door right on the first level and just thought "I don't want to walk around this level to find the key". If it was WASD or just fixed screens that you move to and from with a mouse click then I would have had a walk around and seen what this game had to offer. If I read the other reviews and thought I might be missing an epic story I might have persevered, but that doesn't look like the case.

Each hidden object scene contains ten secret items (hover your cursor over the start to see what they are).  You do not revisit scenes generally so if you want to find the secret items, you should find them right away.
Overall I liked the game but did find it difficult finding some items--they can be small, and some objects you are supposed to open or move to expose other items do not give a visual clue such as a cursor change.

Lemme make a list.
The good:
+ Lots of tactical depth.
+ Has a practice mode where you play vs bots.
+ Also custom game lobbies for practice.
+ Lots of beginner guides on the forums.
+ Very active developers, around 1 new Update every other day at the moment.
+ Very competetive game with leaderboards.
+ Lots of active players, more than 10,000 individual players every day.
+ 4 Races with individual strengths and weaknesses to choose from, plus 1 random race.
The bad:
- Interface not very intuitive, many windows only available through chat commands.
- Games are somewhat RNG reliant, hope this will get fixed at some point by making pathing and unit focusing more consistent.
- If a player disconnects a bot takes over, this is fine for now but I hope they'll implement a more elegant solution in the future (for example if someone disconnects before wave 2 the game will be cancelled).
- Very hard for new players, even though you get all those practice opportunities a tutorial of some sorts would be appreciated.
- Matchmaking is ok for now but could use some improvements. Even though I'm somewhat high elo I constantly get matched with 1200 elo players who have no idea what they're doing. Though this will probably fix itself once even more players start playing the game.
- Features like the cosmetic shop not implemented yet, only 4 races as of right now, buit the base game is definitely there and ready to be expanded on.
Conclusion:
Over all the game is 100% strategy, knowledge and prediction what the enemy will do, it doesn't require a good internet connection nor your constant attention which makes it the perfect game for me and my 2mbits connection to play while also watching some youtube/twitch on the side.
Definitely a recommendation from me.

Let me start by saying this. This game is by far one of the most entertaining and realistic zombie survival games I've ever played. Even in early access, Project Zomboid gives players the true meaning  of horror and hardships in one of the most popular fictious demises of humanity, zombies.  You, a lonely survivor who hasn't been taken by the plague (yet), fight for your very life in a world torn apart by a vicious zombie plague. Loot, farm, fight, and take shelter as you grip on madly to each passing day. Forced to brave the deadly zombie hordes in search of supply.  For those days...may be your last.
Welcome to the zombie outbreak, how will you die, survivor?

If you like highly realistic shooters, then you should definitely check this game out. There's singleplayer and multiplayer, but multiplayer is where the game really shines. The bot AI in this game is really bad, so if you are looking for a singleplayer experience, i can't really recommend this game fot you. If you want to play online, then i suggest watching a couple of reviews and gameplays of the game, because the realism might not appeal to everyone. it's a really unforgiving game, especially in hardcore mode servers. You die from 1-2 bullets, you get no kill cam, you have no crosshair, your soldier gets tired from running really fast, your vision gets blurred from explosions and supression fire very easily and snipers will kill you very often if you are not careful. There are many more things that make this game difficult and realistic, but i'll let you discover them. The game is meant to be played on hardcore mode, so i recomment atleast trying a few matches. It can be extremely fun and satisfying when you are winning, but it can also be very frustrating if you are losing. In order to win a match, a team must play together and have a good communication. It's also very important to have good and experienced player in key roles (commander, squad leader, Machine gunner, etc.) If a team fails to do these things, it is destined to lose, except if the enemy team is even worse in that regard. I also must point out that if you are planning on acting like Rambo- not using any cover, rushing and gunning down everyone, you will be killed countless times by snipers and you won't even get close to the enemy.
All in all, I definitely recomment this game, but before you purchase it, again I suggest watching gameplays and read better and more professional reviews than mine. This is game that many people might not like.

Before I say the good things about this game, I want to point out the flaws
1. The day 1 DLCs are complete bogus, if im paying $60 for a game i should get the whole game.
