While not quite as good as the original, I still enjoyed playing the game. There's no real new ground broken here. If you liked the first game, you'll probably like this one. If you didn't like the first one, this one won't change your mind.
This game is a decade-old and has the design quirks you'd expect given that. There is no autosave, so you need to save during missions yourself. If you don't, you'll find yourself suddenly dead and needly to replay 30-40 minutes of a fight. The enemies, even at the end, can be tough. Make a single tactical mistake and an enemy can land a punch that does 40% damage to some characters. There is not much healing on most maps, so a mistake early on in a mission usually means you don't have enough health for the climax.
On a few maps, a bad team choice can make the mission extremely difficult (which you sometimes don't know until you're 10 or 15 minutes in), e.g. when you discover the Nazis suddenly have flying units and you're stocked up with ground melee units.
Like the first game, you are overwhelmed with characters and I never felt like I got much of a chance to explore many of them. Given how long most missions are, and the how much one poor character (in a team of only 4) can hamper you in a mission, it is easy to "play it safe" and go with the same smallish set.
Despite the flaws, this is still a great RTS with a strong single-player campaign.

Half-Life: Blue Shift was released in 2001 as the second Gearbox Half-Life expansion. In this game, you play as Barney Calhoun, a Black Mesa security guard during the time of the original Half-Life's Resonance Cascade, and the subsequent invasion of Black Mesa by the US military in attempt to cover the event up.
The game is similar to Opposing Force in that it illustrates a part of the world of Half-Life during the time of the Resonance Cascade, though from the eyes of someone other than Gordon Freeman. In Blue Shift's case, you start in a similar environment to Gordon within the depths of the Black Mesa Research Facility as an employee there, and after a casual introduction into basic mechanics and the neat environment Barney works in, you're thrown into combat quickly after the Cascade hits within 15 minutes into the game.
Most of the basic weaponry Gordon has in Half-Life can be used by Barney, from the Shotgun to the Revolver to the Crowbar, and the plot surrounds Barney's attempt to escape Black Mesa and resist against US marines who are pouring in to the facility to cover the whole Cascade up, along the way, you'll solve puzzles, fight baddies, and help scientists to find the way for yourself and others to escape the doomed facility before the impending nuclear destruction of the facility kills your chances.
One of the greatest criticisms leveled against Blue Shift is that unlike it's sister expansion, Blue Shift does not add in any new weapons or enemies, without even recycling the ones in Opposing Force. Barney also does not gain access to any of the neater weapons that Gordon Freeman was able to get his hands on like the Tau Cannon or the Hive-Hand, the biggest gun Barney is able to weild outside of console commands being the RPG. While these criticisms are certainly valid, it's not fair to say it doesn't bring anything new to the table. Blue Shift is decidedly much more story driven than Opposing Force, as Dr. Rosenberg is a very important character to Blue Shift's story and is one of the few persistant NPC's in the original trilogy. Dr. Rosenberg explains alot of exposition about his old lab in the facility wile also serving as one of the few charaters with the knowledge and equipment to actually escape the facility.
The game itself is pretty great; because it was built around the same engine and built around Half-Life as an independent game, it resists many problems itself; most being attributable to those that Half-Life had itself (the flashlight that could stick to surfaces across the room). That being said, the game has a few glitches (saves breaking, certain elevator scenes near the beginning leading to game-overs, Gordon getting stuck on the tram tracks, etc) but none that were utterly game-breaking or capable of ruining the player's experience.
That being said, this game's main problem is its length and the amount of content it introduces. While Opposing Force, the previous Gearbox Half-Life expansion, had within it a fairly long plot, introduced many new weapons, aliens, and even had a boss battle, Blue Shift is fairly short and doesn't really introduce new weapons, (that being said, most of them to my knoweldge use different skins) and in my opinion, serves more as a compliment to the original game by allowing fans of Half-Life to see more of Black Mesa behind the scenes.
In my opinion the game is great and is my personal favorite of the Half-Life expansions and vies with Half-Life 1 for the best original Half-Life title; I've always enjoyed the character of Barney Calhoun, and I find it enjoyable that there's an entire expansion detailing his own escape from the Black Mesa complex. However, I do recognize the flaws that this game has: This game doesn't introduce as much content as Opposing Force did to be considered a different title from Half-Life, and isn't as long as either Opposing Force or Half-Life to have as much of an impact on the average player post-completion. That all being said, I enjoyed what it was, the narrative and story was solid, and I enjoyed the chance to see the Resonance Cascade and the subsequent invasion of Black Mesa from the eyes of Barney. The game has a certain narrative to it that creates an interesting environment that compliments the plot, and because of its length, you spend more time with other characters and as such are able to more greatly build an understanding of their character because you spend more time together. While it's short and doesn't add much to the Half-Life universe, I myself liked it and found it enjoyable, even if it's only around 2-3 hours long in comparison to the original Half-Life being around 10-12 hours in length.
In the end, the game's narrative and plot outshine its gameplay for me; it's interesting to see the quest of a security guard escaping Black Mesa while it's under seize by Xen creatures and the military, and the ending is a complete contrast of the ending of Half-Life, and I can't help but feeling like it hit all its narrative marks in those regards.
I myself recommend it, but whether you want to pay 5 bucks for something like this is your opinion in the end. That being said, I myself got it as a part of the Half Life Complete Steam Bundle, which goes on sale during every major seasonal Steam sale. If you were thinking of getting this title or any of the other games in the Half-Life franchise, I'd suggest you turn to that bundle during a sale, as you get discounts for all the games if you buy it, so it's cheaper than buying each game individually.

"Outlast"
Horror is a tough genre to tackle nowadays, however, one indie studio have managed to revive what we all crave - A blood-curdling, heart-racing, breath-taking horror experience that has all the elements we haven't seemed to find in a lot of horror games these days.
"Outlast", set in the mountains of Colorado, sees Mount Massive Asylum ravaged by someone or something that has left the place overrun with free-to-roam psychopathic patients that just want to rip your head off.
The game has it's fair share of terrifying chases and atmospheric tension, accompanied by a thrilling soundtrack from Samuel Laflamme who got it just right. It's pros are endless, and it's cons are few - One to mention, the story is ever so slightly repetetive, but kept me on the edge of my seat!
"Outlast 2" (stylised as Outlast II) was announced in October 2015, and has since shown a full demo and screenshots (and we're sure there are more to come before it's release!).
Thumbs up to Red Barrels Games for creating this masterpiece of horror - 9/10

TL;DR at the bottom-
I don't even know where to begin with this game.
I'd heard about it a while back and I saw it, thought it looked kinda interesting, and then never bothered picking it up. My friend recently gifted it to me and if I could I would have been willing to spend up to $45 or so for the experience this game tosses at you. The only thing I can say now is that I regret not picking it up sooner. It just hits me in such a way that I can't explain. Everytime I'm walking slowly down a road and there's nothing but cars to the side and burnt houses around, and that ♥♥♥♥ing guitar picks up I just get so into it and feel like I'm actually a survivor.
The Long Dark is a gem among early access games and deserves so much attention. I knew this as soon as I'd put in a good hour. Let me start off by saying that the immersion that this game delivers is phenomenal. It has a great tone and world design to be used for story telling. While the game offers no tutorial and this can be a positive or negative thing, I personally loved it. All it did was make me genuinely want to learn about the game and the world itself more, and as I did, I felt myself get better at it and feel more confident about surviving. The longest time I've survived so far on a character is 30 days counting and there's been numerous points throughout that timespan in which I thought I was going to die and got anxious doing something because I genuinely felt like I was the person wandering through the world. Each time I spotted a bear in the distance or a pack of wolves, I felt like they were a genuine threat and therefore considered my options. Do I try to sneak around them? Do I head in the opposite direction? Do I have ammo or a weapon to fend them off just in case? This doesn't even just count with the wildlife but the environment as well which I cannot stress just how important in a survival game. Every time I saw a side road leading off of the main highway I seriously considered my options. Did I have enough food and water with me in case it's a dead end? Do I have enough daylight left to make it back to the main road if there's nothing down this way? Will I have enough firewood and tinder to create a fire if need be? When I would be staying in a cabin for the day due to a blizzard, I would genuinely consider my options then as well and think to myself if I had enough food to survive the night before I would be able to scavenge for more supplies? The game pushes you to think about these options in a way that I've never felt another survival game do before.
The game does an incredible job at atmosphere and aesthetic and is downright GORGEOUS from every early sunrise and darkening sunset to each howling blizzard or each bright sunny day. The more you're willing to immerse yourself into believing you're truly surviving in the world, the better job it does at delivering a truly special experience. There was a point in which I'd found a safe and when I was trying to crack the code, I actually leaned in on my monitor as though I'd be able to hear the clicks better without realizing it. When there's a blizzard in the game and all you can hear is lonesome ambient guitar music playing and the wind howling in you ear, you feel genuinely alone and feel cold. When you enter a cabin and all you can hear is the wind beating against the house and the creaks of wood echoing, it creates a sense of fear and paranoia because you know that there were people who are probably long dead that used to live here. When you’re walking through a cave and all you can hear is the vast echoes of your footsteps against stone and the hiss of your flare, you feel genuinely cautious.The fact that the game is able to pull this off is absolutely stunning. And above all, you genuinely
like you're a survivor in this new world. You begin to grow attached to your character and genuinely care for them and begin to wonder if you can truly survive the wilderness. The game does an excellent job at small little stories you can pick up on when you're not expecting it. For example you can find a cave in which there's a small campfire with food beside it, or you can be walking through the woods and find a frozen corpse of a man with an axe next to a deer corpse, insisting he died of hypothermia while trying to get food. It's all of these little things that come together that truly help create an enjoyable experience and make me want to get out there and explore the world in front of me. When you walk through a town you begin to really have thoughts of, "I wonder what happened to the people that lived here. I wonder what the story of the people who made it out is" and it's like that for nearly every place.
The only two downsides to this game for me at least are there's been few bugs in which I would climb a rock and randomly sprain my ankles or wrists for no reason and it's pretty immersion breaking. And secondly, there's no randomly generated maps and all loot spawns are always the same regardless of if you were to make a new character or not. If they were to add randomly generated loot and maps, I could play this game for literal hundreds of hours not to say I already plan to, but it would definitely help with the game in the long run and keep me coming back to it.
In short, this game is truly something special for the person that wants to immerse themselves in a world where they feel like they're truly a survivor in the wilderness with nothing but their own decisions on what's best to help you survive the long dark.

~ Daily and Weekly tasks to help keep the grind "fresh" and mix things up.
~ Graphics are not oppressive or excessive. It feels like walking through a casino (though I have not been through many, myself)

~ Rankings for the various games.
Things that were not so enjoyed:

I'll try to avoid spoiling this game to the best of my ability, but I feel it's impossible to really discuss it without any spoilers.
This is not a game to be taken lightly, it's not a game built for fun. I'm not even sure that game is the right term for this, as it's not meant as entertainment. I get the feeling that, regardless of the narrative presented's truthfulness, this is very personal to the creator.
I've seen this game get a decent amount of criticism of just being a "walking simulator," and people say that if you just want to tell a story regardless of the player's choices, you should just make a movie or a book. I can't agree with this. While yes, there's not really any interactivity beyond walking to speak of, and you definitely shouldn't play this if that turns you off of it, but the story wouldn't work in any non-interactive medium. At the end of this... interactive experience... a thing happens, and that thing wouldn't have anywhere near the same amount of impact had you simply been passively watching instead of actively participating.
As for whether I recommend this game, that depends entirely on your position on if a game can be held up on its story alone. There's no gameplay to speak of in this, but the story is an excellent exploration of an idea, and if that appeals to you, then go for it. However, if you feel that games have to have gameplay, then give this a pass.

Carmageddon: Max Damage, formerly known as Carmageddon: Reincarnation is the fourth installment in the Carma series. Developed by Stainless Games and funded by Kickstarter, the game had been in the making since some time in 2011 before the gold release in 2015, to not very favorable reception as the game was badly optimized at the forefront while being quite lackluster in visuals second. While the game was still good fun, this first impression spelled a potentially bleak future for the revival of Carma, as well as the company that got back together to make it a reality.
But unlike some indie games, funded or not that get left as-is Stainless put C:R back in the oven for another year of polishing and added new content in addition to greatly improved performance as well as much nicer visuals as a bonus. A new re-release of C:R going by C:MD with the updates was submitted to get better reception as well as console releases on the Xbone and PS4 to appeal to a larger demographic. As such for niche games like Postal or Hatred, C:MD was met once again with unfavorable critic reception and with gameplay that flew over most non-fans' heads and continued criticism about dated graphics as well as a lack of depth in gameplay or story. However this re-release has been met with much more positivity on Steam than C:R and is really at heart a labor of love for the fans who've been following the series since 1997.
Once again this is a follow-up review to Carmageddon Max Pack and Carmageddon 2: Carpocalypse Now, I will only refer to what is new in this entry, minus covering the absolute basics. C:MD is once again a reboot of sorts for the series, as every game reimagines the universe despite keeping the tried and true formula in-tact. To describe this iteration would be like a fusion between the first and second game, with the former largely being the primary influence in terms of environments, vehicles and gameplay, but the second for its somewhat lighter and cartoon-y tone as well as numerous additions and improvements in the form of user-operable Pups, mini-map, and organizing events into groups. What does not come back however are the missions and permadeath from C2, the latter of which was the largest offense to me in C2, effectively making C:MD the best of both C1 and C2 and none of the bad.
The cops from C1 make a return in their APCs including the mighty Suppressor (now called the SUBpressor as it's slightly scaled down but still packs a punch) to make your life miserable as well as new police vehicles like the Compact Unit: Nil Threat (anyone old enough to play these games will catch Stainless' many dirty gags) which is an armored Smart-car, and the even bigger Super Suppressor. Many opponents from C1 return with reimagined designs and a couple from C2, as do a chunk of C1's environments reimagined in addition to a few new ones as well. You cannot buy your opponents' vehicles like in C2 but you can steal them again like in C1. Unlike C1, all opponents are stealworthy over time as opposed to a select few. Parts shop is back from C1 and instead of using credits earned during an event you collect tokens found throughout the game to upgrade parts for your vehicle instead. Credits are thus almost exclusively used to advance through the chapters, besides in-race recoveries and repairs. You can buy Pups on the go now though using a buy menu during an event, but they're expensive and not required to actually finish the game so spend wisely.
The events are split into 16 chapters, all containing one Classic Carma event which is the meat of the Carma experience, where you win by three ways: kill every pedestrian, wreck all opponents, or complete a series of checkpoints around the circuit. To mix things up new event types were added with Ped Chase, where you and your opponents attempt to splat specifically targeted peds. Car Crusher, which is effectively Carma's deathmatch between you and your opponents. Checkpoint Stampede which is a less violent take on Ped Chase in the form of checkpoints instead of polygonal lives. Fox 'N Hounds, where you or an opponent takes the role of a fox and is chased by the hounds while trying to reduce their time as the fox to zero. Lastly there's Death Race, which is the closest you'll ever get to actually racing, your position matters here and the goal is to complete a series of laps before your opponents do. All modes still have that Carma flavor however and you're still encouraged to play dirty: wrecking an opponent that's doing well will steal their points and give them to you. The first chapter has three events, with late-game chapters including up to six events and ever-stronger opponents, so make sure to upgrade your current ride or switch out altogether if you plan to ram them head on: it'll hurt you more than it will them in their super-powered bulldozer via your toy-like sports car at that point.
Visually the game is unmistakably superior to its predecessors, and while its not exactly on par with today's latest and greatest it's more than adequate and still looks like a recent game, running on a heavily modified version of the BRender engine that powered C1 and C2. The damage model for vehicles has been massively improved and the ped variety is greater than ever before, with the addition of cyclists and mobility scooters as well as nuns. It's all in good tongue-in-cheek fun however as Stainless never wrought anything to be blatantly offensive or shocking for the sake of it. As long as everybody's worth 200 credits at a minimum there's nothing to get one's knickers in a knot over. Sound design is suitably crunchy and punchy, from collecting Pups and colliding with squishy peds to crushing opponents and breaking things in the environment. The soundtrack this time features music by Maximum Sexy Pigeon who do the Carma-fitting metal ala Fear Factory and Morgue who is something of a drum 'n bass and dubstep-y artist. The former is more my jam and just makes sense when it comes to Carma but Morgue got some decent tracks here and to be fair Carma has always had some kind of electronic artist on the soundtrack in addition to a metal one so they're not too out of place.
Criticisms include little but notable, the lack of buying things outside of Pups on the go makes credits feel inherently useless and as the method of progressing through the chapters arbitrary, especially once you beat the game, serving only to beat your friends on the scoreboard for each event. The opponent AI isn't always the best at pathfinding, especially on game modes better suited to multiplayer like Fox 'N Hounds. There's too much reliance on offensive Pups to wreck opponents as opposed to outright ramming even in some of the stronger vehicles with max Offensive and the player is too easily damaged or wrecked even with max Armor in all but the heaviest vehicles so don't be surprised if you get one-shotted by an opponent every once in a while, not counting the police. There's less environments on offer than in previous games and essentially less content overall when compared to C2. This is nothing future updates and fan support can't fix however. But ultimately if you didn't care for the earlier games in the series then C:MD won't be winning you over as it is essentially more of the same and will boil down to what your idea of having fun while wasting time is.
At the end of the day C:MD is a much appreciated return to form for the Carma series and runs neck-and-neck with C1 for me in terms of the best entries in the series and I hope Stainless can manage to stay afloat or at least the small but diehard community to continue bringing us more and better in the future. The Tropico series has been great and although the game keeps its character, it evolves with every series in different directions - which is something the developers can and should be proud of.
I do like the history timeline that was added to this latest edition and I think some of the mechanics in terms of transportation have been improved!
What I would like to see in the next edition is:
- return to more micromanagement of the people. I do think that the managers' system that was introduced in this edition is a very good idea but yet I would like to see more individuality in this and almost would like to be able to employ the closest and best managers to work for me from when I find them until they die.. (pretty much)
- I would like to see more competition from the different faction leaders and more individuality to those throughout the game as part of the resistence, maybe introducing parades, protests etc. against "the regime" so that they feel like real competitive individuals and not just random computer generated people who run against you in elections..
- I would like to see more customisation of your own character and your managers (based on the idea above) and maybe potentially your main opponents (my second point above).. that would further enhance the individuality and the presence of real opponents.
- I would like to see more technology, more choice of buildings of the same type, maybe even be able to somehow affect the cars/transportation your people are using.. (obviously all of that can and probably should be done in following DLCs)
- I think the dynasty idea in this edition has been handled very well and the fact that you can have a number of dynasty members is a great introduction, but I would like to see more traits, more character and, again, individuality in each member.. almost on the principles of traits in Total War series.. or maybe even Sims..
- I think the economy in this edition has been handled amazingly well but I would like to have more control on the import / export and production / consumption of goods. This has been addressed to an extent in this game but I think it would be cool if, for instance, when people only have one type of food - they protest... or for instance you can do edicts which are related to all products in trade and consumption.. the whole geopolitics and trade has to be developed further and resources have to be made renewable or inexhaustible (mainly mines)..
Anyway.. that's just a few ideas off the top of my mind.. and I realize they are very onerous and time/budjet consuming ideas probably.. but I do think that this is the direction that this game has to be evolving into. Nevertheless, amazing work by all and everyone who has been part of this project! The graphics, the gameplay, the character of the game, the sound effects, music, voices, the mechanics of the game... great great job!

 People who like art games and aren't picky about how controls & other gameplay aspects are incorporated. People who don't mind a game with an arguably environmentalist message.
Rituals is a point & click art game, not an adventure game. I want to preface with that. If you don't enjoy walking simulators or games designed primarily to evoke thought and emotion in the player you'll find Rituals extremely boring. On the other hand if you do enjoy similar games I would encourage you to give it a try.
Rituals is not the most emotionally provoking of games and in comparison to others I did find it a little bland but overall it tells an intriguing story about modern human's relationship with an animistic earth. To pick up on the story you do need to read notes & magazines, all of which connect together to offer a loose narrative. That said they're fairly hard to miss as long as you explore the whole game.
My one complaint follows the others that have been mentioned, the controls are a pain to work with. To move you click preset arrows and to look around you click and drag. This separation of camera and movement controls meant I was constantly switching between moving and readjusting camera perspective which felt like a waste of time.
Overall some parts of the game could, and probably should, have been done better but if it's goal is to tell a story and create an interesting atmosphere I feel it succeeded. I'm not sure I would recommend it at $4.99 but if it interests you definitely keep an eye on the price and play when you can.

Rituals is a game that's hard to recommend. While I applaud the developer for creating their own first-person adventure engine to support this game, I'm not sure it came together particularly well. Looking around feels janky and movement via clicking on arrows often becomes tedious. I understand that it's a throwback to games like Myst but it holds the game back. If  Rituals was free-roaming using the Unity engine, or some other such engine, it would have felt significantly better and based on the level design, I'm not sure why that wasn't done.
While there are some basic puzzles in this game, the main draw would be for the storyline and thematic art but it's lack of depth makes it hard to recommend on that level as well. It becomes clear very early into the game what idea the developer is trying to express and the game leaves little room for further interpretation or deeper thought.
I'd be interesting in seeing this developer's future work and seeing what new ideas they can bring to the table but Rituals, on its own merits, can be passed up.

What can I say?  This game's interface looks so simplistic by today's standards, and yet the Indie Stone team has managed to possibly create one of the best post-apocalyptic zombie survival games in existence to date.
In a sea of games set in the rapidly-becoming-trite-and-humdrum End Of The World By Way Of Zombies scenarios, this one outshines them all.  Yes, even in its alpha stage.
In the sandbox game, you create your character and are greeted with the cheery messages telling you, basically, that you're *going* to die.  There's no rescue coming, the end isn't just nigh, it's done come and gone.  You're on your own.  Your goal is basically just to survive as long as you can.  And die you will.  Many, many times, at least unti you get the hang of the game's mechanics and how to avoid becoming some poor deceased fast food worker's lunch.  Barricade windows and doors, erect walls, keep yourself fed and watered, and don't let your character get bored and depressed.  Flee town and start a farm to live off the land, or hole up in an abandoned warehouse and periodically raid the surrounding buildings for supplies, all while avoiding the relentless horde which believably reacts to sight, sound, and smell.
For those of you used to games like Left 4 Dead, taking on a horde of fifty zombies with a shotgun is one of the worst things you can do in this game.  The noise brings every zombie in a five mile radius bearing down on you, and your ammo supply is typically very limited.  Even one zombie hiding in that corner you forgot to check is a threat.  Whoa, there was one in the tall grass you didn't see, and he wasn't dead.  Now he's gnawing on your ankle.  Whoops, is that a bite?  Welp.  You're infected.  Expect to live another couple of days in game before turning.  Or you could just chug that bottle of bleach you found in the bathroom earlier to end it now...
In short, this game delivers one of the most intense and gripping presentations of the zombie apocalypse I've seen in a video game yet.  Pessimistic and gritty, and incredibly addicting, even without the option of mowing down hundreds of cannon fodder corpses.  I've probably logged more than 150 hours in this game in total, and I still can't get enough.
The best part is that the development team is still working hard, cranking out more and more updates, polishing features, ironing out the bugs, and keeping their players informed about what's to come.  This game is well, WELL worth the $15 they're asking for.

Project Zomboid is a great game, even in alpha. You start out as lone survivor in Muldraugh, Kentucky. You scavenge food, fight off the undead and try to keep an eye out all the time.
The game strives to be realistic, so no, assault rifles and automatic turrets won't be in the game. Although Project Zomboid is still in alpha, there're already many features like carpenty, gardening, hunting and fishing. According to the devs, NPCs and cars are also on the list.
However the closer you're coming to the endgame, the easier it gets. You'll have your own garden and grow your own food. No need to leave your fortress. Zombies will be rarely attacted if you stay silent. You really don't know what to do now - minecraft-syndrome.
The devs are aware of that and the community is looking toward  more dangerous zombies and NPCs.
If you really want to try a new, unique zombie game, this is for you. Otherwise, wait for the future builds or the final release. It's worth the money in both cases.

Freedom force vs. the Third Reich is the right kind of nostalgia. The kind that isn't a repeat of something you saw with a fresh coat of paint, but a celabration of WHY we love this thing we love. Stylistically it seems to lovingly and joyfully toss in every silver age (and lots of golden age) comic book trope and cliche both in how the characters speak and look. Expressed no more beautifully than through the amazing hero origin cut scenes between each mission. Cut scenes which I hasten to add are easily the best element for me in the entire game. From the narration, to the story itself, to the personas of each hero...the game just knows what it is and knows exactly what its calling back to.
Gameplay wise the game isn't mind blowing but I wouldn't call it bad. It feels like a slightly looser and far less complex version of the pause/start style of a Balder's Gate or Dragon Age. Teetering on this little border between beat em up/strategy/crpg. You pause, issue commands, target enemies with abilities or allies with buffs and heals, unpause. It works and honestly its a style of gameplay Id love to see given over to actual comic book video games in the future if it evolved some. I mean it makes perfect sense for this kind of strategy light gameplay to be how a super hero team game should play. Now the issues start to nip at the edges when it comes to things like AI pathing and priorities. But really at the pop of a button you can pause anyway so even though it'd be nice to have your heroes act smarter when not under direct orders at all times...it aint nobodies fault but your own that they ever don't have said orders. Imagine one of the old syndicate games but with more verticality and the ability to pause and issue commands. Also I think some of the 'Jagged Alliance' games utilized this mechanic.
For me though the issue with this game I had most trouble dealing with was the length. Mind you I played it in 2 hour stints but by the time I got to the end I felt like it had overstayed its welcome. I had long ago seen the last of the amazing hero origin cut scenes and by the time I stopped felt like the game had become rather drawn out. With missions made needlessly long for the sake of tacking on time played.  That being said I could easily still recommend this title to anyone who is a lover of silver age comic books. Its like the first Freedom Force game but better. It's the kind of thing a comic book fan cannot help but smile at over and over again. so considering how cheap it usually is I firmly suggest giving it a try.

A game with a good premise.  Prays on the fear of being alone with a bunch of freaky animatronic robots.  On top of that, you have a limited amount of power to use in order to keep track of them, to keep doors shut, or to turn on the lights.  When you run out of power, bad things tend to happen, though sometimes good things happen, like beating night 6 as someone with a big smile plays you a pleasant tune.  The game gives you minimal instructions on how it actually works, such as what the lights do, but does give you hints about what you should be doing.  Once you figure out a solid strategy, things mostly fall into place, though sometimes a good friend still slips into the room.  The game isn't that long, took me around 2 to 2 1/2 hours to finish all 6 nights plus play a custom game.  Got a couple of frights out of it.  Also, listening to Bebop scream like a girl as he was murdered on night 3 was worth the price of a little over a buck.  Overall, 7.5/10

This game will get you, it is not a matter of if, only a matter of when....
Day 27.
Close call. My starvation had gotten the better of me, I needed food soon or else I would pass out and possibly never wake up. I had taken residence in a lake side cottage some 15 days before, it had, at the time, been a god-send. Food, water, shelter, and plenty of chairs and shelves to break down for wood, I had made it. Now the food was all but gone, my cottage ran cold most nights, and without the ability to distill water (lack of feul; aka chairs) I had a verrrrrry serious risk of disease from drinking the water that, at this point, probably contained some kind of stool. I was nearing the breaking point, but I had just enough supplies to go reset my traps and possibly live throughout the night to try and catch something, it was all or nothing. I wake up on the 27th day, and the wind is howling, I look outside and it seems as though I am staring at a blank peice of paper. Great. Here I go to die.
I decide that I would rather die frozen in the ground somewhere ( I could be one of those people in someone elses game perhaps) than starving to death in a shadowed cottage so, I take my chances. The long trek begins, I set off across the frozen lake to the spot I had designated for traps when I had first arrived in the area. I am bundled up with the best clothes that frozen people can buy (very comforting when you are trying not to freeze), and set off, resiliently into the morning (or night, honestly couldnt tell it was such a storm). I make my way slowly through the howling winds, unable to detect any landmarks on the edge of the lake, and am effectively, lost. Finally I spot a small island that I had seen days earlier in the middle of the large lake. Great, I am halfway there. I was numb before I left the cottage in the first place so, at this point, I would be lucky to be able to count my toes on one hand (depending if I had fingers either). Finally I limp through the cold to an outcropping off the lake bed, and I see three rabbits frolicking through what must be 2 feet of snow that has fallen within a few hours. Three small, little, tasty, little, small rabbits. In a fit of anger I run after them, I would just eat them raw if need be, im sure cold raw rabbit meat is super tasty anyways. I run out of breath in about two seconds and am forced into the realization that I still need to set my traps, and that this stranded experience has neither turned me into Usain Bolt, or an experienced, versatile hunter. I set three traps, one for each rabbit I was so longengly looking after, and set off back across the frozen tundra. This was a short lived task however, I hear a howl through the wind, but a different kind of howl. This was not wind, this was the hunting pack. I had seen them skulking around the lakes beaches a few days before, and now they had found their chance to take on little old feeble me. All I could think was, "I walk through the shadow of the valley of death, and I am definitely F****** afraid of this evil". I took off, well as fast as my ice blocks of legs could carry me. I had the general direction of a cottage I had seen a few days ago eariler, in relations to my trapping ground. Luckily for me this hunch was correct, I came upon a small abandoned house with the wolf pack in hot pursuit, and slammed the door in their face. Great! Then I realized that I had a grand total of an axe and a flair in my pack, as well as some currently useless medical supplies and about half a slatine cracker. You better believe that was the best damn cracker I have ever had. I had to wait, the wolves were at the door and there was no where to go. I contemplated my options: 1) Die inside 2) Die outside 3) Chop off arm, give to wolves, then die.
Well I went with numbero dos on this one. I ran outside, straight into a wolf. He was one of the ones from the pack but had strayed a bit from them and was more or less on his own. He saw me as easy prey and charged. I fumbled around in my pack for the last flare I had found and chucked it at him right as he was bearing down upon me. Smacked him across the top of the head and scared him off, only he wasnt the only one. Guess who was back. His friends. Well now I am a nice refrigerated raw meat sack to them, and I just♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off one of their buddies, so they were slightly aggravated. I took off across the lake (I could kind of see now, the blizzard had gone from blank page white to more of a constant blast of confetti to the face) and headed for the woods to try and lose them. They slowed but didnt stop giving chase and forced me to look for a quick fix to the situation. As I wheezed my way through the forest, being stalked by the two wolves that were still interested in this easy meal, I finally came upon train tracks of some kind. I saw a derailed train covered in feet of snow and decided to hunker down in that as night was falling. By the time I had pulled myself up and into the train car it was pitch black and I couldnt see my hand in front of my face. I rolled out my sleeping bag that I had luckily brought with me and tried to not freeze to death in the process of sleeping. I woke up at the crack of dawn, essentially dead in every way but spirit. My core body temperature was probably colder than the ice I had slept on. I was, as always, close to starvation and exceedingly dehydrated. I decide to look around this abandoned train car and see if I can somehow survive this disasterous situation.
There it is. The one thing that could have saved me. I had on and off been looking for this singular item since the game began. It is the rifle (now for people who have never played this game, the moment you find a firearm is about on par with winning the super bowl 15 times in a row, 20 if it has ammo) and guess what, it has ammo. (I can see the super bowl rings now....) I feel a type of elation that is impossible to describe. I MAY JUST LIVE. Now comes the trying to live part. I make my way down the tracks as I remember my cottage being relatively close to a set of tracks, whethere these were those, I was completely unsure, but its all I had to go on. Then the second best feeling ever in this game, I saw a red flag flapping against the white nothingness of the crisp air and snow, the flag that adorned the top, of a small shadowed cabin I called home.
10/10 You feel as though you are the character (minus the frostbite)

The Long Dark is a terrifying hardcore survival experience like no other that i know of.  The loot and accessable houses changes each time you die making it all the more challanging to know "the good spots" for sure.  If you are not afraid of wolves already this game will teach to be afraid....be VERY afraid.  They will hunt you down for miles sometimes and there might be a little secret hiding in a certain house involving a wolf so keep your eyes peeled and a flare handy ;).  The weather is also a hard aspect because you might be all geared up for a short trip to another town or something and when you open the door BAM complete whiteout and you have to stay inside draining your hard earned food only to have to go out at night when the weather stops.  Later on you might find a rifle but to your dismay you find out that there can be only so many rounds in this frozen wasteland and when they are gone the rifle is useless AND if you happen to use the rifle in a pinch and manage to miss the target it might jam and well if your not prepared you'll get maulled by a bear or a wolf.  The wildlife doesnt always run away from you brandishing your flare like a maniac.  Since it is freezing cold and your carrying heavy gear you have a high chance of injuring yourself from a fall.
In conclusion buy this game if your at all interested in experiencing these things and if you don't like the above mentioned things i wouldn't buy the game at full price because you won't get much out of it at it's current state.

TLDR: Bioshock is an action/horror shooter taking place in an underwater steampunk city. Unravel the mystery of Rapture’s fall while fighting off demented “splicers.”
The story of Bioshock is told mostly through recordings that you find laying around the levels kind of like voice diaries from a dozen different people. You play an unnamed plane crash survivor who enters a mysterious lighthouse somewhere in the Atlantic Ocean. Inside you find passage into the underwater city of Rapture, where captain of industry Andrew Ryan has built a society based on pure capitalism (like the utopia from Ayn Rand’s Atlas Shrugged). The smartest people in the world have been brought to a single place where they’re free to work without government, religion, or censor watching over them. Piece by piece you find out what turned this “paradise” into the deserted house of horrors that you now need to fight through. Spoiler alert, its’ caused by unregulated genetic manipulation through gene splicing.
Bioshock is a first person shooter using mostly weapons from the game’s time period (1950’s – 1960’s). This means instead of modern assault rifles, you’ll make due with mostly your double barreled shotgun and tommy gun. The game’s gimmick though, are the “plasmids” that you find and buy throughout your adventure. Plasmids are injections of genetic material that give the user super powers such as shooting fire, lightning, etc. You also find a bunch of “gene-tonics” which give you passive bonuses such as reduced damage and improved healing. So, like in an RPG, you get stronger throughout the game by gathering genetic enhancements. There’s also a research camera system where you can take pictures of enemies to gain upgrades through study. It’s kind of tiresome but you get some very useful bonuses.
As mentioned before your enemies in the game are mostly splicers, people who have become addicted to gene splicing and gone insane. Most of them don’t have special powers from the splicing so maybe they didn’t get any of the good stuff. If you’re familiar with imagery from the game though, you’ll recognize the “Big Daddy” and the “Little Sisters” who are the signature characters of the game. The Big Daddies are mini-bosses found in multiple areas throughout Rapture and not only are they tough, they’re surprisingly fast in their armored diving gear. The Big Daddies mostly leave you alone unless you attack, so you don’t really have to fight them if you want to play through the game without buying many plasmids, but you really should or you’re missing out.
Pros:
+The game has an awesome story despite the fact that you’re alone most of the time. The voice recordings, taunting from Andrew Ryan, and guidance from a couple of Rapture survivors are very well done and build a world that you feel like you’re really experiencing.
+There’s a lot going on in Rapture, from hacking mini games, fighting a large variety of enemies, and utilizing a large variety of weapons/ammo types (probably more than you’ll ever use).
Cons:
-There’s an issue (bug) with changing the game’s resolution that causes game crashes. However, once you’ve dealt with it, it ceases to be a problem. (Use alt+enter to go into windowed mode, then change the resolution and alt+enter again to go back to full screen mode).
-I mentioned earlier that the game has a lot of variety, and quite frankly you’ll notice by the end of the game that you probably haven’t used most of the plasmids or weapon ammo types. This is because you’re probably going to stick with the “good stuff” like fireballs and lightning. The other plasmids can mix things up, but when you want to get things done, stick with what works on almost everyone.
Overall Bioshock is an amazing game that spawned an awesome franchise that everyone should play. Yes, it’s a little scarier than you might expect because of the desolate and deserted atmosphere, but don’t let that turn you off. Give the game a try and you won’t regret it.   - 9/10

Red Orchestra 2: Heroes of Stalingrad was. and still is, one of the most realistic first person shooters i have ever come across. If you ever wanted to know what it would be like to be thrown into the bloodiest battle of the second world war, then look no further because this is the game your looking for.
Now enough with the pleasentries, lets get down to the game. It is a first person shooter that challenges players to their very core, even on its easiest levels. Players are forced to think tactically, and make every shot count. This isn't an arnold schwartznegger style game like Call of Duty where you are a lone immortal soldier running around hailing bullets to dominate the battlefield, this game requires teamwork and skill to defeat your opponents, because if the enemy has you in their crosshairs, you will not live to tell the tale. It is a game that teaches you to be humble, to accept that there are times that you will die in the battlefield, but unlike real life, you can respawn and carry on the fight and with every fight there is a lesson to be learnt.
The Singleplayer portrays both sides of the story, and the German Campaign provides you with the tutorials needed to play the game. Step by step you are emmersed into the Battle of Stalingrad, and by the end you feel experienced enough to stand on your feet for the Soviet Campaign. Weapons are based on a class system, however in the single player they are not generous with them. If you prefer a bolt action rifle to a semi-automatic rifle, or a GPMG over a submachine gun, tough luck. because the game decides this for you. Only in multiplayer do you really have the option of choosing classes, and allowing you to play to your strengths. In singleplayer there are only two times you will spawn, at the beggining of the match, or if you fail to hold an objective. The other times when or if you die you are zoomed in on a soldier already in the battlefield, and you have no say what soldier you can zoom into. This means you could start as a rifleman, fall into trouble and die, and become a machine gunner. This may not sound so bad, unless you take into fact that most of the AI on your team have the minds of headless chickens, often running into enemy fire, or even in front of your weapon causing you to shoot your own men. Needless to say, the Singleplayer can be a very frustrating experience filled with problems, but i would recommend playing it atleast once just to get the feel of different weapons at your own pace.
Now Multiplayer is a completly different story, this is the way the game was meant to be played. You have choice over your classes and ranks are based of teamwork and weapon skills, each of the weapons and classes also have their own ranking system which provides you with rewards such as weapon upgrades and even enemy weapons. The maps that are available to you are from the singleplayer with a variety of modes: Territory, Firefight and Campaign. Territory is the classic mode of game, where you are tasked with holding or seizing various parts of the map, if the attacking team takes all of the points, they win, so for Battlefield fans who want a  tougher game, this is worth looking into. Firefight is simply a team deathmatch, but you have to be on your toes, because the enemy accuracy is hightened. Campaign is a long winded version of territory, so if you have places to be, don't bother with campaign because you might be there a while. Its like a tournament, every match you win, you take or hold a peice of territory, if you capture all the territories you win.
Rising Storm is an expansion that brings the Americans and the Japanese into the game, there is no singleplayer mode for Rising Storm but you don't really need one. The maps are as good as the Stalingrad ones and they do a great job in bringing out the claustrophobia and paranoia that those frontlines presented. The only downside is that there isn't that much difference between the two games, if anything it feels more like a proffesional mod that was placed on the original Red Orchestra 2 game. Despite that, its a great experience, and a great addition to the game if you feel you've done enough with the eastern front and want to try somthing new.
In short, one of the greatest things about this game is that it doesn't try to be a crowd pleaser or a populist game like most of the other first person shooters, it provides a particular experience for those willing to step up to the plate. This game is a rare gem, and even if difficult shooters arn't your style, it still reccomend you give it a try. I give the game a 9/10 overall.

First of all: I was so excited about this game when I saw the first screenshots of it, I never had so much needs! I hoped for an intense horror game, but the dissapointment came way too soon...
The positive stuff:
- graphics and atmosphere: Such nice atmosphere which enthralls you within a few minutes of playing
- the idea and the story
- the rides - interesting stuff happens if you ride a attraction
- well.. that was it....
Now the points I really missed in this game and which could've been done way better, because the potential is huge!
- Way too short (I played for an hour) - as above said, there are so many points you could easily put in the game, but it seems the makers went a bit lazy (No offense)
- too less attractions, I thought this place would be huge like the biggest amusement parks in the world, but it only has 4 rides and the horror house - which you can not really call a 'horror' house...
- no scary moments: I hoped for the Chipmunk to hunt you along the park or other creepy things, but sadly - I had ONE jumpscare, that was all.. very meager...
- too less interacting for my opinion... I wished for more extras, like... more interactive huts to inspect, with jumpscares when you look through the window of them, or the mirrors in the horror house, I expected someone to stand behind me. Or the part on the rollercoaster, with the hospital scenes. They were pretty awesome, but still you could've confused the players by doing a stop and let them creep around the hospital for getting more informations about the story and what happened there or something like that! There are so much ideas you could use...
Final words: I am disspointed. Like I said, there's so damn much not used potential, it's really upsetting... For me there's nothing scary in it, I wouldn't call it a horror game at all. But I like it anyways, just because of the amazing graphics, the location and the very nicely done atmosphere!

Honestly, this was mind-blowingly disappointing. It's like they took that initial part of the main game, the part where hardly anything happens, and were like "Yes. This is fun. These experiences are fun to our fellow humans, of which we also are part of the same species." and tried to make an expansion out of that.
Opposing Force cut the Gluon Gun (and a couple of others) for story reasons, but made up for it with a bunch of cool♥♥♥♥♥♥like the Displacer Cannon, LMG, Shock Grub, and AWP. This just cuts out the cool guns completely, so get ready to have TONS OF HUMAN FUN EMOTIONS with just the pistols, assault rifle, and shotgun! Even the rocket launcher is relegated to a single sequence where you fight a stationary tank with so much cover between you and it you have no fear of getting hit.
Likewise, where Op For gave us some neat (albeit a bit bullet spongey) new enemies, Blue Shift is fine with going "YOU LIKE JUST FIGHTING MARINES, VORTIGAUNTS, AND HEADCRABS, RIGHT?" and having nearly every combat encounter be either 3-4 marines, 2-3 vortigaunts, or a single headcrab. You fight maybe four of the bug-gun dudes and each time they're 100+ feet away with maybe a couple Vorts backing them up so it's always a walk in the park. Likewise, you only fight four of the flying dudes who shoot the yellow orbs, and once again they're placed in incredibly easy encounters. The screaming dog things, tentacled mouthed animals, and zombies all get used very regularly on their own and to be perfectly honest all three of those enemy types are so utterly braindead-easy to kill that I'd stress even calling those "fights".
Like goddamn, you're on Xen for a solid 1/3rd of the game, but half the time you're there you're just crawling through alien airvents shooting lone headcrab after lone headcrab. Every encounter is utterly banal and the lack of any sort of challenge is honestly a bit insulting after the "oh god i only have 50 hp and there's 6 of them" thrillride that was Op Force.
Also, the final mission is complete ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. You stand in a room with a button, waiting for a bar to go up, then you press the button when the bar is full to open a teleporter. It takes nearly a minute for the bar to fill up and there's no enemies for almost the entire time. At the very beginning you have to run out to turn a wheel and two scream-dogs spawn, but as said they're a pathetically easy enemy. Between the third and fourth button presses some marines VERY SLOWLY AND VERY LOUDLY cut open a door that's up a ladder and around a corner, in a position where they're of zero threat until you either willingly engage them or make a break for the teleporter, and in either of those cases they're incredibly easy to deal with. The main game and OpFor both had, y'know, final bosses? Story climaxes that ramp up the tension and make you feel like you've accomplished something? By comparison this has about as much wow-factor as watching a 10MB file finish downloading.
The ending is just "uh-oh the teleporter almost messed up! Oh wait, it didn't, we're all good, let's drive to Mcdonalds!" It's like that really cool scene during the intro in Half-Life 2 where Gordon tries to teleport and it goes all wonky and sends him to a bunch of different places, eventually landing him in the wrong place, except this time it's boring and doesn't amount to anything. The rest of the "story" is likewise devoid of any meaningful events.
Also it's hella short. That 2.7 hours includes the overly-long optional tutorial, plus around 20-30 minutes of time I was alt-tabbed or otherwise distracted. OpFor was for comparison something like 4-4.5 hours for the same price.
Half Life 1 is a game with plenty of problems, but at the end of the day it's still an above-average game that set a huge landmark for storytelling in FPSes.
Blue Shift is a harrowing what-if reimagining of if HL1 based its entire core design philosophy around trying to replicate those problems as much as possible, and if you're honestly that desperate for more HL1 content, there's loads of user-made maps that are far more worth your time than this trash heap.

TLDR: Bioshock is an action/horror shooter taking place in an underwater steampunk city. Unravel the mystery of Rapture’s fall while fighting off demented “splicers.”
The story of Bioshock is told mostly through recordings that you find laying around the levels kind of like voice diaries from a dozen different people. You play an unnamed plane crash survivor who enters a mysterious lighthouse somewhere in the Atlantic Ocean. Inside you find passage into the underwater city of Rapture, where captain of industry Andrew Ryan has built a society based on pure capitalism (like the utopia from Ayn Rand’s Atlas Shrugged). The smartest people in the world have been brought to a single place where they’re free to work without government, religion, or censor watching over them. Piece by piece you find out what turned this “paradise” into the deserted house of horrors that you now need to fight through. Spoiler alert, its’ caused by unregulated genetic manipulation through gene splicing.
Bioshock is a first person shooter using mostly weapons from the game’s time period (1950’s – 1960’s). This means instead of modern assault rifles, you’ll make due with mostly your double barreled shotgun and tommy gun. The game’s gimmick though, are the “plasmids” that you find and buy throughout your adventure. Plasmids are injections of genetic material that give the user super powers such as shooting fire, lightning, etc. You also find a bunch of “gene-tonics” which give you passive bonuses such as reduced damage and improved healing. So, like in an RPG, you get stronger throughout the game by gathering genetic enhancements. There’s also a research camera system where you can take pictures of enemies to gain upgrades through study. It’s kind of tiresome but you get some very useful bonuses.
As mentioned before your enemies in the game are mostly splicers, people who have become addicted to gene splicing and gone insane. Most of them don’t have special powers from the splicing so maybe they didn’t get any of the good stuff. If you’re familiar with imagery from the game though, you’ll recognize the “Big Daddy” and the “Little Sisters” who are the signature characters of the game. The Big Daddies are mini-bosses found in multiple areas throughout Rapture and not only are they tough, they’re surprisingly fast in their armored diving gear. The Big Daddies mostly leave you alone unless you attack, so you don’t really have to fight them if you want to play through the game without buying many plasmids, but you really should or you’re missing out.
Pros:
+The game has an awesome story despite the fact that you’re alone most of the time. The voice recordings, taunting from Andrew Ryan, and guidance from a couple of Rapture survivors are very well done and build a world that you feel like you’re really experiencing.
+There’s a lot going on in Rapture, from hacking mini games, fighting a large variety of enemies, and utilizing a large variety of weapons/ammo types (probably more than you’ll ever use).
Cons:
-There’s an issue (bug) with changing the game’s resolution that causes game crashes. However, once you’ve dealt with it, it ceases to be a problem. (Use alt+enter to go into windowed mode, then change the resolution and alt+enter again to go back to full screen mode).
-I mentioned earlier that the game has a lot of variety, and quite frankly you’ll notice by the end of the game that you probably haven’t used most of the plasmids or weapon ammo types. This is because you’re probably going to stick with the “good stuff” like fireballs and lightning. The other plasmids can mix things up, but when you want to get things done, stick with what works on almost everyone.
Overall Bioshock is an amazing game that spawned an awesome franchise that everyone should play. Yes, it’s a little scarier than you might expect because of the desolate and deserted atmosphere, but don’t let that turn you off. Give the game a try and you won’t regret it.   - 9/10

In the year 1997, the feces hit the radiator fan. A racing game so vulgar, crass and violent was released that even the pope* lost his shiz. Carmageddon had arrived in full force, and the gaming world would never be the same. Contestants would strap themselves into motorized death machines, and try to smash the crap out of their opponents while flattening as many pedestrians as possible along the way. Reaching the finish line was optional. Back in the day all this gratuitous gore was shocking and memorable, but this day and age it doesn't carry quite so much in the shock factor department, though it's still a decent way to spend an afternoon.
Thankfully the newest reincarnation of the franchise, Carmageddon Max Damage, has brought things forward into modern times. From the shiny chrome-plated graphics to the bone-crunching sound effects, they've provided the full package here. Also much improved is the game's control system, which quite frankly was an utter crapshow on the older PC games in the series. Everything that made the franchise fan-[CENSORED]-tastic has returned full force, and then some. The classic Carmageddon gameplay mode is here, where you can take the checkpoints, smash all your foes, or tediously hunt down each and every pedestrian to win (blah!).
That's not to say everything is popping up smelling like roses. The load times in particular reek like bull puckey, sometimes taking several minutes to load up the carnage. The framerate tanked a few times on me as well, but with that much highly-detail gut-spewing destruction onscreen at once it's to be expected that the game engine might crap it's pants occasionally. But despite a couple of dingleberries in the mix, this hot mess still comes out on top. It's saving grace is the fact that on the market right now there's just nothing like it at all, and that fact makes it a gleaming polished turd bobbing in a sea of boring cookie-cutter sequelitis diarrhea. So go for it, blow your load (of cash) all over Carmageddon: Max Damage. Just make sure to wash your hands when you're done.
*Greg Pope, MP

I gave Carmageddon: Reincarnation a negative review.  I really didn't want to, but there were some issues in the game that irked me, and the game didn't QUITE feel ready yet.  Fortunately, with the release of Max Damage, the game feels a lot better.  I can safely say now that THIS is indeed the modern Carmageddon I had been wanting to see.
There are still flaws, but none of these games are really perfect.  While the performance has improved, there still seems to be some kind of memory leak that can cause slow down, stuttering, and potentially crashing.  Some of the cars seem to have a real problem with brakes, especially when you've upgraded the engine to tier 4 or 5.  It's like the brakes don't scale with the new power.  There's a few other random bugs, the the music sometimes randomly getting very loud, and the fact that the police APC seems to be missing as a playable car this time out.  [Edit: It appears the APC is indeed playable, but requires fully completing the game.]
On the positives, they added the ability to stun AI drivers with a good hit.  It's such a small change, but it goes a long way.  The game's visually a little more polished, in areas like loading screens etc.  The cars added in are pretty good, and I love that we finally have working trailers.  (Perhaps we can finally see Tanka in its original form?  Though it's not in the game at the moment.)  I absolutely adore one of the new, desert themes arenas.
Some of the end-game vehicles are, of course, fairly over-powered.  But that's always been the case with Carmageddon. TL;DR at the bottom-
I don't even know where to begin with this game.
I'd heard about it a while back and I saw it, thought it looked kinda interesting, and then never bothered picking it up. My friend recently gifted it to me and if I could I would have been willing to spend up to $45 or so for the experience this game tosses at you. The only thing I can say now is that I regret not picking it up sooner. It just hits me in such a way that I can't explain. Everytime I'm walking slowly down a road and there's nothing but cars to the side and burnt houses around, and that ♥♥♥♥ing guitar picks up I just get so into it and feel like I'm actually a survivor.
The Long Dark is a gem among early access games and deserves so much attention. I knew this as soon as I'd put in a good hour. Let me start off by saying that the immersion that this game delivers is phenomenal. It has a great tone and world design to be used for story telling. While the game offers no tutorial and this can be a positive or negative thing, I personally loved it. All it did was make me genuinely want to learn about the game and the world itself more, and as I did, I felt myself get better at it and feel more confident about surviving. The longest time I've survived so far on a character is 30 days counting and there's been numerous points throughout that timespan in which I thought I was going to die and got anxious doing something because I genuinely felt like I was the person wandering through the world. Each time I spotted a bear in the distance or a pack of wolves, I felt like they were a genuine threat and therefore considered my options. Do I try to sneak around them? Do I head in the opposite direction? Do I have ammo or a weapon to fend them off just in case? This doesn't even just count with the wildlife but the environment as well which I cannot stress just how important in a survival game. Every time I saw a side road leading off of the main highway I seriously considered my options. Did I have enough food and water with me in case it's a dead end? Do I have enough daylight left to make it back to the main road if there's nothing down this way? Will I have enough firewood and tinder to create a fire if need be? When I would be staying in a cabin for the day due to a blizzard, I would genuinely consider my options then as well and think to myself if I had enough food to survive the night before I would be able to scavenge for more supplies? The game pushes you to think about these options in a way that I've never felt another survival game do before.
The game does an incredible job at atmosphere and aesthetic and is downright GORGEOUS from every early sunrise and darkening sunset to each howling blizzard or each bright sunny day. The more you're willing to immerse yourself into believing you're truly surviving in the world, the better job it does at delivering a truly special experience. There was a point in which I'd found a safe and when I was trying to crack the code, I actually leaned in on my monitor as though I'd be able to hear the clicks better without realizing it. When there's a blizzard in the game and all you can hear is lonesome ambient guitar music playing and the wind howling in you ear, you feel genuinely alone and feel cold. When you enter a cabin and all you can hear is the wind beating against the house and the creaks of wood echoing, it creates a sense of fear and paranoia because you know that there were people who are probably long dead that used to live here. When you’re walking through a cave and all you can hear is the vast echoes of your footsteps against stone and the hiss of your flare, you feel genuinely cautious.The fact that the game is able to pull this off is absolutely stunning. And above all, you genuinely
like you're a survivor in this new world. You begin to grow attached to your character and genuinely care for them and begin to wonder if you can truly survive the wilderness. The game does an excellent job at small little stories you can pick up on when you're not expecting it. For example you can find a cave in which there's a small campfire with food beside it, or you can be walking through the woods and find a frozen corpse of a man with an axe next to a deer corpse, insisting he died of hypothermia while trying to get food. It's all of these little things that come together that truly help create an enjoyable experience and make me want to get out there and explore the world in front of me. When you walk through a town you begin to really have thoughts of, "I wonder what happened to the people that lived here. I wonder what the story of the people who made it out is" and it's like that for nearly every place.
The only two downsides to this game for me at least are there's been few bugs in which I would climb a rock and randomly sprain my ankles or wrists for no reason and it's pretty immersion breaking. And secondly, there's no randomly generated maps and all loot spawns are always the same regardless of if you were to make a new character or not. If they were to add randomly generated loot and maps, I could play this game for literal hundreds of hours not to say I already plan to, but it would definitely help with the game in the long run and keep me coming back to it.
In short, this game is truly something special for the person that wants to immerse themselves in a world where they feel like they're truly a survivor in the wilderness with nothing but their own decisions on what's best to help you survive the long dark.

If, like me, you like the basic genre of "walking simulators" and if, like me, you're a player of The Secret World, this is a perfect companion piece to the story of Solomon Island and of course Atlantic Island Park in contemporary times.
I've finished the game in about two hours which seems to be standard length for this genre (IIRC I finished Gone Home in a similar time), but might be on the longer side, since I really do try to explore if a game styles itself exploratory. The Park is rather linear in that regard, so there is little exploring of hidden places, but plenty of exploring of scenes, especially in the later parts.
There are a lot, and I mean a lot, of allusions to The Secret World, most of which are not pertienent to the story here, but a nice little touch for Secret Warriors. Beware, if you haven't finished New England in TSW there may be slight spoilers here, depending on how much you pick up and can draw the right conclusions.
The atmosphere can be nothing short of terrifying if you're able to immerse yourself. There is some excellent sound design helping this and some of the scenery and set pieces are sufficiently creepy, even if the're not really innovative. The old standbys (creepy dolls, flocks of birds, etc.) work for a reason.
I don't want to go into story, since in my opinion it's mostly a matter of personal taste if you like a story or not, but let it be said, as mentioned before, that it fits very well within the universe of The Secret World, not only because of atmosphere and "shout outs", but also because of theme.
In the end, I recommend The Park with the caveats mentioned in my review. For me personally it was fully worth the 10 € I paid.

This review is written as of May 10th, 2016. It's my first review.
The Long Dark is a single-player survival experience that takes place in a cold wasteland following a "geomagnetic disaster". You're cold and alone, and the game truly captures that. It has fantastic visuals, a lovely soundtrack and ambience that will make you think you're really struggling for life in this doomed world.
You scavenge for food, clothing, fuel and hunting gear. You have to pry open lockers and crack open safes for the next meal. If you've run the house dry, you plan your trek to the next one between the snow storms and the migrating wolf packs that are hungry and hostile. If you're out of food, you may have to try to hunt your own, but be careful; the wolves may either take your prey, or choose you for their next meal.
The game as it currently stands has an open-world sandbox that will let you choose your own "adventure", of sorts. A story mode is in the works, but by and large, many of the players (myself included) are simply in love with the sandbox mode. I've already spent over 400 hours playing this game before it has even launched. I've definitely gotten my money's worth.
I highly recommend this game. The developers appear to be on top of the game, interacting with the community and listening to their feedback, as well as taking care of major issues with hotfixes as soon as possible. I don't think this game will fall by the wayside like so many others have before it.
Good luck and, if you buy the game, try not to die!

Red Orchestra 2: Heroes of Stalingrad was. and still is, one of the most realistic first person shooters i have ever come across. If you ever wanted to know what it would be like to be thrown into the bloodiest battle of the second world war, then look no further because this is the game your looking for.
Now enough with the pleasentries, lets get down to the game. It is a first person shooter that challenges players to their very core, even on its easiest levels. Players are forced to think tactically, and make every shot count. This isn't an arnold schwartznegger style game like Call of Duty where you are a lone immortal soldier running around hailing bullets to dominate the battlefield, this game requires teamwork and skill to defeat your opponents, because if the enemy has you in their crosshairs, you will not live to tell the tale. It is a game that teaches you to be humble, to accept that there are times that you will die in the battlefield, but unlike real life, you can respawn and carry on the fight and with every fight there is a lesson to be learnt.
The Singleplayer portrays both sides of the story, and the German Campaign provides you with the tutorials needed to play the game. Step by step you are emmersed into the Battle of Stalingrad, and by the end you feel experienced enough to stand on your feet for the Soviet Campaign. Weapons are based on a class system, however in the single player they are not generous with them. If you prefer a bolt action rifle to a semi-automatic rifle, or a GPMG over a submachine gun, tough luck. because the game decides this for you. Only in multiplayer do you really have the option of choosing classes, and allowing you to play to your strengths. In singleplayer there are only two times you will spawn, at the beggining of the match, or if you fail to hold an objective. The other times when or if you die you are zoomed in on a soldier already in the battlefield, and you have no say what soldier you can zoom into. This means you could start as a rifleman, fall into trouble and die, and become a machine gunner. This may not sound so bad, unless you take into fact that most of the AI on your team have the minds of headless chickens, often running into enemy fire, or even in front of your weapon causing you to shoot your own men. Needless to say, the Singleplayer can be a very frustrating experience filled with problems, but i would recommend playing it atleast once just to get the feel of different weapons at your own pace.
Now Multiplayer is a completly different story, this is the way the game was meant to be played. You have choice over your classes and ranks are based of teamwork and weapon skills, each of the weapons and classes also have their own ranking system which provides you with rewards such as weapon upgrades and even enemy weapons. The maps that are available to you are from the singleplayer with a variety of modes: Territory, Firefight and Campaign. Territory is the classic mode of game, where you are tasked with holding or seizing various parts of the map, if the attacking team takes all of the points, they win, so for Battlefield fans who want a  tougher game, this is worth looking into. Firefight is simply a team deathmatch, but you have to be on your toes, because the enemy accuracy is hightened. Campaign is a long winded version of territory, so if you have places to be, don't bother with campaign because you might be there a while. Its like a tournament, every match you win, you take or hold a peice of territory, if you capture all the territories you win.
Rising Storm is an expansion that brings the Americans and the Japanese into the game, there is no singleplayer mode for Rising Storm but you don't really need one. The maps are as good as the Stalingrad ones and they do a great job in bringing out the claustrophobia and paranoia that those frontlines presented. The only downside is that there isn't that much difference between the two games, if anything it feels more like a proffesional mod that was placed on the original Red Orchestra 2 game. Despite that, its a great experience, and a great addition to the game if you feel you've done enough with the eastern front and want to try somthing new.
In short, one of the greatest things about this game is that it doesn't try to be a crowd pleaser or a populist game like most of the other first person shooters, it provides a particular experience for those willing to step up to the plate. This game is a rare gem, and even if difficult shooters arn't your style, it still reccomend you give it a try. I give the game a 9/10 overall.
