Rituals is a short point-and-click adventure game/walking-simulator with a smattering of simple puzzles and a very shallow, almost non-existent story.  I read every piece of text and interacted with every object in the world, yet I still have no idea what the story was supposed to be about.  All I got was some mysticism about triangular places indicating the Earth may be alive, conscious, or have some kind of power.  The company you work for seems to be secretly trying to harness this power. There are two endings, both of which are completely unrelated to the progress you make throughout the game until the final scene.
Rituals isn't really a terrible game, but it certainly isn't good either.  All of the puzzles are self-contained in small environments and nearly all of them simply have you grab one or more items, combine them together, and bring them somewhere else.  The movement control arrows constantly obscure your view, and by locking them to a specific orientation, Rituals forces you to waste time moving the camera around so you can see the arrows before clicking on them.
Even though it takes less than 1 hour to see everything, the game overstays its welcome.

The is - easily! - the single most beautiful game I've ever seen in my entire life. Beautiful, hand-drawn animations make playing "Cuphead" an awesome experience, and the fluid, surrealistic imagery is like something straight out of classic cartoons such as  Fleischer Studios' "Bimbo's Initiation" (1931). Actually, the game is not that dissimilar from said movie, since most everything in the game is always changing shape and form and reality itself is constantly attempting to murder you!
An almost incredible amount of labour has been expended to make literally every frame in every animation look *exactly* like the visual style of 1930's cartoons. Visual tears and distortions have been added to make all animations look "dated". All backgrounds are either watercolor or rotoscoped (google). Snaps, scratches and audio pops have also been added to the soundtrack of period-specific jazz tunes, in order to make them sound "dated" and aged just like in old  Fleischer movies. Even the lingo spoken between the in-game characters is identical to how it sounds in old  Fleischer cartoons. All in all, the visuals, audio and atmosphere are all simpy breathtaking. Since I am a big fan of e.g. Fleischer's old "Popeye" cartoons, my jaw literally dropped the first time I played this game!
Gameplay-wise, this game is both a fun and deeply frustrating experience (in a good way!), in pretty much the same way that the "Dark Souls" series of games is one. In this game, you're faced with a constant barrage of gigantic, surrealistic monsters (and the occasional run-and-gun level), all of which have to be painstakingly defeated, one by one, in order to steal their souls and present them to the Devil instead of your own. Does that sound like a surreal, twisted backstory to the game? You bet! Is it any fun? Oh HELL yeah!!!
"Trial and error" is key in this game, as you frequently have to try the same battle over and over again until you have the patterns of each boss memorized. You get only 3 hitpoints (you can buy more in-game, but that makes your attacks weaker!). The sheer triumph you feel once you *DO* eventually beat a boss far outweighs the frustration you feel as you're still learning, however. It's also important to note that, even in the midst of a heated battle to the death, it is impossible not to admire the marvellous, hand-drawn animations and to marvel over the sheer passion that went into creating this beautiful game!
I very highly recommend this game to every player out there! I would also like to add that I would totally pay money to see a genuine "Cuphead" series of cartoons at some point!
Highly, highly recommended!

So the last time I played Carmageddon, I played the release version of Reincarnation, and while it was okay, it was wracked with performance issues that, at best, hampered playability, and at worst, rendered the game unplayable.
Since the game had everything that made Carmageddon Carmageddon, I lamented the missed opportunity, wrote a somewhat disappointed review, and erased it from my hard drive.
But then, the unexpected happened. The devs commented on my review, for some reason, politely letting me know that the game had been updated since I posted the review, and said I should try it out again. So I did. I downloaded it and, lo and behold, it was far more functional.
This was a delightful little gesture on their behalf, but there was something about it that stopped me from investing myself in it, I can't recall exactly what, but I think that it was a matter of not all the problems being ironed out. So after a while I deleted it once again.
Now, more than a year later (I think), I find out that they've rereleased the game as 'Max Damage', and offered it free to those that owned Reincarnation. So I downloaded it a THIRD time, and I need to tell you that this is what I was hoping for all along. The game runs smooth as silk, and is Carmageddon to the core. Not only are the graphics improved and optimised better, but I feel like there's additional maps that weren't here before, but it could be that maybe I didn't play for long enough in the first place.
In any case, this feels like a Christmas present from the devs. Sure, it's better to get things right *before* asking for cash, but the second best thing is to spend the huge amount of time and effort that must have gone into getting this to where it is, and then ask for no money for it from those that bought the last iteration. I suppose it's a symptom of the landscape that I'm feeling gratitude simply for not being charged twice for what is essentially the same product, but credit where credit's due, they could've asked for more cash and gotten away with it. Instead, they proved themselves to be good guys that also happened to release a great Carmageddon game.
Personal relations aside, the game is Carmageddon. Brutal, hilarious, insane, frantic, and puerile. I find myself laughing out loud regularly, usually as some poor pedestrian gets T-boned between two ridiculous-looking vehicles flying along at 100mph. The sound effects and voices all return and give the experience a really nostalgic-yet-new feel.
The cars still handle like bricks on wheels until you level them up to a certain point, but I can't help but feel that every one of the mechanics, right down to some of  the more frustrating powerups, were implimented based on how much they made the developers laugh. Mayhem is key here, and in this game, it abounds.
The level of variety in terms of race types, and locations is higher than in any other game in the series, although there is still a fair amount of recycling to be found, and the action in the single player can still get repetitive after a time. But that's Carmageddon, and you're listening to a person who played all 36-odd levels of the first one as a child by destroying all 5 opponents every time to finish. So where my tolerance for repetition may be high, others' may not be.
In any case, I think this game works best with a dose of nostalgia. I'm not sure if people coming to the franchise for the first time may get that Carmageddon itself is a rather simple, undemanding thing. In a world of Infinite Warfares and Bioshocks and whatnot, where you're bombarded start to finish with information, and missions, and people yelling, and intricate environments, plowing around an ice flow turning a gaggle of penguins into a red smear, with the singular objective of ramming everyone else until they go 'boom' might not be stimulating enough? I don't know really. But in my opinion, this is the best game of the series, and expertly combines modern conveniences with old-school gameplay, and shows that Stainless really understand what it is that makes a Carmageddon game a Carmageddon game.

Back in 1999 I played both the original and second iteration of Carmageddon. As a kid, it was easy to get lost in such a diverse and action-packed game. Back then, racing games were stuck with linear tracks that left your mind wondering what lies beyond the asphalt. Carmageddon changed this by allowing you to explore large scapes and encouraging you to find secrets. The danage model in the originals were out of this world-- I remember playing Destruction Derby the same year, and although I enjoyed the game, it was nowhere near as advanced as Carmageddon.
Many years later I decided to dive in head first and buy Carmageddon: Max Damage. I know it's not just a "nostalgic" thing for me-- At first I wondered if I made a mistake buying this. The controls were a bit wonky, the gameplay wasn't what I had remembered, the damage model felt cheap and I just didn't understand what I was doing. Surelly, I wasn't going to give up after the first few levels, though.
Suddenly, I unlocked my first vehicle, and the next, and the next.. The controls weren't bad, I just hadn't unlocked and explored the other vehicle options and I still needed to upgrade. As soon as I got some heavier vehicles, I really started appreciating the damage model. My vehicle was so weak that I didn't have an opportunity to see the havok wreaked upon it's body before it blew up. The game all came together for me and I finally realized after 50 hours that I made a great choice.
In the end, I definitely recommend this game if you're looking for something to get lost in for many many hours. I hope Stainless Games continues to update this game. I am excited to see what the community has to offer with CarMODgeddon and I definitely hope to see more players online!

The Park is a first person horror game set in the world of The Secret World. You are a mother whose son has run inside the Atlantic Island Park past closing time. Things seem fine at the beginning but quickly turn dark. What was once a park full of laughter and fun quickly becomes a carnival of nightmares, and your child is lost inside. You will need to face the horros of this evil amusement park to save your child, all the while discovering the history of this twisted offering to childhood imagination. Who built the park? Why have their been so many deaths during its run? And what happened to the children that have disappeared?
The Park is a beautifully done story experience. Enough jumpscares to get your heart racing while enough psychological horror to make you go "WTF". It will run you about 2 hours, maybe more if you want all of the achievements to unlock the game's full history, which for $10 isn't bad. The graphics were flawless, sound was superb, the spookiness of the music often making me want to put down my headphones and turn my head around the screen. The controls are bare, there is no map, and there aren't any enemies per-se, but you won't need them when your mind is the ultimate enemy. All in all it's a great game and I'd recommended it to anyone who likes narrative games,anyone who's a fan of The Secret World, or someone who wants to take a break from action-heavy games like Call of Duty and just have a nice stroll through an amusement park.

The developers of Limbo recently made the game available for free for a short period of time. I was aware that it has a huge reputation, so I thought I might as well take advantage of the offer and see what all the fuss was about.
I'm glad I didn't pay actual money for it.
I will admit that I'm not really a fan of 2D platformers, but I just don't understand the hype.
The story is non-existent. There's no explanation for who the protagonist is, where they are, or what they're trying to achieve. (And no, the single line of explanation on the store page doesn't count, because it isn't referenced in the actual game at all).
The gameplay is frustrating, designed around traps that you can't possibly avoid the first time you encounter them. You have to die first, learn what triggers the trap, and then you can avoid it on the next attempt. The art style is a contributing factor to this, every solid object is the same shade of black, which means many traps are indistinguishable from the landscape. But even the traps you can see, have an invisible trigger point. And don't even get me started about how you drown after being underwater for 0.5 seconds.
This isn't fun, at least for me. Other games that I enjoy are able to make me feel like when I die, its my fault, because I made a mistake. My aim was bad, I used the wrong weapon, I had a poor tactic. But in Limbo, pretty much every death left me with a feeling of "what else could I do?" (with several swear words thrown in for good measure).
The only reason I bothered to finish the game was because I knew its only 3 hours long, and even then I had to really force myself to keep going.
... I just don't get it.

TLD is like playing chess with Mother Nature where you have to figure out the rules as you go along.
A couple bad moves and she will hammer you. Like chess, you have to plan out a game(survival) strategy that considers what "counter" moves Mother Nature can throw at you. To survive the game you have to learn all you can about your environment, weather and animal patterns, where there is shelter, how to make your food last longer, how to make maximum use of your resources as well as those provided by the environment.  The only win is staying in the game as Mother Nature will never lose.
If you try to run and gun this game or just wing it you will die. If you like to run and gun and wing it, this game is not for you.
The Story consist of 5 episodes and currently only the first 2 are available.
The main plot is about two survivors finding each other and to finish a mission where the details are unknown to the player. The first 2 episodes focus on learning the harsh lessons of survival. They serve primarily as a tutorial  where you learn by completing tasks.  Experienced players from the EA may find it tedious and they may find that the mechanics have been tuned so their EA strategies may not work in the story as well.
Survival is the real gem of this game.
The developers have stated that they will continue to update Survival so I expect to see more features and perhaps a few more maps.  Survival was born out of the developers sandbox where the EA players provided feedback on the mechanics to be used in the Story. It had become so popular that the developers decided to make it a part of the game. While it may seem "thin" or lacking depth to some I expect it to be enhanced by the promised updates.
I fell the price is a little high given the current state of the game. With the delivery of the three remaining episodes and depending on the quality of the Survival enhancements the game could be a real bargain.

Skip the wall of text for TL;DR it's just a little backstory as to why I love this game so much.
I have always had a soft spot for tower defense games. Growing up I would play a multitude of TD style flash games and enjoy them greatly for a short time. Later in my gaming career I would play TD mods in vanilla Starcraft 2 like Desert strike or redstone TD. Those got a lot more play from me than the flash games but I'm sure I didn't break 30 hours in either of them and I quickly entered my cringey MOBA phase after that. After I burned out on League of Legumes and built a computer that could run DOTA 2 I dove into that. Sadly Valve took ages to implement the ever important arcade, after all the game started out as a simple Warcraft 3 mod. Well not that simple. Anyway after some Epic Boss Fight and Overthrow I saw Wagamama playing Legion TD on stream and from that point on I was enthralled. I trudged through 5 minute queues just to roll dice on if all 8 people would stay and play favorite tower defense game of all time. Even with just 3 builders I throughly enjoyed Legion TD for probably about 50 hours. It was something that was on and off and it was really difficult to find others to play with. I also favorited it more when my latency was awful. Sadly I didn't see the Kickstarter campaign until it had completed successfully so all I could do was add the steam title to my wishlist and bide my time. Darkness crept into my world and the one TD to rule them all became forgotten. Until I see the Early Access game get a release date. The only reason this game is rated average is all the negative reviews people left in the first 2 days when the game was unplayable. 2 hours of gameplay. That includes a few minutes to go back and pick up the last 3 achievements that I missed. How is it, you ask? It's okay. It's a creepy setting, there's a few parts that made me flinch a bit. The story is laid out pretty well and the environment tells it alright. But if you haven't figured out the entire plot by the halfway point at the latest, I feel very sorry for you. The "twist" was blatantly obvious to me after the first ride and the details about it became almost painful pretty quickly.
I have never played The Secret World (the game that this game is pretty much created to promote), so I can't say for certain, but I feel like if I had played TSW, I would have found this game much less appealing. Having no knowledge of Atlantic Island Park or its history at least gave me a lot to explore and learn.
I was intrigued by the concept of losing a kid in a creepy, haunted amusement park with waning sanity. Unfortunately, it becomes pretty apparent that your character is entirely unrelatable and unlikable and thus impossible to sympathize with and therefore an immersion breaker. The longer I played, the more I thought that that kid was better off lost in a haunted park than with that awful mother.
The most jarring part of the game was the first, I guess... "jump scare" or whatever it would be called. And the one that followed was incredibly predictable because of the first and pretty laughable.
6/10
Atmosphere is good. Story is predictable. Nothing really "scary," just a bit startling occasionally. Obvious Lovecraft inspiration. Notes that should read like a freaked out park goer read more like a badly written H.P. Lovecraft story (maybe on par with one of Lovecraft's childhood stories). Sort, short, short.
It's worth it for 10 bucks. Maybe the full price of 13 bucks, too. If you want something to do with an hour or two of your life, there's worse and more expensive ways to spend it. Remember, though: this game was pretty much made for the purpose of promoting The Secret World. It's pretty much an advertisement that you pay $10 to experience. I'm satisfied, but I can certainly see a lot of people walking away disatisfied.

Look, it's not like I actively dislike this one. I just prefer to save that big blue thumbs up for the titles that I actually enjoy and would not be afraid to recommend. This is not one of those.
Rituals is an interesting one. Got it in the Humble Bundle a little while back and decided to finish it off one day. It seemed like my kind of thing, having grown up on Myst and its sequels. But then, perhaps I set myself up for disappointment.
It's too shallow. Too
Each puzzle is self-contained, a simple object + object + location kind of thing, your inventory reset with each new area. It's almost reminiscent of those escape the room flash games, only with a bit of an ego. And low poly crocodiles.
And just when I found myself beginning to actually care about what the hell was going on in this world, the game ends. Tells you "good job, play it again to find the other ending which is basically the same ending only you make a slightly different choice right at the end". So I did. And was equally stiffed in terms of satisfaction. Take of this what you will. Some may argue that the vagueness leads to everyone's opinions being valid. I say screw opinions, give me facts.
In the end, this game is a bit of a poem. Not a very good poem, mind. One of those love letters to the earth that make zero sense to anyone except the teenager writing them. But there's still at least some value in it. Though maybe not $5 of value.
Hey, at least I got those easy achievements.

I'm shocked that there aren't many reviews for this game, so I figured I could give a thorough one.
Rituals is a 3D point-and-click interactive adventure with nostalgic poly graphics that date back to the 90s.
Graphics:
If you're familiar with the early 3D graphics like from Star Fox on the SNES or a variety of 3D games dating back in the 90s, then you'll understand the graphics. The graphics are low-poly, so they're pretty simple. Not only it's the nostalgia that makes it eye-catching, but the colors used. It ranges from bland gray to colorful green, purple, and orange. Overall, I like the simplicity and the beauty with it.
Story:
The story is revealed through notes and scenes while playing through the game. Apparently, you wake up alone at your workplace and you decide to explore and delve into private places you weren't suppose to, like your boss's office or going into both the men's and women's restrooms. I can say, without any spoilers, that the story links to Earth.
Gameplay:
I'm a little 50/50 on the gameplay here. On one side, I can see why it is point-and-click, while the other side says that it should have been a free-range game. I guess point-and-click was intended to "get to the 'point' " of the game, while we could be wandering for hours if it was a free-range exploration game. I am neutral on this aspect, not because of this, but because of the arrows and interaction. Sometimes, when clicking on the direction I want to go, it doesn't register (yes my mouse works), and some objects are a bit annoying to grab since they are too small or you interact with something else.
Overall:
Rituals is a short game where exploration and colors tell the story about how we perceive earth and unlocking secrets. Today's most point-and-click games rely on 2D graphics, but this takes an extra and interesting step further by using simple 3D. Although the controls are slightly annoying, this game takes us back to veteran gamers' glory days: simple story, simple graphics, and interesting concepts.
Pros:
-Nostalgic Graphics
-Great use of colors
???(depends on how you see it, but I count it as a pro):
-Simple story with some gaps.
-Cons:
Controls are a bit iffy, but not too bad.

Half-Life: Blue Shift is the final expansion pack to the original Half-Life (if you don't count Decay).
The gameplay is what you'd expect in a Half-Life game, the only things that are different are the characters, maps and length of the game. The game is around 2-5 hours long, depending on how good you are at shooter games.
You play as Barney Calhoun, a security guard at the Black Mesa Research Facility who fights his way out of Black Mesa after an event that opens portals which allow aliens to "visit" Black Mesa. As Barney, you run, think, shoot and live through the game solving puzzles, killing waves of US Marines (sent in to "contain" everything) in intense action scenes and, sadly, escort one Dr. Rosenberg, who can't seem to walk 20 feet without needing a 10 second breather.
You have a smaller arsenal of weapons than both Half-Life and Opposing Force, 9 to be exact. This is a major critic point but personally in my experience you won't need the extra weapons since the game is too short to have the need for other firearms. However, the worst part is the escort portion as mentioned above.
You must painstakingly escort Dr. Rosenberg through 20 mins of gameplay, defending him from Aliens and US Marines. Don't even attempt to run, he's slower than a snail and needs as many breathers as the worlds fattest man running 10 meters to the local McDonald's. The only saving grace about this bit is that the game regularly makes checkpoints if either you or Rosenberg die. Combine that with the incredible loading times and it shouldn't take long but it is a chore.
The game runs off the same engine as every other Valve game released before 2004, GoldSrc. This engine cranks the nostalgia to 11 with graphics that can run on a paper bag, loading times that are faster than my one-night stands, and sound quality that is... meh.
Overall Half-Life: Blue Shift is an excellent game that is the cherry on top of the original Half-Life nostalgia cake. Any fan of Half-Life should give this a go, if you want to get into Half-Life, go play Half-Life 1 first, then Opposing Force then this game. It will make sense once you do it.

You know a game is great when you don't even have to spend an hour playing it to know it feels right in every aspect of its design. Cuphead is in short a fantastic and beautiful game. It really is something to behold. It's like an old cartoon come to life, with clarity and a nostalgic bent for all that came before. Not only is it accurate to the times it wants to replicate, it is bursting with creativity.
Every part of this game has been thoughtfully poured over by the devs. Like another Microsoft game, Ori and the Blind Forest, this one resides at the top of its genre in nearly every category of its design. The enemies and bosses are all varied. There are various weapons and specials to beat the game with, and each stage has enough different animations to keep you enthralled from start to end.
You don't need to play this game a whole hell of a lot to realize it is one of the most delicious games out there. And nothing else on the market is really even like it. I would have to go back to a game such as Mickey Mania for a resemblant artstyle. Cuphead also has a wicked sense of humor, though, and overall the stylization of the art and story is decidely adult-oriented in tone. This is a good thing.
The gameplay is utterly perfected, though, there a few issues worth discussing. It's tough like any good bullet shooter or shmup, and you can expect to die a lot. But I wouldn't say it is as tough as the hardest bullet hell shooters, which are impossible to master for most. It has a decent difficulty curve that rewards you for doing things right, and sometimes tortures you for doing things wrong. Luckily, once you customize each button of your controls to your liking the game becomes a lot of fun to pace your way through.
What you will need is your dash for the most part. And that does make the game feel like the extra weapons and abilities are not really all that special. When your invisible air dash is gonna get you through easier, it's hard to need anything else at times. You can certainly try all the other things out, and even the weaker weapons can be fun, but there is definitely a tier list here you will have to follow at times.
Certain enemies and bosses appear cheap, but so far I've not run into anything annoying enough for me to dislike the game. Of course if you are a gamer that wants your games easy, it is possible you might not desire to play this game. Maybe a youtube video would suffice for your enjoyment then.
Overall, Cuphead gets my highest recommendation. A triumpth of art and imagination combusted through fierce gameplay that totally enlivens and lovingly hearkens back to the golden age of shmups and sidescroller shooters. Amazing in every way. I would hope a sequel is planned because we really need another game with this style.

Still holds up.  I played Bioshock when it first released and loved it, and may enjoy it even more now.  I won't bother with too many details as it's widely considered a classic at this point, but if you haven't played this yet for some reason definitely give it a shot if you're even remotely interested in atmospheric shooters with a cerebral plotline.  I'm not one of those hyperbolic fanboys that calls it a "masterpiece" or anything; it has a fair number of problems (some bugs, sloppy combat, pacing problems) but the positives certainly outweigh the negatives by a wide margin.  One bit of advice I will give to avoid what bogged it down a bit on my first playthroughs: don't get caught up with OCD exploration unless you're really looking to pad out your playing time.  It's tempting to hack every turret and med station you come across, I know, but while the mini-games can be fun the first couple times it can grind the game to a halt.  Just enjoy Rapture as the amazing setpiece it is and you'll have a good time.

overall, if you liked the original, your gonna love this game.  it was an insta-buy for me!

The developers of Limbo recently made the game available for free for a short period of time. I was aware that it has a huge reputation, so I thought I might as well take advantage of the offer and see what all the fuss was about.
I'm glad I didn't pay actual money for it.
I will admit that I'm not really a fan of 2D platformers, but I just don't understand the hype.
The story is non-existent. There's no explanation for who the protagonist is, where they are, or what they're trying to achieve. (And no, the single line of explanation on the store page doesn't count, because it isn't referenced in the actual game at all).
The gameplay is frustrating, designed around traps that you can't possibly avoid the first time you encounter them. You have to die first, learn what triggers the trap, and then you can avoid it on the next attempt. The art style is a contributing factor to this, every solid object is the same shade of black, which means many traps are indistinguishable from the landscape. But even the traps you can see, have an invisible trigger point. And don't even get me started about how you drown after being underwater for 0.5 seconds.
This isn't fun, at least for me. Other games that I enjoy are able to make me feel like when I die, its my fault, because I made a mistake. My aim was bad, I used the wrong weapon, I had a poor tactic. But in Limbo, pretty much every death left me with a feeling of "what else could I do?" (with several swear words thrown in for good measure).
The only reason I bothered to finish the game was because I knew its only 3 hours long, and even then I had to really force myself to keep going.
... I just don't get it.

I only recommend getting this game off of a steam key retailer, do NOT spend a lot of money on this game through steam, just not enough content and they are obviously trying to fist us in the butt, so hears a link to get it cheaper.

The Park is something like an atmospheric horror walking simulator. If you despise the idea of a walking simulator, you can stop reading right now. Because that is what you do. There is very little interaction. Instead the narrative is the strong element of this game. You constantly discover new pieces of the story and try to find out what is going on. I won't say more (everything would be a spoiler).
All I can say is that the game gets darker and more intense with every minute. The horror element is not too bad (yes, there are a few jumpscares). And the finale is really nice. I can't say I completely understood what happened in the end (it's a bit open to interpretation). But it left me thinking about the different possibilities, and I spent 20 more minutes in the forum to find out what others think happened. I think this is a good sign, right?
So yeah, I liked it. You just have to ask yourself, are you willing to pay 10 bucks for 90 minutes of entertainment. I am completely fine with the length of this game. But I know many people will not be. So if you are interested, but think 10€ (13€ once the release discount expires) is too much, maybe wait for a 50% sale.

At a first glance, The Park looks like your classic first person horror game that happens to take place in a creepy, abandoned and decrepit amusement park. But it crescendos much more than that.
You play as Lorraine, a single mother who's lost her son, Callum, after visiting the Atlantic Island amusement park.
Upon exiting the park just as closing time arrives, Callum tells her that he misplaced his teddy bear and storms into the amusement park to find it. With darkness quickly approaching and her son missing and ignoring her commands, Lorraine has to enter the park to find him, while strange things slowly begin to occur in the once friendly location.
The story is a bit hit and miss, starting out weak but improving near the end of the game. As you explores the park at night and rides its various innocent yet menacing rides, the plot develops through Lorraine's monologue, which reveal her history and search for answers, and documents that are strewn about the park that reveal its dark past. Funcom have made no secret of the influence from games like Gone Home and The Vanishing of Ethan Carter, and the comparisons come almost instantly as you begin walking around the troubled theme park.
It's also more involved than your average title, as you can ride the rides in the park (a Ferris wheel, rollercoaster, and the like), and look around at your surroundings while doing so. Controls are at a minimum with the ability to move and interact with any items, but I have to say I liked the inclusion of a run mechanic. It makes sense in this context – you’re in freaky hellscape of a park trying to find your son, after all – but it means that moving between sections doesn’t feel like a chore. The Park also uses call mechanic with the right mouse button that not only helps guide you to your next objective, but works brilliantly in the context of the game. Hearing Lorraine call out to Callum with increasing worry and panic is expertly done, as are the responses the player gets. It was these responses along with the swirling visual markers that ensured I knew where I was supposed to be going, although it wasn’t fool proof. There were a few moments where I had to wander around before I was able to get back on the right path, but I didn’t find it too frustrating or time-consuming, thankfully. There's also a decent amount of lore-building involved, and not just because of the Lovecraftian themes that are intertwined with the Funcom-verse. I actually enjoyed reading about various incidents at the park, and how they involve the cast although I did have an issue with some of the the scattered pages and documents you can find off the beaten path, detailing some of the game’s backstory. It seems unfortunate that some of them are nearly unreadable, as the font on these are tiny and blurry. A clearer font, zoom button or a subtitle option would have been an alternative, but as the game lacks it, unless you strain your eyes to read, you’ll be missing out on some of the backstory that ties it to Funcom’s other game, The Secret World.
The strongest part however is the end of the game, which is both fantastic and unfortunate, as it’s such a strong and beautifully creepy finish that is way more terrifying compared to the rest of the experience. If only the game’s setting and story would have more like the last part of the game, it would have been a much more horrifying game.
Overall, The Park is a well crafted narrative-driven adventure game, but there really is no reason to return once you’ve left The Park unless you want to get those missable achievements or analyse the letters and items again to figure out more of the backstory. However, if you want something a little different this Halloween, play this with the headphones on and the lights off.

I generally enjoy mysterious puzzle games that make you try to think about things in a different way, so I thought I'd give Rituals a try.
Pros:
- Good use of both modern and desolate settings.
- Solid music choices.
- Decent art style for a small game.
Cons:
- Puzzles that are far too simple.
-The "big question" answers are handed to you if you are even remotely paying attention.  There is no real moral dilemma here, and no thinking to be done.
- Sound choices are a little out of place at times and very loud.
- A story that makes absolutely no sense and is disconnected from itself, even for this genre.
- Totally out of place humor and design choices.  The game takes itself too seriously and when it tries to make a comment or a joke it comes off as juvenile.
- Very clunky controls.  Just track the player head movement to the mouse movement instead of the whole click/hold/arrow system thing.
-Obviously it has no replay value after you have solved everything, which doesn't take more than an hour or so.  The shortness of the game keeps me from complaining about the odd and arbitrary save system.
Ultimately, I found Rituals uncompelling. This game fails the genre because it requires no thinking, doesn't cause reflection, doesn't tell a coherent story, and in the end isn't really mysterious so much as random.  It seems more like a sketchbook of scenes comprising of cool ideas for a future game that are currently stitched together in an attempt to be artsy.  I hate being overly critical, but I don't think this game is worth your time.  If you enjoy the concept and want to see an indie game that gets it right, check out The Stanley Parable.  For games from larger studios take a look at The Talos Principle or Obduction.

Genius in it's simplicity.
I finally bought this on sale just to see what the fuss was about, and after all the talk of the series being Youtube-bait with its jump-scares and the tiny development cycles of the sequels leading to them seemingly being churned out I was very cynical when starting it.
But I'll be damned if this isn't one of the most palpably tense horror games I've ever played.
Whilst the jump-scare aspect gets the most press when it comes FNAF, the game actually uses the core tenets of true horror to it's advantage. The player's influence on the world around him is limited - the only way you can fend off the creatures is to track the threat and close the doors around you when they appear. Given that operating anything uses up your precious power resources, you're left exposed for most of the game and can only act in your own defence when the threat is at your doorstep. Furthermore, you can only know that the threat is there if you turn on the lights temporarily, and the knowledge that there may be something watching you from the black abyss that lies just outside the door is terrifying in itself. So throughout the game the player is left powerless, exposed, fearing the unknown, feeling like the enemy is one step ahead, and incapable of eliminating the threat, only delaying it. These are the emotions that truly thrill you and scare you. The jump-scare is merely the pay off to the complex and deep tension that the game creates. And it does all this on a shoe-string, exposing just what a solid and simple concept can do for the gamer.
I now get why this game became so popular, and while the things you see and hear on Youtube may make you feel like the game is nothing more than a cheap thrill, I think it's a deceptively simple but masterfully crafted experience.

I played Evolve during the beta, and enjoyed the game immensely. Enough for me to drop money on the largest package. The game was stable, the gameplay was fun, and I wasn't turned off by the pricing model like a lot of others.
Giving you a review from someone that actually OWNS the game (which I think should be a requirement) I can say that Evolve has launched without any server issues, a stable client, and the same gameplay I enjoyed during beta. I guess I've grown accustomed to pricing models that include a la carte costmetic items.
NOTHING in Evolve, aside from pre-order bonuses or cosmetic skins, cannot be simply unlocked through several hours of gameplay. There is a LOT of arm-flailing about how the DLC is sold for this game, and I think much of it is completely unwarranted. A good bit of it is simply untrue. There is nothing at launch that DLC or pre-order owners get that is beyond cosmetic. DLC owners have pre-purchased in advance unreleased monsters and hunters that will come down the line. Otherwise, players will need to buy those new hunters or monsters through the in-game store.
If you buy the base game and nothing else you'll have access to 3 monsters, 12 hunters, and plenty of gameplay to keep you entertained. The beta included only the skirmish mode, which was a single-map experience of monsters vs hunters. The real meat of the game is in Evacuation mode, where you'll play 5 different maps each with 5 different play-modes.
All in all it's a shame that the marketing and pricing model will harm Evolve, because Turtle Rock Studios put a lot of love into the game with a concept built upon the success of Left 4 Dead.

TL;DR: A great survival game that pulls ahead of nearly every survival game I've played before. Worth every penny.
My experiences in The Long Dark have all been entirely different (albeit always ending in my demise) despite picking the same map most of the time. The maps are quite large and connect to each other. The maps are NOT procedurely generated, allowing maps to be created and upon starting a new game, you can head in a familiar direction.
The difficulty can be set depending on how you'd like to play, whether you prefer exploring or hardcore survival. Even playing on the "Pilgrim" (easy) difficulty it provides a solid challenge, eliminating only the threat of animals. My most recent experience was on the easiest difficulty and I still managed to die withing the first few days because I got carried away.
Knowing when you have enough daylight to make it back to camp is essential. I decided to fish my last 2 hours of daylight, only a few hundred yards from what I decided to make my "base". That night of course turned out to be one of the darkest I've seen and of course I had ran out of fuel earlier, not expecting to need any. I lit my lantern that had very little keroseen and started to head towards my shack. Soon I realized I had went the wrong direction after getting turned around in the dark. It didn't take long for my lantern to go out, so I lit the only thing I had left, a flare. I wandered for what seemed like forever, not making any progress. Hypothermia ensued and I was becoming exhausted. I managed to find one of the many fishing huts on the lake I had been fishing on. I decided it'd be best to wait out the night in the shack rather than wandering around cold. To pass the time I decided to fish, there could only be around 4 hours of night left. 2 more hours of fishing and my situation was becoming dire. The night was still black and the temperatures had only become worse. I laid now my bedroll, hoping to rest and warm up inside the sleeping bag while in the fishing shack. Only needed to make it another hour and the sun would begin to rise, lighting the way to my base where I could be warm. As I rested my body temperature just continued to drop and I died in my sleep. This was on the easiest difficulty. (Yes, I obviously suck.)
The game runs well, but can be demanding at times due to the large world and blizzards. The graphics are artistic, but nothing that will knock your socks off, but you can capture some pretty nice screenshots during sunrises or when the night isn't so dark. The game even has a nice soundtrack that can be quite ominous, but fits the setting. The music isn't constant so it doesn't take away from the immersion. Some animal sounds aren't great, such as deer running by, but others can be quite chilling. Hearing a pack of wolves begin to howl in the night while hearing the wind screaming throught the trees creates an amazing atmostphere.
The game doesn't hold your hand. You're thrown in and survival begins the second you start. There are community made maps, but none in game. This is not to say that it has a sharp learning curve though. Crafting is simple and item descriptions tell you how to do certain things (such as curing hides).
The developers are constantly putting out updates and doing everything to turn this into a finished product (even though it feels close to one now). Features such as story mode have yet to be added, but sandbox and challenges are more than enough to keep you entertained for more hours than many triple A titles can.
The Long Dark is an excellent game and is well worth the small price tag. A game that shows no signs of ever being abandoned as many early access games have in the past. The game can be tough so if you're aren't a fan of survival games, it's probably safe to say you should stay away. If you are a fan of survival though, this is the perfect game for you. No zombies, no aliens, just you and the Canadian wilderness.

I really love Tropico games and would not doubt if the entire team is tripping on LSD as they code it. The graphics are solid this time around. They have a much more polished feel over the others. The musics always solid and you can import your own into the game without much effort.
With that being said I'll go into a few negatives. With this one you really do want all of the DLC as too much was withheld from the base game. Once you have everything it's a beauty.This time around you can't zoom out as far as previous versions. There is a script available to undo this but it doesn't work in multiplayer. So now they have multiplayer but it desyncs often which ruins the match. It's definitely playable but there aren't many people online. It helps to know someone with the game if you want all of the achievements because several are tied to multiplayer. I've been trying for a long time to get the final 3 I have left. At least they have it which is a step in the right direction. Then they removed some of El Presidente's previous features. Now you can't follow him around or engage in a shootout. Instead it's all about dynasty members which would be fine... if they let me follow them around, give my speeches, and shoot up the enemy. They must undo this in the next one as it removes part of the charm. I'll also argue that they made it way too difficult to be a ruthless dictator. You'll make money hand over fist being a swell guy, but if you so much as look in the other direction you're going to have a military mutiny. It doesn't matter how well prepared you are for your own troops toppling you. Sure, you deserved it but I invite you to try running a North Korean style of government on this game. You might even find yourself in awe of what that dictatorship has accomplished. It probably is more realistic in that regard but it's also almost impossible since most of the features that could make it a reality aren't available until much later in the game.
There is so much to this game that I am overwhelmed by attempting to describe the positives. Teamsters and construction workers are no longer an achilles heal. The army doesn't wander off during a crucial battle. Traffic jams are no longer an issue whatsoever. Parking garages and metros have been nerfed to the point that there doesn't seem to be a penalty for not having them at all. I'd argue that they went too far but micro managing roads was annoying. The military additions, the espionage, industries, trade, and so on are all well done. You have people flying rocket powered gliders all over the place, blimps, airlines, and so on. It's no longer just micro managing a banana republic and more like you're running a western power. I'm really interested to see what they will do with Tropico 6. I hope they add more wildlife as they removed a bit too much this time, give us back control over El Presidente, and work on the different forms of government. If they do those simple things I'll be happy.

The park is a decent if short game.
I'll admit that most of the jumpscares caught me off guard especially when I was expecting them because there were a lot of spots where you know they would show up and they did.
This is one of those walkabout games where you will spend alot of your time walking and exploring the park as you move from one ride to the next whilst looking for your wayward son.
Spoilers ahead:
My main problem with this game however is it's story.  You start off thinking it's going to be a horror game where you unravel the mystery of what's going on at the park via notes and incident reports.  So at first glance it seems to be a story about how the proprietor of the park purchased the land from a man who commited great atrocites.  The idea being that the park was going to try to be something positive in what would have been a very negative zone.  As you progress through the park and read various documents you learn that there have been various deaths throughout the years starting way back when it was under construction and still occuring even after the park opened it's doors.
You learn that the proprieter actually had an ulterior motive for setting up the park and wasn't as altruistic as he first seemed.  Eventually the park gets shut down by health inspectors and the proprietor retreates to the horror house where his machine was.
but around the third act the game decides to forget all that and switch gears to become about the protagonist and her mindset, trying for a twist that you would have already saw coming from a mile away if you payed the slightest attention to her dialogue.
All i'm going to say as much as I liked the game the last bit of it was the weakest.  I really wish they stuck it out with the regular horror aspect and had us confront whatever was controlling the park.
End spoilers.
other than that though.  It's a real neat tie-in game to an mmo. that knows how to build atmospere and give a general sense of unease even though there are times you can tell when there is going to be a jumpscare well before it happens.

Bioshock is a fantastic game.
This PC port isn't very well optimized, so be careful before buying. Many people found the game unplayable, but I was lucky. Besides a few annoyances, the game ran fairly well for its reputation as one that is broken.
But who cares about that? I don't. You shouldn't either.
Story is definitely one the best aspects of the game. It is pretty well written, and can really get you near the end. The design is also really great. I loved exploring the Art Deco Atlantis that is Rapture, and the levels are full of great detail. The environments also allow you to use it to your advantage, something I found really awesome. The enemies' designs are also neat, the Big Daddies especially.
Bioshock, like most games of the time, is a first-person shooter. And naturally, a first-person shooter should take a back seat to the story and design. The combat is honestly clunky, something that is fixed in later installments. With an exception for Big Daddies and a few other enemies, most of the weapons become obsolete when, with the right tonics, most enemies can be easily disposed with a zap and a 1-3 swings of the wrench. With that aside, it's not bad combat, just kinda off.
As Bioshock is one of my favorite game series, I definitely recommend this game to anyone with something to play it on. Just be aware of the repercussions of the PC port.

Bread is a staple food prepared from a dough of flour and water, usually by baking. Throughout recorded history it has been popular around the world and is one of the oldest artificial foods, having been of importance since the dawn of agriculture.
Proportions of types of flour and other ingredients vary widely, as do modes of preparation. As a result, types, shapes, sizes, and textures of breads differ around the world. Bread may be leavened by processes such as reliance on naturally occurring sourdough microbes, chemicals, industrially produced yeast, or high-pressure aeration. Some bread is cooked before it can leaven, including for traditional or religious reasons. Non-cereal ingredients such as fruits, nuts and fats may be included. Commercial bread commonly contains additives to improve flavor, texture, color, shelf life, and ease of manufacturing.
Bread is served in various forms with any meal of the day. It is eaten as a snack, and used as an ingredient in other culinary preparations, such as sandwiches, and fried items coated in bread crumbs to prevent sticking. It forms the bland main component of bread pudding, as well as of stuffings designed to fill cavities or retain juices that otherwise might drip out.
Bread has a social and emotional significance beyond its importance as nourishment. It plays essential roles in religious rituals and secular culture. Its prominence in daily life is reflected in language, where it appears in proverbs, colloquial expressions ("He stole the bread from my mouth"), in prayer ("Give us this day our daily bread") and in the etymology of words, such as "companion" (from Latin com "with" + panis "bread").

Carmageddon: Max Damage is developed and published by Stainless Games Ltd. Industry veterans and quite ironically, better known in recent years for their video games focusing on Magic: The Gathering. That card game genre alone, is a far cry from their “outrageously” gory, Carmageddon series.

1997 must have been a crazy year as far as PC gaming is concerned. It saw the release of both the first Carmageddon as well as Grand Theft Auto 1. Coincidence or not, both of these titles feature plenty of vehicular manslaughter and their developers were small, independent and UK-based. The controversy surrounding the, new at the time graphic simulation of such violence prompted hundreds of self-righteous mongrels and mouth foaming soccer moms to mindlessly rage and “debate” over the very existence of such video games in the first place. Freedom of expression as well as the fact that a game should never be considered a guide to real life (unless you’re already clinically insane) were placed under questioning amidst exaggerated public outcry. How far can video games go, in depicting the murder of countless on-screen and fully digitalized innocent pedestrians with a vehicle? If you ask me, all that scandal did nothing but to boost sales and interest. Apparently humanity never learns that by banning or declaring something taboo, not only will interest in that subject never wane, but the exact opposite shall occur. I’ve said my piece on violence in gaming and the rant will stop here. I wanted to explain to the younger audience, who might not have been familiar with Carmageddon, about this game’s rightfully unapologetic legacy. Max Damage is the de facto 4th game in the series and it’s more than just a throwback to simpler, but more scandalous times. It stands out on its own very well, since the racing formula it proposes, is far more than just getting from point A to B in the fastest lap time. “Classical” racing is still present, but quite boring given the game we review today. You can alternatively crush your rivals’ cars or run over every single pedestrian or animal present on the map, as original victory conditions. Car combat plays a central role in Carmageddon: Max Damage and is by far the easiest way to win a race.
Unlike previous titles in its series, you’re never pressed by a merciless countdown clock and as long as you hunt down your rivals in a timely manner, the objective is quite straightforward. They will attempt to put you down as well, but such opposition is to be expected and the driver AI was convincing enough. The track and vehicle variety plus customization offer enough breathing room for even the most pretentious of gamers. Featuring both a career mode and free play on the game’s maps, really can’t give anyone an excuse not to become calculated drivers or adept hunters, as the situation warrants. Keeping an open mind is paramount though. While not putting an emphasis on the explicit murder of the innocents found on its race maps, Max Damage has them in ample supply and avoiding them is sometimes impossible.  The game even features a political satire-like mode which replaces the default pedestrian skins (which are themselves a mockery upon today’s society) with everyone’s “favorite” US presidential candidates of 2016. Take your pick, they’re still two sides of the same rusty coin.

The graphics are nothing spectacular, but still manage to convey the simulated chaos while the heavy metal songs fit this genre like a glove. Frame-rate drops were quite unexplainable, but playing at 4K resolution, I never expected constant 60 frames per second anyways. One minor complaint I have to address in regards to Max Damage’s liberal use of motion blur (and even static one!). Apart from the hapless characters and animals you run over, only the vehicles themselves feature good looking and high-res textures, while most buildings and assets lack in-depth attention. And that can’t be masked with so much blur without raising a few red flags.
+ Beautful graphics and soundtrack
+ Plenty of customization options
+ Unique mix of racing and/or vehicle combat
+ Steam Achievements & Trading Cards
- You can’t hide low-res textures with motion blur
- Frame-rate drops
Slaspstick humor, this is not. Unless you replaced wood with a hot iron. Still, the game is proud of its heritage and is an exponent of totally unshackled freedom of speech in video gaming. It doesn’t play by the rules and it shouldn’t either. If some rules are meant to be broken, many others shouldn’t even have been written in the first place. This series is a guilty pleasure of mine. But you know what? I don’t feel guilty at all while playing it and you can agree with me or not. In all honesty, the game is targeted towards a mature audience, but I doubt that separating reality from fiction is an age-restricted domain. Have fun!

in July 2012, FunCom released an MMO called The Secret World. set in the modern day with an occult/conspiracy/horror theme, it'd turn out to be the best-written MMO and one of the best-written and best-acted games of all time. with a strong setting and stronger characters, TSW was primed for popularity among an unfortunately small subset of MMO players: those who wanted to really care about the setting they were in.
one of the areas you'd encounter within a few hours of your picking up the game was the park. it was one of the earliest serious puzzle areas of the game, but beyond that, it was a terrifying environment, both in terms of how it looked and the threats that roamed around it. the Park in TSW was one of the great pieces of level design of all time--comparable to and maybe better than the haunted house in Bloodlines.
enter The Park. The Park is set in TSW's Park, redesigned for a first-person narrative game. there are no challenges in The Park: it's a walkthrough game, just a story being told. it does, however, start with one of the best mechanics I've ever seen in a horror game: right at the outset, you get the ability to shout to find your next objective. giving the player the option to scream and give away their position in a horror game is one of the best ideas I've ever seen. control your own nightmare; make yourserlf feel exposed.
The Park itself (stop reading now if you don't want any inkling of the story) is about a normal person (not a TSW-style chosen of Gaia...at first) wandering the haunted park in search of her son. the plot unfolds through one-page journal entries you find and monologues from the main character. early on in the 90-120 minute experience, it comes clear that the story is really about being a mother, being a single parent, and the stresses and resentments that develop therewith. I won't explicitly spoil how it all works out, but for the TSW fans out there, know that the last scene is a wonderful TSW cameo.
in the end, The Park works. to someone unfamiliar with TSW, it might feel like an Amnesia-esque horror game, minus any threats; to someone who does know TSW, the hooks to Kingsmouth and the TSW setting in general will probably be the most interesting bits. it's short, it's cheap, and it'll either intrigue you about an MMO you should try or excite you about an MMO you have tried. what's to lose?

After playing Evolve for about 3 hours, the experience I have had has been only mildly interesting.
*Long story short, don't buy the game.
I've tried playing as the monster and a couple of the hunter classes and the game doesn't feel like it really takes into account any level of a players personal ability.
My experience of playing the monster (which is undoubtedly the more fun of the two sides) always plays out the same.
First you run away, because you are no match for the hunters at rank 1.
Second you run away some more, because you are no match for the hunters at rank 2, but this period of time is slightly more annoying by the fact that, whatever lead you gained earlier on from your initial run has evaporated and you are now trapped inside a thunder dome with the hunters.
Thirdly you a take stand / bring the fight to them. As the third tier monster you now have some serious clout, but the actual combat with the hunters is lacklustre, as you have to run in and unload as much as you can on one or two individuals, then if managed to take your target down (and I mean actually dead, not incapacitated) then you have a window of opertunity to overwhelm the remaining hunters.
If you fail to kill all the hunters in your first assault in tier three you are essentially screwed, as all that health you lost in your engagement isn't coming back, so the next time you face your foe you are considerably weaker, making it even less likely you'll succeed in your second attempt.
On to the hunters now.
The hunters all feel very bland and individually unimportant (all aside from Maggie who brings a pet who is exceedinly useful in comparison to the others)
The hunters are all very slow and unable to run and gun with the monster who is so fast in comparisson that there is only ever 3 situations where there is an engagement.
As the monster is eating/evolving (ie. stood still).
The monster accidentally ran into you.
The monster is coming for your objective.
The assault is your generic bullet spam class, just ignore everything else and keep firing at the monster.
The Trapper is a useful class, slowing down tracking and well.... trapping the monster.
The medic is... well... a medic, and the support is essentially a second source of damage, sure it has other "useful" things, but I found that shooting the monster was far more useful than anything else.
Another thing I would like to note is that the "hostile environment" in which these battles take place is actually very small, confined and not really that hostile.
At first I thought to myself that I should try to avoid that huge critter (non monster) that is along this path and try to kill it before continuing the hunt, as the monsters footprints head in that direction, only to see a team mate happily hop over it without any problem what so ever, bringing me to the realization that the only thing even slightly dangerous to us was in fact the monster.
The "arena" in which all battles take place is a very dark, gloomy and unattractive local. I never found myself pausing for a moment to look at the amazing view, or stunning detail, because I didn't notice any, I only saw black/brown/Dark Green colors and blue footprints...
I thought to myself "Well at least there is Evacuation mode, that sounds interesting" and in truth it was... for about 10 minutes, which was how long the first battle took, I beat the monster and then realized that it was only going to get harder for them. I would like to say that my first battle against an other player was a close won victory, but it really wasn't and it was going to get even harder for them, as each victory gave the victorious side an advantage and as our first battle was won so easily it stood to reason that with this new advantage the second battle would be even easier.
It was.
It was so easy in fact that we managed to kill the monster in its first stage, it hadn't even got a full armor bar by the time we locked horns.
The first mission had given us a scent masking agent which prevented the monster smelling prey and this had completely thrown off the monster player and he was squashed.
Our mission hadn't even been to kill the monster, it had been to rescue civilians, but thanks to Maggies pet, we knew where the monster was and killed it anyway.
I almost felt bad for the poor monster player, who must have been getting just a little bit frustrated, but not as frustrated as I was when there was an error after we finished the second mission and I was booted from the game lobby and it was at that point I looked back on the prievious 3 hours and thought to myself....
"I do wish I hadn't bought this game."

310 hours dedicated to this game so far and growing! This game has been one of the most entertaining and immersive games I've played yet and this is just the sandbox. I can only imagine what the final, released version will be like with the story included! This review for now will focus on the early access version of the game.
I can't think of any other games like it. A quiet apocolypse has taken place, technology as we know it is gone. The lights went out, never to return. How long can you survive against nature and everything it has to throw at you? There are no zombies. There are no mutants or aliens. Just you, nature and the need to survive. Scavenge what you can from the abandoned regions, hunt for food and find a warm place to spend the night. Just be aware that beyond the safety of your fireglow, green eyes flash in darkness, waiting for you to give them a chance to send you into the long dark. No one is coming to save you, so you'd best be ready to save yourself.
Features:
=======
+No Zombies, no supernatural, no aliens, no occult! Just nature, and it's brutally unforgiving.
+ A gorgeous art style fairly reminiscent of the Group of Seven. Iconic, refreshing and engaging, it's a nice break from photorealism and proof that games can be beautiful and immersive without being overly heavy on realism.
+ Four modes of difficulty with vastly different challenges for all types.
+ Crafting of the basic survival needs, like torches and bows, and animal skin clothing
+ Survival simulation with a unnervingly believable feel. Monitor your temperature, hunger, thirst and energy levels. Think carefully about your food choices and plan your routes carefully. even a small injury could lead to much worse if left ignored.
+ Challenge modes for those who work better under pressure. Added in the newest update, these challenge modes give seasoned players a few scenarios to complete. Originally there were only 2 but it has since grown to 5.
+Comfortably playable with Mouse and Keyboard or with a controller.
+Extremely well done voiceovers for the basic sandbox characters.
+An out of this world sound experience. Every little sound you hear, from the wind in the trees to the clattering of old shutters, has a purpose and has been meticulously planned. A crow flying overhead may alert you to an approaching storm, a strange clang or clatter in a whiteout can point the way to safety. A growl in the darkness can sound your doom.  All of this atmospheric and immersive sound is punctuated by music tracks that serve to elevate the feel of the moment. Rather than play constantly in the background, these short musical interludes kick in to emphasize something and just as quickly fade out again. (The coming of night, the sun rising, A particularly lonely place, or a Change of weather.)
+The game offers no hand-holding. You are dropped in the world and left to figure it out. You will die many times before it starts to make sense, but each time you fail, you get a better idea of how you can apply what you've learned to the next run.
It should be noted that the only real drawback aside fomr the learning curve to the game is the fact that death is permanent. When you die you start again from the beginning, but even that makes for good compelling gameplay as it pushes you to be more careful about how you go about your survival.
Early access means the game is still undergoing serious developement, but even in this current form, it's hard to believe it's an alpha. It's polished and professional with smooth gameplay and challenge that's well worth the full price. If you like sandbox/survival games, this is a great choice. If you like to simply play the game at your own pace and observe the quiet apocolypse, this game is still a great choice. And when story mode releases, I am certain those who like to play games for the storyline will also love it too. Hinterland is making a great first impression with The Long Dark.
A solid 8/10, most likely a 10 once it hits release.

This game is basically a fairly short 3d point and click adventure game. You click on navigation arrows to move between preset locations and can interact with objects. None of the puzzles are overly complex, which is a good thing and makes it seem less like you're solving puzzles of arbitrary difficulty and more like you're moving through the world of the game. That's about the extent of the gameplay.
The asthetic is low-poly and minimalist, but all of the environmets have a decent level of detail given this. I quite liked the graphics, but that's of course a personal preference.
The story and themes are revealed through notes and messages left for the player, and I think the pacing was good. That's all I'll say on the topic for fear of spoiling anything. I enjoyed the level design, as each location felt unique.
My only complaint would be that the controls are a little clunky, as you have to both click on the navigation arrows to move and use the mouse to look around, which can make moving and looking awkward sometimes. I feel like this game would work better as your typical wasd-move, mouse-look walking simulator, but the game is short enough that this small complaint really isn't much of an issue.
I finished it in about an hour of playtime, and am satisfied with my onetime playthough. In my opinion, this game has little replay value, as after finishing the game and getting one ending, you can hit Continue on the main menu to get right back to the final choice and see the other ending. That being said, I do plan on playing this game again with my friends because I think they would enjoy it.

The game is great. It's definitely a good game. The best survival game that exists. It's highly realistic, unforgiving, and extremely immersive. There are multiple difficulties to choose from and tons of areas to explore. While there's no super in-depth end game right now, the beginning is great. Also, the atmosphere is superb. It feels truly lonely, very cold, and, in a sort of magical way, daunting and haunting.
However, there are some problems with Hinterland, the company that made The Long Dark. They're notoriously unresponsive and secretive. They also have a huge tendency to lock threads on both the community forums and on Reddit whenever people get in debates about the game's development or when someone calls out the company's poor PR and development cycle. When criticisms are brought about faults in the game or with the company, they typically completely disregard them and get highly defensive. Then they lock the threads and their reasoning is, every time without fault, "We feel this thread has contributed all it could. Locking it." This is censorship.
The company has, multiple times, made promises. They said, for sure, they were releasing the game back in 2016 and then the date passed and no official release. This is important, because the official release includes Story Mode - the big selling point of the trailers - and people have been wanting this for ages.
Now. Recently, they made a mysterious counter on their website that was counting down, I believe, for a few weeks. Prior to this, for the last few months, they've been completely silent - except for locking threads or giving vague responses to, what I assume they would classify as 'tame' questions. Beyond that, they haven't released a single update for five months.
So, here we have this company, who has broken promises, has had their game in development for years, and effectively censors their community.
But the game is great.
So, I, despite my resent toward Hinterland,must advise you, that, if you're looking for a game without a storyline, but some solid gameplay, but not looking to expect anything from the creators of the game, then I would purchase The Long Dark. To me, it's effectively DayZ in terms of development, but with the quality of gameplay you would expect out of a AAA studio.
If you know how the game plays right now and you're happy with it, and you're content with it not changing, then I would buy The Long Dark. If you're looking for a good deal of progress and development from an accepting company who respects their buyers, then you probably don't want to involve yourself. Also, be careful on the forums and on Reddit. People can get pretty nasty there, both the critics and the defenders of the game.

Project Zomboid is a fast paced, tense, dramatic zombie survival game, with a unqiue and interesting graphic design. The game is basically a "2D" dayz, with a lot less walking. Featuring a large map, however with the art style and graphic design you can see a much larger area and so have a lot more freedom and ability to travel to interesting places. The 2D graphics are a lot like marmite, you either hate it, or you love it, it's almost like a mix of mario and pacman, however don't let that decieve you, the graphics work with the gameplay brilliantly. I suspect that one of the biggest deterents for people looking to buy this game is the graphics, and I highly suggest you to try it out regardless.
The setting for the game is brilliant. The Map features two medium-sized towns which have a wide diversity to them. Both towns feature numerous houses and interested buildings, ranging from convenient shops, to bars, schools, resturants and office blocks. Each building offers various different gameplay aspects and challenges. For example, one perticular officer block is two storey and features a balcony. Myself and some friends set up defensive points in each of the smaller offices in the second floor, and blockaded ourselves on the balcony. As soon as a horde of zombies came our way, we'd all leap into our own personalised office room, kitted out with all our favourite equipment and defenses, and all hunkered down taking out a group of zombies each. This was just one of the varying kinds of gameplay that myself and my friends have come across purely from setting our base up in a different building.
The controls at first are a bit choppy, just moving your character around can be difficult for your first play, let alone fighting off numerous zombies, and the combat at best is rough. With no real way to vary your attacks and from the attack being almost random there are moments when I felt like shouting at my computer screen.
Another downside when it comes to combat and just the entire game, though in some ways it made it more realistic, is the vision arc. When playing witha group of friends as soon as I turn past a certain angle, all of my friends are gone, and suddenly I'm panicking, if I look away for more than three seconds, I loose them. I guess that this is realistic, but It just got more annoying then being a cool feature, in my opinion.
Overall, this games graphics are actually really unique, the gameplay and the maps are very fun and varying. The character creation is just downright brilliant and the game becomes fifty times better when you're playing with friends.
Alone it's kind of boring, the gameplay's choppy and the vision is annoying after more than five seconds. I'd highly suggest you buy this game for yourself and your friends, it's worth it when you play together.
Protip: Get it. You won't regret it.

HALF-LIFE: BLUE SHIFT<
The third installment in the half-life series is once again the progeny of valve teaming with gearbox. It brought fewer new elements into the game than the previous two and wasn't well acclaimed by fans. The game upon release on steam suffers from bugs caused by the engine changing and various other things. The game was also originally supposed to be an exclusive for the doomed Sega Dreamcast. The plot takes place during the events of half-life and Instead of playing as gordon freeman, you play as the ordinary watchman Barney Calhoun(the one you see banging on the door in the beginning of half-life). The story also features some new faces not yet seen in the series.
PROS:
-The story is very well paced and put together very nicely. You play as Barney Calhoun during the cascade and cover up operation in black mesa. Not spoiling the rest in case you haven't picked up a copy in the 20 years its existed.
-The environment is very immersive as it is a long seamless road to the end of the game with, as the definition of seamless implies, zero cutscenes or immersion breaking interruptions.
-The gunplay involves the same weapons from half-life with no new additions. The arsenal available is pleasently loud, very powerful feeling, and quite fun to use when eliminating the enemy.
-The ending is great for what it is
-Has an HD reskin to give a fresh coat of paint.
CONS: (Not even half-life is safe from sin, sorry) Please note that i am extremely aware that this game is an oldy.
-Controls feel floaty and thats not very great to say when this game is a puzzle platformer.
-Same issues as the original, guns feel not very effective at some times and very effective at others. No idea whats going on here but it hasn't deterred me from playing.
-Unlike the other half-life games before this one, this installment is the buggiest out of the bunch. Plentiful missed triggers and some doors not opening like they should all throughout the entirety of the game. Buy at ones own risk.
This game isn't a must have unlike the original but usually it comes bundled with it so give it a play(used to come free). I picked the entire series up in a frantic buy in a summer sale and it was worth it. if anything it's textures for gmod if you don't have much interest in it. With the bugs still not being fixed to this very day we have the second lowest score out of all half-life games that i'll be giving out.
6 blue vests out of 10

The game is very much available elsewhere but hasn't had an offical release on steam. Only thing i can do is go overtime on this one and plant my review here. DOUBLE REVIEW.

A great survival/resource management game, but it suffers from being too easy and lacking content.
At the beginning of the game, there is a challenge to kickstarting your colony, but once you have a steady food supply, it becomes very easy. There are only two uncontrollable threats in the game, fire and disease. One is solved by placing water wells around your colony, the other by having a hospital. There's nothing locked behind research, everything is available from the get go.
It's not a bad game, but because nothing new ever happens, it's quite boring. There's enjoyment to be had by creating a large colony, but that's really it. If you look at the Steam achievements for the game you will see that they're all based around having a large colony (300+ residents), because that's all you really have to do.
And because of the lack of content, I'm going to have to not recommend the game, except for a price you consider acceptable for around
. You can push yourself further, but that's only if you really like building a settlement up.
The one bonus that I haven't properly explored is the Steam Workshop for the game. But most of them are just reskins of buildings, but if you enjoy building, you have more variety available from the workshop.
