Tropico 5 is a very good game.
Pros:
They have made the economy much harder to manage. In Tropico 4 it was just make some sugar farms and you were set.
The era system has also been managed very well, new challenges come with every era and also new buildings, edicts and technologies...
The tech tree adds a whole new perspective the game.
You now have a Constitution where you can change different laws such as voting rights and immigration.
Uprisings, Coups and especially invasions are now a real threat that has to be dealt with, In Tropico 4, foreign invasion never really threatened me at all.
Better combat systems.
Tasks actually have a meaning late-game
The new trade system allows you to sell specific items to a nation of your choice at a higher price to normal.
The swiss bank account actually means something now rather than something you can feel bad about as you earn twice as much money as the country does,
Cons:
You can't control any of your units you just have to hope for the best that they arrive at the combat zone.
Economy is extremely hard to manage late game as more and more buildings are built.
You can't activate martial law and have a happy military. The military loyalty is determined by the people's happiness, meaning that if you issue martial law,ironically, the military will probably start a coup.
Teamsters and Construction workers are extremely slow, and if you put a building on low priority forget about it. I was looking around for any oil deposits and I saw a corn plantation on low priority still being built from the Colonial era.
It literally takes a year to get some wood from one side of the island to the other.
Almanac has been simplified, The economy page only tells you your expenses and revenue, no detail of income or expenditure.
Budgets make a large bustling city cost you $1000 a second.
Overall:
8/10
P.S: At the end penultimo blames the Illuminati.

All in all, I HIGHLY reccomend this game for all, as long as you're willing to die a lot and learn from it.

This is the first review I'll be leaving about a game I have actually not gotten around to playing yet. Little hard to when I have so many others I'm still working on, not to mention, the little time I have to play games, busy updating mods I have made or taken over for other titles. The reason for this review? Check the forums for Edge Of Space and it screams plenty. If you want a game like this, but with support and modability, huge forum, and game play where after spending 100 hours on it, you havent scratched the content? Then buy Starbound. Want a game thats incomplete, crashes, or just don't care losing $15 to $40? Then buy Edge Of Space. I bought it for $4.50 to tinker with if I ever get bored with my other games, and that has not happened.
I visited the forums a few times for Edge Of Space, and the complaints are in the thousands. It's bad enough when I hear of adults getting scammed, but to see how many kids lost their money for a game that had showed promise, and then the dev ran off, thats just wrong.
As of this review, 4 new price deals are now showing. $14.99 standard edition, $24.99 Special Edition.( If there is no one writing code for this game, how on earth can special content be added? it can't! You get the same incomplete game at $14.99 or $24.99) Then there is the 4-pack for $39.99. The last one, Special Edition upgrade $11.99. Zero Times Zero = Zero. Zero + Zero = 0.
As I said before, the games been at $4.50 for a long time. Anyone could have gotten 10 copies for $45.00. Guess the company figured no one would notice a 70% price increase for the holidays.
When I bought this title for $4.50, I already read the complaints not just in the reviews, but the forums as well. If you just want something to tinker with, I suggest waiting till the price drops back to $4.50 or less, or even one of those 90% coupons.
This is not one of those titles where trolls are leaving negative reviews because updates are slow in coming. It's because the people who started this game, just left. Three years ago. Had you clicked the developer link before Steam had updated the game client, you would have gotten a page not found.
Seems the Publisher has no issue of taking peoples money, their link is still active.
Anyway, if I ever get the time, I will update this with information about what game play is possible. Christmas is just around the corner. There are so Many games like this, but MUCH better. Some are early access (EA) some not. I highly recommend Spacebound, Terraria, Dig or Die, Crea, Planet Centauri, Signs Of Life, and Wayward (Small multi-player game but still fun, and cheap too!) All the games I suggested, are either completed or still getting improved but very playable and very little or no bugs at all. Bioshock:
+ There is a really engaging story in Bioshock with a twist that you won't expect. Audio logs which supplement the plotline can be found by exploring the environment and are a welcome addition. The game is set in the underwater city of Rapture and follows two men who struggle for power - Andrew Ryan, leader of the famous Ryan Industries and Frank Fontaine.
+ There are quite a few weapons that can be upgraded, like crossbows, shotguns, pistols, the Tommy Gun, grenade launchers and a chemical thrower which fires liquid nitrogen, napalm and electric gel.
+ A key part of Bioshock is the use of Plasmids, genetic abilities which can freeze enemies solid, incinerate or electrocute them. Unleash a swarm of killer insects or create a decoy target to draw fire away from you. There's many options here.
+ To add greater complexity there are tonics which improve your skills in countless ways. Physical tonics add healing benefits and eve restoration (eve is required to cast plasmids), engineering tonics are crucial to hacking safes, door combinations, gun turrets, vending machines and cameras. Then you've got combat tonics for physical damage resistance.
+ The characters are interesting, the shooting is great, basically it's fun which is the most important pro.

I played Evolve during the beta, and enjoyed the game immensely. Enough for me to drop money on the largest package. The game was stable, the gameplay was fun, and I wasn't turned off by the pricing model like a lot of others.
Giving you a review from someone that actually OWNS the game (which I think should be a requirement) I can say that Evolve has launched without any server issues, a stable client, and the same gameplay I enjoyed during beta. I guess I've grown accustomed to pricing models that include a la carte costmetic items.
NOTHING in Evolve, aside from pre-order bonuses or cosmetic skins, cannot be simply unlocked through several hours of gameplay. There is a LOT of arm-flailing about how the DLC is sold for this game, and I think much of it is completely unwarranted. A good bit of it is simply untrue. There is nothing at launch that DLC or pre-order owners get that is beyond cosmetic. DLC owners have pre-purchased in advance unreleased monsters and hunters that will come down the line. Otherwise, players will need to buy those new hunters or monsters through the in-game store.
If you buy the base game and nothing else you'll have access to 3 monsters, 12 hunters, and plenty of gameplay to keep you entertained. The beta included only the skirmish mode, which was a single-map experience of monsters vs hunters. The real meat of the game is in Evacuation mode, where you'll play 5 different maps each with 5 different play-modes.
All in all it's a shame that the marketing and pricing model will harm Evolve, because Turtle Rock Studios put a lot of love into the game with a concept built upon the success of Left 4 Dead.

Rituals is very lovely little game that really surprised me. If you like point & click games, I can definitely recommend this game to you, but I think it can be enjoyable even for people who are not very big fans of point & click games - like myself. So, let's talk about few things.
Let's start by movement, which is slightly unusual. While the whole game is in 3D, you don't actually move by WSAD keys like you would probably expect. You are moving by clicking on white direction arrows instead. So, you could say the game is on "rails", kind of. This whole moving system looked weird from videos and screens, but it's actually a really nice idea once you get used to it.
What about puzzles? Well, there are some puzzles in almost every level, but don't expect anything that will really challenge you, because all puzzles are pretty simple and straightforward. Which is nice, if you want a game where you won't get stuck. But if you're looking for something challenging, this is probably not the right game for you.
The whole game uses very lovely low-poly graphic style, which is obvious from screenshots. I'm sucker for low-poly, so I absolutely loved it. There is just something very adorable about it. The whole low-poly style is very well executed and colors were picked really well. It's very simple, but it works!
Story is mostly told by gameplay and it's up to you to figure it out. There are some hidden notes expanding the story, but most of it is up to you and your imagination. If I had to describe it without any spoilers, I would probably say that you will find out WHAT happened, but it's up to you to figure out HOW it happened. I would also say that there are some major themes going on, especially environmentalism and existential crisis. Sounds good to you? It is!
What else is there to say? Don't expect some huge soundtrack, because the game uses only minimal sounds and music while you're playing. It's also pretty short game overall. If you play without any guides, you will probably take hour - hour and half to beat it. But if you wanted to finish it as quickly as possible, it would probably take 10 - 15 minutes. It's pretty short. Achivement hunters will be pleased, though, because achievements are very easy to get and it shouldn't take more than 2 hours to 100% this game, if you're playing legit. If you're not, then it will take significantly shorter time.
Overall, I really liked this game, its theme, its atmosphere and its graphic  style. I'm not very big fan of point and click games, but I really enjoyed this one. It's very simple, short and maybe even relaxing. If that sounds good to you, then you should definitely get it, you won't regret it!

This game isn't bad by any means. It's just nothing special.
GAMEPLAY: Click on-screen arrow buttons to move around like the adventure games of yore (think Myst), hold click and move mouse to look around. I'm not sure why this style was chosen, other than to perhaps give players a clearer indication as to where they should be going. But with as simplistic an art style as it has, combined with the ease of its puzzles and the games' short length, this isn't a necessary helping hand. It's not a detriment, nor is it a benefit either. You will primarly be walking around exploring, and otherwise, solving some simple puzzles (I'm hesitant to use that word, as it's mostly just plugging in items into the correct place). No combat to be had here.
VISUALS: Simple, cell-shaded, with lots of colour and fairly minimal detail. It looks nice, and again serves to highlight where you need to go.
AUDIO: Nothing to write home about. There's a general lack of music, no voice acting (aside from some background whispers at one point), and there's very little in the way of exciting events. You'll mostly be hearing footsteps and item uses.
STORY: There's a bit of a narrative to be uncovered here, which has an interesting premise (to do with man's relationship to nature, especially as it pertains to destructive elements) but it's not given much time to be fleshed out. Now I usually hate saying a game is too short, as it leads to games being too long (a much worse outcome), but this is a case where more time would have benefited the message it was trying to convey. Just as I thought I was beginning to see what it was trying to tell me, the game ended, and the connection I felt with its message was cut short.
If you think the premise sounds neat or you want an hour and a half romp around some colourful environments, you could do worse than Rituals. I would advise picking it up on sale though, due to its length and lack of replay value.

No matter what they showed you in the trailer this is a point and click game that is completely linear, with minor elements of exploration. What made this title unique came from its distinctive art direction with low poly models and absent textures. Honestly, it’ll either come off as cheap or classic to you, I personally found it charming since it reminded me of titles such as Little Big Adventure and Ecstatica.
In terms of movement and controls you are railroad to predetermined paths, with little leeway for side areas, but you can adjust the camera angle in first person view and inspect your surroundings in any way you like, so that was a slight variation to the old formula.
As for major themes and plot, you can expect the subject of environmentalism, existential crisis and social unease to be touched upon. However, the game seemed to juggle them around a lot and never making up its mind on which to serve centrally. While the plot may rub off differently to everyone, it came off as a little cheesy to me, but it was enjoyable as a whole in experience.
Lastly, just as other reviewers have said, this title can be completed in around an hour. If you decided to take the plunge without a guide, the length can be stretch to 2-3 hours, depending on how eager you’re on obtaining every achievement. I’ll recommend this if you happened to find this on sale, but you better hold onto the cash if it was in full asking price.

Games like "The Park" make me envision a future where storytelling will be entirely virtual and interactive.  I just finished my first playthrough and am very impressed with the results. The time I spent with the game was not wasted, and I truly enjoyed my experience with it.
That being said, I want to give a realistic review for those of you who may not be as ravenous for truly unnerving horror yarns as I am.
The most glaring issue for me is the difficulty I had reading the notes. I really cant justify sitting super close to the TV just to read something, and I feel like I missed out on the story, which was pretty good when I could understand it. The writing has a very Silent Hill 2 vibe to it and I hope that in subsequent playthroughs I will get to see different choices lead to different endings, since the one I got was pretty dark.
The graphics are actually pretty impessive, but I couldn't find a zoom option to really inspect things up close.  in an exploration and story game,  being able to see things up close and personal really helps with the immersion factor. Speaking of immersion, the camera-bob in "The Park" is pretty weak. A little time researching real measurements of movement for the human head would be a very well spent weekend, you know, like for a future update maybe?
Overall, the game is one of the better offerings, and in a horror landscape that is stuffed with the so called "slender-clones" and poorly thought out indie cash grabs, "The Park" is well above average. Priced at about the cost of a movie ticket, you receive a virtual movie that interacts with you and your friends, every halloween! (or any other time you're in a spooky mood!)
My Humble Opinion: B+

I played this late at night in the dark with headphones as suggested and it is a pretty dark and spooky game.
It's a little slow at the start, especially with the first park ride, but this improves after you get further in. There are some jump scares along the way, but once you become invested in the story I found the anticipation of what was at the end of the journay was what was driving the dark themes of this game.
The game is set in Atlantic Island Park, a location from The Secret World. You do not need to have played that game to understand this one, but there are a huge number of references to characters, locations, and events from TSW so someone who has played the MMO will have a different experience from someone who hasn't. Also, there is a companion mission to The Park now live in The Secret World and playing The Park and then The Seven Silences mission enhances the story significantly.
The graphics are much improved over The Secret World as The Park uses a different game engine and the game performance was strong. There were some very slight hitches in the gameplay, probably caused by background loading that were noticible. This happened about 4-5 times to me.
The sound was great, spooky as expected. The creepy voice on the loudspeakers is a nice touch. You think he is saying something important but no matter how hard you listed you can't quite make out the words.
Gameplay was basic as this is pretty much a by the rails game where you follow one path. Left button actives stuff, right button calls out to Callum and also highlights objects you can interact with. Shift sprints. That's about it for controls, very basic but fitting to the game.
It's a short game, under 2 hours for me and that's exploring everything. One hint is to read everything you find AND if you revist a location or your perspective of that location changes then read everything again as the stuff you've just read may have changed.
I would recommend this game to all TSW players, and you should probably play this before you play Halloween mission in TSW to understand the full story. If you haven't played TSW you can still play this with no issues but you won't understand some of the easter eggs.
Rating.
7/10 if you haven't played TSW
9/10 if you play TSW AND do The Seven Silences mission over Halloween.

310 hours dedicated to this game so far and growing! This game has been one of the most entertaining and immersive games I've played yet and this is just the sandbox. I can only imagine what the final, released version will be like with the story included! This review for now will focus on the early access version of the game.
I can't think of any other games like it. A quiet apocolypse has taken place, technology as we know it is gone. The lights went out, never to return. How long can you survive against nature and everything it has to throw at you? There are no zombies. There are no mutants or aliens. Just you, nature and the need to survive. Scavenge what you can from the abandoned regions, hunt for food and find a warm place to spend the night. Just be aware that beyond the safety of your fireglow, green eyes flash in darkness, waiting for you to give them a chance to send you into the long dark. No one is coming to save you, so you'd best be ready to save yourself.
Features:
=======
+No Zombies, no supernatural, no aliens, no occult! Just nature, and it's brutally unforgiving.
+ A gorgeous art style fairly reminiscent of the Group of Seven. Iconic, refreshing and engaging, it's a nice break from photorealism and proof that games can be beautiful and immersive without being overly heavy on realism.
+ Four modes of difficulty with vastly different challenges for all types.
+ Crafting of the basic survival needs, like torches and bows, and animal skin clothing
+ Survival simulation with a unnervingly believable feel. Monitor your temperature, hunger, thirst and energy levels. Think carefully about your food choices and plan your routes carefully. even a small injury could lead to much worse if left ignored.
+ Challenge modes for those who work better under pressure. Added in the newest update, these challenge modes give seasoned players a few scenarios to complete. Originally there were only 2 but it has since grown to 5.
+Comfortably playable with Mouse and Keyboard or with a controller.
+Extremely well done voiceovers for the basic sandbox characters.
+An out of this world sound experience. Every little sound you hear, from the wind in the trees to the clattering of old shutters, has a purpose and has been meticulously planned. A crow flying overhead may alert you to an approaching storm, a strange clang or clatter in a whiteout can point the way to safety. A growl in the darkness can sound your doom.  All of this atmospheric and immersive sound is punctuated by music tracks that serve to elevate the feel of the moment. Rather than play constantly in the background, these short musical interludes kick in to emphasize something and just as quickly fade out again. (The coming of night, the sun rising, A particularly lonely place, or a Change of weather.)
+The game offers no hand-holding. You are dropped in the world and left to figure it out. You will die many times before it starts to make sense, but each time you fail, you get a better idea of how you can apply what you've learned to the next run.
It should be noted that the only real drawback aside fomr the learning curve to the game is the fact that death is permanent. When you die you start again from the beginning, but even that makes for good compelling gameplay as it pushes you to be more careful about how you go about your survival.
Early access means the game is still undergoing serious developement, but even in this current form, it's hard to believe it's an alpha. It's polished and professional with smooth gameplay and challenge that's well worth the full price. If you like sandbox/survival games, this is a great choice. If you like to simply play the game at your own pace and observe the quiet apocolypse, this game is still a great choice. And when story mode releases, I am certain those who like to play games for the storyline will also love it too. Hinterland is making a great first impression with The Long Dark.
A solid 8/10, most likely a 10 once it hits release.

The game is great. It's definitely a good game. The best survival game that exists. It's highly realistic, unforgiving, and extremely immersive. There are multiple difficulties to choose from and tons of areas to explore. While there's no super in-depth end game right now, the beginning is great. Also, the atmosphere is superb. It feels truly lonely, very cold, and, in a sort of magical way, daunting and haunting.
However, there are some problems with Hinterland, the company that made The Long Dark. They're notoriously unresponsive and secretive. They also have a huge tendency to lock threads on both the community forums and on Reddit whenever people get in debates about the game's development or when someone calls out the company's poor PR and development cycle. When criticisms are brought about faults in the game or with the company, they typically completely disregard them and get highly defensive. Then they lock the threads and their reasoning is, every time without fault, "We feel this thread has contributed all it could. Locking it." This is censorship.
The company has, multiple times, made promises. They said, for sure, they were releasing the game back in 2016 and then the date passed and no official release. This is important, because the official release includes Story Mode - the big selling point of the trailers - and people have been wanting this for ages.
Now. Recently, they made a mysterious counter on their website that was counting down, I believe, for a few weeks. Prior to this, for the last few months, they've been completely silent - except for locking threads or giving vague responses to, what I assume they would classify as 'tame' questions. Beyond that, they haven't released a single update for five months.
So, here we have this company, who has broken promises, has had their game in development for years, and effectively censors their community.
But the game is great.
So, I, despite my resent toward Hinterland,must advise you, that, if you're looking for a game without a storyline, but some solid gameplay, but not looking to expect anything from the creators of the game, then I would purchase The Long Dark. To me, it's effectively DayZ in terms of development, but with the quality of gameplay you would expect out of a AAA studio.
If you know how the game plays right now and you're happy with it, and you're content with it not changing, then I would buy The Long Dark. If you're looking for a good deal of progress and development from an accepting company who respects their buyers, then you probably don't want to involve yourself. Also, be careful on the forums and on Reddit. People can get pretty nasty there, both the critics and the defenders of the game.

Do you like game 'Don't Starve'? Do you wish it had zombies, guns and Baldur's Gate style graphics? Your wish is answered with Project Zomboid.
Project Zombid is a zombie apocalypse survival game that simulates things such as thirst, hunger, panic, boredom, depression/happiness, temperature, and more. The damage system is detailed: maybe that scratch on your arm can be bandaged and you'll be fine... but maybe you're infected.
It has extensive crafting options (got a baseball bat? Great. Got some nails and a hammer? Now you can make a nailbat, and so forth), for long term survival you can even grow crops, go fishing and collect rainwater, after the utilities inevitably (but unpredictably) go out and the food in all those fridges you've been raining begins to rot (barring canned soup, potato chips and other non-perishables.) You can find a variety of weapons to fight the zombie hoardes, from lowly kitchen fare such as spoons, forks and rolling pins, to shovels, fire axes and of course guns (which will invariably attract most of the zombies within earshot).
You can barricade windows and doors so that they take longer to break down. You can build entire structures, even join up abandoned rooftops with wooden platforms. You've got to get your own timber by cutting down trees and sawing them into boards, or simply demolishing existing structures with a sledgehammer.
You can lure zombies into an abandoned restaurant, turn the ovens on and then lock the doors, knowing that the building will burn down before they manage to break free - or do it the quick way, and douse it in some gasoline if you can find it.
The map is massive, with plenty of spots to try and get away from it all by setting up a farm plot with some sturdy fences, or perhaps you'll prefer to barricade a local mall, a supply-filled warehouse or a police station.
The best part is that, though it's still fully functional and entirely captivating, the game is still in development - it's been on Steam Early Access for more than a year, and many more features are planned. Development progress reports are released weekly and game updates usually around once a month or sooner.

At the beginning of the game, there is a challenge to kickstarting your colony, but once you have a steady food supply, it becomes very easy. There are only two uncontrollable threats in the game, fire and disease. One is solved by placing water wells around your colony, the other by having a hospital. It's not a bad game, but because nothing new ever happens, it's quite boring. There's enjoyment to be had by creating a large colony, but that's really it. If you look at the Steam achievements for the game you will see that they're all based around having a large colony (300+ residents), because that's all you really have to do.

I have been playing this game for about 7 months - I picked it up around Halloween last year. My interest in games tends to go in short bursts, but this game has largely sustained my interest the whole time. The developers are doing an excellent job tuning and improving the game, and I love the direction it's going in. I've only ever played a couple of Early Access games before, but I have never seen a development team so active and involved in the community.
Now onto the game experience. It's absolutely beautiful. Watching the videos gives you an idea, but you can't imagine what this game looks like watching the sun rise from the top of a snowy mountain until you've climbed the mountain yourself. Truly the most beautiful game I've ever played - and the replay value is huge. I've started countless new games and even if I try to do things in the same sequence, it's a different game. I love the mechanics of the game and the way things are going. There's something inherently satisfying about stumbling through a blizzard, almost losing hope, and then you see the outline of a cabin poking through the whiteout.
I play games because I like learning the ropes, being challenged, and mastering new skills - and Hinterland keeps that experience going. I've been playing for 7 months, 150 hours, and there are still parts of the game I've never seen, things I've never done, achievements I haven't reached. My playthroughs have lasted anywhere from 1 day to over 100 days, but even the short ones are satisfying.
This game has been worth the money and then some. I can't wait to see what the developers do with it in the future - and I think this game has a bright future. I'm glad I've been along for the ride.

SUPERHOT is the most innovative shooter I've plaed in years!
It's an in joke for those fortunate enough to have played through SUPERHOT. Yes, its a great game.  Refreshing to play a game that does something new with the mechanics as it seems there are so few of those games.  Think Hotline Miami in First Person, then add a time control mechanic (time only moves when YOU move) and it gives you a pretty good idea of the game play.
There is a clever little narative that ties the handful of levels together which becomes quite fascinating. If it were not for the sheer enjoyment of playing through each stage, the story does have enough clout to propel you through the game.
Unfortunately it is very short, which saying is the only real downside, speaks volumes for the quality of Superhot. I clocked in about 4.5 hours and that included the main campaign plus the majority of challenge modes and speed runs that unlock when you beat the game.  The challenges are repeats of the stages in the main game but with twists on the rules. Its fun, but ultimately draws thin after effectively playing through the game multiple times.   Hopefully there will be some additional content released.
The is a meta old school hacking vibe that lets you explore the files on the computer your character is using. There are some real weird and wonderful things to find if you dig around enough. My personal favourite was logging in to a forum and watching a conversation unfold over 15 minutes!
In short then. Absolutely recommended. Just be prepared for it to end before you would like it to.

Overall, this is not an awful game. The story, while somewhat predictable, is decent and the dialogue well-written. Unfortunately, numerous setbacks keep The Park from being something I'd recommend. If you're looking for a horror-type experience, I think you'll find Outlast or even Slender: The Arrival to be better.
My initial experience with the game was less than positive. It took numerous crashes and several Ctrl+Alt+Dels before I managed to get past the main menu and start the game. As far as the game itself goes, there was definitely some things to like. I thought the right-click to shout for your son was a nice feature. The atmosphere is overall well done, but unfortunately short-lived. The game is easily less than two hours long. If you examine everything you might be able to stretch it out to just over two hours.
The gameplay itself could have severely benefited from more depth. I understand that this is supposed to be a story and not gameplay driven experience, but the term "walking simulator" absolutely applies here. I would have liked to see some puzzle-solving elements, or even just ability to toggle the flashlight would have added something. Better yet, since this is not a gameplay driven experience, instead offer more areas to explore rather than the linear path the player is forced to follow. As for the fear factor, anybody with any tolerance for horror games will be left unmoved.
The Park is not terrible, and it definitely makes for a decent experience, but it does not justify it's price of $12.99 at the time of writing. I picked it up on sale for $10.00, and I still feel as though that was too much. I think for a 1.5 hour game such as this, one that has no replay value whatsoever, $5.00 would be a more appropriate price.

OK. So to be completely clear, I have been playing The Secret World since launch, and bought three copies of this game within 10 minutes of it's availability. So this review is not exactly coming from an unbiased perspective.
To start with the mechanics, it was nice and simple. Movement plus three buttons. The right-mouse-click to call for Callum worked well both as a story device and a mechanic to point you to things, however I did feel that it was a little hard to know if you'd missed something sometimes. I would occassionally find myself using it several times, just to make sure I hadn't missed anything. The only other thing I would say about this is that the scraps of paper found in the game were very hard to read. I had to move to about half distance away from my monitor to have any chance of reading it at all.
Moving onto the world. If Funcom proved one thing with The Secret World (they proved lots more than one thing), then it is that they can make a beautiful world to play in. With three years and a different game engine, the awesomeness has only gotten better. I was playing with max graphics settings, and it was really awesome. It wasn't just the visuals though. The audio environment created by Simon Poole was brilliant. I regularly found myself spinning around to look for something I thought was creeping up behind me. I knew that there was nothing there, but I thought there was enough to look. AKA: Brilliant. I remember seeing one instance of a spark passing through a solid wall, but beyond that, I felt it was flawless.
Lastly, the story. I don't want to say too much here, because spoilers. However, I finished the games with several questions. On the most over-arching scale, I found myself questioning which parts were the dark reality of the park, and which were Lorraine's 'reality'. To be clear, I think this is a good thing. I'm also not sure of the whole story of Steve, but I suspect that's because I missed something, though it does also get looked at in The Secret World.
Overall, I loved the game. I had no problem with the story, way less than no problem with the world, and only a couple of issues the mechanics. I will be playing again, no question asked. Would totally recommend this for others.

EDIT: Wow, things have changed since I left my original review, and unfortunately all for the worse.
I used to love this game. Unfortunately, the developers have consistently made such poor decisions that they've completely ruined their own game. There used to be a wonderful UI that was absolutely perfect for the gameplay style. Over time, update after update made the UI more obtuse and unfriendly and slow and tedious and counter-intuitive. The way the UI in this game has digressed can and should be used in game design classes as the perfect example of what not to do.
Aside from the absolutely horrendous UI decisions (which nearly all the EA players hated from the get-go and still hate), the devs have God complex disease like so many devs in the last decade or so. They have a "vision" for the game, so they don't really care much whether 95% of the players hate a new change to the game. As long as it fits their "vision," they're happy even if all the actual players aren't. For a long time I thought the devs actually cared about their community, but it's become clear over time that they were just biding their time to become cruel dictators and they didn't want to disturb EA players too much while we were providing valuable data to help them finish their story mode. Once they had enough data, they stopped listening to the community virtually overnight, it was a very black-and-white change in their decision making.
Anyway, the story mode is something that 0 people have enjoyed, but somehow they managed to take something like 4 years to release it. A big part of that is because sandbox mode became such a hit that the devs were forced to admit that it was worth improving, which they did slowly for a couple years. For a long part of that process, the sandbox mode kept getting better and better, to the point where I wrote my original glowing review below.
Then as soon as most of the community liked the sandbox mode, the changes started. It was as if the devs wrote down a list of everything the die-hard players enjoyed and systematically ruined each element one-by-one. I can't imagine how someone could build such a wonderful game and then turn around and ruin it in inches over the course of about 1 year. It's like the devs are bipolar or something.
To sum up my new edit to this review, I no longer play this game at all and it used to be one of my top 10 of all time. That's a pretty terrible "progression" to a game's development if you ask me. I haven't played story mode, but I read through about 100 reviews and there were 0 people saying good things about it, so I don't feel any urge to try it out. I would not recommend this game because 80% of the things I used to love about it are now gone, leaving only memories and an empty shell of a game that could have been legendary. It's sad to see such a tragic waste of potential, but the only way to get a great experience from this game is to have played it about 2 years ago in EA. If they ever add mod support and someone rolls the UI/gameplay back to the point just before the radial menu was released, I'd gladly play it again. Otherwise, no way.
NOTE: This review is being written for sandbox mode/challenge mode only. Story mode has not yet been released.
I love survival as a theme. I love it in books, movies, television shows, games--wherever. The thing is, most surival games are terrible. They're generally first person shooters with loose "survival" elements that feel tacked-on and far from immersive.
After really wanting to find a good survival game, I finally spent about an hour looking at every game that showed up under the "survival" tag in the store. I saw The Long Dark as the game most likely to be what I was looking for, and it has far exceeded my hopes.
If you're looking for a survival simulator, this is not that. It's a game, and because of that it's not always realistic about available options etc. But a survival simulator would be incredibly boring imo because most of survival is sitting around doing nothing. The Long Dark is much more fun that than, I can assure you.
This game really rewards players for trying new things. The general reward for trying new things is a combination of death and new knowledge. I think the big mistake most players make is protecting their life too much and not taking enough risks. Learning to play this game involves dying a lot of times as you make mistakes. Then as your skills improve, you last longer and longer until eventually you get good enough so that you can last indefinitely.
Much like life, you get out of The Long Dark what you're willing to put into it. If you just huddle down in the first safe location you find, you'll never really get much better at the game and you'll be trapped in that play style until you die or get bored. This game is really a survival game with exploration being nearly as important as the survival element.
That said, the atmosphere in The Long Dark is one of isolation, lonliness, darkness, and a stark beauty that must be seen and experienced to be appreciated. The last game that had this type of impact on me was "Shadow of Colossus" because of the intense atmosphere and focus on exploration. I always wondered what it would have been like if they'd made another similar game without the battles in it.
To me, The Long Dark is a fantastic game that finds the perfect balance between exploration and survival. The new addition of challenge modes hints at a new element of challenge that will expand the game significantly in upcoming updates.
There are plenty of reviews of this game that go into the specifics, so I won't. But I will say this. I started playing video games in the mid-1980s and I've played well over a thousand games in my life so far. The Long Dark is one of my top 10 games overall, and that's an extremely difficult position for a game to achieve.
It's a game that grows on you. I liked it at first, but over the course of about a month I grew to love it, then become mildly obsessed with it. Now it has become the game I default to nearly every day when I'm not busy working etc. As you can see, I've put some decent hours in, so my experience has been deep enough to warrant writing a review in confidence that I've experienced it fully.
One of my favorite things about The Long Dark is the replay value. I've probably gotten $400 worth of fun from my little $20 purchase of this game and I couldn't be more happy about it.
I think the developers are fantastic in their ability to walk the razor's edge of making the game in their vision while also taking feedback from the community seriously. They've been very good about updates and hotfixes and are always expanding the game in ways that add more and more replay value as well as improving the overall experience.
I couldn't give The Long Dark a higher recommendation, it's truly one of the best games I've ever played.

tl;dr: Space Invaders, but you use your combo to power increasingly stronger and varied special weapons!
There's nuances, but every other mechanic complements that premise. For example, to make it easier to keep a combo (i.e. not miss) as you thin out the crowd, when you beat enough enemies in the current wave, you get a screen clear (the eponymous Hangeki) to move to the next. Also, if you do mess up and die or drop your combo, you do slow down, but you can get some of your gauge back by just getting the yellow thingies from clearing the current wave.
TIP: pick up the yellow bits that dead enemies drop! They're the actual gauge juice. Move around a lot: don't clear one column at a time, else you'll have to choose between picking them up and not missing shots (and your gauge drains when you're not comboing).
You equip four weapons (out of many unlockable ones) at the start of a stage, on top of your autofiring base gun. Your power gauge can fill multiple times, and more powerful weapons cost more gauges - they're worth using, as they'll usually destroy enough enemies to appropriately fill the gauge back up. You use the weapons that cost 1 gauge more often (at least when you're new), but it's exciting to strive to keep your combo up for just long enough to get to gauge 2, and even more as you get better at it!
Beating a stage or challenge gets you a new specific weapon to play with, and beating the par time on a stage gets you another weapon. Note that unlike many games with combos, it doesn't *force* you to keep a single huge combo from beginning to end of the stage - it just improves your time overall, there's no all-or-nothing score multipliers.
I haven't fully grasped some mechanics, and the acceleration on your ship is a little weird for such a frantic game (though you also get dodge buttons), but it really felt like I was playing something new!

What I like:
1. Pretty unique and carefully crafted environments. The whole world is huge and will give you dozens of hours of fun just to explore. Some players complain about the lack of maps, but don't worry: The maps are filled with memorable landmarks, each beautifully hand-crafter (lookouts, bridges, odd-shaped rocks, twisted trees, winding rivers...), and before you know it, you will remember.
2. Surprisingly realistic and reasonably challenging system of character's conditions: You will need to pay attention to your body temperature (keeping warm), your fatique (resting regularly), your hydration and your stomach (drinking and eating); beyond these general stats, the game also has a good system of injuries and health problems (food poisoning, bruising, bleeding) and a first aid system with natural as well as artifficial remedies (pain killers or herb tea, just to give an example).
3. Believable wildlife elements - currently, there are rabbits and deer as representatives of herbivores, and wolves and bears as predators. This even allows for a bit of a Rock-Paper-Scissors gameplay, where you can scare a deer to run towards a wolf, then the wolf catches and kills the deer, and then you shoot the wolf, thus getting two kills for one bullet.
4. Great weather and day and night systems. You may get caught by blizzards or travel against strong wind, or you may enjoy clean sky with chilling temperatures.
5. Nice crafting system. While this is not a crafting simulation, the 15+ items you can craft are all useful and add a sense of character progression. The moment when you are finally wrapped in animal furs from head to toe is pretty epic... until the next wolf attack tears half your clothing apart :-)
Highly recommended.

Project Zomboid Early Access (Build 27#1)
--------------------------------------------
Simply the best top down zombie survival horror game ever made with immense depth to craftable items, cooking, farming,  scavenging & looting, building & construct of bases. You will need to prepare for the utilities to shut off at any point, figure out how to craft a fire, maintain a constant water supply, locate seeds to plant & farm, hunt & trap game, fortify & barracade existing buildings or build your own base.
One bite/scratch is often all it takes & you yourself will become one of the undead. If this happens no worries though, just fire up a new character & continue in same game world, any bases built will still be there & you can even visit the zombified you and end their suffering. +100
Has multiple modes (Survival, Sandbox, Last stand, Multiplayer)
Survival - Survive for as long as you can in open sandbox world, the utilities (gas/electric) will go off soon & at any point.
Sandbox - Same as survival but allows for custom game preferences.  Changing the zombie lore (weaker/harder, faster/slower), changing the infection mortaility and transmission methods, reanimation speed & decomposition effects, enabling utilities gas/electric to stay on for anything upto 5 in game years.
Last Stand - Challenge mode - You alone in house must defend against the waves of zombified hordes.
Multiplayer - Not tried it as of writing so won't comment, the general concensus however seems overall positive.
If you are more interested in the base building aspects of this game rather than the survival then you may want to check out the NecroForge mod for PZ which is an in-game item spawner & then you can pick a spot and get building without worrying about supplies.
You may want to check out...
• Project Zomboid Map Project (Benjamin 'blindcoder' Schieder). Superb map thats gives a greater overall scope for you to plan your survival.
• The Project Zomboid Wiki over at
for information on all aspects of PZ from crafting to charcter building.
• The PZ mods such as NecroForge, Zspawn etc
Pro
----
Immense depth to craftable items
Massive game world (Will only get bigger nearer to full release)
Multiple game modes - Survival, Sandbox, Last stand, Multiplayer
NPC's are coming which will add even more depth to gameplay
If you come for a zombie horror or apocolypse base building simulator you won't be disappointed
Con
----
Needs a rotate ability - sometimes when base building I will find somthing I cannot destroy (Railings etc) as its behind another object or simply I'm just unable to select to destroy - could be mitigated easily with a rotate function.
Needs armour crafting out of stuff like phone books & duct tape, ice hockey gear etc.
Need more clothing items such as raincoats, wellies, thermals.
Needs power generator (siphon fuel from garage/car) or solar panels from houses that can be crafted into providing usable power for your base for fridges, lights.
Needs an mp3 or walkman that requires batteries, which when listened to will raise mood.
Needs a flaming samurai sword.
Build 27#1 Verdict - 9/10 (It will only get better)

310 hours dedicated to this game so far and growing! This game has been one of the most entertaining and immersive games I've played yet and this is just the sandbox. I can only imagine what the final, released version will be like with the story included! This review for now will focus on the early access version of the game.
I can't think of any other games like it. A quiet apocolypse has taken place, technology as we know it is gone. The lights went out, never to return. How long can you survive against nature and everything it has to throw at you? There are no zombies. There are no mutants or aliens. Just you, nature and the need to survive. Scavenge what you can from the abandoned regions, hunt for food and find a warm place to spend the night. Just be aware that beyond the safety of your fireglow, green eyes flash in darkness, waiting for you to give them a chance to send you into the long dark. No one is coming to save you, so you'd best be ready to save yourself.
Features:
=======
+No Zombies, no supernatural, no aliens, no occult! Just nature, and it's brutally unforgiving.
+ A gorgeous art style fairly reminiscent of the Group of Seven. Iconic, refreshing and engaging, it's a nice break from photorealism and proof that games can be beautiful and immersive without being overly heavy on realism.
+ Four modes of difficulty with vastly different challenges for all types.
+ Crafting of the basic survival needs, like torches and bows, and animal skin clothing
+ Survival simulation with a unnervingly believable feel. Monitor your temperature, hunger, thirst and energy levels. Think carefully about your food choices and plan your routes carefully. even a small injury could lead to much worse if left ignored.
+ Challenge modes for those who work better under pressure. Added in the newest update, these challenge modes give seasoned players a few scenarios to complete. Originally there were only 2 but it has since grown to 5.
+Comfortably playable with Mouse and Keyboard or with a controller.
+Extremely well done voiceovers for the basic sandbox characters.
+An out of this world sound experience. Every little sound you hear, from the wind in the trees to the clattering of old shutters, has a purpose and has been meticulously planned. A crow flying overhead may alert you to an approaching storm, a strange clang or clatter in a whiteout can point the way to safety. A growl in the darkness can sound your doom.  All of this atmospheric and immersive sound is punctuated by music tracks that serve to elevate the feel of the moment. Rather than play constantly in the background, these short musical interludes kick in to emphasize something and just as quickly fade out again. (The coming of night, the sun rising, A particularly lonely place, or a Change of weather.)
+The game offers no hand-holding. You are dropped in the world and left to figure it out. You will die many times before it starts to make sense, but each time you fail, you get a better idea of how you can apply what you've learned to the next run.
It should be noted that the only real drawback aside fomr the learning curve to the game is the fact that death is permanent. When you die you start again from the beginning, but even that makes for good compelling gameplay as it pushes you to be more careful about how you go about your survival.
Early access means the game is still undergoing serious developement, but even in this current form, it's hard to believe it's an alpha. It's polished and professional with smooth gameplay and challenge that's well worth the full price. If you like sandbox/survival games, this is a great choice. If you like to simply play the game at your own pace and observe the quiet apocolypse, this game is still a great choice. And when story mode releases, I am certain those who like to play games for the storyline will also love it too. Hinterland is making a great first impression with The Long Dark.
A solid 8/10, most likely a 10 once it hits release.

Great game.  Easy to sink hours into it without knowing.  Much of my time spent was trial and error trying to find the best strategy to get to the modern era.  Once you understand how to get to the modern era, the game really opens up.
Some things I notice people say about this game...
1) too hard, almost impossible
- It really is not.  There are plenty of strategies online to help you get started if you do not care to try the campaign/tutorial.  Not saying the campaign/tutorial are the most helpful, but I don't think the developers intended to spoonfeed people the knowledge of how-to-win in said modes.
2) terrible graphics, same as Tropico 4
- Ehh, to each his own.  Game looks incredible to me, running between 80-110fps @1440p.  Never played Tropico 4 so can't compare.
3) Tropico 4 is better.
- Have not played Tropico 4 so I can't really compare.  From what I've read, most people liked Tropico 4 better because it was way easier.
4) broken mechanics.  you lose everything when you move to a new era.
- No, you do not lose everything.  Some of your managers might lose their jobs (I think this is a thing), but you definitely do not lose everything.  I notice most people that hate this game do so because they don't understand how to succeed in each era and move onto the next.  There are multiple ways to do this but the key is knowing when to modernize and what to modernize.  Old houses/buildings need to be replaced with new ones to keep people happy.  If you have power available but don't build a plant, your approval rating will steadily decline; same goes for not supplying electricity to people.  Seems like a logical mechanic.
5) it's impossible to keep everyone happy.
- Well duh! That's how real life is too!  You have to attack your weakest stat, be it crime safety, religion, food, etc. at the right time in the right era, and that largely depends on your constitution and overall playing strategy.
6)DLC
- Totally optional.  Only Waterborne and Espionage add anything worth having and even then, the game is completely playable to the bitter end without any DLC.  The DLC does not make this game, period.

As a veteran SHMUP girl but also a casual player, I do recommend this game!
It's got retro graphics but it's intense, it's fun, and there's lots of weapons; even if someone isn't a top shooter, that person still will get even at least one weapon per stage cleared, adding lots of replay value. The further one goes and does well, the more he/she gets better weapons (like in Silpheed: The Lost Planet) and can edit up to four in prep for the next battle (Gradius)
The soundtrack has quite a catchy beat and is quite charming (like in Stage 3 on the Highway Zone, it's catchy!) as well as can get quite badass (like in Stage 2: the Supercell Area), and even up to how tense some bosses can be in familiar titles like Deathsmiles, Castle Shikigami, and Touhou (such as the final boss) adding a hint of sudden hard-rocking atmospheric music to a powerful climax of an opponent!
Speaking of which, the game has a fair difficuly curve as well, one can do quite well in the first few three stages and then it will challenge a/the pilot(s) of the Hangeki fighter(s) to how well he/she/they can fight. Stage 4 is where the action may kick up and become really exciting (in my oppinion).
Make sure to learn how to utilize the fighter's weapon settings well, as the hostiles will not hesitate to litter the screen with lasers and streams of bullets later ahead of the game! There's plenty of lives and infinite continues regardless of not doing so well, so it's also very benevolent regardless of how strong the opponents later can be. Never give up.
There is ONE gripe however, beware of a sudden "Out of Memory!" error which could hit harder than the game's true last boss himself!
Oh but one last plus: Did I forget to mention that one can bring a "wing in arms" along the way locally? (There is Co-Op!) and this will make many of the fights much easier! Have fun!

You know a game is great when you don't even have to spend an hour playing it to know it feels right in every aspect of its design. Cuphead is in short a fantastic and beautiful game. It really is something to behold. It's like an old cartoon come to life, with clarity and a nostalgic bent for all that came before. Not only is it accurate to the times it wants to replicate, it is bursting with creativity.
Every part of this game has been thoughtfully poured over by the devs. Like another Microsoft game, Ori and the Blind Forest, this one resides at the top of its genre in nearly every category of its design. The enemies and bosses are all varied. There are various weapons and specials to beat the game with, and each stage has enough different animations to keep you enthralled from start to end.
You don't need to play this game a whole hell of a lot to realize it is one of the most delicious games out there. And nothing else on the market is really even like it. I would have to go back to a game such as Mickey Mania for a resemblant artstyle. Cuphead also has a wicked sense of humor, though, and overall the stylization of the art and story is decidely adult-oriented in tone. This is a good thing.
The gameplay is utterly perfected, though, there a few issues worth discussing. It's tough like any good bullet shooter or shmup, and you can expect to die a lot. But I wouldn't say it is as tough as the hardest bullet hell shooters, which are impossible to master for most. It has a decent difficulty curve that rewards you for doing things right, and sometimes tortures you for doing things wrong. Luckily, once you customize each button of your controls to your liking the game becomes a lot of fun to pace your way through.
What you will need is your dash for the most part. And that does make the game feel like the extra weapons and abilities are not really all that special. When your invisible air dash is gonna get you through easier, it's hard to need anything else at times. You can certainly try all the other things out, and even the weaker weapons can be fun, but there is definitely a tier list here you will have to follow at times.
Certain enemies and bosses appear cheap, but so far I've not run into anything annoying enough for me to dislike the game. Of course if you are a gamer that wants your games easy, it is possible you might not desire to play this game. Maybe a youtube video would suffice for your enjoyment then.
Overall, Cuphead gets my highest recommendation. A triumpth of art and imagination combusted through fierce gameplay that totally enlivens and lovingly hearkens back to the golden age of shmups and sidescroller shooters. Amazing in every way. I would hope a sequel is planned because we really need another game with this style.

+ Great atmosphere and a few jump scares.
+ Intense on Insane mode difficulty which doesn't allow for saving or check points.
+ Night vision looks really nice.  Batteries are scarce on Insane mode.  You'll stop dead in your tracks as enemies pop out of the shadows before your eyes.
+ Great for speedrunning.
+ The Whistleblower DLC (sold seperately) is well made and pushes the envelope further than the base game.  Outlast's DLC is a worthwhile expansion if you want more.
- Mostly linear.  Outlast has been described as a "virtual ghost train".  Not entirely fair as there are various rooms, hiding places, and strategies you can use to survive, but in the vast majority of cases, there's one path out of each danger zone.
- Story is mostly cliched, typical horror stuff.
- Unskippable cutscenes.  One mid-game cutscene lasts around four minutes.  Great the first time you see it, not so much if you're constantly replaying on Insane mode.
- Quite short.
Personal recommendation:  As you can probably tell, I think the value here is in Insane mode.  Play it on Insane mode until you complete it, then go achievement hunting on the lower difficulties if need be.  The game really thrives when death is something you fear.  You don't get that with checkpoints.  The Whistleblower is also a worthwhile addition if you want more, especially at its regular sale price.

Note: This review is after my first play through of the game
I originally saw trailers for The Park months before it came out and once it became available to pre-order on Steam, I bought it; there was the advantage that it was also on sale but this was my first ever pre-order on Steam and I am happy to say, I was not in any way disappointed.
To be clear, the game tells you it is a narrative driven game, much like games from Tell Tale or the game Gone Home, this means actions are limited in place of following/taking part in the story. So to those who expect anything else, you only have yourself to blame.
I really enjoyed this game, the atmosphere is immersive as it blends a perfect mix of visuals and audio to keep you tense and constantly pressing the right mouse button. The game itself is short but that is not neccessarily a terrible thing, games do not need to be long they only need to be entertaining and padding them out with repetitive game play often only takes away from the experience.
If you are new to horror, this may not be a bad choice, the game is very easy to get into and easier to get lost in.
Edit: I am seeing a lot of reviews complaining about the game being a narrative driven game. I am not sure why because the game, the trailer, the developers all said it is a narrative driven game. People had the same complaints about Gone Home and the Vanishing of Ethan Carter but you never hear people complain about about any other game like this "It didn't say it was twin-stick shooter" or "it didn't say it was a third person shooter", so why should a game have to apologize for what it is?
If you don't like narrative driven games, don't buy them.

Hangeki is a simple tactical shmup that supports two local players. It's pretty well done with a focus on having a vast array of diverse weapons that you can unlock as you clear stages and challenges. It starts of simple, with you keeping up a combo by destroying enemies and picking up items constantly to level up and unlock your stronger weapons, which also require keeping that combo bar up. This combination will keep you always at the edge trying to destroy things as fast and efficiently as you can.
When a wave reaches a "critical" point after destroying enough enemies (shown on the upper side of the screen as a white progress bar), you can trigger the "Hangeki" to make all remaining enemies explode and trigger the next wave. Survive all the waves in any given stage and you'll face the area boss, which are also ery creative, challenging and force you to think a bit outside of the box by launching sudden melee strikes (ok, they give you a millisecond warning at the very least!) or drop waterfalls of lasers+bombs and more.
So, yep, a tactical choice between weapons, permanent aggression and knowing the enemy waves leads to victory. And mastering the controls: the ship is really fast which makes players prone to mistakes due to overconfidence in movement.
In some aspects, it reminded me of Super Crossfire (another good shmup in a similar vein although with a fixed position instead of free movement, unfortunately it's not on Steam despite having an awesome PC version) but with a mixture of the old Wipeout/Psygnosis style in the design of the weapons, which I found very cool. You in fact get achievements by completing stages using weapons from the same manufacturers, like Hangeki Initiative or Crystalix.
Expect the difficulty to ramp up fast as you progress through the stages and good luck with the challenges, some of them are going to make you cry but, still, this is a shmup and if you like those, you are certainly going to enjoy Hangeki.
Special mention to the music (freaking awesome, comes in ogg format inside the game but seriously needs an official OST release!!!) and the local co-op: banish the anti-social in you and bring a friend, bring two 360 pads and stay alive! The co-op is great, although a bit chaotic (nothing compared to the madness Jamestown's 4-player local co-op is though) it's highly satisfying to clear stages with friends.
Definitely recommended it for those who like shmups, those who don't perhaps will need the discount incentive to budge. Give it a chance, you'll be surprised.

The Park is a spooky "walking simulator" style game that emphasises mood and lore over gameplay and longevity. Originally started as a Funcom tech demo, it's important to know going into it that it's only maybe 90min or so long and is essestially you just going through scripted motions.
That said, Funcom is always good at layering the mood on nicely and while I found the first half of the story to be slow and a bit "by the numbers" it picks up nicely in the second half. The first half also presented me with a few stuttering frame-rates at points as well, but this too disappeared after the half-way point.
I am a player of The Secret World for full disclosure so I may have gone into this with a bit more foreknowledge on The Park, and recognized some things in-game that people that don't play the MMO will not know, but I don't think you need to be at all familiar with TSW lore to enjoy it. Though the ending will make a bit less sense...
I'd give it a 7.5/10. Worth the $10. Probably a fun one to stream.

I have enjoyed this game a lot. It has a steep learning curve at first, but the challenge was fun, and I had a good time coming back for more. It's an intense survival experience and even when your character is doing good, you're still constantly on guard because things have a tendancy to go downhill fast in this game. It has been a fun adventure!
Unfortunately, there are some terrain issues, and your character can easily get stuck. There is no way to remedy that situation, other than quit the game and pray your save goes back to before your error. There is no /stuck command to assist your character or ability to jump, so be very careful where you wander, as the game is not friendly to that sort of exploration. A rather counter intuitive and frustrating thing in a game that claims to be a sandbox.
A quick example: Most recently I stepped off a ledge in a cave to take a quick shortcut, and my character caught the edge of a cave rock formation. The game bumped her onto the top of the formation and she is permanently stuck there, as the game does not recognize any sort of pathing for her to exit. Without a /stuck command, ability to jump, or utilities that will allow you to pull your character off such structures, my character is official stuck for good (when she walks to the edge it's like she's walking into an invisible wall). Exiting the game without saving did me no good, since I had this awful idea that perhaps the game would recognize my location as an invalid pathing option if I rested. Doing so did not reset my character to a valid pathway. :( So, she's stuck there... until she dies.
This is a pretty crucial error in my opinion, and until something is implimented that will allow the player to fix terrain issues like this, I'll be shelving the title. Once a feature that allows the player to remedy situations like this is implimented, I would highly recommend the game.

Rituals is a short and simple point and click adventure where you control an employee trying to uncover the truth behind a secret project his company is working on: as you uncover clues you start having weird visions that urge you to go forward.
-while the graphics are truly low poly they work well and sport a decent style
-the story is quite interesting and urges you to discover what your company is working on
-the narrative is done well mixing reality and visions to good effect
-good level variety
-it controls in a somewhat old fashioned way with directional arrows and screens where you can look around by dragging the mouse around so don't expect to roam freely
-a few puzzles can be a bit obtuse, thankfully if you're stuck you can find hints on the forums: a puzzle on the second level also left me stuck for a bit as I missed a small object in one of the screens
-the directional arrows are a bit too big and can get in the way when you're reading a document or trying to interact with something near the lower middle of the screen
-very short, I finished it in 45 minutes taking my time to explore and reading documents: a speedrun (to see the other ending) can be done in 10 minutes once you know where to go and how to solve each puzzle
Rituals is a decent adventure with a story that is fairly interesting and backed up by a good narrative overall, most puzzles are pretty straightforward and the few levels you go through are varied enough to hold your interest. It seems the dev wants to convey a message regarding how the human race interacts with nature and, having finished the game, I can say he was fairly successful in doing it: he'll probably not win any points for originality but he did a good job in providing a mistery to solve and a decent plot to back it up.
It's a shame the game is so short cause I'd have loved to see this done with a bigger budget to provide a lengthier, more fleshed out story...as things stand Rituals is still worth at least a playthrough in my opinion: it's not worth the asking price though as there's not enough content so wait for a bundle (like I did) or a big sale.

Rituals is a simple but quite satisfying point and click that can be completed swiftly. It is very much an adventure lite.
The story is immediately intriguing and begs the player to find out more, though the second location is a little confusing until more of the background and plot is revealed. I would have liked to have seen the plot expanded upon and fleshed out much more as the premise does grab the attention.
The game took me 90 minutes to complete and I used no hints, though one rather hungry animal puzzle had me scratching my head for about 20 minutes. The puzzles are therefore straightforward and not a cerebral explosion. There is no real freedom of movement as you simply click on the directional arrow to move, but this does serve to move the experience forward at a comfortable pace.
The graphics are simple but very clear. I thought they fit the scenario and plot very well. There are no voices and only simple sounds, but again this actually added to the atmosphere.
For a simple, 90 minute game, I would not like to pay full price but as I got the title for just a couple of dollars, I will happily recommend it.

Arcade aficionados and score-chasing 1cc'ers rejoice;
is the counter-attack of leaderboard-driven, score-breaking, retro action you've been waiting for.
Those of us old enough to remember the warm glow and the busy sounds of a bustling arcade remember a time when games were more of a social and competitive interaction where we wouldn't just play to simply say we finished but to perfect it and surpass the scores of those who came before you. Games like
,
, or Toaplan's
were never a matter of simply "beating the game", these old classics were all about the points, maximizing your runs and learning every little detail about the game to get that perfect playthrough.
captures this arcade spirit all too well with it's bite-sized levels full of adrenaline and replayability as it pushes you to come back to each stage to try and try again with new weapons and gained skills or techniques.
On the surface
shows a similar concept and style to the row-reducing gameplay of
with enemy variation akin to
and it's many spinoffs. The similarities stop here, however, as the combat itself takes a much more modern bullet-hell approach to the chaos involved in dodging and timing your
'counter-attack' which acts as a finishing bomb and is how you will advance each wave. Fans of the more recent
will instantly fall in love with the combination of old-school enemy formations with the frenetic satisfaction of modern visuals and pacing. Unfortunately that game never saw a PC release, but I'm happy to say
fills the void just fine.
The game is as flashy as it is punishing requiring full engagement of your audio/visual sensories and can almost be a bit overwhelming with how much is going on, but that's exactly how us shmup enthusiasts like it. Your eyes will be busy and a lot of your practicing will be focused on where you train your center of vision. You'll learn to strike a balance between watching enemy ship patterns at the top to anticipate which bullet-types are incoming and keeping track your powerup meter in order to time and aim your special weapons perfectly. One misplaced shot and you'll be back to dodging and waiting for your next weapon or
to powerup, costing you valuable time and points.
Victory in
is also handled in a very unique manner when it comes to the classic shmup formula, as you aren't simply trying to shoot down each enemy to score. Your score, instead of being based on a mundane points-by-kill basis, is reflected by the quickness and diligence in which each wave is dealt with and how fast you're able to trigger your
through sustained chains and repeated successful shots. This creates a much more competitive and skill-based atmosphere on the very important, addictive and well designed leaderboards. If you love leaderboards you'll love
.
boasts an impressive arsenal of unique weaponry counting in at 51 pieces of unlockable equipment, and they all pack a serious punch in their own right. These range anywhere from a piercing cannon that's capable of incapacitating an entire vertical row, seconds long shielding for that sudden moment of invincibility in the roughest of times, and huge rolling waves of flame that can take out large lines of enemies. These are only some of the beginning weapons, and as you play you'll continue to unlock better, more insane weaponry that will push you to revisit past levels and reattempt your score with new-found strategies.
This is a game crafted with a serious devotion to the arcade culture, and a detailed love for the shmup genre. It's a classic shooter with modern flair that I can wholeheartedly recommend to anyone from the most old-school of arcade veterans to the most hardcore and modern of Cave or
-styled bullet-hell fanatics.

First know that RO2 and Rising Storm are sold for $20 each. You gain the ability to play the other when you purchase one of them, but you will not be able to pick anything but rifleman class or level up.
By far one of the most interesting experiences in online gaming. Merril's Mauraders' two servers are the only ones I found worth playing for realism mode (one for Rising Storm, one for RO2) I can't really speak for the single player campaign or any other game modes as I haven't been drawn to play them. Enjoy the wide variety of characters you will experience producing a number of different sounds, songs, and racial profiling statements over mic chat. There are some really good teammates you will get that will lead you or follow you to topple your enemies. There are also abstracted young ones who like to get tunnel vision and charge foward, throwing a grenade into the trench you're sitting in without so much as checking their map to see what's in front of them, or that they are still behind the frontline. Enough about that.
The game is a lot like playing a Battlefield game. Squad leaders are the beacons that their members can spawn on, so their positioning and protection is key to avoid losing ground. There are a few gameplay modes but I have only played realism campaign in which both sides vie for a number of territories in an attempt to control more or wipe out completely the enemy force until the other breaks. This is done by either team attacking or defending. Usually it will rotate between maps. There is a lot of importance in having experience with the game and the maps played, because you need a good Team Leader that understands the tactics that the team should follow in order to best help the campaign overall, not just each individual battle. If you have the audacity to learn about the game and become a good leader please play this game because it's a way better experience with good team leaders and people that can cooperate. Those of you who play team games like CS:GO or 'MOBA's and always blame your team for everything need not apply.
The realism is there; bullet drop, suppresion, wounds that affect your performance... Bullet drop feels very accurate and satisfying especially using a bolt-action rifle. You will feel like a marksman when you lead a shot on a running target from many meters away. You can even adjust for elevation on some of the guns. The suppresion is interesting but can also be very annoying in things like one-on-one gunfights where someone begins to shoot at you and you get aimpunched without them actually hitting you. It can also be tough to tell exactly where enemies are firing from - it seems like muzzle flash isn't nearly as noticable as it should be on darker maps. It can also be strange to not really be able to hear which direction machine gun fire is coming from sometimes. The bullet wounds had me disconnected a bit when my forearm was injured and my soldier decided to throw a grenade with that arm instead of his good one. Let's just say it didn't get thrown very far. Besides that I guess I should talk about how rediculous the amount of recoil is on the mg42 where people will climb through windows with it and hipfire the thing without much trouble laying waste to everything. It's not nearly as bad as the flamethrower in Rising Storm, but Japan has knee mortars, the ability to kamikaze-grenade without losing tickets / set traps, and banzai charge (allowing them to sometimes eat bullets for breakfast) .. so I guess it's sort of fair.. These things set Rising Storm apart from RO2, but I enjoy both. But if you do suck at shooters and decide Red Orchestra is too real for you, just play Rising Storm and load in before everyone else, pick allies and get the flamethrower and just spray it in the general direction of the enemy for free kills.
The main problem with this game is if you run it at certain graphical settings rendering goes into space. You will see through everything on and off. Terrain, walls, train cars, cars, fences... will provide a false sense of security when you think you're being sneaky and in reality someone's game decides to give him free 'ESP' (wallhacks) and he knows you're there. I have more of an issue of it happening to me because it just feels really boring and cheap at that point to just see every enemy around you, but this should not really happen to anybody. My friend said to use the console command 'Umbra calling' but it doesn't help. Granted I could play on higher settings but I should not have to just so that more than half of the level renders. Not to mention switching graphical settings 99% of the time means forcing you to restart your game. I think it's mainly a problem with RO2 and not really Rising Storm, but I still wouldn't recommend them for $20 a piece.
Final verdict; Wait until it goes on sale.
