After reading the overly positive reviews and being a fan of dark games, I decided to give this "classic" a try and I must say that I am very... underwhelmed. Not everything is bad about this game of course:
+The story is interesting without being incredible
+The style is unique and gives a special flair to the whole experience
+The power allocation system is not out of the ordinary but still entertaining
Now to the negative part of my playthrough:
-The gameplay is very simplistic and quite boring, you end up killing the same kind of ennemies over and over again in the same way
-Objectives are often unclear and long to achieve which takes away a lot of the fun
-Speaking about fun, this game is not fun in any way and I was very glad when I finished it
-The game gives you the illusion of choice but they only matter in the ending cinematic and not before
-I expected more from the ending since the storyline was the best part of the game
-Although being labelled as a scary game with jumpscare, there wasn't a single thing in this game that was a little bit frightening and the little to no jumpscares were either predictable or very dull
Conclusion:
After finishing the game, I felt like I was missing out on something, on a part of the game that makes it so amazing in the eyes of the mojority of the players. I would not label it as a bad game because of it's uniqueness and it's features that set it apart from other games. However after a few hours of playing it, I just rushed through the rest of it to finish it as quickly as possible. This game was disappointing and not only because of the big hype around it, this game is just plain monotonous.

+ Great atmosphere and a few jump scares.
+ Intense on Insane mode difficulty which doesn't allow for saving or check points.
+ Night vision looks really nice.  Batteries are scarce on Insane mode.  You'll stop dead in your tracks as enemies pop out of the shadows before your eyes.
+ Great for speedrunning.
+ The Whistleblower DLC (sold seperately) is well made and pushes the envelope further than the base game.  Outlast's DLC is a worthwhile expansion if you want more.
- Mostly linear.  Outlast has been described as a "virtual ghost train".  Not entirely fair as there are various rooms, hiding places, and strategies you can use to survive, but in the vast majority of cases, there's one path out of each danger zone.
- Story is mostly cliched, typical horror stuff.
- Unskippable cutscenes.  One mid-game cutscene lasts around four minutes.  Great the first time you see it, not so much if you're constantly replaying on Insane mode.
- Quite short.
Personal recommendation:  As you can probably tell, I think the value here is in Insane mode.  Play it on Insane mode until you complete it, then go achievement hunting on the lower difficulties if need be.  The game really thrives when death is something you fear.  You don't get that with checkpoints.  The Whistleblower is also a worthwhile addition if you want more, especially at its regular sale price.

The game follows a depressed mother looking for her lost child in a really creepy amusement park named Atlantic something. To give my personal review of this game, I will answer a few questions the reader might have in mind.
1. Is this actually a game?
If you, like me, consider that an interactive software needs some sort of obstacles, adversity, or problem solving to be considered a game, then no, it is not a game. The Park won't ask you to solve any puzzle, nor will it ever hide from you the means to progress, and there is no conditions for failure.
2. Is it an enjoyable experience?
For me, it was.
3. What are the game's strengths?
While the story of this game is not the most original (especially if you are already familiar with Salomon Island), it still keeps you interested, and wanting to discover more as you go. Another strength is in the game's ambiance, carefully and successfully crafted mainly through carefully used sound effects and lighting.
4. Any blatant flaw?
A few technical flaws, most notably during the first quarter of the game, can be a little bit distracting. I experienced stuttering during the first part, and noticed what I would call a lack of polish during the same part. Thankfully, once I walked into the actual park, I did not notice any of that anymore.
5. Is it worth the price?
If your personal equation is based on a "time versus money" reasoning, then no, clearly not. The average time needed to beat The Park is well under two hours, and it has little to none replayability. However, that time is well spent, so if you don't mind paying 10 bucks for an hour or two of entertainment, go for it. And you can always wait for a sale.
6. Should I buy it because of the items for The Secret World?

Below you'll find both a written and video impression on the game.
Hangeki to break it down is what Space Invaders would be if it had a proper sequel. It's fast paced and flashy, but under all that there's a challenging score attack game. Hangeki challenges the player to use their arsenal efficiently so they can continue their kill chain and maintain a steady charge for a "Hangeki" blast to clear the screen. The game's target audience, the people who loved classic arcade games, should find this very interesting. Those who might not be as inclined into score attack style games, it's always worth it to do a little more research.
Though the game is fun, and is a unique take on classic arcade shmup, it's not with out it's flaws. There are 2 notable design flaws that hinder the player's ability to quickly read the battle field. The game demands efficient use of your special abilities in order to keep your kill streak going, but since the ability HUD is small and placed on the bottom left corner, it forces the player to take his/her eyes off of the main focus, the ship, in order to glance at their abilities. The bullets from the enemies I think are too small and blends in with the back ground. Couple these 2 issues with the bullet hell nature of this genre, along with all the other micromanagement that you'll have to do, it adds frustration in areas where it otherwise would be fine.
Overall Hangaki is an enjoyable score attack game that evolves the old classic arcade shmup genre. For those who are interested in this sort of game, Hangeki is probably a good fit.
Pros:
- Exciting gameplay
- Flashy visuals
- Evolves the classic arcade "shmup" genre with it's own flavor
- Encourages replay
Cons:
- Could induce seizure or epilepsy. I am not exaggerating, this is a real possibility with this game
- Could prove repetitive to some

Don't let my playtime fool you, I've spent more hours with this game than you can imagine.
I am a major Carmageddon fan and near widdled with joy when I heard C:R was coming.  Like many I backed the kickstarter, participated in the forums, reverse-engineered the file formats and wrote editing tools so others could mod the game but still I felt, way deep down, that things weren't quite right.
Then one night, over a candlelit meal, Nobby broke down into tears and said "Errol, things just aren't right.  We know this and we'll make it better."
"Will there be elephants?" I asked, rather breathlessly.
"Elephants as far as the eye can see." he replied, wiping his eyes with the tablecloth.
I knew in my bones he was speaking the truth so I left him to it.
Days went past, days turned to weeks, weeks to months and all was quiet.
The doubt, the dread, the panic began to grow once more.  Did Nobby really speak the truth?  Maybe I was too caught up in my nostalgia to see clearly?
Then, one glorious day, the sun burst over the horizon and shone sparkling down upon Carmageddon: Max Damage.  This was it, this was the game I had been yearning for all those years.  The light-hearted violence, the purile british humour, the basic stupid fun.  All there.  Life was good...
I was on the phone like a shot.  "Nobby," I said, "this is fantastic.  You have outdone yourselves.  But Nobby,  where are the elephants?"
*click* went the telephone as Nobby hung up.
~~~ twelve months later ~~~
On my darkest days I fear the elephants may have been a ruse, a ploy, an... elephantasy, but I shall remain strong.  "They're coming" I tell myself.  "They're coming..."

On the surface this is just a flashy stand alone demo for the game Broforce that offers around 30 minutes of play. The bottom line is that the Expendabros is a fresh, dynamic, fun, 2D platforming pixelated, FREE shooter that is a sheer joy to play.
This game of course parodies the Expendables 3 movie and features parodies of Arnold Schwartenager, Jason Statham, Wesley Snipes, Dolf Lungren, Randy Couture, Terry Crews and of course Sylvester Stalone. There was some painstaking amount of detail in the artwork for the game and a lot of brief, yet hilarious cut scenes, especially for a free game. It is a beautiful game with a lot of vibrant, bright colors while still having an aura of grittiness. There is always a lot happening on screen and blood spattering all around.
Aside from the obvious, there's the actual game itself, this is a cleverly designed 2D shooter that lets you shoot through terrain, make your own paths. Not just that, but you can wall climb just in case you ever shoot yourself a hole. The controls are easy, movement, shoot, melee, jump and special. You can only shoot left and right thankfully and that works for this sort of game. The controls are so simple, but its the destruction that makes the game so complex. Blowing up barrels will destroy walls, shooting gas tanks will send them flying and murdering enemies, burning bridges, shooting down towers. Shooting down power supplies, making them explode on enemies beneath. Saw blades you can dislodge and send them rolling into foes. Its so much silly fun that feels more cartoony than violent.
At the start of each level, you have one Expendabro. This bro is randomly selected out of bros you've already unlocked. You then play through the level, and you'll find other bros to rescue from cages. To unlock bros you need to rescue a certain amount of bros. So if you have only Arnold and Stalone unlocked, you'll only rescue Arnold or Stalone until you rescue them enough times to unlock someone new. Each Expenpendabro has different guns and specials. Stalone has a standard two pistols and a triple grenade. Couture has a flame thrower and napalm. Statham has knives that shoot like a gun and a knife shower special with a high arc. Dolph has a sticky grenade launcher and a RC bomb car. Terry has a chaingun that will push him backward for how powerful the gun is and a special that will make him leap across the screen. Wesley has melee only that can destroy projectiles and some kind of flying melee special making him the Wolverine of the group (Wesleyrine).
Since the cages have random bros that you've unlocked in them, this allows for a lot of play diversity and replayability. You can't switch bros unless your current bro dies, then you respawn back to the last checkpoint and you play as a random bro remaining that you've rescued on that level. The level doesn't reset itself, the terrain still stays ruined as you destroyed it. In a way, it makes a new level. If you lose all of your bros you restart the level and the terrain resets. These levels are short, but again its legitimately so much fun to play even if a speed runner can get through each level in under a minute. Each level has multiple paths, but with the destruction you can make your own paths. Wall in your way? No problem when everything is destructible. At the end of each level, you'll 'get to ze chopper,' and jump on to have it carry you away. It all adds to the creativity and cleverness this game and its devs have to offer.
There is a wide array of enemies and they add a lot of personality to the game even if they get out shined by famous parodies. There are attack dogs that will eat enemies as well as you, fat attack dogs, standard soldiers, suicide bombers that don't attack, but explode when dead, bro seeking missile launchers, giant chaingun soldiers, big fat bosses, rocket trucks, and many more types of enemies. There are pigs too, but they don't attack, they're there to be adorable. They react to your bullets, they'll hear you and come running. Sometimes they run away. You can use your melee for stealth kills. When you destroy ledges they're standing on, they can fall to their death. They can burn, be beheaded by gunfire and run around without their head until they drop dead. Seeing attack dogs eat corpses. Throwing a grenade, having it cling onto an enemy who then panics and runs away straight into a saw blade completely unplanned or unscripted. Again, there's a lot of charm than it is horrible violence. There's always a lot going on screen.
Expendabros did what every great demo does and it made me want to play Broforce even if I didn't want to see Expendibles 3. Oh and did I mention it can be played with 4 players on screen at the same time? Chaos ensues. FREE. FREE. FREE. FREE. FREE. FREE. FREE. FREE.

This will be a bit long, so just bear with me.
A truly great game. Rather unique and open-world. There are hardly any restrictions in the game, although you might want to keep your head clear of such reckless thoughts in this survival game, or else you'll likely get killed early-on. The longest I've survived was 11 days, which I still feel quite swell of. As others have said, PZ isn't just an average zombie game that gives you a shot-gun and has you blowing zombie brains all over with no actual back-story (Did I mention that?), it's an excellent zombie game that gives you choices and has your heart pacing to run from that monger zombie pack... That's every-where. I also have another unique thing to say.
YOU CAN OPEN EVERY SINGLE DOOR IN THE GAME! VERY few games have this ability. Skyrim, Oblivion, Minecraft... And PZ are the only games I've ever seen like this. GTA 5/4/3/2/1, Watch Dogs, Brink, and a bunch of other still-cool games haven't implemented this. Not only can you open every door in the game, but you can barricade every door in the game, break down every door in the game, and look through every door in the game (As long as it has a window.)
ALSO! Another unique feature! The entire damn thing is pre-loaded! While you're waiting a possibly grueling 5-10 minutes, you don't realize that you dun have to wait for any more loading! Well, except for a second or two as the map loads. No long pauses between frikkin' opening doors, no quick loads between 6-week-long ship rides, PZ never loads again (Save for the occasional quick map load.) I've never seen these two, simultaneously, oh wait Minecraft. Never mind.
Now, lemme cover some of the "features" this game says it has.
Sandbox zombie survival game. ---- No lie here. You can do a very many of things that allow this to be true. Check.
Full line of sight system and real-time lighting, sound and visibility mechanics. Hide in the shadows, keep quiet and keep the lights off at night, or at least hang sheets over the windows. ---- Lol yup. They didn't just implement a quick attention system where, if you come with-in a certain range, they 'see' you. No matter what. If you're sneaking, zombies will likely not detect you if they're more than 3 meters away. If you sneak up on a zombie trying to burglarize a posh house and steal it's meaty, succulent, intelligient riches, it won't likely notice you until you're fondling it, if you have the Graceful ability. Check.
Vast and growing map (loosely based on a real world location) for you to explore, loot and set up your fortress. Check out Blindcoder’s map project:
---- Well, maybe. I haven't explored all coners of either map, although it didn't take long before I hit the ocean, and couldn't swim. NOOOO!!! Now I'll never earn my Blue Ribbon for Best Swimmer! Bah. No check.
Use tools and items to craft weapons, barricade and cook. You can even build zombie proof forts by chopping trees, sawing wood and scavenging supplies. ---- Yes. Check, check, check, check, check, oh wait, really? Check. Scavenging for supplies is simply *Italicize*Essential with a capital "E"*italicize* during the early part of the game. Later on, you can grow your own crops, but it'll likely take a little while before you can successfully build/find a secure, efficient, and sufficient garden/farm. If you don't, you'll die with-in the first hour. Check.
Deal with depression, boredom, hunger, thirst and illness while trying to survive. ---- I have actually encountered all of these during my play time. And, I may be speaking out of my♥♥♥♥♥♥ but they seemed to have an excellent system of seeing your character's needs. Say they've been damaged. You/They don't know exactly how much damage they've taken, nerve bundle for muscle tissue (Which is ridiculous. Do you know exactly how many veins/arteries have been punctured when you're shot in the arm? Yes? Well you too.), but you have an icon that gives you a generalization of how much they have. Not too precise, not too broad. Check.
Day turns to night. The electricity falters. Hordes migrate. Winter draws in. Society is in freefall. Day turns to night with-in a reasonable time allotation (You can alter this in Sandbox mode.) I haven't actually first-handedly experienced the electricity being cut off, but then again, I've only survived for eleven days at max.  Hordes migrate. I dunno, maybe. Winter draws in. Again, only eleven days. Society is in free-fall. Aye. Possibly check, not sure.
Farming, trapping, fishing, carpentry, character customization, skills and perks that develop based on what you do in-game. Check. 'Nuff said.
Hundreds of zombies with swarm mechanics and in-depth visual and hearing systems. Correct. They will group with each other in close packs if you accumulate enough. And if you have moderate-sized pack even, don't run. Hide. You can't run, but you can hide. (See what I did there?) Now trust me, you want a rather large sized house, break in through the window, lock your-self in the top floor, stay quiet for a good day, and hope for the best. Check.
Proper zombies that don’t run. (Unless you tell them to in the sandbox menu). Check. You can alter the speed of the zombies in Sandbox mode, but normally they max their speed out at a solid jog.
A ton of amazing atmospheric music tracks by the prodigy that is Zach Beever. Ohmigosh, yas. Zach made tracks that can make you scared, sad, bad♥♥♥♥♥ excited, and maybe even... Happy?(?) I dunno, but check.
Instant action ‘Last Stand’ mode, on top of our Sandbox and Survival mode. I dunno, haven't played Last Stand.
Full, open and powerful Lua modding support. I'll just say "Check" for now.
Online multiplayer survival with persistent player run servers. Yes. Check. Multiple player-created servers, but they seem to be a bit of a pain to enter.
Over-all, horribly great game. It's addictive, yet it's the kind of addiction that you love to hate. In the right way. Also, another thing. You can-not save in the game. Well, when you log off, your progress is saved, but if you die, you die. You have to start all over again. 'Course, you can spawn a brand-new character near your last character's death place.
9/10.
Although, I still do have a few suggestions.
1. In Sandbox mode, you should certainly be able to modify your character far beyond just the Survival perk pick. You should be able to alter their speed, strength, biological defenses, physcial defenses, mental defenses, and their ability to survive with/with-out certain things/mental states.
2. You should be able to add as many survivors as wished in Sand-box mode.
3. I kind of think the perk pick in Survivl should be a bit more lenient.
4. This game should become big. Like, WoW-big.

One of the most difficult tropico games, given you choose the right settings or workshop scenarios. Lots of fun but if you are easily frustrated play at lowest settings. Some of the dlc is not worth the price but some is. The reviews are pretty accurate and will let you pick which dlc you want. Tropico 5 expands on many areas other Tropico games have not delved into while getting rid of some of the old features (some which were pretty good). As a Tropico game goes this is without a doubt the most unique. In a good way or a bad way is up to the taste of the gamer in question.
1. Economy.
The economy is much better and more realistic. There are now features like trade routes, which when used effectively can help a lot. Used without the foreign relations penalties in mind can now result in foreign invasions, and trade route embargos. The settings for sandbox maps are more generic in presentation but work just about as well as other Tropico games. Some building upgrades tend to work a bit differently than Tropico 4. I am sorry that i do not know how to adequately describe the changes, yet i find them welcome. If you like the challenge of making money you will enjoy this.
There are also buliding managers that provide various bonuses and in some cases both bonuses and penalties to your buildings and even perhaps surrounding buildings. This means citizens now have roles. Some are good roles like supervisor. Some are bad like rebel or with the espionage expansion foreign spy.
2. Military.
The military game of Tropico 5 has new features. Not only do your troops fight the rebels but ANYONE who attacks your island or your rule. There is still the potential for coups, although personally i find it easier to maintain the military factions' approval than previous Tropico's, but this does not mean the military portion of the game is easier. In fact even on the easiest settings it is more challenging than many other Tropico games. Something else that should be mentioned is there are a lot of military options even in vanilla Tropico 5. If you add dlc and the Espionage expansion you get even more. I think the military game is more realistic as well. YOu can also see the stats of you troops which now operate in squads. There are three stats, attack power, health and number of units in the squad. Troops also do not surrender as easily. Sometimes they will not surrender at all choosing to fight to the last man which i think occurs more often with high miltary loyalty.
3. Foreign Relations.
This has been changed quite a bit as well. In the colonial era it is really hard to get invaded by the crown. Pirates can invade but are usually easily beaten. I think this is a good balance choice by Kalypso. Nothing is worse in a strategic game than jumping in and being outnumbered and outgunned from the very start, with no chance of preperation. However if you do not prepare for the next eras being invaded by superpowers is much more risky. In the colonial era, the main effect with having bad relations with the crown is lack of trade routes, which can hurt your income and lack of yearly funds sent from the crown, which is not vital but every little bit helps. Latter foreign relations get more tricky to manage, especially in the modern era. Much like Tropico 4 there are 5 factions. Only two can invade you that i know of. The dynamics of trade routes become much more complicated, although Tropico 5 gives you various ways around that, if you invest wisely. You can now import trade goods directly from foreign powers as well as minor powers, smugglers and in the colonial era pirates. With the waterborne expansion smugglers become a more viable option with the smugglers docks building. The Espionage expansion makes significant changes to foreign relations. You now have spies and more ways to detect the roles of citizens. Police stations now help detect the roles of citizens. As a sidenote police stations can now serve the additonal role of fire station with an upgrade. Spies can be used for various missions some of which i am still familiarizing myself with. The ones i am familiar with are steal money and steal technology. That's right Tropico 5 now has research and scientists. Frankly there's not enough of that. It is very reminiscent of a certain mission in Tropico 4 with the exception of the scientists producing the research points. Yet i digress. Nations will now demand more from you including more frequent survival from foreign invasions missions. Most of which occurs in the World Wars era. Embassies are much more functional than the foreign minitry building and provide more options for manging foreign relations. There is a cost for every foreign action, so in actuality foreign relations is harder in my opinion.
Island Factions.
Throughout most of Tropico 5 i find the importance of island factions is not nearly as important. Actually with the exception of the military faction I ignore the others. Yet this is because the constitution you develop on your island influences them a lot. With the right options island factions can be a dominant force, or firmly under your control which is how i play. If you give a lot of power to the factions on your island i can imagine those factions being more important than in previous tropico games. Factions can now influnce protests.... well as far as i can tell. There are both faction protests and citizen protests.... as far as i can tell. Citizen protests you can buy off, negotiate to do certain tasks to appease them, or send in the troops. Yet this is all fuzzy to me because i never have protests the way i play. I may have a island wide uprising on occasion which my troops will usually put down, but never protests :). Also with the right constitution option it is now possible by all appearances that some military faction supporters can now fight as militia, which is handy during foreign invasions and those nasty island wide uprisings :). It is very possible to have an army of 200 without much effort by the end of the game. One other thing is edicts now can more directly affect miltary strength. Those militia from the milittary faction work almost as well as modern infantry when used with the right to arms edict. Problem is rebels are stronger and those citizens who join the uprisings. Anyone who invades your island and faces 5 squads of modern infantry, 3 tanks squads, 2 apc squads, fighter bombers and cruise missiles ( which is usally what i run with in the modern era, will be promptly, efficiently and quickly squashed with a minimum of effort and collateral damage. Watch out for those fighter bombers they can kill your citizens.
In summary Tropico 5 offers many ways to play. In fact more ways than previous incarnations with the addition of multiplayer and workshop content. I give the economic aspect a 9/10. The military aspect a 10/10, the Foreign relations aspect a 10/10, and the Island Factions aspect a 7/10.

There is something enchanting about having a game actually tell you its story without telling you the story directly. Even if the story has been done before, depending on the execution it can lead to a somewhat surreal experience. Such is the case with Rituals, developed by Tymon Zgainski, and published by Mudvark. Rituals never directly tells you what its story is, rather showing small clues and letting the player figure it out for them. This way of indirect storytelling plays to the game's strengths, allowing the player to be the one that dictates what the story is about beyond the skeletal narrative that the developer set up, relating to civilization and nature.
When starting out in the game, the first thing the player will notice is that they can't move freely. They're on a set track that gives them various options to go through on a set path. You use your mouse to click on the arrows in front of you and to move your characters head so they can look around. There are still options of exploration, which gives the player a chance to really figure out just what is going on in the mysterious office building they've worked their way up in. You can go all over the office building or the other explorable areas, but you can't interact with everything which is a little disappointing, considering it would be interesting to be able to turn on all of the computers and investigate more that way. However, the way that it's set up does give the player plenty of chances to learn more and more about the world they're in. The player doesn't know anything other than what they find out themselves or what they can interpret. This game makes you think about what the developer was trying to get across with their work, some parts are more obvious than others, but it gives you a chance to theorize on just what is going on in this office building.

A solid game game with mechanics and a gameplay loop that is fun and rewarding, even to someone who is not an avid RTS or strategy game player.
I picked this up shortly after a recommendation from a friend, and the time I have spent with it have not been disappointing. The tutorials that this game provides are a drag (as far as tutorials go), but I have to give credit to the developers: they are concise and helped me get going right away. I understood the mechanics and what needed to be done very well and that made the features and tools the game provides much less daunting.
The best compliment I can give this game is that, as a non-RTS enthusiast, I found the game relaxing and an excellent time killer. All the times that I made it to any significant number of people that I was in charge of would always end with my adults dying faster than I could educate my children. I think that says more about my inability to micro-manage. With all the things that your people need in order to be healthy and happy, the game has the potential to overwhelm. But if you take it at regular (or even paused) time, I'm sure that with some practice even the most novice of players could create a self-sufficient and truly inspiring town.
Numerically, I give the game a 7/10. It is a good game, and I found myself lost in it more than I anticipated I would. I still don't find myself swearing by RTS games, but this game puts up a good argument towards convincing me to convert.

I tentatively recommend this game.
It is a simple point-and-click puzzle game.
Interesting story, presented in a very simple way, with a few things hidden in corners that expand the details a bit. Nothing too obtuse or difficult to understand, beyond the basic part that requires a suspension of disbelief.
So the good is: I found it fun, the puzzles were interesting, kept me occupied for a few moments, but were not terribly difficult, so it was right in that range to quickly make me feel engaged in solving it, without ever being frustrating. The world building was simple, but effective, the audio was atmospheric, and I felt engaged in playing it the whole time.
At its core I would describe it as: minimalist, but it uses everything to its greatest potential, so while minimalist this also means no wasted space in the design and atmosphere.
The bad: I have played it through twice, with 100% achievement completion in one and a half hours, and that is just the  stats Steam gave me; I was not sitting and playing the whole time, and took my sweet time checking empty spaces and corners for secrets, so the actual gameplay time for playing it twice is under an hour.
There is also no replay value; once you know the puzzles, it takes just a few minutes to get from start to finish, and would take just one if not having to wait for animations and scenes. Once you get both endings there is nothing left for you, beyond getting 100%, and you are likely to get the few secrets and achievements on your way to the end anyway.
I only missed two myself. One because I went forward not realizing I couldn't go back, the other because it involved using a simple and obviously wrong way to try to solve a puzzle. The latter is easy to find when you look at the achievement list.
It is fun, but when you objectively compare it to the market, the game to cost ratio is kinda.. low on the game side. It would be very easy to get a lot more enjoyment for the same cost.
But that is the only hiccup, and while I feel $3 to $5 may be a more appropriate price, I don't actually regret purchasing and playing this.
So I tentatively recommend it. It's good, but be warned, for your $10, you will get about an hour of gameplay.

Easily the definitive Flatout game, developed by the original developers BugBear. Flatout 2 has provided plenty of fun for a guy like me, who likes racing games with a more arcade-y feel.
You've got your traditional race mode, which equates to crashing opponents into obstacles and crossing the line first, silly stunt modes that let you live out your inner ragdoll butcher, and derbies, which are the only mode really worth playing, and you do exactly what you expect to do: Survive being blown up while blowing everyone else up.
Much like Need for Speed and Burnout, Flatout 2 had a boost system, which has you rewarded with juice in your boost bar by hitting destructible objects and dealing collateral damage to your rivals. And that's essential for combating the game's biggest flaw: Rubberbanding. No matter how good you are, or how fast your car is, the opponents will always find a way to blow past you unless you wreck them. And you CAN wreck them. It's satisfying.
Speaking of opponents, they all behave differently. You know which ones you can use a punching bag or which ones are going to try and run you off the road. And this was in 2006, which I think is a pretty nifty feature for its time.
I won't recommend the game at full price, but it's definitely worth it on sale if you're hoping to get an arcade racer that let's you live out your inner murder fantasies built up from years of being stuck in traffic.

If you were jonesing for a peaceful, Disney-animated stroll down memory lane, you’re in the wrong dimension. Welcome to 193404. Mickey Mouse? Never heard of him. Donald Duck? Who? Satan? Oh yes, we know him. He’s very real and out to get your souls. However, if you’re able to beat him in a fiddling contest you might just make it out alive...oops, wrong story. Set in the backcountry of 30s rubber-hose animation, Cuphead has you blasting and biffing your way through odds that would make Popeye cough up his spinach. You’re on a quest to save yourselves from a contract with the Devil (that you got into because the lord of Hell is obviously known for being trustworthy) by collecting the souls of his rubber-hose animated debtors. This game takes all the best aspects of Mario, Metroid, and the bones of cryo-frozen Walt Disney’s corpse and smashes them all together into a masterpiece. The look and feel of the game is phenomenal, and is one of the only reasons you’ll have to not want to snap your screen in half when you die for the 404th time in a row on the same level. Don’t be fooled my it’s childlike exterior, though, for this houses a harsh and unforgiving interior. You’ve got three lives and tiny blue lasers shot from your finger. Time to wage a war on Satan that would give Doomguy a run for his money. Despite the difficulty, the game never feels overwhelming or crushing. It’s that perfect level of difficulty where you know you’re able to beat it if you just keep trying. And that’s what you’ll do. Much like the Devil’s contract thag Cuphead and Mugman fell into, you’ll either finish it or die trying.

An interesting game. I mostly grabbed this because I am a fan of The Secret World MMO, and this game is set within that universe. I appreciated the deeper insight into the the park and its denizens.
This is less of a game than an interactive short story... and by interactive, you're really just picking things up and examining them. There is no combat or puzzle solving or any other aspects of a traditional computer game that you may be expecting.
That aside, it was fairly creepy... especially with headphones on so you can hear the nuances of the sound effects. It would have been much creepier in the dark, but the sun was still up when I decided to try it out.
The only bad things I have to say about it are that it is short (finished it in less than 2 hours) and towards the end, there are elements that repeat over and over. While I know that is there to elicit a psychological effect, I started to get bored of the repetitiveness of it. I also felt the ending was a bit lackluster, but fitting. With the buildup, I guess I was expecting something more dramatic. I was also hoping for more paranormal elements, given the tie in with The Secret World.
Anyway, for the price, this game is worth playing if you're a fan of the psychological horror genre, or you're a fan or player of The Secret World MMO. Just try to play it in the dark with headphones on. :)

Introduction:
This is a team based (4v4) competitive Tower Defence game in which you build towers against waves increasing difficult mobs. The twist of Legion TD is that at the end of the game you send your towers (they are actually living creatures not a stone tower in the literal sense) against the enemy team's towers in a showdown. And hence the difficulty lies in you have plan not only for the waves of mobs, but towards the enemy team as well.
At higher levels of gameplay I can definately forsee build orders like Starcraft 2. There can also be pocket strategies in which one particular player does not build towers but focus on generating income through mining. So therefore I believe this game is complex enough to develop a competitive scene.

(I admit I have only seen these advanced strategies in Legion TD 1/Warcraft 3, but the selling point of Legion TD 2 is its authenticity to LTD1/War3.)
The good:
1) Plays exactly like Legion TD custom map on Warcraft III /Starcraft II. If you liked that you will like this. No controversial/unpopular mechanics changes so far.
2) No Lootboxes (for now). Very rare these days.
The bad:
1) I cannot imagine what their server infrastructure is like.  This game on launch has experienced server capacity issues on the levels of Diablo 3 and Simcity 2013. No one can ever login because they are stuck at the log in screen and if you do miraculously login, you can't play a game because your username is NULL as you cannot connect to the server that holds your username as well.
I bought this on launch 20 November 2017 and found myself having connection issues. That's fine. I waited a few days and came back 23 November and it is still experiencing connections issues.
This is raising serious issues for the game's longevity. This sort of multiplayer only game need a large player base to sustain matchmaking of various skill levels, and I would hazard a guess a significant portion of the population has already refunded the game due to the game LITERALLY UNPLAYABLE.
At this rate I wonder what is your server infrastucture is like. Is it a Pentium 4 3.0 Ghz powered by a hamster wheel?

Carmageddon is a great game that lives up to it's predeccesors (especially the one we don't talk about). The cars look great and the handling is somewhere between arcadey and simulation resulting in some effort required to control each vehicle.
The soundtrack is pretty good too at least it doesn't offend my ears. There's both dubstep and metal present which doesn't bother me but does for others so bear that in mind.
It's no oil painting but by far and large the game in general looks good, there's several large environments to run rampant in and plenty of pedestrians to magle in a variety of ways. Or simply watch them dance if you get the groovin ped power up.
Speaking of powerups, there's plenty. Some take the form of weapons to better help dispose of other racers by launching anvils or mortars in their direction or just launching every racer around you by using the repulser and watch them fly. Or if it's vehicular manslaughter you're going for there's more than enough powerups to deal with that ranging from dismemeberment to electro rays and good old fire.
There are a few different game modes to switch things up a litlle which you can find on the store page so I won't go into it here but to say they are extremely fun, fox n hounds being my personal favorite.
Multiplayer is not quite as active as I'd like but there is a dedicated community to keep multiplayer games active, the biggest problem being that you have to unlock everything in singleplayer to use it in multiplayer. Thankfully it only applies to the host.
All in all, if you're looking for carnage and hilarity involving cars and open world exploration you can't do any better than this game.

Rituals is a short, but atmospheric game filled with weirdness and some light puzzling.
The first thing you'll notice is the low polygon art style and graphics that the game runs with.
We see these kinds of things often with one man studios who don't have the time to go overboard with the graphics.
(I.e The Music Machine a while back)
And in Rituals the artstyle is very well refined and polished giving the game that old school feeling even when it doesn't look that old.
This transfers into the gameplay as well , as you don't move with the traditional WASD keys, but just with the mouse as you click on arrows that take you where you need to go.
This fits the game, but I still don't see why I couldn't do the same thing as a free roaming person.
Other issue is also the mouse movement as you have to hold and drag with the mouse if you want to look around anywhere. This again might be a way to capture nostalgia from older games, I don't know, but it would have been nice to at least have an option to toggle that on and off.
Otherwise the gameplay consist of exploring and finding things of interest related to the plot in the playable area and solving some light puzzles (just don't overthink them).
A very short experience. It took me over an hour with looking at everything and overthinking the puzzles, but one can beat it in under an hour easily.
There are two endings so you might get some replay value from that.
Considering the shortness of it I would wait for a sale, but definitely worthy of an look.

This is a tough game which sucks you into a very real environment in which you can die at almost any time.   No, it's not zombies or aliens;  it's just you in a very hostile, extremely cold environment populated by mammals with sharp teeth and claws.  You get a gun, if you're very lucky, but mostly it's you and your wits.
You've got to keep a close eye on your health, the weather; your fatigue, hunger and thirst levels.  Hypothermia's a risk, so keep an eye on the air temperature and your clothing (I once unwittingly took my jeans off and promptly froze to death - it's easy to die) and no, you can't hide in a cabin you've found - you'll go nuts.  That's Cabin Fever, folks, so there's no real place to hide in this game; you just keep moving, foraging, avoiding bad beasties, and planning ahead - ALWAYS plan ahead.
The last thing you need is a desperate run through a freezing blizzard for shelter because you've not set aside fuel for a fire, which means you don't have enough water from melted snow.  Not good.   Dying of cold and dehydration in temperatures of -42F is not fun.
That said, it's a beautiful game to play; the skies and changing weather conditions are gorgeous to look at, and the realisation of the basic concept is outstanding.
A game which could (should) be boring, is anything but.  In fact, it's bloody tiring and stressful at times.  Sticking your head out of a window to check on weather/wildlife isn't an option - oh no, you've got to go outside, and if Snufkiin the hungry wolf is on the doorstep waiting for his Scooby Snaks it's bad luck for you as you get a brisk massage from his welcoming fangs.
The incidental music is great, atmospheric, and it's...... cold.   In fact, this is a game which sucks you in so much you can actually feel physically cold when playing it.
When you've slugged your way through a storm, health failing, and you find - Glory of Glories - a hut with a stove - well, it's like you've literally saved your life.
In short, this game, currently available in Sandbox and Challenge modes, is an absolute beauty.  When the full Story version is released, it promises to be terrific.
Whatever your preferences, you should give it a go.  It certainly converted this FPS addict to survival games, and it makes you think.  Hard.  All the time.
It's different, in every way, and it's for grown ups only.

What enabled the resonance cascade? Surely, Freeman might have put the final nail in the coffin, but what more factors could have affected the outcome? A broken supercomputer, a malevolent Russian infiltrator; or perhaps an oversleeping scientist. The possibilities are torrential, and in retrospect anything seems conceivable ... perhaps the catastrophe could have been avoided?
, a Black Mesa security guard. His job is simple; main objective: to protect facility equipment and research personnel. He may have Level 3 security clearance into the top-secret Sector B, but don't be deceived - Calhoun is an ordinary guy. But he is about to experience something extraordinary.
  The 16th of May started out just like any other day: the halls of Black Mesa are still somewhat empty,  tired staff grumbles their discontent over yet another early morning, the complex has not yet sprung to life. Calhoun is savoring the silence of the break of day; but suddenly something breaks the silence. Gunshots from down the corridor echoes throughout the vacant rooms. Down the hallway the shooting range has fallen victims to its first wielders, confirming the outset of a new day. A few guards steps through the entrance and greets Calhoun, as if just to confirm it further.
  For an outsider the halls could be hard to navigate, but for the employees it's perfunctory. A left turn; another left; straight forward and to the right: Barney enters the locker-room. It's mandatory to wear your bulletproof vest at all times, and today is no exception. His locker creaks uninvitingly - as if auguring the imminent event - and it sends his 9mm pistol (it's standard-issue among the wardens) toppling to the ground with a resounding clunk. Some turned their heads, others couldn't be bothered. He picked it up and shifted its weight in his palm. The cold metal sent chills down his spine. Chills, in the most delightful meaning of the word. Barney Calhoun is ready for duty….

The gameplay is just amazing, promoting strategy and tactics, going slow and carefull instead of just head on solo rambo mode. The maps are cool, some are hard for one side ( I.E. Defender/Attacker ) but they're mostly well balanced, and well designed.

Get this game on sale. Chances are high you'll only play it once (and my walkthrough, at least, took less than 2 hours), and while it's worth buying it for that, it's much better if you can get it for 1 or 2 dollars (and it gets discounted regularly).
For the most part, I really enjoyed it. It's less a game and more a guided movie, of sorts, and if that doesn't appeal to you then I wouldn't recommend this.
However, if you're interested in a sort of interactive story, I think The Beginner's Guide approaches some really interesting topics and does so through the world of video game creation, which I really enjoyed. I will say that I found the ending somewhat frustrating (there was some heavy-handed leading early on in the game that make you think one thing, and think it for VERY valid reasons, then reverses it for a cheap sort of 'rug pull surprise' moment that seemed unearned) but I was still left thinking about it when I was done, and thinking about some of the moral dilemmas it brought up. For an experience that's not any longer than most movies, that's pretty impressive.

This game has to be one of the biggest let downs for me this year for the indie horror scene. We have all seen our fair shares of terrible indie horror games on Steam but this one was just so promising.
This game is wildly short, in all honestly you can finish it in about 1 hour and still get the full message the game is trying to convey. Don't get me wrong this game has some really awesome parts to it that makes it stand out, such as its creepy setting, art style, and beautiful visual fidelity from the Unreal Engine 4.
I will give it to the art designers, they did a wonderful job but fell really short.
This game puts you in the shoes of a mother who has lost her child in a theme park, you must find him as you physologically unravel the mother's mind. This sounds like a good idea, and honestly delievers in some aspects, but in the strongest points it falls so short that it hurts.
In this game you will experiance four slow moving boring rides, with little to no personality. It is a damn shame since the art team did such a great job at the park's design itself. In a spooky carnival maybe you should of put more creepy physological design into it, and turned the speed up a bit more. Every ride in this game is a choir. Yes, a literal chore.
I found the acting actually quite good for a small indie team, and it delievers great on that part! I loved the mother's role as she gets more and more insane as the game progresses. That being said, she really is the only actor in the entire game, so good job nontheless.
The main villian you meet in this game has a really sweet design too! I love how he looks, just so creepy and well thought out. I very much enjoy this aspect.
Also what about that horror part? Is it spooky? Will it make it hard to sleep after this game?!?!? The short and easy answer is no. I wouldn't even call it a horror game, as it only has about 2 jump scares that even work and nothing phsycologically hit me. Such a sad, and dissapointing aspect.
If this game was longer I believe it could of been passable, but with its boring and lack of personality rides, bland story, and overall lack of creepy design I have to say I don't reccomend it but like what it was trying to be. Maybe if they spent more time on it and tried harder, they would of had a great game and experiance on their hands.

ok..so this game
i haven't ever been mad at a game just for being the game that it is before
i've been mad at bad gameplay, but never anything like this
the park is a "horror/explorative adventure game", which really just means its a horror game with no combat/health/ai/actual danger, which instantly takes all of the impact out of any real scares the game could have. Because of this it focuses completely on small jump scares. The game is less than 2 hours long (more about this later) and there's literally about 4 jumpscares and thats the entire horror aspect of the game
you'd think that since there are zero quality scares in this horror/adventure game it would be more about the adventure and the amazing cinematic story right? i thought so too, but the thing about this game..from the first announcement they said the game was only meant to be an hour or two long, so i'm really confused about how the planning for this story went. The gameplay is literally walking around between cutscenes reading occasional letters on the ground that don't really form a complete story anyway, and the "twist" is predictable within the first 5 minutes of the game or maybe even in the trailers.
-This game, in its short time, uses every horror stereotype/cliche known to man and completely ruins all of them..i cant go into much detail without spoiling the "story" though.
-the first 30 minutes of the 2 hour game are just riding amusement park rides. (its spooky because you're the only one on the ride! ooooh!)
-There are 5 characters in this game and only 1 of them has a single shred of personality and it's totally ripped apart, changed and ruined by the end of the game although there was barely anything there to start with.
-You get no time with the kid before he goes missing so you have no emotional bond or reason to actually want to find him
-the mother is the only character in this game with more than 2 lines unless you count the kid's prerecorded whisper when you press the mouse button to yell for him
-there is SO MUCH unexplained in backstory and lore, but the main story is so uninteresting that by the time the game's over you dont care about what you missed
-it tries to copy the repeating hallways trick from things that did it amazingly like PT but completely ruins it..without any real scares this is just repetitive busywork to extend the game's already short playtime
Overall The Park was a game i was originally very excited for from the first trailers, but was extremely dissapointed with the bad voice acting, short underdeveloped story, boring characters, weird mechanics, and lack of actual horror
TL;DR 1/10 cuz i got to ride a rollercoaster, thank god for steam refunds

Blue Shift is a game for the Half-Life completionist; or perhaps more accurately, people who buy a Half-Life bundle.  If you've finished HL1 and Opposing Force and feel like another couple of hours of that, only not quite as good, Blue Shift might be able to satisfy.
The main problem is that this is short and has very little new content over HL1.  No new weapons, no new enemies, not even all of the ones that showed up in the main game.  It also lacks the polish in its set pieces that the original has, and has rather more back-tracking than other games in this universe.  That said, the gameplay is still enjoyable; it's still Half-Life, even if the weakest incarnation.
Gameplay aside, there's little other reason to play this.  The story of one security guard's escape is rather low-key and underwhelming.  Yes, the player character shares the name of the NPC from HL2.   But as a silent protagonist, he has no personality and might as well be anyone.  There is some world-building as we see more of Black Mesa, including its history with teleportation experiments, and its done fairly competently.  But it's not enough by itself to play this.

When I first got this game I didn't really think much of it. But as time goes on, I keep playing city builders and thinking "that wasn't bad, but Banished did it better." That excludes Rimworld... Rimworld is still my favorite, but more of a survival game than a builder game.
The game is reasonably complex in terms of needs and availability of resources, and gives you decent controls and info to manage your town. It isn't too simple, and it isn't too difficult. It's a pleasant balance. It does have a little learning curve. Some builder games take you through a tutorial for getting started, but I usually feel like "oh, ok, so that's a walkthrough for the early game," so I like the fact that this doesn't do that.
The later game becomes routine, almost an idler, as is common for building games. You get cookie-cutter building layouts that keeps things balanced and just keep slapping em down as newcomers file in. As long as you don't do anything stupid, you really can't lose at that point. I don't like that aspect, but it's kinda standard for this type of game.
There are a few AI glitches. People sometimes group strangely. It's common for a single old widows to monopolize houses, while the town is full of adults living with their parents because they can't find open housing. And if young couples don't have their own homes they don't have children, and you can get in trouble with your entire population getting past breeding age without making any babies. There's workarounds to shuffle people up, but it's a pain they don't do it automatically. It's quiet too. if you don't notice that people have stopped having children, you might suddenly find your entire town dying of old age without any young people to backfill.
Overall, it's a solid, city-building game. While it's not amazing in any single aspect, but it's above average in almost every aspect. Great for relaxing evenings.

TL;DR: feeling of input lag, UI blocks visibility of oncoming walls, game creates left index finger convulsions by tapping E to kill enemies that give you half a second to run from their oneshot, but if you kill them game slows down to make sure you won't use muscle memory.
This game is really close to be really good difficult fast paced game. But it's not. Things that makes me mark this review as NOT recommend are:
1) "input lag" (time offset to be correct) to change lanes - game don't allow changing lanes too fast (why?) so if you press button to quick 2 times you may end up changing lane just once. It gets frustrating on faster levels when you need to change lanes in one direction very fast and you actually can't do it if you press too fast.
2) Arrows showing where to go on blue blockades actually BLOCKS visibility. If you want to look at oncoming walls to predict where to change lane you can't. Game forces you to look on colors because pooping arrow just covers too much space.
3) Enemies are problem. They just add artificial difficulty. You shoot guided missiles at enemy by pressing E. You don't lose anything by pressing E when enemy is not present and actually it helps avoid enemy fire because you will shoot missiles very early when enemy appears. So I personally made habit of tapping E whole game. Next problem with enemies are their aim. Well, this is not surprising that you are one-shot for enemy, but the reaction time that game gives you is just too short to do anything. I think it's around 0.3 - 0.4 sec MAYBE 0.5 second but it's often still too little to make any other move than pressing left or right no matter what is on that lanes. It's indicated by cross appearing on your ship. So, if you are not changing lane constantly you will end up getting shot. Oh, and my favorite are situations when left side is wall, right side is wall, and then mighty cross appears on your ship. Good thing I press E constantly so game is restarted in like second.
And then,  when you get somewhat used to changing lanes with input lag, looking on floor not walls and pressing E while dancing here comes
4) SLOW DOWNS - like really? If you shoot down enemy or get speed up every 15 sec games slows down for a second. Why is it so bad you may ask? It should help, game is very fast blah blah. Yes, sometimes it helps. Sometimes. But often you are getting ♥♥♥♥ed by it because in games that fast it's muscle memory that makes you complete level. So I get terribly often in situations when I see two walls in front of me and I want to change lane between them. Game slow down but my hand still presses left or right button and yet I see that first wall still hasn't passed because of slow down and I crash in it. It also messes with Q-pressing timing when you want to instantly get unblocked.
I really feel bad for this game because it's concept is very good and I still sometimes play it for speed feeling but gets destroyed by details. To make this game fun devs should delete that time offset, move arrows up, give more time to react on enemy aim and delete slow downs. To compensate for difficulty there could be some punishment for pressing E when there is no enemy or Q when non - blocked.

This is a solid game hands down, powered by a great engine and a creative asymmetrical game play model. I have played in Big Alpha, the Open Technical Beta, as well as put in about 6 hours of game time launch night. And my play experience has been the same every time, its phenomenal.
The maps are fantastic, with plenty of variety and almost always give a tense and/or creepy vibe when hunting monsters. There is plenty of wildlife other than the monster that can kill you so you always need to keep you alert, and changing weather conditions that can make the game play more interesting. They are also huge vertically as they are horizontally, giving hunters and monsters paths to sneak past one another or to setup places of engagement.
For the hunters in the standard Hunt mode, it's a game of cat and mouse, where teamwork especially utilizing in-game voip is vital for success. With 12 hunters broken down into 4 classes, they all have their own unique abilities which can be combined to create a deadly hunting party for any given map, monster, and game play style. There is a learning curve, especially playing with new people and monsters you haven't seen much before, but this will all smooth out with time.
For the monster players, you're on your own... well not so much, you can use the more aggressive wildlife to your advantages when picking engagements or as cover when evolving. You can be the predator and go loud or play it more sneaky depending on what monster you choose and what game mode you are playing. All the monsters feel great, and everything seems well balanced.
All in all, this game is fantastic and I can't wait for additional content to come down the pipeline. As for all the whiners who are leaving poor reviews based on the price tag or DLC, well I don't know what to say other than it looks like that most of these people have played in Alpha/Beta, but don't even own the game. The DLC isn't pay to win, so let's just stop that right now, and the price point is fairly modest but so are the ambitions of this game. And for me it's money well spent, a game that will satisfy me for years to come as long as you♥♥♥♥♥♥heads don't poison the pool for no reason. I even bought a copy for my friend I like this game so much.
Buy this game and join the hunt.
Edit: Sept 2016 - When this game re-launched under "Stage-2 Beta", they had a good place to start. Since then they have ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ized the game and many of the original core gameplay elements have changed for the worse.

The Park is a Game by Funcom, the minds behind The Secret World and it plays in the Amusement Park from the same game. If you are solid in TSW Lore, skip this next paragraph if not this might help
An old man decided to harness the magic power of Solomon Island, he did so by constructing a park and using it as a Magic Circuit. However, Usually those kinds of things never go well, and it so happens that the Magic very much tainted the Park. And so during construction and while the park was running terrible accidents and way too much death happened - Until the Player Character comes along and finishes/fixes what the old man once started.
This game happens before that happens.
The Park is one of those experiences you want to be over and you want that to be soon. In a good way. The game can be finished in about 2 hours and leads you through something I never really considered to be scars - a deserted Amusement Park at Night. (Given we are in ♥♥♥♥ed Up Land, but yes.)
The Game opens with a message telling you that it "might play around with control and Audio settings" - just to f**k with you and yes, controls feel a bit sluggish at times, especially towards the end.
the Story is conveyed through the Main character, a mother whose son ran off into the Park to look for his lost teddy bear, talking to herself and occasionally when you Press X To Jason. You will also find reports, Letters and newspaper clippings, but thats not the norm here.
the Atmosphere is just creepy. the park is very small but still manages to creep the living♥♥♥♥♥♥out of me at times. when you step into the rides you'll find that the game does not play with the usual Horror Game Frights, but more relateable ones. Audio - there is almost no music, save for a few notes around some rides and soundwise I didnt pick much up either, However onething providing mild discomfort was that at times whey would play a Bassy sound.
Overall the game is (very) short for its price, but an Experience to be had. It also extends on one of the major points in the first area of TSW.

TL;DR; This game is great recreation of a fan-favorite WC3 mod and the dev team is quick to respond and takes the community seriously.
Please do not be dissuaded by the negative reviews (none of which this game or its dev team deserves). Every negative review here (and I've read most of them) is written by someone who is impatient and does not understand game development at all - let alone what early access means. Early access is a way to greatly include the community in the development process and help the (2 man) development team to iterate on an already solid game *before it is fully released*. It also is a time for them to work out infrastructure issues - which we are currently experiencing. If you can't be patient with an early access game that is being actively developed then you should not purchase it and leave nasty, uneducated reviews. If that is you, just be patient and wait until the game is fully released to review it.
I am personally impressed that this game is made by a 2 man team and I'm not surprised they're having infrastructure problems. At the time I'm writing this it can take up to 5 minutes just to get into the lobby server. This is frustrating enough on it's own but to make things worse you reenter the lobby queue every time you finish a game. From my understanding this is only a temporary solution while they prop up more servers to handle the load which was 20x more than they anticipated at launch (so cut them some slack). I do appreciate their responsiveness to the community and, although this is a headache, I will gladly be patient while they work out the kinks. They've done a great job recreating and improving on the original WC3 mod and I am in no way dissapointed. I'd like to see improved lobby/menu UI which feels a little amatuer at the moment but that, again, is totally understandable as a 2 man team. I think this game has the potential to be a huge success and I'm happy to help support them. Can I donate more money to help?

The Beginner's Guide isn't what it seems on the surface. What starts as a look into the mind of an indepedent, isolated game developer turns into a story of self-reflection and curiosity. If there was just one word to summize my feelings, it would be "invigorating".
Towards the end of the game, you have some time to yourself (the player). You have to think of all that transpired, all that happened and wonder, "Have I done this?", "Am I one guy or the other?", or even "What's next for me?" This game -- while not a game in the traditional sense of the word -- is an eye-opening adventure that will get you to think about yourself and the implications of what this game has to offer.
If you're like me, you'll empathize with both of the characters in this short, insightful piece behind the mind of the Stanley Parable.

First of all, I like this game pretty much. I never played it back in Wacraft III (or atleast I can't remember to have specifically played this game). However, I like it the way it is today.
BUT let me warn you:
The game is still in EARLY ACCESS, that means:
The server are still not able to endure the sheer amount of players who try to login. Depending on the time of the day you have login times ranging from some seconds up to umpteen minutes. And that's just the login time for the lobby server. Right after that you can find a game pretty easily, IF you want to play alone, that is. If you want to try to play with one or more friends together, it gets even trickier. You don't always have a friendlist and can't invite your mates. Suddenly you are in a party with some random people, and when they start their queue you will be queued too!
Then, when you finished your game, you're right back in the login queue to get back to the lobby server, even to see your statistics. If you're unlucky you are unable to queue again (especially when trying with multiple people).
BUT when you get all that to work and bring the time or enough other stuff to do whilst in queue times, then this game is pure bliss. Especially for a mathematic driven person like me. You don't really need much skill or fast mouse movements to master this game, all you need is a really good game knowledge, the ability to use that knowledge, to adapt to your enemies and maybe some decent team mates (it's hard to win when one of your teammates goes afk wave 1). Even tho the players will be replaced by bots when leaving the game entirely. And they still have the ability to reconnect into the game later on.
I really can recommend the game itself, even tho the server stability is definitely not given yet.
Thanks for reading my review.

In anticipation of Playdead's latest offering "Inside" I decided to play this first, as it was free and I never got around to it. I have to say, I am thoroughly impressed with the game despite it not being the kind of game I would normally play. The atmosphere is haunting, the lack of music is foreboding and the plethora of sudden deaths are always surprising and, in many ways, depressing.
Limbo is an atmospheric puzzle-platform game. You will spend all your time running to the right and then stuff will block your progress of running to the right. The game controls very smoothly in comparison with a game like Deadlight, which was clunky and altogether unenjoyable to play. There are only three controls--running, jumping and pushing/pulling. That's it. The game is so simple and yet each puzzle is different and new in a way a much longer game wouldn't be able to recreate. I hear the game is short, but in every way that is preferable. There's absolutely no padding and the atmosphere is just dripping with personality. Plus, there are collectibles you can go back and try to find.
Overall, even if you don't normally like creepy games, give Limbo a try. I don't think you will regret it.

So... Welcome to the least politically correct driving game around, probably.
Short version: If you're looking for a racing game with few rules, many blood stains, low-brow comedy and unplanned comedy, you probably want to give this a go.
Good enough graphics & sound, varied selection of cars to get (with some cool new ones to go along the classics that have always been there), tight controls (highly depending on the vehicle you drive, some aren't designed to be controllable), and more than enough people and livestock to run over for bonus points.
Also, a bunch of different game modes for variety, a reason to explore the maps (that's now  how you get the tokens you need for vehicle upgades),
TL;DR wall of text version:
First, there was Carmageddon. A fun little racing game where you get to roam a wide map to pick your own shortest route to the checkpoints, thus completing laps to win the race. Or, you know, you could just total your opponents instead and be the last one standing. That works too. Oh. And beware of the pedestrians along the track. They're worth points if you make them go SPLAT! and you'll need those points to pay for repairs & stuff. As added bonus, splatting the last ped on the map is another way to be declared winner.
For some reason, that "More pedestrians equals more points!" bit caused a bit of controversy as well.
Then came Carmageddon 2. Which was technically superior to the first in many ways, and was every bit as nuts. It also introduced some godawful timed & scripted missions to♥♥♥♥♥♥people off until they track down the cheat codes to skip those. Hum. I suppose that's the risk of trying to innovate, sometimes what sounds like a good idea doesn't really work out in the end.
Next up, Carmageddon TDR2000. Which introduces crazier vehicles (yay!), messes up the driving physics (boo!) and has pretty much every stage be a timed & scripted mission, thus repeating Carma 2's big mistake several times over (WHY WOULD YOU DO THIS? ARGH!). Suffice to say, this is the black sheep of the series. And that came out back in 2000, after which the series pretty much died.
Until about 15 years later, when the aptly-subtitled Carmageddon: Reincarnation brought things back to life. (That's not counting a fairly troubled Early Access period; the early builds were in all honesty complete♥♥♥♥♥♥in terms of performance and general feel, and the game wasn't really playable until a massive overhaul shortly before release sorted out the biggest issues)
The official release version was still rough, but playable and enjoyable enough to bring back the happy days of driving like a maniac and unleashing the Pedestrian Electro-♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ Ray on unsuspecting crowds. All in all, not stellar, but it did prove the general idea is still valid in this day and age.
It got a bunch of updates along the way, and then promptly disappeared from the digital stores where it was sold.
That's because for console release, there was this updated version titled "Carmageddon: Max Damage". With more spit & polish and stuff. So the devs decided that should replace Reincarnation on Steam as well.
With all the work put into it by now, this really is a worthy successor to 1 & 2, and it's a perfect game to just pick up & play for some relaxing mindless violence.

When I first got this game I didn't really think much of it. But as time goes on, I keep playing city builders and thinking "that wasn't bad, but Banished did it better." That excludes Rimworld... Rimworld is still my favorite, but more of a survival game than a builder game.
The game is reasonably complex in terms of needs and availability of resources, and gives you decent controls and info to manage your town. It isn't too simple, and it isn't too difficult. It's a pleasant balance. It does have a little learning curve. Some builder games take you through a tutorial for getting started, but I usually feel like "oh, ok, so that's a walkthrough for the early game," so I like the fact that this doesn't do that.
The later game becomes routine, almost an idler, as is common for building games. You get cookie-cutter building layouts that keeps things balanced and just keep slapping em down as newcomers file in. As long as you don't do anything stupid, you really can't lose at that point. I don't like that aspect, but it's kinda standard for this type of game.
There are a few AI glitches. People sometimes group strangely. It's common for a single old widows to monopolize houses, while the town is full of adults living with their parents because they can't find open housing. And if young couples don't have their own homes they don't have children, and you can get in trouble with your entire population getting past breeding age without making any babies. There's workarounds to shuffle people up, but it's a pain they don't do it automatically. It's quiet too. if you don't notice that people have stopped having children, you might suddenly find your entire town dying of old age without any young people to backfill.
Overall, it's a solid, city-building game. While it's not amazing in any single aspect, but it's above average in almost every aspect. Great for relaxing evenings.

If you ever wanted to experience the battlefields of WWII from the soldier's perspective, this game is for you.
Red Orchestra is an amazing WWII FPS. This isnt a run-and-gun arcadey COD game. This is a survival game where you must always stay in cover and keep your head down or it will be blown off. Staying in the open is a death sentance as you will be killed in one shot by the basic rifle. The two teams will usually run into eachother in a meatgrinder of attrition until one side runs out of reiforcements. As far as I can tell, the only real way to play the game is realism mode.
Red Orchestra is an experience like no other game I have played. This is what you will get:
- Running with your comrades as you are mowed down by machine guns.
- Getting blown to pieces by a well placed artillary strike.
- Having your squad leaders give you orders (and occasionally arguing with eachother hilariously)
RO has a relatively high learning curve. You have to learn how to search for enemies while both you and them are in cover. The first to spot, aim, and fire will usually win as you will likely die to a single shot.
This game is about getting positions. The LMGs will get into a punishing position and halt an advance (through spamming everywhere) until he is taken out from the good positioning of a sniper. Once you learn how to find a good position, you can find yourself getting a large amount of kills. But as I said, this takes learning of maps, and learning how to use cover effectivly. While you are not in a good position, you will be getting killed quickly by those who do.
Well this is less of a reveiw and more of me rambling about the game, where more experienced players could tell you much more. So I will just end with my rating. 9/10
