Atmospheric but short,
tells an exciting story in the small amount of time you’ll spend with it, while leaving you sufficiently creeped out.
You begin the game as Lorraine, a mother who has some obvious issues. Your son, Callum, tells you he can’t find Mr. Bear, so you head back into the park, and thus begins your adventure.
is a first-person exploration game. You can add walking simulator on top of that, if you like. As Lorraine, you travel to several different areas of the park, all within a few minutes of each other. You’ll go on a (creepy) tunnel of love ride, a (creepy) rollercoaster and, of course, (creepy) bumper cars. Along the way, you’ll find notes, which help tell the backstory of the park, several items to examine, see things that aren’t there.
Funcom wasn’t lying when they said that
would be a short experience. If you choose not to explore every nook and cranny, and not read all the notes, you can easily complete it in half an hour. I completed it in 45 minutes, and that was with reading every document I came across and examined everything I was able to. (Don’t let my time played fool you; the rest of the time played is letting the game idle to unlock the cards, and a quick replay to get screenshots and video for my achievement guide.)
While a quick experience, it’s a good experience. They’ve done an excellent job with the creepiness factor. If you’ve been around horror games (or any horror medium, for that) long enough, you likely won’t be disturbed or otherwise “scared” of what the game has to offer. The story is entertaining, and really paints a portrait of Lorraine as, well, you’ll find out soon enough.
.
is very atmospheric. The amusement park itself is dark and foreboding, rides and equipment are run down and rusty. Some of the ending sequences are very well done, and evoke a feeling of P.T. On that note, there’s also a Silent Hills-esque feeling that I had when wandering around.
. If you’ve played The Secret World long enough, you’ll get a few references. Considering
is a spin-off of TSW, that’s to be expected. There’s nothing major, but they’re fun little “oh, that’s interesting” moments.
. For the most part, Lorraine is voiced quite well. Most of her dialog seems natural, and doesn’t feel forced. The further into the story you progress, she sounds more and more desperate and afraid when you use the shout mechanic.
. The world looks nice. The rusty ferris wheel enshrouded in fog, the rollercoaster that feels like it’s going to fall apart, the statues of Chad the mascot spread throughout the park, everything looks well detailed.
. There are a few jump scares, only a few. They are well placed, don’t seem forced, and they don’t ruin the immersion too much.
. Lorraine, Callum and the very limited number of other people you meet do not look good. At all. They are passable, but they look like they belong in a game that hasn’t come out this decade.
. Right-clicking has Lorraine call out for Callum, in a variety of ways.
As the story progresses, it’s interesting to see how her dialog and voice change, but overall, the mechanic is pretty useless. When you use it, it puts a sort of retracting blur effect on items of interest, such as notes. But, considering that the game lacks any puzzles, and everything is presented to you in plain view, it seems out of place.
. I debated putting this as a con or not. Funcom specifically stated it would be a very short experience, so there should be no excuse for buying the game and being surprised at how quickly you’ll get through it. It’s a good experience in the short amount of time, but if you’re looking for something to last longer than what your coffee stays hot for, you may want to look elsewhere.
is a fantastic experience. It’s short, but contains a great deal of story telling and immersion. It’s interesting to see what happens, and to find out what’s actually going on. It’s atmospherically horror, with only a few jump scares, and will certainly entertain you for its duration. At its low price, I consider it good value for money, but as always, your mileage may vary.

An entirely linear "interactive" story by Funcom which has some mild scare bits, a story that leaves you with a bad aftertaste in your mouth, and a whole lot of issues in terms of gameplay.
- The XBox Controller's B button won't allow you to "back" out of menus. Nor does the "back" button.
- The "headthrobbing" quickly gets on one's nerves.
- The player character narrates the story from time to time - turning off running while she talks. This is really obnoxious since the game is essentially a walking simulator. You advance the story by going from one park ride to another and there's a lot of ground to cover in between them.
- Talking about running; you can't run until you get to the point where the game tells you what key to use to run. Forget trying it before that point as that particular key is not "active" until that point.
- Interaction hovertext is glitchy and may appear in random positions and half out of the screen while you pass by an item, or appear in the center of the screen when you're nowhere near the item.
- Especially in the rollercoaster part of the level there are some longer texts which only flash by and are impossible to read as a result. Even when playing the game twice.
- The game is so linear it could have been "on rails" if not for the part where you're searching for badly hidden interactive objects along the road. They even go so far as to put you in the middle of a round area, and then put the bogeyman on the road so you can only go around it in one direction.
- On lower resolutions, the scraps of paper you find are impossible to read. On a laptop with a resolution of 1366x768 I could not read the letters on the papers I found even with my nose pressed against the screen! Really a big oversight.
- Areas shut off from being revisited once you exit them, the game literally demanding the player to push forward to the next area, up until you've found everything you need for the story to progress to the House of Horrors, when all of the park is suddenly open and accessible for no apparent reason.
- The in-game lore is a little "out there" for people who have not played The Secret World and understand the players at work there. There's barely any information for people to piece that story together properly, except for a lot of mentioning of places found on Solomon Island, something the player would have no attachment to one way or another if they have not played The Secret World.
- Apparently the spoken "Don't let them take me" is supposed to be "Don't take me" according to the subtitles.
- I guessed at "the big reveal" about ten minutes into the game and only had it confirmed in the last FMV of the game.
- Did I mention the game is really short? We're talking less than 2 hours playtime here.
I'm happy to obtain the special items for my TSW account, so I at least have something for my troubles, but there's no replay value here besides trying to complete the achievement list if you missed anything on your first go.
I really wish Funcom had put some more effort into making the game more engaging. This could have been so much better, considering the park's background story. Instead they put the focus on something entirely unrelated and used the park as a backdrop. Such a shame.
Lastly, just so I'm not a complete negative Nancy; there were a few good things about the game;
+ The atmosphere is great. It's what was to be expected; dark places, wind howling, the occasional sound that makes you wonder if you really heard it.
+ The chipmunk is sufficiently creepy and pops up in places you least expect him to be in. He's not overused, but the amount of his appearances are just right for the length of the game.
+ The rides are decently thought out even if it's clear they're separate instances. It's not as seamless as I would have liked, but it's barely a bother considering the limited amount of games which have good carnival rides in them.
+ The role of the bogeyman when it concerns the rides was a nice touch.
+ The house of horrors had just the right amount of creep to it, although I had expected some more events when interacting with things like the faucet or some of the doors.
+ For players of The Secret World, there was a nice amount of additional lore to gather.
Still; I do not recommend this game in this state. This was not the right place to have a story about post-natal depression. It would have been better served following the trail of death from the park's opening to its inevitable closing, and go in deeper on the cause for the supernatural events that took place there.

The Park is an excellent game! It's the video-game equivalent of "The Shining" except without all the sweetness and light. It's spooky, it's got some good scares, and it's a compelling horror story. I've heard it panned as "a walking simulator" and that's a fair complaint - BUT it's not meant to be a FPS, quick-time-event, combat game. It's a story-game - where you explore your environment, interact with objects, and learn what really happened that fateful day at Atlantic Island Park. This game is absolutely best experienced in a dark room with headphones on.  The sound and voice acting are phenomenal.

The concept of this game is simple: avoid the white barriers until sixty seconds have passed. Sounds simple enough. However, at fifteen second intervals, the game speeds up. And it will continue to until you either reach the end of the level, or you die. The latter result will happen much more often then the former unless you have incredible reflexes. While the gameplay moves way too fast for me, the performance was smooth and I didn't find any bugs or glitches in my brief playthrough. In short, a low cost (and well made) Unity game that gave me a nasty migraine after twenty minutes of playing it. If you like extremely fast-paced "avoid-'em-ups" and are willing to deal with it's insane learning curve, then it might be worth your time.

In anticipation of Playdead's latest offering "Inside" I decided to play this first, as it was free and I never got around to it. I have to say, I am thoroughly impressed with the game despite it not being the kind of game I would normally play. The atmosphere is haunting, the lack of music is foreboding and the plethora of sudden deaths are always surprising and, in many ways, depressing.
Limbo is an atmospheric puzzle-platform game. You will spend all your time running to the right and then stuff will block your progress of running to the right. The game controls very smoothly in comparison with a game like Deadlight, which was clunky and altogether unenjoyable to play. There are only three controls--running, jumping and pushing/pulling. That's it. The game is so simple and yet each puzzle is different and new in a way a much longer game wouldn't be able to recreate. I hear the game is short, but in every way that is preferable. There's absolutely no padding and the atmosphere is just dripping with personality. Plus, there are collectibles you can go back and try to find.
Overall, even if you don't normally like creepy games, give Limbo a try. I don't think you will regret it.

When it comes to a sense of place, and of being, I don't think I've been as fully immersed in a game as I have in The Long Dark. Here's how it works...
You wake up in the snow after your plane has gone down. WIth no idea as to where you are, cold, shivering, you need to find shelter fast and keep a sharp eye out for predators. Once you've found a cabin or such, you need to start thinking about the basics of survival. Water. A warm place to rest. Food. Clothing that can survive the harsh blizzards. A weapon to fend off wolf attacks. To gain the answer to these problems you must explore. At first you'll find yourself raiding abandoned cars and houses, trying not to think about the dead bodies scattered here and there following an as yet undetailed catastrophe. But the cans of pop and candy bars and such you scavange are only a temporary answer. Soon you'll have to look to be self-sufficient.
Survive the first few nights and odds are you can survive a couple of weeks. Survive those two weeks and you might survive a month. Survive that and... who knows? The genius of the game is that it perfectly balances risk, need, fear and greed. You can get carried away and suddenly discover that you've neglected something vital - something life endangering. Forget to stay stocked with fuel and you could perish from being marooned in a cave by a blizzard. Fail to carry bandages with you and you might bleed out from a wolf bite on the snowy wastes. Dehydration especially is a danger. (And no, like in real life simply eating snow will not save you.)
It can be a punishing game at first. Nothing is explained. I didn't know how to make tinder plugs or melt snow in my first game and quickly died after I ran out of my last can of fizzy goodness. But I made darn sure I figured it out the next game. The more you play, the more you find yourself thinking logically and weighing up the risks. Which is all well and good until you become obsessed about getting a bearskin bedroll and end up dooming yourself to be a chewy snack for DiCaprio's growly chum. Happily there's an excellent forum at the Hinterland website, which is very friendly. I strongly recommend it if you have trouble sussing out the game mechanics.
Lastly I want to talk about what makes this game truly special. It's the marriage of beautifully crafted graphics with to my mind the best sound design since Battlefield: Bad Company 2's War Tapes. At first glance the graphics appear simplistic. But you quickly come to appreciate them as being truly evocative, especially in terms of weather. Seeing the deep tread of your footprints as you hear the muffled scrumpf of snow underfoot. Watching a sunrise from the porch of your farmhouse in the morning; a hot cup of coffee a personal treat to celebrate narrowly surviving a blizzard the previous day, as you finally recognised the tell-tale signs of an oncoming storm. Looking up to see the high altitude trade winds carrying aloft the first wave of a fresh snow. And the chilly haunting fog that closes in as you return home in the late evening, a brace of coneys over your shoulder. Even simple things like waking up in the cabin and hearing the walls creak and the windows rattle as the wind blows outside... man, this game is the most atmospheric I've ever played.
So sure it's tough. And yes, wolves are unnaturally terrifying. But as soon as you come to terms with your inevitable death. As soon as you begin to treat it not as a game but as a real question of survival for yourself. And as soon as you learn to let go of trying to max everything out and just enjoy... existing... in this wonderful world HInterland have crafted. Well, then you'll find you've made something really special. Plus you can keep a journal in game!
Any gripes? Each map could do with a forge, and whetstones really shouldn't break after a couple of dozen uses. (I know, game mechanic, but it's unnecessarily cruel.) Also rifles should have a longer effective range and arrows should be more available. Some items, like the maple needed to make a bow, seem unnecessarily rare and tricky to find.) And there should be a little starter guide with a few early-game lifesaving tips bundled with the game in the main menu. And I wish my character would quit complaining all the time about being hungry! It's good to be ravenous and make supplies last!
Despite these niggles the game as it stands at this point in Early Access really is something quite magnificent. It is a transporting game that will have you feeling terrified at times, proud at others and most of all have you feeling that the little farmhouse in the valley has become a place of your own, a place that you can call home in a hostile world. With a story mode to come this game only looks set to become better, but for now I feel that I've definitely got my money's worth on the entrance fee. Congratulations HInterlands for recognising that surviving the natural world can be more thrilling than surviving yet another rehashed zombie invasion, and that the simple joy of felling a deer and filling one's pantry with venison as significant a victory as saving the planet in a shoot-em-up from the evil Emperors RaxinFraxin and Dixdastardlax.
9/10

Very mixed feelings about this title.
Graphically and performance-wise, Carmageddon Max Damage is OK. Its previous version, Carmageddon Reincarnation, definitely had some problems in that respect but Stainless did manage to resolve nearly all of them. I have not experienced any crashes or slowdowns with Max Damage at least. Note that the game has fairly heavy requirements so if you are close to the minimum CPU and/or memory, you will probably suffer and have to tone down your settings.
Other than that, the game pretty much "feels" like Carmageddon 1 and 2. You race, you crash into opponents, you mow down pedestrians, pedestrians run/wheel away screaming. "I was in teh war!" Oh yes, they are all there ...
If you already lost me, then I assume you never played one of the earlier titles. In that case, realise that Carmageddon is NOT A RACING GAME. This is a game about wreaking havoc and death & destruction. If you are looking for a racing game, or a game with realistic vehicle behaviour, or stunning graphics or whatever, this is not the game for you. Carmageddon is all about pure and uncensored fun, nothing more, nothing less.
So is it a good title then, you ask? Is it better than Carmageddon 1 and 2? (I've chosen to ignore Carmageddon TDK because it blows.)
Well, yes and no. In a way it plays exactly like the earlier titles, but with improved graphics. That is a good thing. Except for the awful car handling, which is still exactly the same as I remember it 20 years ago (seriously of all the things you could change you kept the worst bit?). The developers included a few extras, like additional controllable powerups and a few more race modes, but nothing that warrants a new purchase. Get this title only if you want Carmageddon with shiny new graphics.
But ... there is always a but ... The game has severe balancing issues. The opponents in Carmageddon 1 and 2 were always cheating ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s; able to zoom accross the map without care for the terrain and its pitfalls if you had no direct line of sight to them. That is still the case, but the game now even goes beyond that. The opponents are a lot more stronger than you: they can crash you in a few hits, while it takes you forever to whittle them down. They are almost always faster than you, but the second that you step into their car (after you stole it), that very same car drives like a dead snail even after you spent your scarce upgrade points on it. Opponents can reach checkpoints in nearly impossible to reach places easily when not visible, but the second you are near them they stumble and fumble to reach that same checkpoint.
Not that this makes the game a lot harder ... it is actually very difficult to lose an event against the AI players. Nevertheless, that cheap behaviour might have been acceptable 20 years ago when CPUs were not powerful enough to handle complex AI, but nowadays computers can handle AI calculations so there should be no need to aid the computer-driven cars that way.
The balancing issues suck a good portion of the fun out of this title: the obligatory (!) missions where you have to grab checkpoints to score points become exercises in frustration as opponents can crash you sometimes in a single hit, stealing your points, while you it takes you so long to steal a point of your own that other players meanwhile scored an additional 2 or 3 points. Similarly you see AI cars winning in races, despite the fact you saw them drive off a cliff or against a wall barely a minute earlier.
Summarizing, I cannot in good conscience recommend this title at full price. It has its fun moments, no doubt about that. And those who played the previous entries in the series will get their kick. But the balance problems and forced checkpoint-grabbing/racing minigames are so frustrating that you will never play this game for long stretches of time. Get this at a good discount.

I've got some majorly mixed feelings on this game. For context, I've played a LOT of Tropico 1 & small amounts of Tropico 4 before playing 5.
Positives:
-The era setup is neat, and provides more variety over the course of both sandbox games and campaign missions.
-Great sense of humor by the writers. Every single building in the game has funny flavor text, the radio announcer is sarcastic as hell, and the mission dialogues are (mostly) great.
-The campaign's good. Its missions do a good job of slowly introducing you to game mechanics & new challenges, and alternate between two different islands that you slowly build up over the eras.
-The core gameplay is still rock solid. Not much has actually changed from previous games, but the formula works.
Neutral:
-The dynasty system is definitely different from past Tropicos, but I'd hesitate to call it better or worse. Replacing traits with manager skills takes a layer of interest out of it, since all the skills are completely positive now. It also leads to your dynasty becoming overpowered as it gets more members, since each one brings a global effect(bonus starting money, cheaper buildings, etc) along with the usual manager effect. On the other hand, it's less over-centralizing than the trait system was - you're not going to be changing your strategies to fit your presidente anymore.
Negatives:
-The almanac needs serious work. My biggest complaint is that many economy figures track over the entire span of a game. It's tolerable in the campaign, but renders the almanac nearly useless in long-running sandbox games. Being able to see yearly figures would help enormously. (There are graphs provided, but they're much less useful than being able to see raw numbers.)
-The fog of war is more of a nuisance than anything. Instead of naturally uncovering as your settlements get closer to it, you have to send out military expeditions(at $1000 a pop) to remove it. But there's a technology in the World Wars era that removes the fog of war completely, so it only really matters in the Colonial era.
-The military is godawful. It's sad that guard towers(which automatically fight enemies) are so much better than actual military units(which have to slooooooowly travel across your island to engage).
On the whole the game is enjoyable, but I'm not sure I'd recommend it to somebody who already owns 4.

Many will get mad over this post, but I do not care. I absolutely do not recommend this game if you have ever played any citybuilding games before. If you're new to this genre or play this because you watched a Youtuber play it for a few seconds, then ignore this post.
However, if you've grown up on city builders and played the gems that are Caesar III and Zeus, even Rollercoaster Tycoon and Anno 1404 (or others), then this will bore the HELL out of you. I've seen things moving when I'm not touching anything, not moving the mouse, not turning, not moving at all - but it's super slow.
One turn off is the game is constantly yelling "SUPER HOT" at me when I finish a level or "scenario" and I find that it already got annoying, and the white backgrounds are too white in some places and I can't turn the gamma down enough so I can clearly read anything that's on the replay/upload part of the screen. Minor stuff, really.  Just left-click and keep going.
The game's concept is simple.  You're in a scenario where people are trying to kill you.  Mostly time only moves when you do.  Constant "bulle ttime" - sort-of.  You can punch, shoot, throw stuff, chop (so far, at 14 minutes of gameplay) so there are several ways to deal with opponents.  Gun out of ammo?  Chuck it in buddy's face.  Oh, he had a gun? All the while two other guys are shooting at you, so move the right way before those bullets get to you.
As of 2017-01-24 it's on sale.  Go get it, or at least check out some gameplay footage.  Let me tell you one more thing.  I'm very critical of games.  I usually develop hatred of a game within the first hour or two of gameplay.  It usually (but not always) takes even longer for me to say I enjoy a game.  I've got under 15 minutes played as I write this, and I'm telling you to give this game a shot.

For being recently revived with Fl4tout, I feel like I should get into this review. This game is a racing game, but it's not a usual racing game. Why is that? Well, Bugbear, the devs, used a specific engine and used it for car damage, making it seem realistic, at least for the time. That is why this game is remembered, including the great modes.
This game has normal races, where you race for 1st using nitro and reckless driving as well as shortcuts. There are also derbys where you go and be the last one standing, but you can't coward away since you have to smash others, otherwise, your timer goes down and you die. There are also Olympic Events? Yeah, you can LAUNCH your driver out the window and do things like a long jump, cards, and other crazy stuff. I can't make that stuff up. This game also isn't easy, unless you grind money and upgrade like crazy, you will be challenged! To me, it seems underwhelming, but you might like it.
The game's music is all licensed stuff by different bands. I would go into the bands used, but I can't remember the names. I didn't find it too memorable anyway. When EA licensed music in say, their sports games, I can usually remember it, so this is weird.
The game's graphics use NVidia hardware from the 2000s, as this was released in around 2003-2005. It still looks really good and like I said earlier, the game's damage model is fantastic. Not as good as say, Wreckfest, a game also by Bugbear that will finally reach full release in 2018. Now if this game was remade in HD, we would all be going crazy because we wouldn't be able to handle the awesomeness.
Some other things to know is that this game had online, and when I say 'had,' I mean it because GameSpy, the onnline system used, is now down. It's disappointing to see online be gone, but you can do local multiplayer still. This PC version also allows mods, and many mod cars exist, some better than others. Some mods actually recreate real sports cars like NASCAR and such, and others let you drive an egg. And I thought the drivable toilet mod in GTA V was strange. You can set up a controller, but you can't use it in menus for some reason. Only in gameplay. The controls work fine, I just wish the controller worked everywhere.
Overall, this game still holds up. While the difficulty can be overwhelming at times and the races can be sometimes not the best designed, you can still have mega fun. It is worth the 9.99 price it has, and the game is also on PS2, PSP, (Flatout Head On) XBOX360 (Flatout Ultimate Carnage), and on
. You can get this game at many places, but I recommend either this version, or the PSP version (portability).

After reading lots of other reviews it seemed like this game was generally regarded as very fun, but shorter than most people expected.  It does seem like I'm in the minority, but sadly I didn't find any aspects of this game actually *fun*, and I really wanted to like it.
The core mechanics seem to be built around the idea that you should carefully time your actions and plan things out, but in reality it just comes down to jittering yourself back and forth to move the timestep along predictably.  It's not satisfying at all to see the replay at the end of the stage, which I guess was supposed to make your path through the level look impressive and meticulously timed - instead it's just an up-to-speed version of the spastic nonsense that you had to do to dodge all the enemies and projectiles.  I didn't feel like beating the levels was ever an accomplishment, and dispatching the enemies was tedious instead of exciting.
While it's clear a lot of time was spent making the UI look like an old scanline text prompt, it's mostly just irritating.  Even if it's masking loading times or something, delaying every action behind animations and obnoxious screen garbling just makes the whole thing feel unresponsive.  Maybe that was the goal, I don't know.   I also can't tell if the minimalist art direction was chosen on purpose, or just done because it would be far cheaper and faster not to have model decent looking assets and textures.
I didn't find this game to be a fun shooter or a fun puzzle game.  I honestly have no idea why other Steam users described this as a "great game" or an "awesome experience."  At best it feels like a very polished tech demo with some disjointed story elements.

Nothing ruins something more than an onslaught of ridiculously obssessive fans that like to bang on about something, because a part of your interest in a game is automatically jaded from the large likelihood of a game not being as brilliant as they want to tell you.
No, don't get me wrong. In its entirety, Five Nights at Freddy's is pretty good. But because of the 12 year olds that haven't heard of four simple words, "Resident Evil" and "Silent Hill", the Five Nights at Freddy's game has turned from being a potentially brilliant series into nothing more than a mainstream fad. Once FNAF 4 comes, and give it a few months, and I guarantee this series will be banished into the abyss of obscurity. It happened to Amnesia, it happened to Slender. It's the hard truth of the mainstream gaming community.
But I digress. When Five Nights at Freddy's does something well, it does something, reeeeallly well. It's not "just jumpscares". Heck, the only jumpscares that happens is when you die. What this game excels at is tension. The lack of movement and vision allows your paranoid imaginations to run free and plays you into the hands of the animatronics. The almost silent room, with the exception of the fan that's draining your energy like the AAA gaming developers drain my soul, is crippling, and really allows you to sink everything in, the fact that you only have one shot to keep Freddy, Foxy, Chica, and Bonnie away from you or your done for. Somehow, practically all of the elements of this game combine to somehow work, despite pre-rendered animations, simple gameplay, and stock children cheering sound effects.
Is Five Nights at Freddy's talked about to death? Absolutely, but Scott's not to blame for that. I hate flying. Even with the facts that indicate a accident is far, FAR from likely, I’m still on the edge of♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥myself. It’s not what could happen during a flight, its the fact that I’m spitting distance from the ♥♥♥♥ing stratosphere. Thats kinda what I feel about Rapture. A nearly beautiful  and nearly flawless in concept, but essentially enabling UNREGULATED, UNSTABLE, ADDICTIVE SUPER SERUM use in a goddamned fish tank, makes the whole thing far from desirable.
BioShock is one of those games used as a shining example of gaming as art, or how an interactive narrative should be done. While the narrative is rather fantastic, I don’t see how adding a art deco style to something makes it artsy. A pretty damned good design, but thats where it stops, as it’s simply design. Going with the theme of what’s “pretty damned good” about BioShock lie in mostly with it’s strong story and combat.
Finding yourself victim to a plane crash over the city of Rapture, you soon delve down into the briny deep to the underwater dystopia for sanctuary. What you find is a dying city, full of genetically spliced psychopaths, are a range of weapons that don’t really deviate from the standard formula of melee, pistol, shotgun, machine gun, explosive, and exotic weapons. What I do enjoy is your not restricted to two weapons, leaving you with an entire arsenal at your disposal. It compensates for your ability to break into Fort Knox by having ammunition relatively scarce, resulting in a very balanced and cohesive experience, complemented with satisfying gun recoil and accuracy. All modifiable at one time use upgrade stations, offering sizeable bonus to damage, ammo consumption and capacity.
Still, plasmid use is what BioShock is where seeks to bare its teeth. Essentially powers that rely on a mana bar for use, plasmids offer an interesting spin on game play, giving you a second option if your ammunition drys up. While there are a quite a few to choose from, you won’t really need to deviate beyond some core combat powers, being fire and lightning attacks. Rendering other options rather muted, being used once for experimentation and never again. All also upgradable for a certain amount of ADAM, which acts essentially as money.
Going with the theme of genetic manipulation, the player is granted a variety of passive buffs in the form of gene tonics. Each can either improve combative abilities or aid in hacking minigames. It’s rather marginal, but Irrational Games needed some place to crame those pesky RPG elements.
Complementing BioShock’s solid combat mechanics are the surprisingly variant baddies to murder. Be it the hulking Big Daddies, gun toting Lead Heads, or wall crawling Spider Splicers, they all offer a certain depth to combat, giving every weapon and plasmid a purpose. Making larger fights rather tense and exciting. Though, enemy types tend to be grouped together early on, damping the game a bit.
Storywise however, BioShock shines brightest. It offers legitimate intrigue and speculation early on, helped along with the absolutely stellar voice acting lent. Providing a clear cut objective that ties in with the world that you find yourself in, as you interact with various key political figures of Rapture’s past glory. Providing a twist that was so smartly written, you can’t help but feel it was hurt by it being told through a cut scene. As you are almost always behind the controls, you are the one that is carrying the story along, not a cut scene. It’s very reminiscent of Half Life in this respect, keeping you engaged with the plot the whole way through.
Having given this game non stop praise, the only negatives I can find is with its later half, which is more level padding and far from necessary. Everything else is spot on and virtually excellent, with it’s tight and engaging story and characters, coupled with its solid combat system, I can’t really live with myself if I didn't say BioShock can be considered a genre benchmark.

Not a good horror game, not a bad horror game. Just not much here at all. The scares don't really start until you've basically left the actual park. The park itself has nearly no scares of any variety. There's maybe 3 or 4 jump scares, some decent psychological scares (but only at the very end when you're not really in the park). It's got a pretty eerie atmosphere though.
Controls are clunky and slow and unintuitive. The shout mechanic is literally just a waypoint marker.
The story is decent given how very short the game is. I care just enough about the mother to want to know what's going to happen and the newspaper clippings really give the park a chilling history. Too bad the park itself doesn't take advantage of ANY of it's back story. Unfortunately the game kinda just... ends. No emotion from the final scene. Length is also a serious problem. Taking my sweet time I managed to beat the game in 1.5 hours. There's nothing to explore and the very short story is severely drawn out by slow movement speed and even slower mandatory rides. There's less substance here than your typical Saw or Paranormal sequel.
Graphics are decent but performance is meh at best. Given the lack of draw distance, high res textures or overly detailed objects I'd expect to be able to max 60 this game at 5760x1080 with my computer (GTX 980Ti, Intel Core i7 4790k) but even with reduced settings could only get about 40-50 frames. Hardly terrible numbers at all. No serious dips and no choppiness. The graphics themselves are very decent. They more than do the job and don't detract from the game. The occasional animations however do detract from the game. They're simply bad but fortunately there aren't many animations at all. Also the triple screen support is quite excellent I'm happy to say. I didn't have to do any tinkering to get it to work and there is nearly zero screen warp on the outer edges.
Overall I cannot recommend this game. Though it's not bad it excels at absolutely nothing including being scary. I won't even say I was disappointed by the game as it has decent moments. Do I regret my 10$ purchase? I don't. But Layers of Fear is a substantially better game in every way for about the same price. Still living classic. But... sadly, just barely.
In the time Age of Wonders was released (year 1999), it was something technically and conceptually in-between of the Heroes of Might and Magic 2nd and the 3rd volumes. Visually it was prettier than the 2nd HoMM, and by the scale of maps it was at least on the level with HoMM 3. The story was gross by the size... but kinda second-rated and very much Tolkien-based, only the halflings were much more sturdy and agressive fighters again, just as fierce as goblins.
Basically it is still looking much like HoMM - you have some main hero, a map with castles you need to conquer first and develop right after that, with the gold you can gather on the map. Unlike HoMM, you can send your troops without a leader (a hero), to move further and repossess some stuff laying on the land. Also, the battle system is not the same as in the HoMM and King's Bounty series. It's turn-based all-right, there are grids, yes, but there are much more space, with the vegetation and buildings all around, and the view perspective is just like as on the big map. I gotta say that battle system, while certainly not so refined and deep as in the HoMM, feels kinda better for that feeling of bigger perspective of the battlefield.
All in all, it plays solid enough even now... But only if you're used to such old concepts, visuals, and other technical limitations of the games made 20 years back. However.. I wouldn't recommend to buy it now, if it's not of some nostalgic or explorative interest.
The game is dated way too bad. I can easily play HoMM 1 and 2 on my GOG account, but with Age of Wonders I have trouble. The resolutions, the stability, other strictly technical issues... Sorry, people, it's just a rotten hull for the most part of gaming auditory nowadays, and I don't see any measures to recover and resurrect it.
Well, my mark is 6.7/10, but... it's a dance with a mummy.

I've always struggled a little in finding a good definition for art. Maybe it's just because the only forms of it that I personally enjoy are literature, and games. The first, as a rule, is self-explanatory. A book (at least a good one) has a purpose, and will take you somewhere. Video games have an even greater drive, a very focused destination that the player will intimately understand. Sometimes the formula is changed, sometimes tropes are played with and you get a game that isn't linear. Even the games with expanding worlds and never-ending playability have a singular purpose. After all, if it didn't, why would you play?
So when it comes to other forms of art, I sometimes have trouble with the fluid, abstract definitions that come into play. "The curtains are blue", and meaning beyond that can end up feeling pretentious or just superfluous. You don't need more. Or, so I thought.
This game doesn't have a sense of completion. It's not even a game, in that sense. It's on a computer, you choose what your character does, but you're not going to play this like you are going to play something else.
I think this is art. I think this is a person's perspective on art, and how people have different perspectives.
It took me a hundred minutes to play this. No real re-playability. But I'd call it worth it. A glimpse into the mind of someone else, and not necessarily the mind that the developer is talking about.

The Park… an interesting, although generic, title. One that you might not necessarily link to an amusement park (unless you already took a look at the screenshots). What we all want to know, however, is this: is it a walk in the park or is there more than meets the eye here?
When I say ‘walk in the park’ I mean that quite literally actually. It’s a semi-interactive game but all you do is basically walk. It’s what people call a ‘walking simulator’ these days, and for good reason. There’s usually not much to do in games like this and they’re dependent on the story being told. Anyway, you walk along a set path (you can branch off into a different direction, but that’s it) while the story is being told by monologues and objects found in the game world and, of course, scripted events. These objects are usually found in the form of documents and books and can sometimes be interacted with, but it’s all very limited. Players of Gone Home will know what to expect. Usually the written material lies hidden in plain sight and sometimes it requires a tiny bit of exploring, but even without exploring you should understand the story without too many problems. Besides reading you will also be able to get on the rides. In fact, the rides are the biggest part of the story.
Since the game is quite short (one to two hours) I can’t really go into the story as much as I would like. In fact, I can’t go anything it all without spoiling something. Just saying something short could spoil (a part of) the experience and it wouldn’t be fun for (potential) players, as well as the developer who put (a lot of) time, money and effort into it. If you eventually decide to play this game and you finished
enjoyed it within two hours of playtime then do yourself a favor and don’t try to request a refund. It would be quite insulting to the developer and good art should be appreciated.
The atmosphere is grim and tense and overall the look of the game is dark and moody. It fits the story very well. There are some good scares, but thankfully it’s kept to a minimum to maximize the effect. If that makes any sense at all.
Performance is all over the place and there are some visual glitches. While fine tuning the graphics (i.e. setting everything to Ultra) my entire screen became very blurry. The only way to fix it was to set the graphics settings to Auto. But then the framerate kept going up and down. Unfortunately, it was the only way to get decent visuals so I eventually decided to just play it that way. For game a short as this one I expected solid performance so it’s quite disappointing to see that it hasn’t been optimized properly.
The audio design is magnificent: the ambient music is good and the voice acting is nothing short of amazing. The sound effects, while reasonably limited, are solid and help immerse you into the story. One of the best parts of the game.
As you may have seen already the visuals are also quite pretty. All of the models have good detail and okay-ish/decent textures, but since the atmosphere is already quite dark most people won’t notice or simply won’t care. In the end it’s nothing groundbreaking and that’s why it’s such a shame that the game can’t manage to keep a steady 60FPS.
The Park is a short one to two hour experience. It’s linear, but there’s a lot of information (written and spoken) implemented and therefore you might want to play it a second time. I doubt you’ll come to back it after that, though. There’s really not much else to do.
While The Park might not be the best walking simulator out there it does a good job at trying to tell an emotional and thrilling, at times even intense, story. It succeeds mostly, but still has some flaws.
It might not be everyone’s cup of tea due to the lack of interactivity but if you can look past that (and the horrible performance) then there’s a good game to be found here, with some great storytelling.
Pros:
+ Moody and dark atmosphere with pretty visuals
+ Immerse and interesting story
+ Sound design is just excellent
Mixed:
+/- It has a short length, which I personally don’t consider a con, but it definitely could’ve been a little longer
Cons:
- Feels a bit like an experiment
- Hardly any replay value
- Performance is all over the place/Very unoptimized
- Can feel very passive at times
(Ratings aren’t calculated based on a formula, but on my personal feelings)

I have an unusual feeling after playing this game, I dont know why, but it seems like I am inspired by this game......for somethings. It is not even a game, but the meanings inside this "game"  are more meaningful than other games, so why dont you come and try this unconventional "game" ?

First things first, this game is indeed short. It took me about 1 and 1/2 hours to beat the game. Is it worth it? Yes.
I pay more then that to see a movie which is usually the same length or shorter. The Park is a psychological thriller in which you play a troubled mother searching for her lost son inside a creepy amusement park. The game plays like other narrative games, so there is no combat. As you progress throughout the game the narrative unfolds in the form of mostly notes and internal dialogues.
There aren't any puzzles. You can call out in the game for Callum, and that will help you figure out where to go. Your voice does change depending on whats happened and whats currently happening, and I found that really cool. The atmosphere is good, so is the music. Graphics are also good. However, some notes are a bit hard to read.
What is most important to me when I play a game for it's story is that it provokes an immotional response, and The Park does that.
If you enjoyed games like Dear Esther and Gone Home you will enjoy this game. Also, if you're looking for a dark supernatural story driven experience, you will find a pretty good one here.

First off, Cuphead is a gorgeous game with an authentic soundtrack that somehow doesn't get old the 40th time you reset a boss fight. The mechanics are pretty simple and never require you to do much more than memorize a boss' patterns as first encounters will often result in quick deaths upon phase changes.
One area that doesn't quite work perfectly is the shmup shooting sections. The bosses are all fun and frantic, but having things fly by in the foreground obscuring your view of projectiles is a big no-no. Also, projectiles spawning in from off-screen, such as Dr. Kahl and his robot, seems somewhat unfair.
Unfortunately for my taste, luck plays an all-too-important role in some boss encounters where certain patterns will just require you to take a hit without much to do about it on your part. And with a default of 3HP in a fight (and no way to heal during a fight), a bad pattern almost always results in a death or a reset.
That being said, the bosses are wonderfully unique, creatively designed, and all very impressively put together. Each fight has its quirks and they all work together to flesh out the running and shooting. My favorite would have to be the first boss in the last area, with a sampling of 9 mini-bosses before the final encounter, it's a neat encounter that adheres strikingly well to its theme.

I hate flying. Even with the facts that indicate a accident is far, FAR from likely, I’m still on the edge of♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥myself. It’s not what could happen during a flight, its the fact that I’m spitting distance from the ♥♥♥♥ing stratosphere. Thats kinda what I feel about Rapture. A nearly beautiful  and nearly flawless in concept, but essentially enabling UNREGULATED, UNSTABLE, ADDICTIVE SUPER SERUM use in a goddamned fish tank, makes the whole thing far from desirable.
BioShock is one of those games used as a shining example of gaming as art, or how an interactive narrative should be done. While the narrative is rather fantastic, I don’t see how adding a art deco style to something makes it artsy. A pretty damned good design, but thats where it stops, as it’s simply design. Going with the theme of what’s “pretty damned good” about BioShock lie in mostly with it’s strong story and combat.
Finding yourself victim to a plane crash over the city of Rapture, you soon delve down into the briny deep to the underwater dystopia for sanctuary. What you find is a dying city, full of genetically spliced psychopaths, are a range of weapons that don’t really deviate from the standard formula of melee, pistol, shotgun, machine gun, explosive, and exotic weapons. What I do enjoy is your not restricted to two weapons, leaving you with an entire arsenal at your disposal. It compensates for your ability to break into Fort Knox by having ammunition relatively scarce, resulting in a very balanced and cohesive experience, complemented with satisfying gun recoil and accuracy. All modifiable at one time use upgrade stations, offering sizeable bonus to damage, ammo consumption and capacity.
Still, plasmid use is what BioShock is where seeks to bare its teeth. Essentially powers that rely on a mana bar for use, plasmids offer an interesting spin on game play, giving you a second option if your ammunition drys up. While there are a quite a few to choose from, you won’t really need to deviate beyond some core combat powers, being fire and lightning attacks. Rendering other options rather muted, being used once for experimentation and never again. All also upgradable for a certain amount of ADAM, which acts essentially as money.
Going with the theme of genetic manipulation, the player is granted a variety of passive buffs in the form of gene tonics. Each can either improve combative abilities or aid in hacking minigames. It’s rather marginal, but Irrational Games needed some place to crame those pesky RPG elements.
Complementing BioShock’s solid combat mechanics are the surprisingly variant baddies to murder. Be it the hulking Big Daddies, gun toting Lead Heads, or wall crawling Spider Splicers, they all offer a certain depth to combat, giving every weapon and plasmid a purpose. Making larger fights rather tense and exciting. Though, enemy types tend to be grouped together early on, damping the game a bit.
Storywise however, BioShock shines brightest. It offers legitimate intrigue and speculation early on, helped along with the absolutely stellar voice acting lent. Providing a clear cut objective that ties in with the world that you find yourself in, as you interact with various key political figures of Rapture’s past glory. Providing a twist that was so smartly written, you can’t help but feel it was hurt by it being told through a cut scene. As you are almost always behind the controls, you are the one that is carrying the story along, not a cut scene. It’s very reminiscent of Half Life in this respect, keeping you engaged with the plot the whole way through.
Having given this game non stop praise, the only negatives I can find is with its later half, which is more level padding and far from necessary. Everything else is spot on and virtually excellent, with it’s tight and engaging story and characters, coupled with its solid combat system, I can’t really live with myself if I didn't say BioShock can be considered a genre benchmark.

I heard tale of a virtual adventure. "Cuphead" the name rings in my head, echoing endlessly in the abyss of my cranial cavity. An article informing me of its many challenges sparked my interest. Me being an avid adventurer myself, I pondered the thought of engaging in the nostalgia riddled title. I open my Steam client and search the name, alas, there it is, popping up first on the list, superior to all others related to it's theme. Winking with a sinister charisma, as to make a mockery of my manhood. I click the page open, watching previews, & reading reviews. 10/10s, 5 stars, applause all across the forum. I'd had enough....Cuphead was to be mine.
I smack my finger on my mouse, triggering a purchase toward my Steam wallet & the deed was done....it WAS mine.
I anxiously wait for the download. Palms sweaty, knees weak, eating my mothers spaghetti as I twiddled eagerly, thinking of all the adventures I would endeavor. And all the glory that would follow.
The download finishes & I pummel my mouse on the icon, enthralled in my purchase. Like an obese child being offered a second piece of cake. And just like that the game opens and the title appears with the main character dancing with a Mickey Mouse swagger, only with a cup for a head & an irresistible personality, the one they call..."Cuphead"....I now understood the banter...& this was it...my weekend was already looking up.
I start the first level and to my surprise its already difficult, racking up deaths too and fro. I already wanted to quit in my vexed state but no...quitting is for♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ I finally get proficient enough to advance a level and with triumph arrive at the boss level. "HURRAH!" I exhale with pride, but am soon hit like a stepchild in a broken home. Death after death like a zombie I revive Cuphead over and over again... "THIS. IS. ♥♥♥♥ING. IMPOSSIBLE." I scream. My lungs near collapsing in my passion for victory. And upon antoher death I feel something isn't right.
But I must win.
Amidst the dodging and raining enemies,...my eyes begin twitching....my minuscule brain POUNDING, yet, I kept playing with the pride of 50 lions, but as my frustrations grew strong...I was growing weaker. Oh no. It was what I had feared....an aneurysm. Ive ventured too far in to it & alas...it's too late for treatment. My friends. These will be my last words...as I am currently internally bleeding in to sheer darkness. I realize that I could have made it to the hospital in the time it took to write this review...but I had to warn all my steam family of the upcoming dangers they may face.
THIS IS MOST IMPORTANT TO ME!
So, with the last of my strength...I leave you all with these final words...
"Cuphead - 10/10 a sheer masterpiece....would risk internal bleeding again"
*gasp* God speed brothers and sisters.

After reading lots of other reviews it seemed like this game was generally regarded as very fun, but shorter than most people expected.  It does seem like I'm in the minority, but sadly I didn't find any aspects of this game actually *fun*, and I really wanted to like it.
The core mechanics seem to be built around the idea that you should carefully time your actions and plan things out, but in reality it just comes down to jittering yourself back and forth to move the timestep along predictably.  It's not satisfying at all to see the replay at the end of the stage, which I guess was supposed to make your path through the level look impressive and meticulously timed - instead it's just an up-to-speed version of the spastic nonsense that you had to do to dodge all the enemies and projectiles.  I didn't feel like beating the levels was ever an accomplishment, and dispatching the enemies was tedious instead of exciting.
While it's clear a lot of time was spent making the UI look like an old scanline text prompt, it's mostly just irritating.  Even if it's masking loading times or something, delaying every action behind animations and obnoxious screen garbling just makes the whole thing feel unresponsive.  Maybe that was the goal, I don't know.   I also can't tell if the minimalist art direction was chosen on purpose, or just done because it would be far cheaper and faster not to have model decent looking assets and textures.
I didn't find this game to be a fun shooter or a fun puzzle game.  I honestly have no idea why other Steam users described this as a "great game" or an "awesome experience."  At best it feels like a very polished tech demo with some disjointed story elements.

The Park is a brief, thoroughly disturbing, but brilliant game.
It's not exactly what you'd expect from a standard horror game. There aren't a lot of jump scares, or monsters, or danger. The parts that I'd say are frightening are very few -- though they definitely get the adrenaline flowing -- and it's not even possible to die or "lose."
What makes The Park so unnerving is not the bit where you're lost in a haunted amusement built to harvest the souls of the innocent. No, it's learning about Lorraine and her struggles as a mother. I don't want to give too much away, but this game is far more intimate and emotional than you'd expect from a horror game. It's over very quickly, but it's worth every penny.

I got a ton of these.
In all seriousness, I understand how so many people seem jaded.  DLC has gone off the rails before and burned people.  Then 2k steps up with a big ol' DLC Party Cake for Evolve and everyone goes rabid.
What they don't notice is that the game really is a solid piece of work with a great IP, and that DLC for this kind of game is sorely needed.  I'm sure TRS wanted to give us as many monsters and hunters as they could make, but they are constrained by actually finishing the game and paying for its creation.  If the game had 10 Monsters, all fully unique and balanced, people would still complain about lack of content and if they announced even a single monster DLC over that 10, they would complain about 'not getting the full package'.
During the Alpha I was fully in the "no where near enough content for AAA price".  Then as the beta approached I started early on the hype-cycle, pre-ordered before it even started and played as much as I could.  I completely forgot about 'amount of content' complaint, because the game did have the content I wanted.
The legitimate complaints I see about 'lack of content' come from people who I expect were wanting something they could sit down and play on a lark.  Pubbing in the low levels, you can do that, but you will get wild swings in skill that CAN make the game 'boring' (i.e. you got stomped, or 'faced a monster who constantly ran', or you played against a hunter team that spent half its time arguing and the other half letting the medic die to a tyrant "because the medic didn't know how to break a stun lock."
Evolve isn't an FPS, but new people will treat it as one and expect that skill curve.  Evolve is about as close to chess as an FPS can get.  If you want a game of instant gratification and constant shooting, stick with an actual FPS.

We got our hands on Funcom’s new psychological horror game The Park to see how a game that cites Gone Home and Dear Esther as inspirations. Personally, I thought there was also quite a large Silent Hill 2 influence in there as well.
The whole game takes place in an amusement park on the premise that your son, Callum, has lost his teddy bear. While you head over to talk to the guy behind the counter, you hear Callum (at least we assume it’s Callum) running behind you and into the park. This begins your journey into the park and into insanity.
As we mentioned, you’re a mother to a small boy (Lorraine) and you have to look for Callum by calling out his name (which provides some clues and also some responses from him) and riding on the rides in the park. There’s not really much you can do while you’re on the rides, but we would suggest looking around as much as you can. This is where you end up seeing things and where the sound design comes into its own, but more on that later.
There isn’t really any other mechanics apart from that. It’s more of a psychological experience / experiment rather than a game. But sometimes it’s better that way without having to solve puzzles to progress the storyline. It’s what made Slender one of the biggest horror game franchises in the past.
Graphically we were getting around 30 fps on average, but that improved later in the game to 60. It may have been something running in the background. It looks pretty nice and the park seems quite well designed for a horror setting. The pristine look soon vanishing for an abandoned look once you get to the top of the entrance. The game requires a level of darkness to really appreciate, but at times it can be a bit tricky to see if you use their recommended settings. The game doesn’t have much in the way of characters, but every now and again you might view Lorraine (the protagonist) in a 3rd person view or Chad The Chipmunk with his evil looking red eyes.
Chad, it seems, is one of those park mascots that you normally get in large amusement parks to entertain the guests. It soom becomes apparent, however, that not everything is right with Chad. Someone has scrawled a poem on his statue and your first encounter with him leaves you feeling incredibly uneasy. There’s more to the Chad story, but we don’t want to give away any spoilers here.
The sound design in The Park really work well to create the atmosphere of an abandoned amusement park and the way sounds come and go as you walk around or ride the rides can make you pretty tense. The banging and splashing on the swan ride really made me feel uneasy. The voice acting isn’t too bad and is fairly believable as Lorraine becomes ever increasingly frantic in her hunt for Callum. There are times when your ability to call out is removed, but that’s generally only on the rides.
It’s nice to have a horror game that isn’t all about jump scares. Yes, there are one or two in the game, but they’re not the be-all-end-all of things. The fear comes from that sense of thinking something is going to happen soon. Is there something hiding behind that rock? Will that teddy bear suddenly move?… WHAT THE HELL WAS THAT?! NOPE! NOPE! NOPE! If played properly with the lights low and headphones on with the volume up, this game can (and probably will) put the willies up you. It gets even more sinister as you learn about the park itself and Chad… Damn you, Chad… The ice-sculpting chipmunk…
The game is only a short one. Its story it told in the space of one to two hours and is a great late-night romp for anyone looking for something a bit different to what’s currently going around. As an added bonus, if you also play Funcom’s The Secret World, this game will unlock some special items in that game for you (imagine running around as a giant killer chipmunk… You’re welcome).
Overall, it’s well worth a look and one that should do well for Halloween. If you do play The Secret World, then it’s a no brainer to get this one. Otherwise, you can still grab this, turn out the lights, turn up the volume and have yourself a scary evening.

I love anything to do with zombies, and I especially love the survival games where the developers take everything into consideration. This game has it's pros and cons. However, I find that the cons outweigh the pros. I find the viewing feature interesting. It's only a matter of opinion, but I like it. It shows you what you would see if you were ACTUALLY in that situation. We're only human, and we can't see 360 degrees around us at all times. Also, I think the game needs NPCs. I won't list this as a con, considering the developers are working on creating NPCs already. It saddened me the first time my character woke up in the middle of the night, hearing a gunshot. I later looked it up on the internet, and there are no NPCs to which the gunshot was fired. It would be nice to be able to team up with them, or kill them and take their loot. Also, perhaps an animal system would be nice. Adding animals could do nicely for a different way of hunting for food. Perhaps the developers could add companions, such as dogs to fight alongside you.  Multiplayer mode is alright, but I find that I prefer single player mode over multiplayer mode. The traits system is also something that you don't see in most survival zombie games, so I would list that as a pro. Lastly, I find that this is one of the games that I play when I'm bored. But, sometimes, this game gets boring itself. It's strange how I find myself building up my character, only to have them die. I think the developers should create some sort of lake, or pond that our characters could retrieve water from once the water and electricity ran out.    Until the developers update the game a bit more, I'll be uninstalling.

Edit #2:
Summary:
- Beautiful graphics.
- Immersive gameplay, truly survival (Stalker Mode) or simply adventure without risk (Pilgrim) or a mix of both.
- "Maps" are big, difficult to navigate (without maps) and a lot of things to explore (Don't search for maps, the game is better that way). 5 maps + transition zone, never runs out of things to do.
- Sandbox Mode + Challenge (Short survival challenge) only, no Story Mode yet (coming soon)
- Occasional bugs here and there. Sandbox is almost bug free, Challenge mode still have some.
So, maybe spending almost 8 hours playing the game nonstop and failed the challenge both times due to bugs really got to my head so I'm here to make things straight.
- First, the game is still in early access so there will be some dumb bugs happen, not as frequent  and sandbox mode is almost perfect, the bugs are still around in challenge mode however (For Tireless Menace, stay off the railroad once you get to Mystery Lake's Train Crash, the bear will teleport left, right, then very close to your left/right, if it happens, use your flare gun after it teleported the second time).
- Second, the graphics is beautiful, you have to agree that TLD have a very different vibe compared to other survival games. The polygon-ish textures are very attractive plus lighting is on point.
- Third, the gameplay, if you like playing single player and open world adventure.I know there's 5 big regions (Mystery Lake, Coastal Highway, Desolation Point, Pleasant Valley, Timberwolf Mountain) plus the transition zone between each (Ravine, Crumbling Highway, Abandoned Coalmine). The regions have increasing difficulty, Timberwolf being the hardest region and Mystery Lake being arguably the easiest (I personally think Coastal Highway is much easier). It will takes you personally at least 3 hours to prepare gears and get enough supply to travel from Mystery Lake to the next region, to which then you will spend more time preparing yourself. The shortest playtime it takes me to travel from the starting region to the last region (Past 2 regions in between) was 6 hours, that being I have maps opened. Without maps, it will take you a lot of time to explore the region you're in and made the experience tenfold better.
So what do you do in The Long Dark? You survive, as long as possible, sounds easy right? Nope, not really, stocking for crazy amount of supply is not really possible (Food/Medicine rots over the time, even if you don't take it or it's on the other side of the world, everything starts rotting once you start the game), supply runs low once you stay in a region for too long  and predators does respawn + weapons are really hard to craft or maintain as well as ammo. Eventually you can't stay in one place for very long and will be forced to move, which keeps you on your toe and you can't carry everything to a new place.
Overall, this is still a great game despite occasional bugs but it is very minimal in sandbox mode. Also, the main campaign (Story Mode) is expected to come out in the future and the team brings update somewhat monthly so this is a great game to have even now. When you're bored, tired, want to get away, you hop in the game and just play. When you're bored, you can always move to another region and start a new suffering for yourself.

With The Park, what you see is what you get, and I consider that a very good thing. My playthrough of the game, making my way through it fairly quickly and not exploring as thoroughly as I could have, clocked in at just over an hour and a half. This is a short and sweet, narrative-driven horror experience. There are no chase sequences, there are no quicktime events, and there is no stealth gameplay. This is pure and simple a Haunted House type experience, where the game tries to creep you out and startle you, immersing you in the world of The Park, without ever actually putting you in any danger. The lore of things adds another layer, with many notes, newspapers, and other environmental objects being scattered around to clue you in on the true history of the Atlantic Island Amusement Park. Each note is fascinating and well worth the read, and I only wish they would have made the text font a bit bigger.
The Park is a game if you want a short and sweet horror experience. It never overstays its welcome, it's wonderfully paced, and it will succeed at creeping you out and getting you to jump when you least expect it. To me, that's worth the price of admission, any day of the week.
WARNING: As of the time of this review, the game does suffer from some stability and framerate issues, so if you're on the fence, wait for a patch to improve these issues before grabbing it.

I've got goosebumps, and that's someone who's been a horror fan since he was a kid saying that.  The atmosphere was spot on, and provided just enough teasing to keep pushing you on throughout, without relying on constant jump-scares.  Not once did I wish to stop playing or take a break.  I was intrigued, and I wanted to experience what was going on.  So, if you're afraid of a "walking simulator" and that it'd bore you, don't.
If you see any complaints on story, you won't see it from me.  People these days seem to expect a novel or epic level conclusion, but for the size of the game, that'd either leave it rushed or leave too many holes.  Instead, it's as it should be, the level of conclusion you'd expect out of a short story.  That's what this game is, a short story.  Expect and take it as such.
Downside?  Of course.  Replayability is limited, as there are no choices or puzzles to make.  Those who will get the most use of this game are those who are already fans of The Secret World, as it fills in more detail into a fan-favorite location.  However, that's not much of a downside, and just more of a bonus.  Though, as a longtime TSW player, I can't easily see if anything is unanswered due to all the little tie-ins that were added in the background.

Playing this is like taking a guided tour through a horror story.
What Funcom does well, it does brilliantly.  Despite not being as recognized as is Bioware for story-telling, Funcom excels like no other developer in that category.  Their games tell the best stories.
The Park is a great short story that unfolds before the player from a first-person perspective.  The story will have more meaning to players of Funcom's MMO The Secret World, but the story stands on its own.  Familiarity with TSW's lore is not required to enjoy The Park's story, but there are numerous references that TSW players will likely enjoy.
I would not hesitate to reccomend this game to a friend.  But that reccomendation would have this accompanying caveat - be aware that this is a very short video game.  The length worked well for the story and the pricing was appropriate for the entertainment value.  But as most video games are much longer, it's worth mentioning the short length of The Park so that doesn't become one the playthrough's surprises (those surprises, by the way, work surprisingly well).
Bottom line, this is a good game and a must-buy for any fan of horror stories.

My mom comes home. I get off the computer.

It's pineapple. Just like an icicle.
I start to cry.

I played this just recently. I didn't have time in the past for it. This strategy is old so do not expect superb graphics. Suprisingly this game allows You to use modern resolutions (even full HD, but then everything is so small than You can't play). If You are old gamer and know Master of Magic then this game will be for You. It has lots of MoM to offer. Generally this is kinda HoM&M with much bigger battlegrounds during combats. Unfortunately AI is not so good so many times You can win battles which You shouldn't. Tutorial doesn't explain everything, f.e. when combat occur then all forces bordering combat hex are also joining the fight which has great impact to gameplay.
There is 10 different cities with their forces (12 units). Part of them are similar between races, but part are very different. Each unit have abilities (stronger = more expensive ones have more abilities) and basic stats which can increase while leveling them (units can level up twice). Most important units are heroes. They have level caps in each map and finally You will be able to reach rank 30 in last mission. Heroes are most important units and later on can be terminators to almost everything. Your main hero will travel through all maps in campaign, but You be able to move at least second one as well (all depends of points You have to spend on heroes, units, items and gold/mana between maps).
Another important matter which is not mention in tutorial are magic schools. Your hero have seven slots and one school can go to rank 4 (4 slots). That is important to have access to certain spells. I suggest to study which schools gives which spells, decide which You want to use during campaign and then put proper magic into Your slots.
Game offers two campaigns (light/dark) with 12 missions each. During them I could choose different paths sometimes.
I played one campaign (cleaning all maps from all enemies and discover everything) and took me 85 hours.
Music is fine and I didn't feel to shut it down and start to listen my own.
I'm looking forward to play AoE2 and then AoE3.

10/10 - A MUST have for those who can deal with heavy introspection...
The game is not really a game. It is a deeply personal and subjective experience, and journey into the innermost self, of you, the creator and the subject. And possibly of everyone else youever know or meet.
it is a dark experince, a bright expeience, a lost and confusing experience, and a sharply clear experience. All at once.
I don't know that I actually could spoil this for anyone, since it really is something deeply personal, and I feel the experience will be different for each person who explores this path. I do think it would not be terribly good for anyone without some good, solid self-awareness, or at least some self-awareness, looking for more. Probably not a good experience for anyone who is badly broken, totally not self-aware and those looking for soething kight, easy, and with no deep meanings or thoughts. It is hard to call it "enjoyable", perhaps "worthwhile" is a better term.
This experience made me stop and look at my own life, my deepest worries and fears, my reason for being, my motivations, my faults, my flaws, my wants and needs, my darkest places got ripped open a bit, just a bit. But it also made me think of my joys, my successes, my dreams, my impact on the world around me, the postivie things I have done. It's not all dark, but it could sure suck you into the depths if you have a tendancy to go there anyway.
Not a "pew-pew-pew" and grief you friends and total strangers kind of game. This does require a higher level of attention and thinking to even feel like you understood any of it. And after playing it, I am left with so many thoughts of "What if", "Should I, Could I, Would I" and "Could I have done better". Not in the game, but IRL. Really moved me deeply and shook me. And will keep shaking me for some time. Deeply human. It is so very deeply human...
Thank you for making this game, and making me wake up while walking the path you guided me on. I will walk this path with you again, and see what else it reveals about myself and others around me. And I hope Coda is happy and well, out there smewhere.

Not sure why this got bad reviews when it came out, to be honest. Okay, yes, it's quite short, only about 4-5 hours long, and it re-uses the same hazard course as the original game. And I don't know if anyone else got this but I got a bug that caused my gun to start firing as soon as I loaded a previous save. Used quicksaves instead. The ending is a bit abrupt too.
But who cares really, everything that made Half-Life great is here too - the tight, contiguous level design (the Duty Calls level is really clever, as is Power Struggle), the oh-so-satisfyingly gory blasts from grenades, the nice little tie-ins to previous games - for example you start in the same position as Freeman saw you in the first game banging on a door to be let in, and the G-Man makes another mysterious appearance. There are some cute touches like family pictures on Calhoun's locker to give some context, and makes it feel as if the whole thing's worth fighting for. And ho ho, I love the dry humour at the beginning of the game, where it says "Subject: Barney Calhoun. Secondary priority: Safety of research personnel." I smiled at that. Well done Gearbox.
