The game launched 2 days prior to me writing this review. I haven't been able to play due to severe server issues. Why these issues you might wonder:
Well, because the devs expected only 400 to maybe 600 people to play the game in the first few days. The amount of unique logins have reached 25k+ until now, only 49 hours after release. 25000. They prepared effectively for 500.
But since the game was released, they were trying their best to fix the servers, so that evens it out and I am not going to let that affect my early point of view of the game.
To the game itself:
Even though it might seem like a Tower Defense game where you have that one most effective strategy and certain most effective units (which would be expected, since the generated "waves" attacking your "towers" each wave are the same), this is not at all the case. Each game differs a little bit, due to the enemies being able to send mercenaries on your lane to attack your towers alongside the preset wave. And these little differences affect your game in a way that is crucial and changes your every game you play.
Graphics:
Simple. Nothing special, animations feel a bit off and "clumsy" at times. Especially when it comes to high attack speeds, the animations of certain units do not work very well. But overall, it can be looked at and doesn't cause your eyes to get cancer. 6/10.
Interface:
Simple, intuitive and it seems like thought was put into it. You can basically ping everything you see and make all important announcements to your team by pinging. Nothing I could think of to improve the UI, except for the design. The functionality is definetly on point, which is the most important aspect of the UI for a game like this. 9.5/10.
Gameplay:
Oh, Boy.
As mentioned in the short opening section, it is more unique than you might expect of your average tower defense game and fits perfectly for competetive play. You can do complex tactics, but also very simple ones that are effective for beginners. The towers and attacking monsters feature different attack and defense types and also different abilities. This game, like many other competetive games, have a steep learning curve and here, intelligent and strategic thinking is the key to success, not reaction time or quick thinking (although you need to be quick in order to not miss waves, so you cant just take all the time in the world to think of the best available tactic). You also need to observe the way the enemy builds his lane, so you can attack adjusted to his units. Due to the lack of action which one might lead to playing even more, 9/10.
Overall impression would land on a solid 8/10. Might get better with time and server fixes.
Wait until the servers are fixed before you buy the game, though.

Edit #2:
Summary:
- Beautiful graphics.
- Immersive gameplay, truly survival (Stalker Mode) or simply adventure without risk (Pilgrim) or a mix of both.
- "Maps" are big, difficult to navigate (without maps) and a lot of things to explore (Don't search for maps, the game is better that way). 5 maps + transition zone, never runs out of things to do.
- Sandbox Mode + Challenge (Short survival challenge) only, no Story Mode yet (coming soon)
- Occasional bugs here and there. Sandbox is almost bug free, Challenge mode still have some.
So, maybe spending almost 8 hours playing the game nonstop and failed the challenge both times due to bugs really got to my head so I'm here to make things straight.
- First, the game is still in early access so there will be some dumb bugs happen, not as frequent  and sandbox mode is almost perfect, the bugs are still around in challenge mode however (For Tireless Menace, stay off the railroad once you get to Mystery Lake's Train Crash, the bear will teleport left, right, then very close to your left/right, if it happens, use your flare gun after it teleported the second time).
- Second, the graphics is beautiful, you have to agree that TLD have a very different vibe compared to other survival games. The polygon-ish textures are very attractive plus lighting is on point.
- Third, the gameplay, if you like playing single player and open world adventure.I know there's 5 big regions (Mystery Lake, Coastal Highway, Desolation Point, Pleasant Valley, Timberwolf Mountain) plus the transition zone between each (Ravine, Crumbling Highway, Abandoned Coalmine). The regions have increasing difficulty, Timberwolf being the hardest region and Mystery Lake being arguably the easiest (I personally think Coastal Highway is much easier). It will takes you personally at least 3 hours to prepare gears and get enough supply to travel from Mystery Lake to the next region, to which then you will spend more time preparing yourself. The shortest playtime it takes me to travel from the starting region to the last region (Past 2 regions in between) was 6 hours, that being I have maps opened. Without maps, it will take you a lot of time to explore the region you're in and made the experience tenfold better.
So what do you do in The Long Dark? You survive, as long as possible, sounds easy right? Nope, not really, stocking for crazy amount of supply is not really possible (Food/Medicine rots over the time, even if you don't take it or it's on the other side of the world, everything starts rotting once you start the game), supply runs low once you stay in a region for too long  and predators does respawn + weapons are really hard to craft or maintain as well as ammo. Eventually you can't stay in one place for very long and will be forced to move, which keeps you on your toe and you can't carry everything to a new place.
Overall, this is still a great game despite occasional bugs but it is very minimal in sandbox mode. Also, the main campaign (Story Mode) is expected to come out in the future and the team brings update somewhat monthly so this is a great game to have even now. When you're bored, tired, want to get away, you hop in the game and just play. When you're bored, you can always move to another region and start a new suffering for yourself.

This game is addictively INCREDIBLE! This is probably the best game I have come across. I have been a long time fan of the AoE series games, but I feel like something is always missing because there is only so much you can do with it--200 population cap, (almost) the same kind of people/soldiers etc. Yes yes I know AoE is not a city building game, but I finally found what AoE is missing for me: the building aspect, the ever-developing aspect and the community aspect.
This game made me feel like I'm the president of a little village, and because of the many realistic elements it has, such as deaths, marriage, diseases etc, I feel very connected to this little world and want it to thrive. I want to build a school for it, I want to make stone paths for people to walk and I want to make sure people have a herbalist to visit for their health.
I'm currently playing it with some mods, but I played my first village (died off of old age) without any mods and I honestly don't think I was missing anything. The mods are very cool, but sometimes the gazillion things I can make aren't necessarily a turn-on, because it can start to feel like you are playing a HD version of Minecraft. However, I do think that these things are so heavily incorporated that they negatively impact the game, so I most of the time prefer to have all the options than not.

Tropico 5 is yet another sequel to Tropico, a series of city-building games as dictator of Banana Republic. This one was released in 2014 by Haemimont Games. At least they waited 3 years since Tropico 4. Now with multiplayer!
It also came out for Xbox 360 and PS4. Xbox One version is planned. Don't know of any good difference. So relax and enjoy PC version.
Technically there was a huge slashback because the game requires videocards that support DirectX 11 and nobody ever reads System Requirements. Or maybe it wasn't written at launch, I didn't check back then. Also, some complaints about bugs, but most of it probably got fixed by now.
Multiplayer community seems to be here. It employes chat-room and I can see a dozen of players here, with messages popping up that somebody is making a new game. So it may take 5-10 minutes to get game running, but at least it's not empty. Most often you see games of World War era with tons of starting money and no victory requirements, I guess that people here favour deathmatch type of games.
So, Tropico 5.
Main plot of this part is that Penultimo grew a moustache.
Unlike Tropico 4 which barely added anything to Tropico 3, Tropico 5 changed few things up. I don't know about others, but I am thankful that I don't have to do more of same tactics and that it became a bit more challenging in mechanics too.
I mean, from one point some may think that game got dumbened down. For example, you set one of 5 pre-defined budget on each building unlike previous Tropico games where you could set any wages you wanted to each building. But where Tropico 1 was so difficult that you had to care about such thing, in Tropico 3 and 4 it mattered little, as in those games you just slammed production and then Industry building onto island and would go on fiesta as money rained on your head, once in few years increasing wages for everybody by one to keep them happy. At least Tropico 5 budget increases effectiveness as well, like Teamsters can carry more.
Yea, it's not Tropico 1. But at least they refocused around to make it more interesting, less fluff. Or at least different. Because after playing Tropico 3 and 4 I am happy with some core difference.
You now can advance through the four eras. To reach each new era you usually have to research all era's stuff and then do little quest of sorts. I actually love strategies where you can advance through era, combining both historical interest along with seeing all your units and buildings getting upgraded (Where is Empire Earth on Steam, Rebellion?!). Not so much here, being too tongue-in-cheek for historical and not updating looks of everything as often. But hey, still something.
- Colonial era. Allows only extraction of island's raw resource. Out of industry there is only Lumber Mill, which is like a middle between Woodcutting and Furniture anyway. Out of foreign powers there is only The Crown and it's pretty linear, as you have to increase revolution supporters on island, mostly by side quests. Also, no healthcare at all. Watch Royalists die. No elections, but your time on governer's seat is limited and you have to do The Crown missions to increase them. Interesting, but linear.
- World War era. Now with two foreign powers and more classical Tropico gameplay with elections. You now get access to industry to finally make tons of money. Just make sure to have a good standing with both factions when advancing to next era.
- Cold War era. You now have access to tourism. I actually didn't figure out how to make tourism effective, I still would focus on production as always. I did notice that Tourism houses are quite expensive, hm. It probably isn't so nice that it gets introduced this late.
- Modern Times era. Now a whole bunch of foreign powers, but only US can invade you. Have access to everything. Not much else to say.
Another awesome thing is trade system. In Tropico 4, which introduced it, I remember it being as something automatic and then I stopped caring. Here you have limited ships which can carry limited amount of recources per once and you have to set each ship to any trade routes that you got. You may find out that the only industry export is for steel for 10 years, so you can choose to build Steel factory. And then find out that your Iron mines ran out and you now have to import some iron. It's quite good addition.
Then comes a whole bunch of small differences. Like, budget instead of wages. Or you can set a manager for each building for additional bonuses, reminding me of Tropico 2. Hm, actually some music track reminds me of that part too, that game was focused on Pirate theme.
You also have improved battles handling. You can't control them, but battles now look like battles and offense will try to destroy some of infastructure, quickly moving between then, until getting to the palace. While defence still rushes dumbly all over the map from the base. Build watch towers to slow down offence, yep.
Or the wacky way that buildings are being built. Seems like the construction workers have to touch it once for it to slowly get 17% or so built automatically by itself for next few seconds. But I had little issue with constructions in this game, so it must work better with this AI.
Or you have now a whole dynasty of El Presidente on a map. But in this game you can't control them at all, only set some as managers. So they are just there hanging around for bonuses. And hey, you got use for Swiss bank now as you get to upgrade family.
Actually, you can't do some micromanaging things of dictatorship now. Like, no golden statue to waste money on. Or you can't move your presidente to attack rebels or speed up construction. Or you can't easily win votes by promising things. Though no complaints as it brings some challenge back, selling bonds to get money to do something fancy to impress people with.
Heck, people even say that it doesn't even have a prison to arrest people into.
Even though I remember that I could build some prisons in Cold War era. Wait.
Ohhhh, they updated game since then: putting save feature into multiplayer, implenting Steam Workshop and putting a prison building for free. Nice. You would think that they would make it part of their tiny DLCes.
Oh, and there is campaign. It's quite nice. Humor. The Order. You now have few island and game will make sure that you will revisit all of them, having to do stuff on top of your early mistakes.
Sadly, announcers and music is a bit less awesome. Especially radio announcer, who is some girl who keeps inviting men to Jolly Roger for fun times. And punishes players for building lumber mill by proving the world that she can do the most annoying sound ever. At least each tiny DLC now promises a new music track.
Well, and multiplayer. You can play it competevily and cooperatively. It's still works as good as you can imagine such city-building to be. Mostly that army rushing isn't all that fitting to game's pace and that players don't really interact much otherwise. But hey, at least some of random objective are challenging, like getting 100000 of team money. Can share recources and connect roads with same team too.
Oh well, I can see it being really nice with friends.
Tropico 5 is interesting part, trying to reform some parts of gameplay and I like some of the stuff that it does. It's a bit more challenging than Tropico 4, but it doesn't have as much of Dictatorship funzies. As for me, I am happy that it's not more of same like T4.

First off:  I have to mention that if you are not interested in Racing Games as such AT ALL, this game is NOT for you. But if you have even the slightest interest in racing and ramming others off this game might keep you busy for... quite a lot of time.
Now at this point and time you are probably asking yourself: why is this weird guy with an even weirder profile picture reviewing an 11 year old game?
Well, let me say this right now: this game held up AMAZINGLY well. Now just to make this clear, I am a HUGE racing enthusiast. I've played countless hours of NFS U2 and MW back in the day (on my trusty ps2) and i own a lot of current Racing Games aswell.
So I (inevitably) stumbled across this game when I was in a desperate search for *GOOD RACING GAMES* on Google one day. After booting it up I was immediatly greeted by some stellar music. What kind of music? ,you ask.
Well mostly rock to be honest but i do want to mention that the choice of music in this game is strangely similar to the older NFS parts (like Underground 2 and Most Wanted 2005). So if you liked the choice of music in those games, your'e gonna LOVE the Soundtrack of this one.
But the similarities don't end there. By now you've probably noticed that I speak quite fondly of this game (hence the recommendation). But who should consider buying this game?
While playing this I was stuck asking myself: why am I enjoying this so much? I am playing an 11 year old game right now and im having more fun than that one time I played NFS 2015. Until it struck me: This game resembles what I liked about the older NFS games with a couple of twists.
Firstly, the music as mentioned before but not only that! The Physics also closely resemble the driving of NFS U2 etc. But at the same time you can absolutely WRECK people when they get near you.
Did you ever want to get REWARDED for well... basically cheating? Well, look no further! When you finish off an enemy (most likely by making him drive into the trusty tractor of some poor old farmer) you actually receive bonus Nitrous. Which... makes you go fast as♥♥♥♥♥boi ( ͡° ͜ʖ ͡°). The driving is almost exactly like in Underground 2 (without these HORRIBLE drift events).
And all of that simply makes the driving... fun. Yeah, which somehow is hard to come by in the modern racing games industry.
Obviously the graphics arent quite on par anymore... I'ts 11 years old what did you expect? But at no point did I think that the game was actually ugly. I mean it's no Driveclub or Forza Horizon 3 but with this hectic and action filled gameplay you don't really pay attention to your surroundings anyway.
So WHO is this game for?
Group Number 1: Fans of the old NFS games who somehow did not get to play this.
Group Number 2: People who like things like Derbies and ramming others off of the track.
Group Number 3: Racing fans who just want to try something new.
If you were stuck with simulation games for the last couple of years and want to try something fresh and new this might just be it. Playing something so ridiculously dumb is just really refreshing.
And lastly Group Number 4: People who are new to racing.
Obviously most modern racing games have a difficulty setting and allow you to turn on COUNTLESS assists but this game is different. Obviously the steering of this game isn't very realistic but exactly that kind of driving style is what i would recommend for beginners. The game is really forgiving  for new players and still challenging for the Veterans.
So basically: I would recommend this game to anyone who has even the slightest interest in Racing Games. Just dont expect any visual customization of your cars... Because there is none.

If you enjoy unique competitive games then Evolve is the best there is! It is  4v1, hunters (first-person) vs. Monster (third person), across various modes with the most basic and balanced in Hunt (which is where most if not all of my experience comes from).
In hunt the monster must feed on wildlife so that he can evolve to stage 3 (upgrading skills and HP pool along the way) and destroy the power relay to win the game. The monster can evade the hunters by sneaking (crouching conceals tracks and prevents bird activations which hunters can see anywhere across the map), and by intelligently engaging the hunters.
The basic classes for the hunters are instantly recognizable in medics, supports, assaults, and the trapper. There are 3 available hunters in each class. Each with unique equipment that's familiar to the class but changes the playstyle of both the individual hunter, team, and even how the monster must engage the team.
There are 3 monsters available each that drastically changes how the hunters must hunt, and fight the monster. A total of 3 monsters and 12 hunters across a wide variety of maps, and a few unique well designed modes. The possibility for gameplay is insane when you throw all these tools at players in a competitive environment.
The graphics are great and its all very well optimized (ran great both an FX-8350/280X/8GB and a i7-4790k/GTX970/16GB).
And the best thing is all DLC promised for this game so far (6 new hunters, 2 new monsters, free maps) is designed in a way to not split the community up. That's something I personally hate in competitive online games, so I am very happy to see that Evolve will not be doing that. All the future maps will be free, and if you don't own a hunter/monster you can still fight against or with those DLC characters. You can even join a game or hotswap to a DLC character if a player drops. This gives you a way to even test the DLC before you pay for it. (The AI even will choose DLC characters you don't own in single player!!!)
Great design, great execution. Can't wait to see the evolution of this game now that it is in the public's hands.

A fantastic little game.
Yes, it's short - but IMO it's short for a specific reason... it told the story it needed to tell.  No added 'fluff', no additional grindy parts.  In my opinion, it wasn't longer because it didn't *need* to be longer.
No spoilers, but The Park takes us to some very dark corners of the human psyche, insanity, motherhood - all while in a place that is doing... well, precisely what it was intended to do.  Weaving in the story of the Atlantic Island Park's history alongside the story of a mother looking for her son is no mean feat, but I thought Joel Bylos & Company handled it very well.
The Park doesn't throw tons of gore at you and scream "BE AFRAID DAMN YOU!  BE AFRAID!!!"  Instead it relies on clues, hints and 'lore' to paint a picture of what's going on - and a rather grisly picture indeed, if you think about it.  There are a few jump-scares, but I thought they were sparsely-used and effective.
And the roller coaster.  Oh.  My.  God.  The roller coaster.
The nods toward TSW were awesome.  'Nuff said.
Some of the notes were a little hard to read - I had to lean forward more than once... but I only consider that a minor quibble.  Subtitles would be nice for Lorraine's voice-overs though.
Do I recommend this game?  Yes.  Even if you haven't played TSW, The Park is an enjoyable (albeit very dark) romp.

10/10 - A MUST have for those who can deal with heavy introspection...
The game is not really a game. It is a deeply personal and subjective experience, and journey into the innermost self, of you, the creator and the subject. And possibly of everyone else youever know or meet.
it is a dark experince, a bright expeience, a lost and confusing experience, and a sharply clear experience. All at once.
I don't know that I actually could spoil this for anyone, since it really is something deeply personal, and I feel the experience will be different for each person who explores this path. I do think it would not be terribly good for anyone without some good, solid self-awareness, or at least some self-awareness, looking for more. Probably not a good experience for anyone who is badly broken, totally not self-aware and those looking for soething kight, easy, and with no deep meanings or thoughts. It is hard to call it "enjoyable", perhaps "worthwhile" is a better term.
This experience made me stop and look at my own life, my deepest worries and fears, my reason for being, my motivations, my faults, my flaws, my wants and needs, my darkest places got ripped open a bit, just a bit. But it also made me think of my joys, my successes, my dreams, my impact on the world around me, the postivie things I have done. It's not all dark, but it could sure suck you into the depths if you have a tendancy to go there anyway.
Not a "pew-pew-pew" and grief you friends and total strangers kind of game. This does require a higher level of attention and thinking to even feel like you understood any of it. And after playing it, I am left with so many thoughts of "What if", "Should I, Could I, Would I" and "Could I have done better". Not in the game, but IRL. Really moved me deeply and shook me. And will keep shaking me for some time. Deeply human. It is so very deeply human...
Thank you for making this game, and making me wake up while walking the path you guided me on. I will walk this path with you again, and see what else it reveals about myself and others around me. And I hope Coda is happy and well, out there smewhere.

Half-Life: Blue Shift is the second expansion from Half-Life 1. In it, you play as Barney Calhoun, a security guard who works at Black Mesa, the same facility in the main game. Several times through-out the game, you'll spot Gordan Freeman, which is a really neat touch. It really interwoves with the actual game's story.
The same type of story events play out just in different areas of the story. For example, the resonance cascade from the beginning of HL plays out with you on an elevator instead of in the test chamber. If you just chose to play this game without playing HL1, you'll be just as clueless as your hapless security guard.
Compared to Opposing Force and the main game, this game is VERY short, and not as exciting as the other two. Unlike Opposing Force, this game doesn't add any new weapons. All of the weapons you get in this game are just from the main game. Nothing new. This game also doesn't have as much replay value as the other games. It's just super short and really stale when compared to the main game and it's first expansion.
Aside from it's lack of enough excitement, this game is still true to what a Half-Life game is supposed to be, with surprise enemy attacks, to great sound design, to mind destroying puzzles.
If you REALLY love Half-Life, I recommend this game. It's not as bad as I made it out to be, so definitely check it out if you're into Half-Life.

DISCLAIMER: I, and every other consumer who purchased "Carmageddon: Reincarnation" have recieved this product for free. Carmageddon: Reincarnation was a failure. It was buggy, very poorly optimized, and rough all around, and it had gotten to the point where the Carma: Re brand was tarnished. So, after several somewhat effective, yet still failed attempts at bringing the game to its fullest potential, Stainless Games made a great business decision and took a year away to copy and paste Carmageddon: Reincarnation into a new project, optimize it beyond all belief, polish it, add new creative content content, fix bugs, and turn it into the game we expected to recieve when we purchased Carmageddon: Reincarnation. Stainless games certainly redeemed themselves, and I thank you guys for this great game!
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
There's a common criticism that this game is not a 2016 game or "it belongs in 1999". I think that criticism is somewhat unfair, though partially true. I don't think Stainless Games should have heavily modernized this game. I think they did a great job at bringing back an old game with fresh graphics, mechanics, and content. Is the formula a bit dated by today's standards? Kind of, but I love it just the way it is, and it's a great, full experience that was crafted to revive old memories with a fresh coat of paint and some new toys to play with. Also, there's no corporate bull crap going on. No annoying microtransactions, no "Supply Drops", no insulting DLC practices, and when Carma: Re failed, Stainless Games did not abandon it or make half-a$$ed attempts at dodging negative PR. No, they worked all day and night and brought us what we asked for in Reincarnation, and took some of the loss by giving us owners of the failed game a new product. Now THIS is what a great development team looks like. Take notes, "Early Access Randomly-Generated Open World Survival Sandbox #9540271620100698953210192" scrubs.. If you loved the old Carma games, or you love entertainment with little story, offensive humor, and epic action, pick this up, and you just might be one of those people that this game caters to. ;)

I remember when BioShock first came out and me and my older brother were in awe at how amazing it looked as the plane crashes into the ocean and flames engulf your vision in that opening cut-scene, we thought that this was the best looking a video game would ever get.
A lot of time has gone by since then, and we were wrong,
this game is still really good and has stood the test of time. This game has a great story that can be progressed even further with the use of the audio logs scattered around the landscape and the game play mechanics are still outstanding and unique to this day, the use of
and lack of ammo makes for some very thought provoking moments.
The roar of the Big Daddys coupled with the soft murmurs of dialog from the Little Sisters from another room evoke a feeling of fear as you remember the last encounter that left you with little to no ammo or eve. In this game you definitely feel like you are nothing and could just be destroyed by anything any second, and this is very rare for games to do these days and is a great thing to experience.
BioShock excels at evoking feelings whether it be the sadness or regret of harvesting a little sister or the nice feeling you get when you rescue a little sister and she runs off after thanking you profusely. But this game is somewhat unforgiving to you if you are yet to decide which route you want to take.
If you want a good ending, do not harvest any little sisters. SAVE THEM ALL.
I harvested two and I was considered evil by the games standards which is something that I found disappointing as I thought there might be a system that would tally a ratio of harvests to rescues but that is not the case.
Just remember:
There are also a few game-breaking glitches where alt+tab'ing will sometimes mess with the resolution or make it crash, I also came across a bug where the game lost 3 hours or so of save-games so I was forced back, and the game also crashed on the final cut-scene forcing me to replay the last section.
Definitely worth playing, even today, you might just want to change some controls but after that you're good to go.
tl;dr: Great game, even for today's standards, a bit unforgiving, and a bit buggy. Tends to crash. Still really good!

I will try to review this game the best way that I can in its current form.
I remember playing FlatOut 2 when I was younger, though it was mostly overshadowed by the greatness that is Burnout 3: Takedown. Now I'm not here to compare the two games, but let's just say FlatOut is the younger, more playful little brother and Burnout is the more serious older brother.
FlatOut has some undeniably good charm that makes it good, and by good I meant really good. Destructible environments, visible car damage, entertaining mini games, the driver being flung out of the car like a ragdoll after a deadly car crash, and all of these are nice, yes, especially when you're like 10 and the only thing you want is to have fun. All the times that I was like "LOL MY DRIVER'S FLYING" after I hit a steel post or a wall, or when I'm playing the mini games and I'm just laughing my♥♥♥♥♥off even though I'm not hitting the target, just watching the driver flying around like an idiot and watching the replay and slowing it down was entertaining at that age, but for a much older audience, the novelties runs off quick, and sometimes it just gets frustrating.
See if you're looking for a solid racing game, where the goal is to race and be the first place, then this game will seriously tear your brain out. The destructible environment means alot of debris is scattered around the map, meaning a pipe or a traffic cone gets snagged on your wheels and you're pretty much gonna crash, adding it up with the fact that the physics of the game is ♥♥♥♥♥♥ so sometimes your car trashes around like an idiot until you get back on the ground or the game lets you respawn your car which at most cases it wouldn't so you'd be spending like 5-10 seconds trashing around like an idiot and you'd be back at last place in the last lap just five seconds away from the finish line. Oh, and the ramps which were designed to encourage you to use are death traps that will either give you a Nitro boost or trash your car, better to avoid them most of the time, the nitro boost isn't that much of a help anyways unless you're losing. There are also segments of the game that feels bugged where your car just suddenly slows down for no reason at all even while driving on a straight path. Either it's part of the game or a design flaw, I'm not entirely sure.
Next up each of your AI enemies has a personality which I wasn't aware existed back then because I was a stupid kid who just crashes my car, and these personalities can be annoying, very annoying. Half the cars are racing and half are just there to ruin your game. Like this AI Sofia is just there to race, you'll mostly see her being first or second, but the others like that Katie will just literally go out of their way to swerve and bang you to a wall, It either adds up to the difficulty or just ruins the game, and for the most part it just ruins it. And even if the option to wreck your enemy's car exists, the game isn't really designed for it to take place, the tracks are too short for it to occur and you don't even get a bonus for crashing an enemy car to a wall by leading him there. You only get points for directly hitting them unlike in Most Wanted where if you push an enemy to a wall you get nitro boosts.
Also the minigames runs out of novelty once you learned how to play them, but are still fun to play from time-to-time, especially the darts and the poker games since they change targets unlike the other ones, and the Derby is really hard to win in, but is a nice touch to the game. You can finally wreck that ♥♥♥♥♥ Katie who keeps hitting you in the tracks.
Lastly there is very minimal customization and the car choices is quite small. This isn't really a problem, but hey, back then NFS is out and you can even change the rims on that game. Even San Andreas presented more customization than this game(Then again, that is an unfair comparison since GTA isn't a racing game) I don't even get why they didn't add the color wheel scheme for the car colors which has been out back since N64(Ridge Racer 64 has the said feature). You only have like five different colors for each car or something. These are not really that much of a problem, but is worth noting IMO, since customization is a big thing nowadays.
Now even after every negative thing I have said, the game is good. It presents a difficulty that gives you time to master maneuvering around the debris littered around every map and avoiding enemy AI's that are there to just slaughter you. The tracks are well designed IMO, with the splitting lanes and sharp curves that require mastery in passing through and the entertaining places that you pass around in(the mall segment was nice, but it was better in California Speed, lol) really gives a nice touch to the game. The destructible environment can be annoying at times, but I would be lying if I say I don't deliberately crash myself into windows and gas tanks just to see them break or explode. Despite the car choices being very minimal, it gives you options which fit their design. Driving on a road? Well use this car, Joining a derby? Use that car. They all have very well-balanced stats that gives you freedom to choose what you want and if you're doing the career mode you can also upgrade them to suit your style better.
The graphics is also very beautiful despite the age, and don't get me started on the soundtrack. One of the best soundtracks in gaming. Really pumps you up and sends you back to the game's era.
I suck at rating so I'll just say the game is good go buy it, if you don't want to pay the full price then wait for a sale, it's always on sale anyways.

Cuphead is a game that suprised me with its 1930's aesthetic and brutal difficulty. It is truly one of my favorite games, and here's why:
- I never felt that any boss in particular was 'bad' or 'lacking,' because each phase of every boss makes the boss even more interesting than the last. The amazing hand-drawn animation on them was a true feast for the eyes.
- The 'Run and Gun' levels are a nice change of pace for an otherwise boss-oriented game. Each location is different than the last and houses enemies that introduce stage-specific mechanics. For example, flipping you onto the ceiling to platform.
- The overworld presentation is very nice, and each of the 4 worlds (One of which has 2 stages) have different themes than the last. If 4 worlds seems like too little than fret not, because standard 7-8 levels (excluding the final world which has 2) in each of them will keep you busy for hours.
- The music in this game is absolutely perfect and could seriously be one of my favorite sountracks of all time. I found myself humming at least half of the total amount for a week straight.
There were a few things about Cuphead that did detract from my experience however, and are as follows:
- Hitboxes on certain enemies can be iffy at times (I experienced problems on 2-3 stages at most)
- Many weapons and charms are rather useless and I found myself sticking to the same build for basically the whole game.
- A+ or S ranks can be extremely difficult to obtain, and I feel as if the requirement to not take damage is a bit much (Take note that I have an A+ on every boss but 2, mostly because I did not want to deal with the hitboxes).
These small complaints should may only apply to me, yet I thought I would include them either way. Do not let this affect your opinion too much.
Overall, Cuphead is a superb game that kept me entertained the whole way through, and is definetely worth a buy.

Age of Wonders is a game that will appeal to most fans of turn-based strategy, and some (including myself) who generally prefer real-time action in games. With a large variety of races, magic spells, and independant units, there is plenty of flexibility to suit your individual playstyle; play for a sheer numbers advantage as Orcs, rapid expansion and pressure as Halflings, exploit the tricky specialty units of the Dark elves and Azracs, or employ any combination of these and several other races. While not quite as protracted as a game such as Civilization, matches are relatively slow-going, which will appeal to people who may dislike RTS games that favor players with intense focus and rapid action over premeditation. This game also has decent RPG elements with highly customizable leaders, heroes, and a rudamentary loot system. I've spent quite a bit of time just trying out different strategies for hero building.
The downsides of this game include an almost exclusive focus on military victory. Economic development is only used to fund more units, which may dissapoint fans of cultural or scientific victories in similar games. Diplomacy is possible, but shallow and primarily serves to expedite conquest. The AI opponents can be annoying in that they always seem to know what towns and resources you have neglected to defend, and a match can rapidly devolve into a fight from behind if you are not attentively garrisoning your empire.
Combat will not appeal to everybody. The RNG elements can be aggrivating, and players may feel 'cheated' out of a victory in close matchups. I'd recommend watching a gameplay example of tactical combat before purchasing, as this is a significant part of the game for players that want to minimize losses by avoiding automatic combat.
The graphics hold up well, with an appealing palette, detailed sprites, and a varied landscape.
Overall, I'd definitely recommend this game to a fan of strategy and RPG. If they enjoy single-player games. Sadly it's not 2003 anymore, and you will be hard-pressed to find people to play with via TCP or Email.

I remember when BioShock first came out and me and my older brother were in awe at how amazing it looked as the plane crashes into the ocean and flames engulf your vision in that opening cut-scene, we thought that this was the best looking a video game would ever get.
A lot of time has gone by since then, and we were wrong,
this game is still really good and has stood the test of time. This game has a great story that can be progressed even further with the use of the audio logs scattered around the landscape and the game play mechanics are still outstanding and unique to this day, the use of
and lack of ammo makes for some very thought provoking moments.
The roar of the Big Daddys coupled with the soft murmurs of dialog from the Little Sisters from another room evoke a feeling of fear as you remember the last encounter that left you with little to no ammo or eve. In this game you definitely feel like you are nothing and could just be destroyed by anything any second, and this is very rare for games to do these days and is a great thing to experience.
BioShock excels at evoking feelings whether it be the sadness or regret of harvesting a little sister or the nice feeling you get when you rescue a little sister and she runs off after thanking you profusely. But this game is somewhat unforgiving to you if you are yet to decide which route you want to take.
If you want a good ending, do not harvest any little sisters. SAVE THEM ALL.
I harvested two and I was considered evil by the games standards which is something that I found disappointing as I thought there might be a system that would tally a ratio of harvests to rescues but that is not the case.
Just remember:
There are also a few game-breaking glitches where alt+tab'ing will sometimes mess with the resolution or make it crash, I also came across a bug where the game lost 3 hours or so of save-games so I was forced back, and the game also crashed on the final cut-scene forcing me to replay the last section.
Definitely worth playing, even today, you might just want to change some controls but after that you're good to go.
tl;dr: Great game, even for today's standards, a bit unforgiving, and a bit buggy. Tends to crash. Still really good!

A very odd type of game. Coming from the creator of the Stanley Parable I kind of expected it to be some sort of meta, fourth wall breaking type of game. And in a sense it is, but if you're expecting more like Stanley Parable you'll be disappointed.
The entire thing runs for just shy of 90 minutes. During that time you are presented with a fictional story about the creator's relationship with another game designer. Towards the end it unravels into what probably is supposed to be a deeper emotional meaning, but it just completely misses the mark if you ask me.
The entire thing had me bored about 15 minutes into it and the only real reason I kept playing it is because hell, I bought it at some point and I read it wasn't that long a game so I wanted to finish it. But honestly this is just a mashup of simple Source engine maps. The sort of maps you'd expect to see from a starting map designer who still needs to get a grasp on his tools. The narative is supposed to bind it all together but in the end it's just not very interesting.
I can appreciate the weird meta type games like Stanley Parable, but this game takes it a step too far to the point of becoming so 'weird' that it becomes pointless. Watch a playthrough of this game on YouTube and you'll get 100% the same experience.
There are no alternate endings or different solutions. It's just a walking simulator set in some rubbish maps with a cheap narative. It's not worth playing and it certainly isn't worth the 9 dollars they're asking for it. Would refund if I could.

Relying heavily on The Secret World lore which I consider to be the most interesting one in world of MMORPGs (just my opinion, no need to prove me wrong), The Park is short and sweet narrative experience. Feeling more like an interactive movie than a game, The Park lets you play a role of young mother searching for her son lost in a local theme park. As the time passes, you'll soon realize something sinister is out there, but the real question is: where's the sinister at - around or inside of you?
Gaming mechanics are pretty simple and the experience is basically a linear ride (no pun intended) reminding me a lot of rail shooter mechanics (although you can walk). That could prove to be a fatal decision in other games, but The Park tends to let you soak up the gloomy atmosphere and enjoy the little horror details. A wonderful and traumatic story is being told not only through words, but also through colors and sounds.
If you're too old to be trick or treating (is that even possible?) or you're simply sick of annual Halloween marathons, do yourself a favor - get The Park, turn off the lights, put on your headphones and turn it up.
Ride of (for) your life!

Like many kickstarted games, Carmageddon: Reincarnation got a publisher after a successful crowd-funding campaign, only to have that publisher push out an incomplete product. The developers worked on the game and did improve it; however, in the end they decided a full re-release was in order and that game is Carmageddon: Max Damage. There are a lot of little improvements, including better damage physics. (You don’t lose a tire against Val Hella when merely being grazed by her car, for example.) There are also more maps / tracks, plus a few more cars. If you bought Reincarnation, you got this one for free, but if you mixed reviews scared you away the first time, now is the time to grab Max Damage.

A 64 player FPS that captures the Pacific Theater and Eastern Front of WW2, including excellent immersion and setting specific mechanics while requiring strategy and a certain amount of skill to win a game.
This game feels much more difficult than your average FPS that allow you to be a one-man-army. If you attempt to run in and take the enemy head on, the chances are you won't make it out alive. But before you die, you may have the chance to help your teams mates capture the enemy objective or take out a mounted machine gun which had your team mates pinned. Such a death feels not frustrating but satisfying, knowing that you've saved the lives of your squad. This game is not about getting the best kill to death ratio, nor is about getting the highest number of kills. This game is about working together as a large force to take or hold objectives. This game doesn't punish you for a death, it punishes your entire team. Where the game implements respawns in terms of a limited amount of reinforcements per game, no one is allowed to spawn if they're depleted.
When you land those successive shots with a bolt action rifle, it feels earned and satisfying.
Definitely worth a buy if you want an FPS that includes more strategy, immersion and skill than your Medal of Duty: Battlefield.

If you want to ♥♥♥♥♥ and moan about DLC, I hope they delete your reviews.
I'm going to give a review of the GAME, not the talking points that whiny little ♥♥♥♥♥es feel entitled to harp on because "♥♥♥♥ greedy AAA studios". You people can jog on and go back to Occupy Wall Street or whatever. Your opinion is worthless.
Graphically, you're not going to see this game's full potential on anything less than modern hardware. For example, I did the Alpha and Beta test on an old Radeon HD 6850 / 1GB , then played last night on a HD 7950 / 3GB. As expected the graphical difference was immense. Yet, I was getting pretty slick performance without trying to push the card beyond reasonable expectations. Occasionally I got a small stutter when loading textures while moving around the map but that's more of a hard drive bottleneck I believe.
The game itself has a lot of unlockables, meaning you have to play each class / monster and reach certain goals to progress. The playstyle differences between the core classes are different enough that when playing against humans you'll have to learn to adapt slightly in nearly every game. It's always going to be a little different. Against CPU opponents you'll get more varied tactics depending on the bots. The AI itself is interesting but you can tell sometimes when they're stuck in a loop because of narrower goals, such as the monster hitting Level 3. Seems the bots tend to hike back to the power relay and fortify for a final battle which means you have leisure time to gain armor or buffs before swooping in for the kill as the monster.
If you don't learn to play your classes you're going to have a very bad time. The monster is great for when you just don't want to work with bad players but you really have to learn some stealth mechanics (SNEAK EVERYWHERE) or you're fairly easy to track. Does the game break when people don't effectively play their classes?  Eh, to a mild degree but again the onus is on the players to master their roles, and anyone familiar to class-based teamplay understands this concept. You can win without that skill, but the difficulty increases dramatically.
We'll see if the game has longetivity, but I see it as no different than previous titles by Turtle Rock (Left 4 Dead) in that there's a bare-bones background story but the majority of gameplay *will* seem fairly repetitive without the human aspect. If you spend a lot of time in solo play, you'll get bored quickly. You need to ask yourself if this style of game is really what you find fun because if it is, I see Evolve having a long shelf life. I can't say I enjoyed this game. It's hard to write that. The game is clearly special, from a sound design and visual esthetic perspective. However, from a gameplay perspective, it's terrible.
And I don't say that just because I'm bad at the game - I am. But that's not why I didn't like it. I didn't like it, because so much of the game expects you to play by trial and error. There's visual and sound cues, sure. But that doesn't make it better when you're still trying in vain to figure out what you're doing wrong and you've died 27 times in the same spot. Almost worse is when you know what you are supposed to do, and you still can't quite manage to get that one jump timed correctly. To add to that, there's moments (many of them) where you're not dying (no, really) and you simply have no clue what the game expects of you.
Maybe I'm thick-witted and slow-fingered. Maybe I'm just tired after work. Limbo punishes me for everything that I do wrong and some of the things I do right. But that's not why I play games - I play them to have fun. Limbo isn't fun; it's annoying, obtuse, and requires regular backtracking and exploration of areas that you don't even know exist.

The Park isn't a game in the strictist sense. In terms of what you actually do as a player your only options are to shout out for the protagonists son and to toggle between run and walk. The primary interactive elements come in the form of interactable documents within the world which you can choose to examine on discovery as well as a few rides which you may choose to ride upon or not.
However what the game lacks for in terms of direct gameplay it makes up for in atomosphere. The developer clearly was hoping to capture the creepy factor of an abandoned amusement park, in this they have largely been successful. The game is not overly reliant upon jump scares and rather focuses on the pyschological horror of a protagonist who clearly has deep seated mental issues.
The storytelling is excellent, going in I expected the plot to be fairly straight forward as Lorraine (The player character) became increasing panicked to get her son back. Without spoiling anything I can say that she is a far more complex character and the plot goes to some very dark places.
Overrall the game is an excellent horror experience with quality voice acting, writing and world building. However it lacks much interactivity and is decidedly short. The side information found through documents is also likely to be less interesting to those who aren't invested in the wider The Secret World universe.

A very odd type of game. Coming from the creator of the Stanley Parable I kind of expected it to be some sort of meta, fourth wall breaking type of game. And in a sense it is, but if you're expecting more like Stanley Parable you'll be disappointed.
The entire thing runs for just shy of 90 minutes. During that time you are presented with a fictional story about the creator's relationship with another game designer. Towards the end it unravels into what probably is supposed to be a deeper emotional meaning, but it just completely misses the mark if you ask me.
The entire thing had me bored about 15 minutes into it and the only real reason I kept playing it is because hell, I bought it at some point and I read it wasn't that long a game so I wanted to finish it. But honestly this is just a mashup of simple Source engine maps. The sort of maps you'd expect to see from a starting map designer who still needs to get a grasp on his tools. The narative is supposed to bind it all together but in the end it's just not very interesting.
I can appreciate the weird meta type games like Stanley Parable, but this game takes it a step too far to the point of becoming so 'weird' that it becomes pointless. Watch a playthrough of this game on YouTube and you'll get 100% the same experience.
There are no alternate endings or different solutions. It's just a walking simulator set in some rubbish maps with a cheap narative. It's not worth playing and it certainly isn't worth the 9 dollars they're asking for it. Would refund if I could.

This is one of my "dat childhood" games, but I'll try and be as unbiased as possible.
Let's deal with the technical side of things first: visually, this game still looks fairly decent for a game made in 2006, the cars and lighting especially, and it has one of the best damage models out there (not in terms of realism, but in terms of level of satisfaction and impact). The soundtrack is legendary by now and all the various car sounds, crash sounds and everything else is just pure perfection. Performance? Runs like greased lightning. All the puzzles fit, in short.
Gameplay wise, this game is also pure gold.
The tracks are great, I really don't know what else to say, they're challenging but not frustrating, the environments are pretty varied (city, desert, forest...).
The cars are also done extremely well - there's something in there for everyone and the various stats are balanced in a skillful and sensible way: want an insanely fast car? Well, it's not going to be durable and it might be a nightmare to handle. Want a tough car? Top speed meh, handling ok. Want a car with great handling? Sure, but expect to get overtaken on long straight sections because it simply doesn't have the juice.
That means that in the end, you'll have to pick a car to suit your driving style or adapt the driving style to the car you're driving. I'd actually say this gives the game quite a lot of replay value because you can either try racing with cars you didn't touch during career or even re-start a career with a new profile and picking different cars. Career mode is structured in a way that you work your way up from rat-rods and racecars to proper street racing beasts, so gameplay never gets stale: each tier, the AI picks different vehicles (though some gravitate towards a certain type) and the special events change; in other words, there's plenty here to keep things interesting.
Speaking of AI... I rarely see racing AI done this well. They've all got a really short, loading-screen backstories/descriptions and it's just marvellous how well their behaviour matches those descriptions. "Jason Walker: aggressive and unpredictable" etc. - will either race like a maniac or decide he wants to slam your♥♥♥♥♥into the wall. "Sofia Martinez: an ice-cold professional racer who isn't lured into crashes easily" - will mostly elbow her way to the front and win by just driving well, sometimes even actively avoid other cars. Each character is assigned a color and their car is always that color regardless of class so you can easily tell who is who. It's such a small detail yet implemented SO well that it gives the other participants on the track a tangible personality and some races or cups start to feel like it's personal sometimes.
When you're fed up with plain old racing, you've also got stunts: these are quirky physics events like "darts" and "ski jump" or "bowling", all built around the idea of launching your driver through the windshield as a kind of projectile. They're fun distractions and a good way to give your head a rest (they also appear as special events in career mode), and they're challenging enough, though not terribly hard.
Then there's other special events like NASCAR-style oval tracks and "figure eight" racetracks... like I said, this game is full to the brim with quality content. I assume Multiplayer's pretty dead, but it has party mode and local LAN - I can tell you from experience party mode is freakin amazing.
In terms of negatives, there is really no major fault I can find, other than the slight "RNG" elements that happen naturally because of the various crap strewn across the tracks as the race progresses. This is a great way to keep you on edge, but sometimes it can be a little frustrating to lose a 5-lap race because you got thrown into the air by a paintcan. Then again, when a near-metric-tonne object traveling at full speed hits something, anything can happen and that element of danger and insanity is an integral part of the FlatOut experience. Not a major fault, but it sometimes can be unnecessarily frustrating. Also slightly related, the "Reset" button is pretty overpowered, you can literally reset if you just stop while not cornering properly, which might make the game too forgiving for some, but an easy way to remedy that is just not using it.
Overall, this game is great and if you're a racing game fan, you should DEFINITELY play it (chances are you probably have). If you're new to racing games, also pick it up because it's really a fairly unique entry in the racing genre.

Occasionally I got a small stutter when loading textures while moving around the map but that's more of a hard drive bottleneck I believe.
The game itself has a lot of unlockables, meaning you have to play each class / monster and reach certain goals to progress. The playstyle differences between the core classes are different enough that when playing against humans you'll have to learn to adapt slightly in nearly every game. It's always going to be a little different. Against CPU opponents you'll get more varied tactics depending on the bots. The AI itself is interesting but you can tell sometimes when they're stuck in a loop because of narrower goals, such as the monster hitting Level 3. Seems the bots tend to hike back to the power relay and fortify for a final battle which means you have leisure time to gain armor or buffs before swooping in for the kill as the monster.
If you don't learn to play your classes you're going to have a very bad time. The monster is great for when you just don't want to work with bad players but you really have to learn some stealth mechanics (SNEAK EVERYWHERE) or you're fairly easy to track. Does the game break when people don't effectively play their classes?  Eh, to a mild degree but again the onus is on the players to master their roles, and anyone familiar to class-based teamplay understands this concept. You can win without that skill, but the difficulty increases dramatically.
We'll see if the game has longetivity, but I see it as no different than previous titles by Turtle Rock (Left 4 Dead) in that there's a bare-bones background story but the majority of gameplay *will* seem fairly repetitive without the human aspect. If you spend a lot of time in solo play, you'll get bored quickly. You need to ask yourself if this style of game is really what you find fun because if it is, I see Evolve having a long shelf life. Play with friends will be even more fun. However if you have a short attention span, little patience, and no desire to work as a team you'll probably not enjoy the game as much as others.
Just don't expect people to have any respect for your opinion if all you want to complain about is the DLC.

The Long Dark is a good example of an early access title. Upon release I gave it a go. It was not much, a survival game with okay graphics and barebones crafting. But now... It's a really fun and immersive title. It has since gone through various updates adding things such as mechanics, new game areas, and improved graphics. The developers have made slow but substantial updates that made the game better in many ways.
At heart it's a standard survival fare. There's a crafting system, looting system, and status bars like many others. It differs from the other games with an intuitive menu system that has been refined in many updates to make it look flashy and show info. You have to manage sleep, thirst, hunger, and your body temperature. You crash in the canadian wilderness as a result of a geomagnetic storm, wiping out all technology. You're tasked with lasting as long as you can. You have to eat and drink and sleep. Resources are scarce which is a clever way to make you run around and explore the huge map. When I say huge map, I mean HUGE. The Canadian wilderness is broken into many sections, each varying in difficulty and terrain. One area is a large frozen lake, an easy area to scrounge for items. There's a dam with supplies and warmth but it's very dark. One of the new areas is a hazardous mountain meant only for the most experienced players (I still can't brave the mountain). The other selling point is its graphics. Throughout its development, the game has made some style changes, and I believe the update coming in late April will make it even better. It's asthetics share many things with the game Firewatch, with its flat and beautiful painted looks. This, paired with the weather effects and bright colors, makes it a stylized and immersive game.
While this game is good, there might be some things that players might be turned off to. Firstly, the game is hard at first. It doesn't tell you you need to eat or sleep until you REALLY need to. Status managment is key. Second, the game world might be too big for some. It's easy to get lost, and it doesn't help that the only maps are found on Google. Third, to encourage exploration, supplies are scarce, and the fact taht certain areas are designed to be harder might mean you have to move out of your comfort zone faster than you would like.
All those things above aren't bad things, and the game is great even with them. It's one of the best survival games in Early Access.

Short and sweet -- LIMBO is the game that you can play when it's dark and rainy outside. Keep in mind that the atmosphere, the sounds and the setting is prone to suck you in and hold you in a firm grip as you play. LIMBO is most likely an experience that you've never had before - it looks like a simple game, but trust me on this one: It is way more than what meets the eye.
The storyline is not very long, around 2-3 hours. Yet, the length and pace felt great. LIMBO's uniqueness and uncomfortable "the silence is speaking" vibe makes you fill in the empty spaces yourself as you explore this dark place. As you can only see contours of objects for the most part and cannot speak to people you get this unpleasant feeling of isolation. You are completely on your own, so in order to survive you need to come up with clever solutions in this realm of LIMBO, which is rewarding once you get it right :)
This unique and unsettling atmosphere, the great design, and the phenomenal soundscape makes LIMBO a true one-of-a-kind experience. A simple yet very deep game that I totally recommend for the person who seeks a new and refreshing adventure!

As always in public feel free to criticize me.
I don't see why someone would say that the physics are arcade like for this game in many aspects.
The game rewards keeping in control of the car graciously as in reality.
Certainly the traction of a car with four wheels with front and/or back wheel drive
seems sound to me.
When you start to skid the energy of the body of the car no longer flows through the
front tires for turning and so the front tires become a force of resistance at the front of the car
and you lose a good turning radius especially if you continue to use the gas.
Using the gas for the front wheels while you are skidding will only serve to create a pulling
force in the direction the front tires are turned to.  Meanwhile you're skidding because you're already going
too fast and adding gas to the equation will continue to suffer your turning radius.
So with or without control of the car the physics seem sound to me in this game.
I feel like I can take that red muscle car and go for a slaughter run with sound physics although the
power-ups provide for additional wacked out physics.  They seem to be the arcade like part of the game.
I love this game flat out.  Especially when I play to complete the laps because the track is always a bit different
when you need to continously run over pedestrains to put time on the clock.  This will test your racing skills.
My advice for keeping control when the front of your car is bobbing left and right is to lay off the gas and
then when the car has slowed down a bit hit the gas when your car faces frontward to pull it straight.
And use the hand-brake only when you need to throw out the back end to hit pedestrians or on a hairpin turn
or if you need to do a 180.
Great mix of arcade and what seems to be sound physics concerning traction.
I'd be happy to be informed about what physics have been made arcade like aside from the effects of the power ups.
I don't know if they got it wrong for tracked vehicles or vehicles with six wheels as I'd have to experiment to find out.

Short answer : If you're a fan of destruction derby games and/or hate Politically Correctness and are up for some good wrecking and dismembering fun, just buy the game! The devs have done a wonderful job and deserve it!
Alright, been a fan of Carmageddon for almost 20 years (since 1997).
This new game is actually a reimagining of the original carmageddon (maps, cars and of course gameplay) with many new elements and features.
To get it out of the way, the damage code is just splendid! This is an in-house engine and you can tell the devs have worked their asses off just for the physics and damage.
The only thing you should be cautious of, is pick the right difficulty, cause HARD difficulty, is NOT fair at all. You'll be wrecked, mangled and♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥quite a lot.
Now the gameplay : It has the classic Carmageddon gameplay meaning that there are NOT "you're wasted once - you're out of the session" instances. You can repair over and over and head for the bastehrds!
You can finish the game with 3 ways. Killing all peds, destroying every opponent or finishing the laps.
I'd recommend destroying opponents, cause it'll fetch you more money in the long run, but you can do any of the 3.
Graphics are good looking, not high-end, but you won't care too much anyway, once you'll delve into the gameplay and the mind of Max Damage (he's the bald driver that smiles holding the steering wheel).
You of course have the option to have a bit more detail especially if you have a good GPU.
I, with my humble GTX 750Ti, am getting 40-80 FPS at all times on 1080p. Mostly it's stabilized at 60FPS, but there are a few instances that drops at 43-47.
Now the handling has improved very much compared to C:R. And it's definitely an improvement over C:R in all aspects.
It also has awesome vehicle tech. We have 4-wheeled cars, 6-wheeled cars, tracked-wheel cars (tank like vehicles), and well... Bicycles and more-than-6-wheeled cars. That means you can implement ANYTHING you want if you're a modder, and the game already has heavy trucks and trailered cars.
So this game is absolutely recommended. Even if you're not a fan of destruction derby games, you're bound to have lots of hours of fun playing this. But remember. Play either on Easy or Normal (there is no achievement for hard mode anyway).

This game is essentially what Reincarnation should've been. When I first bought Reincarnation I was met with a gloriously fun game hampered by poor performance (even with my i7 5820k processor and GTX 1070 graphics card, couldn't run the game at 1440p max everything without drops in frame rate). The game had frame drops, and would occasionally drop down to 7fps ish and never come back up until you restarted the game. Then one day Max Damage appeared in my library. I opened it up and I was met with a version of reincarnation with more original characters, great gameplay, and great performance. The powerups are all very unique, both in name and ability. The vehicles feel heavy, more... real. The soundtrack is very nice as well. And while the soft body stuff might not be on the same level as something like Beamng.Drive, it's still pretty damned good. And on top of that, MAX IS BACK! I love it, just as good as the first two, and definitely a good way to make up for the disaster that was TDR. Overall, it's definitely a more loveable game than reincarnation, and it's definitely worth $20. Seriously. Buy it now.

The Park. Gets it right. It's first and foremost a twisted and disturbing story. A haunting tale befit any campfire story telling time. It is dressed up in well done art design, and a fantastic nightmarish setting of an evil mysterious theme park at night. The game goes beyond the sharp textures and high poly models to incorporate reflections, shadows, and intense surreal moments to draw you into the nightmare. What I loved the most is the audio work followed by the pacing, that heightens this short game to a much broader level. Each hour is fantastic, and the build up to the end is superb and not to be missed.
- The audio work
- The outstanding pacing, slow at first, heavy on the clues, the fast paced blurs and intesified scares leading to a mind blowing conclusion
- Art design
- Mr. Hat
- They killed Freddy Faz Bear in a van? WTF
- It's short. Even if three hours is packed to the rim with details and thrills. I want more.

Note: I changed my recommendation to negative, due to the lack of continued support for this game. It is overall a good game, but bugs and simple flavour-killing lack of diversity are not being addressed at all by the developers, who instead came up with far less useful DLCs adding e.g. military buildings to the already overblown diversity, etc. My initial review for this game was positive, though the lack of further development and eveb basic support made me change my mind.
Anyway, the plus for the game:
The game is still quite amazing in terms of how it feels. True, like many of the posters have noted, it lacks some features present in Tropico 4. However, it also has numerous improvements.
Among the pros, I would like to note:
- Nice graphics (especially the nature).
- Funny (albeit fewer) radio comments and funny edict and challenge commentaries.
- Basic but enriching research compontent.
- Much better military component.
- One can now keep older buildings and build them in later eras. No longer will a hurricane force you to reconstruct everything a la Hong Kong like in Tropico 4 MT. I love this part as it makes the cities look much more organic, with historic cores, CBDs and 1970´s stile social housing coexisting in harmony.
- Improved economic system and high diversity of industrial supply lines.
- Upgraded diplomacy.
- The population limit is rather adequate.
- I think the political system is better, icluding tought competitive elections with faction leaders (rather than 17 year old farmer girls).
- Better optimization as compared to T4.
Among the cons, of which there are numerous as opposed to T4:
- Some useful buildings no longer present (tourism attractions are now all but a skeleton). Ditto for some interesting edicts.
- Rudimentary tourism component. I cannot stress this enough. All tourists have just 1 male and 1 female skin, and buildings and attractions have been dumbed down to "barely existing".
- Colonial epoch very basic, albeit a useful learning tool early on.
- Information cumbersome and poor. Tropico 4 almanach was much better. The one in Tropico 5 is broken and the developers have never bothered to fix it, focusing on wacky DLC instead. Also, one can no longer use overlays like housing occupancy, which is a shame.
- Lack of ability to zoom up to street level, without mods.
- Building and person skins are reduced to a bare, unrealistic, simplified minimum. Gone are the super-diverse, gritty yet detailed looks of Tropico 4, replaced with some generic undiversified construction patterns.
- The DLC policy is weird, and most DLC buildings are extremely odd (and in my opinion poor choices). You will still not get a chance to build separate police and firemen buildings, or to have 2 different skins for tenements, but you have 4 types of floating buildings and 12 types of military random edifices. These game design choices are difficult to understand for me.
Overall, still a very good game. After buying it, I said I will not return to Tropico 4 any time soon, despite missing certain features. In the end, I did, as the lack of support and weird design choices have robbed Tropico 5 of its full potential, and have made it go - IMHO - along the Kalypso path of increasingly sub-par games.

I am rating this game good for a couple of reasons. Though I have not played much of this at all, probably not even long enough to critique it properly, I would like to state that this game's difficulty is well balanced for what type of feeling it's trying to create, the levels are well done visually and gameplay wise as well, not to mention that it is random enough to have a slightly different experience when replaying the level because of a move performed by the boss or enemies, whether it was graphically appealing or just as simple as an idle animation. Cuphead is, what it looks like so far to be, a short game with what I think is an adequete replay value ( if it wasn't, then dying so much in this game would not be as "fun" as it is. ) and, as I stated before, amazing hand drawn 1930's art style and music that almost perfectly replicates that era of cartoons. I do not think this game is for everyone, as it is ( at least to me ) a very challenging game, obviously suited for people who want to feel the adrenaline pump more than just sitting at a desk clicking away at some objects or people. The only complaints I have for this game are the occasional glitch that might force me to task manager the application off the face of my toolbar and the fact that it doesn't have options to minimalize a few things to run well on older pcs ( but I doubt that doing that would be as easy said, considering that all of it is hand drawn. ) Overall, I see cuphead as an exellent game to pick up if you enjoy an older vibe of cartoon and a 90's feeling of platform shooting games ( such as the older megamans ) with a touch of the occasional repression of rage and maybe a bit of crying, as well. ( that's if you're not too good with coordination or if you're Dean from VentureBeat. )

I've only made two purchases in Steam that I didn't like. This game is one of them.
Really, this review puts it better than I could:
To echo the main points of his review that I most agree with...this game is too pretentious, too obvious, too "convinced of its own profound meaning." Wrapping up a story of human frailty in depression, that then turns into
depression, that then turns into an unresolved musing on self-worth...it all gives the APPEARANCE of wisdom literature. But then you try to find meaning in it. So you begin to peel back the layers of artsiness, of story-without-plot, of game-not-game. And at the end of it all, it's hard to get anything more concrete out of this than "I laughed, I cried, it moved me Bob."
At it's core, you're left with a pile of pretentiousness that must be True Art because we all know that True Art is Angsty, and BOY does this game crank up the Depression-o-Meter!
To put it another way...it has no conclusion, just raw emotion. It was designed that way on purpose, I know. But a story that has no conclusion, has no profound meaning. You're simply whisked away on the narrator's journey of thoughts on his friend, on emotions, on his own insecurity--the end. You're supposed to experience these feelings by proxy. All feeling, no real concrete thoughts.
This game is NOT like the Stanely Parable...except in one way. The Stanely Parable's narrator is like the player in a lot of ways. The same can be said of this game. The narrator doesn't have a clue WHAT to conclude. You, the player, will also be denied any conclusion.
Well, here's MY conlcusion on the whole thing.
If you want to simply experience an author's stream-of-consciousness and his own expression of human frailty, buy this game. But if you want an actual STORY--or even something with any MEANING--this game isn't worth your $10, it's not worth your 1.5 hours.
...
Still don't believe me?
Go read the most highly rated positive reviews of this game. You'll notice they all talk about FEEEEELLLLLLIIIIINNNNNGGGG. But I challenge you to find even five that actually draw concrete, expressible meaning out of it.

This is one of those "one gimmick" games.  The central gimmick is fun, but get ready to be frustrated. Most of the levels are pretty easy, and the games makes random changes to the scenarios each time which keep it interesting. The final-final level, however, is setup such that minor changes in randomly-generated outcomes make a huge difference. In fact there is one situation in the very opening of this level which if it isn't aligned within a certain tolerance, you just have to keep restarting until you get the right alignment. That isn't fun.
My other complaint is that the story is fairly thin, and the player is forced to endure these time-gated cut scenes, some of which include randomly mashing the keyboard. Even more egregious is the not-subtle full-on marketing pitch at the end. This is NOT one of the most innovative shooters I've played in the past couple of years, sorry guys.
The final level is so tight that other... bugs? Secret arbitrary rules? become starkly highlighted, making the game feel a little half-baked. I got it on sale and it isn't too expensive, so I'm willing to forgive a lot. At the end of the day, at first blush this looks like a tightly-crafted puzzle game, but once you get deeper you realize it is not. I would love to see what someone like Zachtronics could do with this gimmick.
